interview.chapter01.q01.question: What is a Substation Automation System (SAS), and what are its main functions?
interview.chapter01.q01.answer: SAS is an integrated system that monitors, controls and records substation equipment through IEDs, communication networks, station computers and gateways. Protection remains a separate safety-critical function, even when information is exchanged with SAS.
interview.chapter01.q01.step01: Identify primary equipment such as breakers, disconnectors and transformers and the associated secondary IEDs.
interview.chapter01.q01.step02: Collect status, measurements, alarms and events from IEDs using the configured protocols.
interview.chapter01.q01.step03: Present validated data on the HMI and record events with timestamps.
interview.chapter01.q01.step04: Issue authorized operator controls through the configured control model and interlocks.
interview.chapter01.q01.step05: Forward selected operational points to the control centre through the gateway.
interview.chapter01.q01.scenario: During FAT, change a simulated breaker auxiliary contact and confirm the IED input, SCADA point, alarm/event record and gateway indication update correctly.
interview.chapter01.q01.takeaway: Explain the complete signal path rather than describing SAS as only an HMI.
interview.chapter01.q02.question: Explain the difference between a protection relay, BCU, RTU, gateway and SCADA server.
interview.chapter01.q02.answer: A protection relay detects abnormal electrical conditions and initiates configured protection actions. A BCU performs bay-level monitoring and control. An RTU acquires and transfers field data, a gateway exchanges or converts information with external systems, and a SCADA server manages station-wide supervisory data and operator functions. Product architectures can combine these roles.
interview.chapter01.q02.step01: Identify which device owns each field signal and control output.
interview.chapter01.q02.step02: Check the device communication interface and protocol.
interview.chapter01.q02.step03: Determine which system hosts point mapping, alarms and control permissions.
interview.chapter01.q02.step04: Verify the end-to-end indication and command route in the approved drawings.
interview.chapter01.q02.scenario: A feeder status reaches the local BCU but not the remote control centre: verify BCU acquisition, station communications, gateway mapping and remote protocol transmission in order.
interview.chapter01.q02.takeaway: Avoid assuming every project has a separate physical device for each function.
interview.chapter01.q03.question: Describe the end-to-end flow of a breaker status from the yard to the HMI.
interview.chapter01.q03.answer: A breaker auxiliary contact provides a hardwired input to a bay device. The IED represents that state in its data model; SCADA receives it via reporting, polling or another configured integration path, maps it to a database point, and displays it on the single-line diagram.
interview.chapter01.q03.step01: Verify the breaker auxiliary contact and input wiring using approved test procedures.
interview.chapter01.q03.step02: Check the binary input and the IED logical status, for example XCBR.Pos where applicable.
interview.chapter01.q03.step03: Verify the relevant DataSet, reporting configuration and active MMS association when IEC 61850 reporting is used.
interview.chapter01.q03.step04: Confirm SCADA database address, quality, inversion and display binding.
interview.chapter01.q03.step05: Check timestamp, quality and state transitions at the HMI.
interview.chapter01.q03.scenario: The breaker is physically open but HMI shows closed: compare the field contact, IED value, report and mapped HMI tag to isolate the first mismatch.
interview.chapter01.q03.takeaway: A green network link does not prove the signal mapping is correct.
interview.chapter01.q04.question: What is the difference between station bus and process bus?
interview.chapter01.q04.answer: The station bus typically connects bay IEDs to station-level clients, HMIs and gateways for monitoring, control and peer communications. A process bus connects process-interface devices such as merging units and protection/control IEDs for sampled measurements and related process signals. Actual topology depends on design.
interview.chapter01.q04.step01: Read the network architecture and identify devices on each bus.
interview.chapter01.q04.step02: Identify MMS, GOOSE and Sampled Values traffic where used.
interview.chapter01.q04.step03: Review bandwidth, VLANs, multicast handling and redundancy requirements.
interview.chapter01.q04.step04: Check whether the project uses conventional copper wiring, digital process interfaces or a hybrid design.
interview.chapter01.q04.scenario: If SV traffic is missing at a protection IED, inspect merging-unit publication, process-bus switch forwarding and subscriber settings instead of troubleshooting the HMI first.
interview.chapter01.q04.takeaway: Do not claim every IEC 61850 station uses Sampled Values.
interview.chapter01.q05.question: How do you verify a newly integrated IED in the SAS?
interview.chapter01.q05.answer: IED integration must be checked from the physical and network layers through the configured data model to the operator interface. A successful ping or MMS association is only one part of acceptance.
interview.chapter01.q05.step01: Check IED model, firmware, configuration revision and approved engineering files.
interview.chapter01.q05.step02: Verify IP settings, network port status, VLAN and time synchronization.
interview.chapter01.q05.step03: Establish the required protocol connection and browse expected data objects.
interview.chapter01.q05.step04: Validate reporting, measurements, indications, alarms and controls against the signal list.
interview.chapter01.q05.step05: Record evidence, defects and retest results in FAT/SAT sheets.
interview.chapter01.q05.scenario: A new feeder relay communicates but measurements remain zero: compare actual injected/available values, IED data objects, scaling and SCADA mapping.
interview.chapter01.q05.takeaway: Never perform live switching just to demonstrate connectivity.
interview.chapter01.q06.question: What is the difference between an alarm, event and SOE record?
interview.chapter01.q06.answer: An event records a state change or occurrence. An alarm is an event or condition configured to require operator attention. Sequence of Events (SOE) uses precise event timestamps to reconstruct the order of operations; its accuracy depends on device timestamping and clock synchronization.
interview.chapter01.q06.step01: Confirm the originating device and event condition.
interview.chapter01.q06.step02: Verify timestamp source and time-sync status.
interview.chapter01.q06.step03: Check alarm priority, acknowledgement behavior and return-to-normal logic.
interview.chapter01.q06.step04: Confirm the event is stored and ordered correctly in SCADA/SOE logs.
interview.chapter01.q06.scenario: After a feeder trip, compare relay trip assertion, breaker-open indication and HMI alarm timestamps to reconstruct the sequence.
interview.chapter01.q06.takeaway: Do not confuse event arrival time at the server with the original device event time.
interview.chapter01.q07.question: Explain local, remote and supervisory control of a circuit breaker.
interview.chapter01.q07.answer: Breaker control is permitted only through the selected authority and the approved electrical and operational interlocks. A supervisory command may involve select-before-operate, authorization and feedback verification. Control behavior depends on the IED control model and project philosophy.
interview.chapter01.q07.step01: Verify the Local/Remote selector and current control authority.
interview.chapter01.q07.step02: Check user permissions, operational permits and interlocking status.
interview.chapter01.q07.step03: Confirm the configured control model, target point and command parameters.
interview.chapter01.q07.step04: Issue commands only in an authorized test environment or approved switching procedure.
interview.chapter01.q07.step05: Verify command result, breaker feedback, SOE and any failure indication.
interview.chapter01.q07.scenario: HMI close button is disabled while the breaker is healthy: inspect Local/Remote mode, interlock conditions, permissions and SCADA command configuration.
interview.chapter01.q07.takeaway: Never bypass interlocks to make a test pass.
interview.chapter01.q08.question: What is redundancy in SAS, and how do you test it?
interview.chapter01.q08.answer: Redundancy reduces single points of failure through duplicated networks, servers, power supplies or communication paths. PRP and HSR are examples of IEC 62439-3 seamless network redundancy; redundant SCADA servers and gateways may use separate application failover mechanisms.
interview.chapter01.q08.step01: Identify the redundant elements and their intended failure behavior.
interview.chapter01.q08.step02: Verify both network paths or server nodes are healthy before testing.
interview.chapter01.q08.step03: Record baseline communication, alarms and client connections.
interview.chapter01.q08.step04: Perform a controlled single-failure test with approved isolation and supervision.
interview.chapter01.q08.step05: Verify continuity, failover indications and recovery; document any loss or delay.
interview.chapter01.q08.scenario: During FAT, disconnect one approved PRP LAN path and confirm the IED remains reachable through the other path without a service interruption expected under correct PRP operation.
interview.chapter01.q08.takeaway: PRP/HSR and RSTP do not have identical failover behavior.
interview.chapter01.q09.question: What checks do you perform before starting FAT for a SAS project?
interview.chapter01.q09.answer: Factory Acceptance Testing demonstrates that the configured system meets agreed functional requirements in a controlled environment before shipment or site installation.
interview.chapter01.q09.step01: Review approved architecture, signal list, SLD, network diagram and test procedures.
interview.chapter01.q09.step02: Confirm software versions, licenses, IED configurations and backups.
interview.chapter01.q09.step03: Verify test equipment, simulated inputs and safe output isolation.
interview.chapter01.q09.step04: Check station communications, time synchronization and database loading.
interview.chapter01.q09.step05: Execute witnessed test cases, record results and manage punch-list closure.
interview.chapter01.q09.scenario: A breaker simulation is shown on the IED but not on the HMI during FAT: log the discrepancy, trace mapping and reporting, correct under change control and retest.
interview.chapter01.q09.takeaway: FAT is not a substitute for site wiring and end-to-end SAT verification.
interview.chapter01.q10.question: A device responds to ping but shows communication failure on SCADA. What do you check?
interview.chapter01.q10.answer: Ping verifies only basic IP reachability. The SCADA application may still fail because the application port, protocol association, device settings, security policy or data/report configuration is incorrect.
interview.chapter01.q10.step01: Check SCADA driver logs and exact failure timestamp.
interview.chapter01.q10.step02: Verify target IP, port and service availability; for MMS commonly TCP 102.
interview.chapter01.q10.step03: Inspect VLAN, ACL/firewall rules and routing where relevant.
interview.chapter01.q10.step04: Check IEC 61850 server settings, association limits, certificates/security where deployed and client configuration.
interview.chapter01.q10.step05: Use an approved packet capture to confirm whether the TCP connection and application association complete.
interview.chapter01.q10.step06: Retest reports and points after the association is restored.
interview.chapter01.q10.scenario: A replacement IED uses the correct IP but SCADA cannot establish MMS: compare the enabled server service, access settings and client configuration with the approved baseline.
interview.chapter01.q10.takeaway: Never conclude that IEC 61850 works simply because ping succeeds.
interview.chapter02.q01.question: What is IEC 61850 and why is it used in substation automation?
interview.chapter02.q01.answer: IEC 61850 is a family of standards for power utility automation communication and engineering. It defines standardized data models, abstract communication services and configuration language, enabling consistent integration across equipment vendors. It does not guarantee plug-and-play interoperability without engineering.
interview.chapter02.q01.step01: Identify the IED roles and communication requirements from the project architecture.
interview.chapter02.q01.step02: Review logical devices, logical nodes and data objects in the IED model.
interview.chapter02.q01.step03: Identify the services used: MMS for client-server access, GOOSE for event exchange and SV where process-bus sampling is implemented.
interview.chapter02.q01.step04: Engineer communication and datasets through the appropriate SCL files.
interview.chapter02.q01.step05: Validate interoperability with end-to-end functional tests.
interview.chapter02.q01.scenario: A new vendor relay supports IEC 61850 but its breaker position is missing in HMI. Check model reference, report dataset, RCB and SCADA mapping rather than assuming standard compliance guarantees correct mapping.
interview.chapter02.q01.takeaway: Mention interoperability, standardized semantics and engineering files—not just Ethernet.
interview.chapter02.q02.question: Explain the IEC 61850 data hierarchy with a breaker status example.
interview.chapter02.q02.answer: The typical reference hierarchy is IED → Logical Device → Logical Node → Data Object → Data Attribute. For example, a breaker logical node XCBR can expose position through Pos; its structured value and quality attributes are used by the client. Exact references and instance names depend on the device SCL.
interview.chapter02.q02.step01: Open the ICD/CID or browse the live IED with an IEC 61850 client.
interview.chapter02.q02.step02: Find the relevant logical device and XCBR instance.
interview.chapter02.q02.step03: Locate Pos and its structured attributes such as stVal, q and t as implemented.
interview.chapter02.q02.step04: Check actual field changes against stVal and quality.
interview.chapter02.q02.step05: Use the full configured reference in SCADA mapping and reporting.
interview.chapter02.q02.scenario: SCADA shows stale breaker position: compare physical auxiliary contact, XCBR.Pos.stVal, quality/timestamp and HMI binding to find the first incorrect stage.
interview.chapter02.q02.takeaway: Do not assume XCBR1 or a particular logical device name is universal.
interview.chapter02.q03.question: What are Logical Nodes, Data Objects, Data Attributes and Functional Constraints?
interview.chapter02.q03.answer: A Logical Node groups related function data (for example XCBR for circuit breaker, MMXU for measurements). Data Objects represent information such as Pos or A; Data Attributes contain typed values and metadata. Functional Constraints classify attribute usage, such as ST for status, MX for measurements, CO for control and CF for configuration.
interview.chapter02.q03.step01: Inspect the IED SCL DataTypeTemplates and instantiated data model.
interview.chapter02.q03.step02: Identify the target logical node and data object.
interview.chapter02.q03.step03: Check the functional constraint of the needed attribute.
interview.chapter02.q03.step04: Confirm whether the client uses read, report or control services for it.
interview.chapter02.q03.step05: Validate the data type and expected values in the SCADA database.
interview.chapter02.q03.scenario: A measurement is configured as a status attribute in the client and fails to decode: review the reference, FC and attribute type against the live model.
interview.chapter02.q03.takeaway: FC is part of addressing and service semantics; it is not a network layer.
interview.chapter02.q04.question: What is the difference between MMS, GOOSE and Sampled Values?
interview.chapter02.q04.answer: MMS maps IEC 61850 client-server services to a TCP/IP-based stack and commonly supports reading, reporting and control. GOOSE uses Ethernet multicast for time-critical state/event distribution. Sampled Values carries sampled measurements, commonly on process-bus networks. Network and application engineering requirements differ.
interview.chapter02.q04.step01: Identify which producer and consumer require the data.
interview.chapter02.q04.step02: Use MMS for station-client access and reporting when appropriate.
interview.chapter02.q04.step03: Use GOOSE for engineered peer-to-peer event/state exchange.
interview.chapter02.q04.step04: Use SV only where the architecture includes sampled measurement publishers and subscribers.
interview.chapter02.q04.step05: Validate VLAN/multicast handling, data content and timing against the project design.
interview.chapter02.q04.scenario: A subscriber misses a GOOSE trip signal even though MMS reads work: inspect GOOSE frames and subscription engineering, not just the TCP/IP connection.
interview.chapter02.q04.takeaway: GOOSE does not require IP addressing in its conventional Ethernet mapping.
interview.chapter02.q05.question: What is an SCL file and how do ICD, CID, SCD and IID differ?
interview.chapter02.q05.answer: SCL is the XML-based Substation Configuration Language used to describe IED capabilities, instantiated configurations and system communication. ICD generally describes device capabilities, CID an IED-specific configured instance, SCD the system-wide engineering configuration, and IID an instantiated IED exchange description. Exact export workflows vary by vendor.
interview.chapter02.q05.step01: Collect the vendor-provided capability file and approved system design.
interview.chapter02.q05.step02: Import device descriptions into the system configuration tool.
interview.chapter02.q05.step03: Assign IED identities, communication addresses and required datasets/controls.
interview.chapter02.q05.step04: Engineer GOOSE subscriptions and reporting relationships.
interview.chapter02.q05.step05: Export appropriate files, download to devices and verify consistency with the approved SCD.
interview.chapter02.q05.scenario: A replacement relay has a new firmware build: compare its data model and supported services with the existing SCD before reusing the previous CID.
interview.chapter02.q05.takeaway: Never rename an ICD to CID and assume that changes its contents.
interview.chapter02.q06.question: What is a DataSet in IEC 61850 and how do you verify it?
interview.chapter02.q06.answer: A DataSet is an ordered collection of data references used by services such as reporting and GOOSE. Its membership and ordering must match the publisher configuration and consumer expectations; inclusion alone does not guarantee delivery.
interview.chapter02.q06.step01: Locate the DataSet in the live model or SCL.
interview.chapter02.q06.step02: List every member and verify the reference and functional constraint.
interview.chapter02.q06.step03: Confirm the expected values and data types at the source.
interview.chapter02.q06.step04: Check which Report Control Block or GOOSE Control Block references it.
interview.chapter02.q06.step05: Trigger a permitted test change and confirm the expected consumer update.
interview.chapter02.q06.scenario: A new alarm does not appear in SCADA after mapping: confirm the alarm attribute is actually a member of the DataSet associated with the active RCB.
interview.chapter02.q06.takeaway: Distinguish dataset membership from report trigger configuration.
interview.chapter02.q07.question: Explain Buffered and Unbuffered Report Control Blocks (BRCB and URCB).
interview.chapter02.q07.answer: Report Control Blocks define how a server sends reports for a DataSet. BRCBs can buffer eligible events while a client is disconnected, subject to server limits and configuration; URCBs generally do not retain a disconnected backlog. Both require correct client ownership/enabling and triggers.
interview.chapter02.q07.step01: Identify the RCB name, DataSet reference and configured report instances.
interview.chapter02.q07.step02: Check RptEna, reservation/ownership and client association status.
interview.chapter02.q07.step03: Inspect TrgOps, OptFlds, integrity period and buffer settings as applicable.
interview.chapter02.q07.step04: Cause an approved value change and observe whether a report is generated.
interview.chapter02.q07.step05: For buffered reports, test disconnection/reconnection and review entry handling under the approved procedure.
interview.chapter02.q07.scenario: HMI reconnects but historical changes are missing: check whether the client uses URCB rather than BRCB, and review buffer overflow/entry behavior.
interview.chapter02.q07.takeaway: BRCB is not a substitute for historian retention or SOE time synchronization.
interview.chapter02.q08.question: What are quality and timestamp attributes, and why do they matter?
interview.chapter02.q08.answer: IEC 61850 data can carry a value together with quality and time information. Quality helps consumers identify validity, test/substitution or other conditions; timestamp supports event ordering. A displayed value without its quality context can be misleading.
interview.chapter02.q08.step01: Browse the value, q and t attributes for the target data object.
interview.chapter02.q08.step02: Check IED time synchronization and source timestamp generation.
interview.chapter02.q08.step03: Force only an approved simulated fault or communication-loss condition.
interview.chapter02.q08.step04: Confirm HMI quality indication and alarm behavior.
interview.chapter02.q08.step05: Compare SOE timestamps against source records and the time reference.
interview.chapter02.q08.scenario: A breaker indication remains displayed after communication loss: verify that SCADA marks stale/invalid quality rather than presenting it as confirmed live status.
interview.chapter02.q08.takeaway: A correct value with invalid quality should not be treated as a healthy indication.
interview.chapter02.q09.question: What is the IEC 61850 control model and what is Select-Before-Operate?
interview.chapter02.q09.answer: IEC 61850 supports control models including direct operate and select-before-operate (SBO), with normal or enhanced security variants depending on the implementation. The server validates selection, authorization, interlocks and command conditions before operation; command termination and feedback must be checked.
interview.chapter02.q09.step01: Read the configured ctlModel for the control object.
interview.chapter02.q09.step02: Verify local/remote authority, permissions and interlock conditions.
interview.chapter02.q09.step03: For SBO, select the object before issuing the operate command within the configured time.
interview.chapter02.q09.step04: Observe command response, termination where supported and actual device feedback.
interview.chapter02.q09.step05: Record unsuccessful control causes and avoid repeated operation without diagnosis.
interview.chapter02.q09.scenario: A breaker control works locally but SCADA returns command rejection: check ctlModel, selection ownership, origin/authorization, local/remote and interlocks.
interview.chapter02.q09.takeaway: Never bypass electrical interlocks or operate live plant for an interview demonstration.
interview.chapter02.q10.question: How do you troubleshoot an MMS association failure when ping works?
interview.chapter02.q10.answer: Ping confirms only ICMP reachability. MMS access depends on TCP connectivity, the IEC 61850 server, application association and client/server configuration. The commonly used MMS TCP port is 102, subject to project security arrangements.
interview.chapter02.q10.step01: Confirm correct target IP, VLAN, routing and link status.
interview.chapter02.q10.step02: Check whether TCP port 102 is reachable and permitted by network security policy.
interview.chapter02.q10.step03: Inspect IED MMS service settings, client access limits and server logs.
interview.chapter02.q10.step04: Capture traffic to identify TCP establishment and application association errors.
interview.chapter02.q10.step05: Compare configured client parameters and approved IED baseline, then retest reads and reports.
interview.chapter02.q10.scenario: After relay replacement, ping works but SCADA says disconnected: the replacement may have MMS disabled or a changed access configuration.
interview.chapter02.q10.takeaway: Separate network reachability, MMS association and report delivery as three different tests.
interview.chapter02.q11.question: How do you verify GOOSE publisher/subscriber engineering?
interview.chapter02.q11.answer: GOOSE requires a valid publisher DataSet and GoCB, a network that forwards the multicast frames, and a subscriber engineered to interpret the publisher message. Matching expected configuration revision and DataSet structure is essential; supervision must detect missing or stale messages.
interview.chapter02.q11.step01: Confirm publisher GoCB is enabled and points to the intended DataSet.
interview.chapter02.q11.step02: Verify destination MAC, APPID, VLAN settings and frame transmission with a capture.
interview.chapter02.q11.step03: Check subscriber input mappings and expected publisher identification.
interview.chapter02.q11.step04: Review confRev, stNum, sqNum, timeAllowedToLive and subscriber supervision status.
interview.chapter02.q11.step05: Perform a controlled FAT stimulus and verify the subscriber logic input and expected output safely.
interview.chapter02.q11.scenario: GOOSE frames appear in Wireshark but subscriber status remains invalid: check confRev, DataSet structure and subscription bindings before changing switch settings.
interview.chapter02.q11.takeaway: Successful packet arrival does not prove correct application-level subscription.
interview.chapter02.q12.question: What is the correct end-to-end procedure for integrating a new IEC 61850 IED?
interview.chapter02.q12.answer: IED integration includes engineering-file validation, physical and logical connectivity, IEC 61850 service configuration, point mapping and witnessed functional testing. The process must follow approved project documentation and change control.
interview.chapter02.q12.step01: Verify device model, firmware, ICD/CID/SCD consistency and backups.
interview.chapter02.q12.step02: Configure approved IP, VLAN, time sync and required IEC 61850 services.
interview.chapter02.q12.step03: Confirm MMS association and browse data objects and quality attributes.
interview.chapter02.q12.step04: Validate DataSets, RCBs, GOOSE subscriptions and control model as applicable.
interview.chapter02.q12.step05: Map points to SCADA/HMI and gateway; test status, measurements, alarms, SOE and controls under safe conditions.
interview.chapter02.q12.step06: Record FAT/SAT evidence and close defects through controlled retesting.
interview.chapter02.q12.scenario: A multi-vendor relay communicates but HMI measurements are wrong: inspect source units, data type, magnitude reference and scaling before editing the HMI display.
interview.chapter02.q12.takeaway: Present a testable integration sequence, not just a software tool name.
interview.chapter03.q01.question: Explain how IEC 61850 MMS communication works between an IED and a SCADA client.
interview.chapter03.q01.answer: MMS is the application-level client/server service used for IEC 61850 station-bus data access. An IED typically acts as the server and SCADA, gateway or engineering tools act as clients. MMS supports reads, writes where permitted, reports and controls. IEC 61850 MMS is commonly carried over TCP port 102 using the ISO-on-TCP stack.
interview.chapter03.q01.step01: Check the approved SCD/CID file for the IED IP address and MMS access point.
interview.chapter03.q01.step02: Verify physical link, VLAN, routing and TCP 102 reachability.
interview.chapter03.q01.step03: Establish MMS association and browse logical devices, logical nodes and data attributes.
interview.chapter03.q01.step04: Enable or reserve report control blocks as required by the SCADA driver.
interview.chapter03.q01.step05: Verify live indications, quality, timestamps and authorized control services.
interview.chapter03.q01.scenario: An IED responds to ping but SCADA is offline: isolate TCP 102 connectivity, MMS association and reporting separately.
interview.chapter03.q01.takeaway: Ping does not confirm MMS service or successful reporting.
interview.chapter03.q02.question: What is the difference between a DataSet and a Report Control Block (RCB)?
interview.chapter03.q02.answer: A DataSet is an ordered collection of references to IEC 61850 data objects or attributes. An RCB defines how a server sends changes from that DataSet to a client, including triggers, integrity reporting, buffering and report identifiers. A DataSet alone does not transmit reports.
interview.chapter03.q02.step01: Browse the DataSet and confirm each required FCDA reference.
interview.chapter03.q02.step02: Locate the RCB and confirm its DatSet reference.
interview.chapter03.q02.step03: Review RptID, TrgOps, OptFlds, IntgPd and BufTm.
interview.chapter03.q02.step04: Enable reporting using the correct client ownership procedure.
interview.chapter03.q02.step05: Change an approved test input and verify report content, quality and timestamps.
interview.chapter03.q02.scenario: Breaker status is visible on direct MMS read but not updating automatically: the DataSet may be correct while its RCB is disabled or incorrectly configured.
interview.chapter03.q02.takeaway: DataSet = what to report; RCB = when and how to report.
interview.chapter03.q03.question: Compare Buffered Report Control Block (BRCB) and Unbuffered Report Control Block (URCB).
interview.chapter03.q03.answer: BRCB retains report entries in a server buffer during eligible client disconnections, within its capacity and implementation limits; URCB does not provide the same buffered delivery. Neither guarantees unlimited storage. BRCB uses concepts such as entry identifiers and purge behavior, while URCB is suitable where buffering is not required.
interview.chapter03.q03.step01: Identify the RCB type and supported client allocation in the IED.
interview.chapter03.q03.step02: Configure DataSet and trigger options consistently with the SCADA client.
interview.chapter03.q03.step03: For BRCB, check reservation/ownership, RptEna, entry handling and buffer status.
interview.chapter03.q03.step04: Generate test changes while connected and verify received reports.
interview.chapter03.q03.step05: In FAT, test controlled disconnect/reconnect and review missing or replayed entries.
interview.chapter03.q03.scenario: SCADA loses connectivity for 20 seconds; after recovery the engineer checks whether a BRCB can replay buffered state changes without buffer overflow.
interview.chapter03.q03.takeaway: Buffered does not mean guaranteed recovery under every failure condition.
interview.chapter03.q04.question: What are dchg, qchg, dupd and integrity triggers in reporting?
interview.chapter03.q04.answer: Trigger options determine when a report may be generated. dchg detects data value changes for attributes that support it; qchg detects quality changes; dupd handles supported data-update indications; integrity produces periodic reports at the configured integrity period. General Interrogation (GI) is a client-requested reporting mechanism, not the same as periodic integrity.
interview.chapter03.q04.step01: Inspect the target attribute and its supported trigger behavior.
interview.chapter03.q04.step02: Review RCB TrgOps flags and IntgPd value.
interview.chapter03.q04.step03: Create a controlled value change and verify dchg reporting.
interview.chapter03.q04.step04: Simulate an approved quality change and verify qchg reporting.
interview.chapter03.q04.step05: Request GI and confirm the expected DataSet values are reported.
interview.chapter03.q04.scenario: SCADA shows correct status after GI but misses later changes: check dchg and whether the IED data object actually generates change triggers.
interview.chapter03.q04.takeaway: Trigger settings must match the data behavior and project requirements.
interview.chapter03.q05.question: Explain the purpose of BufTm and IntgPd in an RCB.
interview.chapter03.q05.answer: BufTm is a report buffering interval that can group eligible events before transmission; IntgPd sets the periodic integrity reporting interval when integrity is enabled. Both are configured in milliseconds in the IEC 61850 data model, subject to device implementation. They serve different purposes.
interview.chapter03.q05.step01: Identify the required event reporting latency and network loading requirements.
interview.chapter03.q05.step02: Check the approved RCB BufTm setting and avoid unnecessary delays.
interview.chapter03.q05.step03: Check whether integrity is enabled and its IntgPd value.
interview.chapter03.q05.step04: Generate two controlled rapid state changes and inspect resulting reports.
interview.chapter03.q05.step05: Verify SOE source timestamps and report arrival behavior.
interview.chapter03.q05.scenario: An alarm reaches SCADA later than expected: compare IED event timestamp with report arrival and inspect BufTm plus client processing delays.
interview.chapter03.q05.takeaway: Do not confuse event timestamp, report transmission time and HMI display time.
interview.chapter03.q06.question: What are RptID, DatSet, ConfRev, OptFlds and SqNum in reporting?
interview.chapter03.q06.answer: RptID identifies the report stream; DatSet identifies its data source; ConfRev indicates relevant DataSet configuration revision; OptFlds controls which optional report fields are included; SqNum supports report sequence tracking. Exact optional fields and handling depend on the IEC 61850 edition and implementation.
interview.chapter03.q06.step01: Open the approved SCD and locate the relevant RCB.
interview.chapter03.q06.step02: Compare RptID and DatSet reference with the SCADA driver configuration.
interview.chapter03.q06.step03: Verify ConfRev expectations after DataSet engineering changes.
interview.chapter03.q06.step04: Inspect optional fields such as timestamps, reasons and DataSet references as required.
interview.chapter03.q06.step05: Capture or log consecutive reports and review sequence handling.
interview.chapter03.q06.scenario: After an IED configuration update, SCADA rejects reports: compare DataSet membership and ConfRev against the imported engineering database.
interview.chapter03.q06.takeaway: Treat a configuration revision mismatch as a controlled engineering change.
interview.chapter03.q07.question: How do you enable a BRCB for a SCADA client during integration?
interview.chapter03.q07.answer: The client must use the RCB access and ownership procedure supported by the server and its IEC 61850 edition. Typically the engineer checks availability, selects or reserves the correct instance as needed, configures permitted parameters, and sets RptEna. Multiple clients may need separate RCB instances.
interview.chapter03.q07.step01: Check the server-supported BRCB instances and any existing client ownership.
interview.chapter03.q07.step02: Confirm the client references the correct RCB and DataSet.
interview.chapter03.q07.step03: Apply the supported reservation/ownership procedure before writing protected settings.
interview.chapter03.q07.step04: Set or verify trigger options and other permitted parameters.
interview.chapter03.q07.step05: Enable RptEna and request GI if supported and needed.
interview.chapter03.q07.step06: Test updates and monitor ownership/reconnection behavior.
interview.chapter03.q07.scenario: Two SCADA clients attempt to use the same exclusive RCB instance; one fails to enable reporting. Assign supported instances rather than forcing concurrent ownership.
interview.chapter03.q07.takeaway: RCB ownership and reservation are device- and edition-dependent.
interview.chapter03.q08.question: Why can an IED be online in SCADA while its status points do not update?
interview.chapter03.q08.answer: An MMS association proves that the client and server communicate, but individual report subscriptions, DataSet references, triggers, point mappings and quality processing can still be wrong. Diagnose from source signal to HMI rather than restarting the network first.
interview.chapter03.q08.step01: Check the physical input and the live IED data attribute.
interview.chapter03.q08.step02: Read the same attribute directly using an approved MMS browser.
interview.chapter03.q08.step03: Verify DataSet membership and RCB DatSet reference.
interview.chapter03.q08.step04: Check RptEna, reservation, triggers and GI behavior.
interview.chapter03.q08.step05: Confirm report reception and SCADA database point mapping.
interview.chapter03.q08.step06: Verify display inversion, quality and timestamps.
interview.chapter03.q08.scenario: XCBR.Pos.stVal changes in the IED but the HMI stays closed: find whether the change disappears at DataSet, report reception or SCADA mapping.
interview.chapter03.q08.takeaway: An active association is not equivalent to valid point-level telemetry.
interview.chapter03.q09.question: How do you troubleshoot MMS connection failure when ping succeeds?
interview.chapter03.q09.answer: ICMP reachability tests a different service than MMS. Possible causes include blocked TCP 102, disabled MMS server, incompatible application parameters, client limits, device security settings or invalid association configuration.
interview.chapter03.q09.step01: Verify target IP and network route from the SCADA host.
interview.chapter03.q09.step02: Test TCP port 102 with an approved tool and check firewall/ACL rules.
interview.chapter03.q09.step03: Capture TCP handshake and ISO-on-TCP/COTP and MMS association traffic.
interview.chapter03.q09.step04: Review MMS server enablement, permitted clients and session limits.
interview.chapter03.q09.step05: Compare client/server communication settings with the approved SCD/CID.
interview.chapter03.q09.step06: Retest read access, report enablement and application stability.
interview.chapter03.q09.scenario: After a relay replacement, ping works but MMS fails; compare the replacement firmware/security configuration and server access point before editing SCADA tags.
interview.chapter03.q09.takeaway: Troubleshoot at the first failed protocol layer, not from assumptions.
interview.chapter03.q10.question: What is General Interrogation (GI), and when should SCADA use it?
interview.chapter03.q10.answer: GI is a request from the client to the RCB to send a report containing the relevant DataSet values, provided the IED and RCB support the operation and reporting is properly enabled. It is useful for initial synchronization and recovery but does not replace change reporting.
interview.chapter03.q10.step01: Confirm the correct RCB is enabled and accessible to the client.
interview.chapter03.q10.step02: Initiate GI using the SCADA driver or approved test client.
interview.chapter03.q10.step03: Verify the report contains expected DataSet entries and quality.
interview.chapter03.q10.step04: Compare displayed values with the current IED states.
interview.chapter03.q10.step05: Then test ordinary dchg/qchg reporting without relying on GI.
interview.chapter03.q10.scenario: After SCADA server failover, GI refreshes current states; subsequent breaker operations must still generate change reports.
interview.chapter03.q10.takeaway: GI verifies current state synchronization, not continuous event delivery.
interview.chapter03.q11.question: How do quality and timestamps travel through MMS reports and affect SOE?
interview.chapter03.q11.answer: Reported data may include source data values, quality and timestamps depending on DataSet membership and report options. SOE accuracy requires reliable source event timestamping, time synchronization and correct SCADA processing. Server arrival time is not necessarily the event time.
interview.chapter03.q11.step01: Inspect the relevant stVal, q and t attributes in the IED data model.
interview.chapter03.q11.step02: Verify IED SNTP/PTP/IRIG-B synchronization as applicable.
interview.chapter03.q11.step03: Check DataSet and optional report fields needed by the client.
interview.chapter03.q11.step04: Generate a safe test transition and compare IED log, MMS report and HMI SOE.
interview.chapter03.q11.step05: Test communication loss and verify invalid/stale quality is handled correctly.
interview.chapter03.q11.scenario: The HMI displays a breaker state after loss of communication: verify that the quality indicates stale or invalid data and does not imply a live measurement.
interview.chapter03.q11.takeaway: Always interpret value together with quality and time.
interview.chapter03.q12.question: How would you execute a complete FAT test for MMS reporting and document the result?
interview.chapter03.q12.answer: A good FAT test demonstrates traceability from approved signal list and IED configuration to actual MMS reporting and SCADA display. It includes normal operation, quality behavior, reconnect scenarios and recorded evidence, without operating live plant.
interview.chapter03.q12.step01: Review approved signal list, SCD/CID baseline, RCB allocation and test sheet.
interview.chapter03.q12.step02: Establish a stable MMS association and record server/client details.
interview.chapter03.q12.step03: Check DataSet contents and RCB parameters against the approved design.
interview.chapter03.q12.step04: Stimulate approved simulated binary and analog values; verify value, scaling, quality and timestamps.
interview.chapter03.q12.step05: Test GI, change triggers and controlled disconnect/reconnect behavior.
interview.chapter03.q12.step06: Record screenshots, packet/log evidence, pass/fail observations and punch items.
interview.chapter03.q12.step07: Retest corrected defects and archive final configuration versions.
interview.chapter03.q12.scenario: During witnessed FAT, one feeder alarm is absent from reports: trace its FCDA reference, add it through approved engineering change control, reload the affected configuration and repeat the witnessed test.
interview.chapter03.q12.takeaway: A complete test includes documented evidence and controlled defect closure.
interview.chapter04.q01.question: What is IEC 61850 GOOSE and why is it used?
interview.chapter04.q01.answer: GOOSE (Generic Object Oriented Substation Event) distributes configured data changes from a publishing IED to subscribing IEDs using Ethernet multicast. It supports time-critical interlocking, status and protection-related signaling without requiring an MMS client connection. Performance depends on engineered network and device behavior.
interview.chapter04.q01.step01: Identify the publishing IED and required source data objects.
interview.chapter04.q01.step02: Configure a DataSet and GOOSE Control Block (GoCB).
interview.chapter04.q01.step03: Configure multicast destination, APPID and VLAN parameters as designed.
interview.chapter04.q01.step04: Map subscriber inputs to the published DataSet members.
interview.chapter04.q01.step05: Verify supervision and functional behavior under approved test conditions.
interview.chapter04.q01.scenario: During FAT, a simulated protection pickup in one relay is received by a second relay through GOOSE, with physical trip outputs isolated.
interview.chapter04.q01.takeaway: GOOSE is publish/subscribe Layer 2 traffic, not an IP/TCP session.
interview.chapter04.q02.question: Explain publisher, subscriber, DataSet and GoCB in a GOOSE application.
interview.chapter04.q02.answer: A publisher sends GOOSE frames containing values from a defined DataSet. The GoCB controls the GOOSE publication and identifies the message. A subscriber is configured to accept the correct publisher message and bind its DataSet members to internal signals.
interview.chapter04.q02.step01: Confirm the exact FCDA members and ordering in the publisher DataSet.
interview.chapter04.q02.step02: Check the GoCB reference, GoID, DataSet reference and confRev.
interview.chapter04.q02.step03: Verify APPID, multicast MAC, VLAN ID and priority against the network design.
interview.chapter04.q02.step04: Import or configure external references (ExtRef) in the subscriber.
interview.chapter04.q02.step05: Validate message reception and subscriber signal quality.
interview.chapter04.q02.scenario: A subscriber receives Ethernet frames but its interlock input remains invalid because the ExtRef points to the wrong published member.
interview.chapter04.q02.takeaway: Receiving a frame does not guarantee correct subscriber mapping.
interview.chapter04.q03.question: What is the role of stNum and sqNum in GOOSE?
interview.chapter04.q03.answer: stNum is the state number and normally increments when the published DataSet state changes. sqNum identifies retransmissions for a given state and generally advances as repeated frames are sent. These fields help analyze changes, continuity and retransmission patterns.
interview.chapter04.q03.step01: Capture publisher traffic with a mirror/SPAN port or approved capture method.
interview.chapter04.q03.step02: Apply the Wireshark display filter goose.
interview.chapter04.q03.step03: Observe stNum when a safe simulated input changes.
interview.chapter04.q03.step04: Observe sqNum across retransmissions while state is unchanged.
interview.chapter04.q03.step05: Correlate frame sequence with subscriber diagnostics.
interview.chapter04.q03.scenario: A relay input changes once; the capture shows a new stNum and a burst of retransmissions with advancing sqNum.
interview.chapter04.q03.takeaway: Do not confuse a new state with a retransmission of the same state.
interview.chapter04.q04.question: Why does GOOSE retransmit even when there is no new event?
interview.chapter04.q04.answer: GOOSE uses repeated transmission to improve reliability and allow subscribers to supervise publisher availability. Immediately after a state change, transmissions are frequent, then spacing generally increases toward a steady-state interval as configured by the device.
interview.chapter04.q04.step01: Review the configured minimum and maximum retransmission intervals.
interview.chapter04.q04.step02: Capture traffic before and after a controlled state transition.
interview.chapter04.q04.step03: Measure actual frame spacing in Wireshark.
interview.chapter04.q04.step05: Compare results with vendor documentation and project requirements.
interview.chapter04.q04.scenario: A network capture shows rapid GOOSE frames after a simulated trip indication and slower periodic messages afterward.
interview.chapter04.q04.takeaway: GOOSE is not a one-time event packet; supervision relies on repeated traffic.
interview.chapter04.q05.question: What are APPID, multicast MAC, VLAN ID and VLAN priority in GOOSE?
interview.chapter04.q05.answer: APPID identifies an application stream within the GOOSE frame. The destination multicast MAC directs Ethernet multicast delivery. IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tagging can segregate traffic and carry priority information. All parameters must agree with the engineered network and device configuration.
interview.chapter04.q05.step01: Read publisher GoCB communication settings from the approved SCD.
interview.chapter04.q05.step02: Check the destination MAC and APPID in captured frames.
interview.chapter04.q05.step03: Verify VLAN tagging and priority behavior on ingress/egress switch ports.
interview.chapter04.q05.step04: Confirm the subscriber expects the correct stream.
interview.chapter04.q05.step05: Retest after any controlled network configuration correction.
interview.chapter04.q05.scenario: Publisher and subscriber are connected to one switch but GOOSE is absent at the subscriber because the switch port excludes the publisher VLAN.
interview.chapter04.q05.takeaway: VLAN mismatch can block GOOSE even when IP ping succeeds.
interview.chapter04.q06.question: What is confRev and how can it cause a GOOSE subscription failure?
interview.chapter04.q06.answer: confRev is the configuration revision associated with the published DataSet definition. A subscriber may reject or flag messages when the received revision does not match its engineered expectation, especially after DataSet structure changes.
interview.chapter04.q06.step01: Compare publisher DataSet contents and order with the approved SCD.
interview.chapter04.q06.step02: Check the publisher confRev in Wireshark.
interview.chapter04.q06.step03: Inspect subscriber expected confRev and subscription diagnostic.
interview.chapter04.q06.step04: Update and distribute validated engineering configuration to affected IEDs.
interview.chapter04.q06.step05: Repeat subscription and signal-level FAT tests.
interview.chapter04.q06.scenario: An engineer adds a new DataSet member to the publisher; GOOSE frames arrive but the subscriber reports a configuration mismatch.
interview.chapter04.q06.takeaway: Changing a DataSet can require coordinated publisher and subscriber engineering.
interview.chapter04.q07.question: How do you configure GOOSE communication between two different vendors?
interview.chapter04.q07.answer: Cross-vendor GOOSE engineering requires consistent IEC 61850 data references, DataSet structure, communication parameters and subscriber mapping. Vendor engineering tools may import SCD files differently, so interoperability must be verified end to end.
interview.chapter04.q07.step01: Export or obtain correct ICD/IID information for each device.
interview.chapter04.q07.step02: Engineer publisher DataSet and GoCB in the system configuration.
interview.chapter04.q07.step03: Assign approved multicast MAC, APPID, VLAN and priority.
interview.chapter04.q07.step04: Import SCD or configure subscriber ExtRef mappings in its vendor tool.
interview.chapter04.q07.step05: Download validated configurations and test every mapped bit and supervision state.
interview.chapter04.q07.scenario: A Siemens relay publishes a breaker interlock and a Schneider relay subscribes; the engineer verifies the imported ExtRef and a controlled simulated state transition.
interview.chapter04.q07.takeaway: SCD exchange helps interoperability, but actual functional testing is still required.
interview.chapter04.q08.question: How do you troubleshoot GOOSE when both IEDs ping but no GOOSE is received?
interview.chapter04.q08.answer: Ping tests IP connectivity; GOOSE uses Ethernet multicast and does not depend on the TCP/IP path used for ping. Troubleshoot physical delivery, switch VLAN/multicast configuration, publication, subscription and message compatibility separately.
interview.chapter04.q08.step01: Check link state, optical levels, switch errors and the correct physical ports.
interview.chapter04.q08.step02: Capture publisher traffic and verify GOOSE frames are transmitted.
interview.chapter04.q08.step03: Inspect VLAN membership, tagging, multicast forwarding and filtering on the path.
interview.chapter04.q08.step04: Capture near the subscriber to confirm frames arrive.
interview.chapter04.q08.step05: Check APPID, destination MAC, GoCB reference, confRev, DataSet and ExtRef mapping.
interview.chapter04.q08.step06: Perform an approved functional retest and record evidence.
interview.chapter04.q08.scenario: Both relays respond to ping, but GOOSE is lost after a switch replacement because the new trunk does not carry the configured VLAN.
interview.chapter04.q08.takeaway: Always separate network delivery failure from subscriber configuration failure.
interview.chapter04.q09.question: How do you identify a GOOSE subscription fault in Wireshark?
interview.chapter04.q09.answer: Wireshark can decode GOOSE Ethernet frames, allowing inspection of source/destination MAC, VLAN, APPID, GoCB reference, DataSet, confRev, stNum, sqNum and timeAllowedToLive. Captures must be interpreted alongside IED diagnostics.
interview.chapter04.q09.step01: Capture traffic using an authorized mirror port or test TAP.
interview.chapter04.q09.step02: Use display filter goose and select the expected publisher.
interview.chapter04.q09.step03: Verify frames arrive at the intended capture point.
interview.chapter04.q09.step04: Compare APPID, GoCB reference, DataSet and confRev with approved engineering.
interview.chapter04.q09.step05: Observe stNum/sqNum during a safe simulated event.
interview.chapter04.q09.step06: Check subscriber diagnostic counters and input values.
interview.chapter04.q09.scenario: GOOSE frames are visible at the subscriber switch port, but the subscriber rejects them due to an unexpected confRev.
interview.chapter04.q09.takeaway: A packet capture proves network arrival, not successful application binding.
interview.chapter04.q10.question: What is timeAllowedToLive and what happens when a publisher fails?
interview.chapter04.q10.answer: The GOOSE timeAllowedToLive field indicates how long a subscriber may wait for a subsequent valid message before treating the stream as timed out. On loss, subscriber quality or supervision status should change according to device logic and engineered fail-safe requirements.
interview.chapter04.q10.step02: Verify the subscriber supervision or communication-health signal.
interview.chapter04.q10.step03: Under approved FAT conditions, isolate the test publisher or test link.
interview.chapter04.q10.step04: Measure the time until subscriber timeout indication.
interview.chapter04.q10.step05: Verify configured fail-safe behavior and recovery after publication resumes.
interview.chapter04.q10.scenario: During FAT, an interlocking subscriber raises a GOOSE communication-failure alarm after the publisher is disconnected.
interview.chapter04.q10.takeaway: Loss of GOOSE must be handled by designed supervision, not assumed to mean FALSE.
interview.chapter04.q11.question: How do you test GOOSE-based interlocking safely during FAT?
interview.chapter04.q11.answer: Test both functional state changes and communication-failure behavior against an approved cause-and-effect matrix. Live breaker operations and protection trip outputs must not be used as casual communication tests.
interview.chapter04.q11.step01: Review interlocking logic, expected publisher signals and test permits.
interview.chapter04.q11.step02: Isolate trip/close outputs and establish approved simulated input conditions.
interview.chapter04.q11.step03: Confirm publisher and subscriber communication healthy.
interview.chapter04.q11.step04: Apply each simulated permissive/blocking condition and record subscriber response.
interview.chapter04.q11.step06: Document actual versus expected results and retest any defect.
interview.chapter04.q11.scenario: A simulated disconnector-not-open signal must block a breaker close permissive at the subscriber; verify logic indication without operating the breaker.
interview.chapter04.q11.takeaway: Never bypass interlocks to pass a GOOSE test.
interview.chapter04.q12.question: How is GOOSE different from MMS reporting?
interview.chapter04.q12.answer: GOOSE is Ethernet multicast publish/subscribe for rapid IED-to-IED data distribution. MMS reporting uses an established client-server association over TCP/IP to deliver DataSet changes to SCADA or other clients. Their engineering, transport, diagnostics and use cases differ.
interview.chapter04.q12.step01: Identify whether the consumer is another IED or a station-level MMS client.
interview.chapter04.q12.step02: For GOOSE check GoCB, multicast, VLAN, APPID and ExtRef.
interview.chapter04.q12.step03: For MMS reporting check client association, RCB, DataSet and report triggers.
interview.chapter04.q12.step04: Use Wireshark filters goose and tcp.port == 102 as appropriate.
interview.chapter04.q12.step05: Verify application behavior and quality handling for each service.
interview.chapter04.q12.scenario: A breaker status updates on HMI via MMS while the peer interlocking relay does not receive its GOOSE subscription: troubleshoot the two paths independently.
interview.chapter04.q12.takeaway: Healthy MMS does not prove healthy GOOSE, and vice versa.
interview.chapter05.q01.question: What is SCL and why is it important in IEC 61850 engineering?
interview.chapter05.q01.answer: Substation Configuration Language (SCL) is the IEC 61850-6 XML-based engineering format for exchanging IED capabilities, substation structure, communication settings and signal relationships between engineering tools. It supports coordinated multi-vendor configuration; it does not replace testing of the actual running IED.
interview.chapter05.q01.step01: Collect approved project architecture, IED capability files and vendor engineering requirements.
interview.chapter05.q01.step02: Validate XML/SCL schema and vendor-specific constraints.
interview.chapter05.q01.step03: Integrate IEDs and network settings in the system configuration tool.
interview.chapter05.q01.step04: Engineer DataSets, reports, GOOSE subscriptions and control mappings as required.
interview.chapter05.q01.step05: Export approved configurations and verify the downloaded IED against the master design.
interview.chapter05.q01.scenario: An ABB relay and Siemens relay need GOOSE exchange: their capability descriptions are imported into a system configurator and the final subscriber bindings are verified in each vendor tool.
interview.chapter05.q01.takeaway: SCL is a configuration exchange format, not a real-time protocol.
interview.chapter05.q02.question: Explain ICD, CID, SCD and IID files with their practical differences.
interview.chapter05.q02.answer: ICD (IED Capability Description) describes a device type or capability template. CID (Configured IED Description) describes one configured IED, often for download. SCD (Substation Configuration Description) describes the coordinated system including multiple IEDs and communications. IID (Instantiated IED Description) represents an engineered IED instance for exchange within a multi-tool workflow. Exact vendor import/export behavior varies.
interview.chapter05.q02.step01: Start with vendor ICD or supported capability export.
interview.chapter05.q02.step02: Instantiate the actual IED and configure its name, logical devices and communication interfaces.
interview.chapter05.q02.step03: Combine the participating IEDs in a project SCD and engineer subscriptions.
interview.chapter05.q02.step04: Exchange IID files when the workflow calls for individual IED updates.
interview.chapter05.q02.step05: Generate vendor-accepted CID or equivalent download file and verify installed configuration.
interview.chapter05.q02.scenario: A vendor supplies ICD for a new bay controller; after integrating it with the station SCD, the configured device-specific file is exported for commissioning.
interview.chapter05.q02.takeaway: An ICD is not automatically the final commissioned configuration.
interview.chapter05.q03.question: What information is contained in an SCD file?
interview.chapter05.q03.answer: An SCD can include the Substation electrical hierarchy, IED instances, AccessPoints, ConnectedAPs, subnetworks, IP addresses, logical nodes, DataSets, ReportControl, GSEControl, GOOSE addresses and subscriber ExtRef links. Presence and detail depend on project engineering and tool support.
interview.chapter05.q03.step01: Open the SCD in a trusted SCL viewer or engineering tool.
interview.chapter05.q03.step02: Inspect Header and Substation sections for project identity and topology.
interview.chapter05.q03.step03: Inspect Communication for SubNetwork, ConnectedAP, IP and GSE addressing.
interview.chapter05.q03.step04: Inspect each IED/AccessPoint/Server/LDevice/LN for DataSets and control blocks.
interview.chapter05.q03.step05: Inspect Inputs/ExtRef to confirm intended subscriber signal references.
interview.chapter05.q03.scenario: A GOOSE subscription is missing after an SCD update; compare publisher GSEControl and subscriber ExtRef paths before modifying a relay.
interview.chapter05.q03.takeaway: An SCD is the integration baseline; do not assume every runtime setting is fully represented in it.
interview.chapter05.q04.question: Describe the complete SCL engineering workflow from design to FAT.
interview.chapter05.q04.answer: The workflow starts from approved functional requirements and vendor capability data, produces a coordinated system configuration, exports device-specific settings, and validates the deployed behavior through controlled tests.
interview.chapter05.q04.step01: Freeze signal list, architecture, IED list, naming rules and network plan.
interview.chapter05.q04.step02: Import capability files and create unique IED instances in the system configuration tool.
interview.chapter05.q04.step03: Configure DataSets, RCBs, GOOSE publishers/subscribers and communications.
interview.chapter05.q04.step04: Run schema, cross-reference and vendor compatibility checks; review changes.
interview.chapter05.q04.step05: Export device configurations, download under controlled procedure and record versions.
interview.chapter05.q04.step06: Test MMS reporting, GOOSE behavior, quality, controls and failure handling during FAT.
interview.chapter05.q04.scenario: During FAT, a subscriber rejects a GOOSE stream; the engineer checks SCD cross-references, regenerates the affected vendor configuration and repeats the approved test.
interview.chapter05.q04.takeaway: The exported XML is only an intermediate deliverable; FAT evidence closes the loop.
interview.chapter05.q05.question: What is the difference between IED name, logical device and logical node in SCL?
interview.chapter05.q05.answer: An IED name uniquely identifies a configured IED instance in the SCL project. A logical device groups logical nodes within a server. A logical node models a defined function, such as XCBR for breaker information or PTOC for overcurrent protection. Data references combine these levels and the data object/attribute path.
interview.chapter05.q05.step01: Identify the IED instance name in the SCD.
interview.chapter05.q05.step02: Open the intended AccessPoint, Server and LDevice instance.
interview.chapter05.q05.step03: Find the LN class and instance, for example XCBR1.
interview.chapter05.q05.step04: Confirm the Data Object and Data Attribute used by the signal list.
interview.chapter05.q05.step05: Verify the complete reference in the IED browser and SCADA mapping.
interview.chapter05.q05.scenario: After changing an IED name in an engineering tool, report and GOOSE references are reviewed because references that depend on the old name may become invalid.
interview.chapter05.q05.takeaway: Never confuse an IED physical label with its IEC 61850 object reference.
interview.chapter05.q06.question: How do you configure DataSets and Report Control Blocks using SCL?
interview.chapter05.q06.answer: A DataSet identifies a collection of data attributes or functional constraints. A ReportControl references a DataSet and defines reporting-related parameters. Buffered and unbuffered behavior, trigger options and client reservation must be checked against the IED capability and runtime implementation.
interview.chapter05.q06.step01: Identify required SCADA points and appropriate data attributes including quality and time where available.
interview.chapter05.q06.step02: Create or verify DataSet FCDA members and functional constraints.
interview.chapter05.q06.step03: Create the supported ReportControl referencing that DataSet.
interview.chapter05.q06.step04: Set supported trigger options, integrity period, buffer time and report identifiers.
interview.chapter05.q06.step05: Check available RCB instances and client ownership expectations.
interview.chapter05.q06.step06: Download configuration and verify report enablement and actual updates with a client.
interview.chapter05.q06.scenario: SCADA can read XCBR.Pos by MMS but gets no change report: inspect the DataSet FCDA, ReportControl datSet reference, TrgOps, RptEna and client configuration.
interview.chapter05.q06.takeaway: The number of BRCB instances is a client/IED design decision, not always a fixed count.
interview.chapter05.q07.question: How are GOOSE publisher and subscriber references represented in SCL?
interview.chapter05.q07.answer: The publisher typically defines a DataSet and GSEControl under its logical node, with communication addressing in the GSE section. The subscriber uses Inputs/ExtRef references to identify required publisher data. Vendor tools may require additional mapping to internal logic.
interview.chapter05.q07.step01: Identify the publisher DataSet members and GSEControl name.
interview.chapter05.q07.step02: Confirm GOOSE MAC, APPID, VLAN ID and priority in the Communication section.
interview.chapter05.q07.step03: Check the subscriber Inputs/ExtRef attributes against publisher IED, LD, LN, DO and DA.
interview.chapter05.q07.step04: Check engineering revision and subscriber binding status in vendor software.
interview.chapter05.q07.step05: Download both sides if required and test in an isolated approved environment.
interview.chapter05.q07.scenario: GOOSE packets arrive on the subscriber port but the logic input remains invalid: verify ExtRef references, DataSet member order, confRev and the vendor internal mapping.
interview.chapter05.q07.takeaway: Network arrival is not the same as valid subscriber mapping.
interview.chapter05.q08.question: What is confRev and when should it change?
interview.chapter05.q08.answer: The configuration revision (confRev) is used with GOOSE and reporting configurations to identify relevant changes. For GOOSE, a subscriber may reject messages if the expected revision or DataSet structure does not match the publisher. Tools manage revision behavior differently; confirm against the applicable standard and vendor documentation.
interview.chapter05.q08.step01: Record current publisher configuration and subscriber expected revision.
interview.chapter05.q08.step02: Review the changed DataSet/control-block configuration and affected subscriptions.
interview.chapter05.q08.step03: Regenerate and validate system configuration using the approved workflow.
interview.chapter05.q08.step04: Update the affected IEDs and verify both sides agree.
interview.chapter05.q08.step05: Capture a valid test message and check confRev and subscriber status.
interview.chapter05.q08.scenario: After adding a GOOSE DataSet member, the subscriber reports configuration mismatch until its engineered subscription is updated.
interview.chapter05.q08.takeaway: Never force a revision number without understanding the actual DataSet and subscriber configuration.
interview.chapter05.q09.question: How do you troubleshoot an SCL file that fails to import into a vendor tool?
interview.chapter05.q09.answer: Import failure can result from malformed XML, unsupported SCL schema/version, invalid names, missing references, unsupported IED features or tool-specific restrictions. Diagnose from the first meaningful validation error and the vendor import log.
interview.chapter05.q09.step01: Save the original file and capture exact error, tool version and firmware.
interview.chapter05.q09.step02: Run an XML parser and SCL schema validation appropriate to the file edition.
interview.chapter05.q09.step03: Inspect namespaces, schema edition and required sections.
interview.chapter05.q09.step04: Check duplicate IED names, broken references, DataSet members and unsupported options.
interview.chapter05.q09.step05: Re-export using a compatible engineering-tool workflow; compare the diff.
interview.chapter05.q09.step06: Re-import and record evidence before deploying any configuration.
interview.chapter05.q09.scenario: An IID exported by a newer vendor tool is rejected by an older system configurator; compare supported SCL editions and use a vendor-supported exchange path.
interview.chapter05.q09.takeaway: Do not remove unknown XML sections blindly just to suppress an import error.
interview.chapter05.q10.question: What are common SCL configuration mistakes in multi-vendor integration?
interview.chapter05.q10.answer: Common issues include mismatched IED naming, duplicate network addresses, unsupported logical node/data object paths, inconsistent DataSet member order, missing ExtRef bindings, wrong functional constraints and configuration revision mismatches.
interview.chapter05.q10.step01: Validate unique IED names and communication addresses.
interview.chapter05.q10.step02: Compare publisher DataSet FCDA members with subscriber expected structure.
interview.chapter05.q10.step03: Check functional constraints and data attribute references.
interview.chapter05.q10.step04: Verify RCB ownership, report instances and trigger options.
interview.chapter05.q10.step05: Run vendor interoperability checks and packet-level tests.
interview.chapter05.q10.step06: Maintain an issue log tied to SCD revision and IED firmware.
interview.chapter05.q10.scenario: SCADA shows an invalid measurement after a relay replacement because the new model exposes a different logical-device instance; update mappings through controlled engineering.
interview.chapter05.q10.takeaway: A syntactically valid SCD can still contain semantically incorrect mappings.
interview.chapter05.q11.question: How do you manage SCD revisions and change control during FAT and SAT?
interview.chapter05.q11.answer: A controlled SCD baseline prevents divergent engineering data between station tools and deployed IEDs. Every change should have an owner, reason, approval, impacted IED list, regenerated outputs and retest evidence.
interview.chapter05.q11.step01: Back up the approved SCD and affected IED configurations before changes.
interview.chapter05.q11.step02: Create a change record identifying exact affected signals and services.
interview.chapter05.q11.step03: Review the XML diff and validate references, addresses and subscriptions.
interview.chapter05.q11.step04: Export updated device files using the documented engineering chain.
interview.chapter05.q11.step05: Deploy only with authorization and verify communication and functional tests.
interview.chapter05.q11.step06: Archive final approved SCD, device files, version list and FAT/SAT evidence.
interview.chapter05.q11.scenario: A late GOOSE signal addition affects two relays and SCADA; the team updates the master SCD and retests publisher, subscriber and station reporting before closure.
interview.chapter05.q11.takeaway: Avoid making undocumented changes directly on an IED that are absent from the master configuration.
interview.chapter05.q12.question: How do you verify that the downloaded CID matches the approved SCD?
interview.chapter05.q12.answer: Compare the deployed IED identity, communication settings, logical-device/data references, control blocks and subscriptions with the approved baseline. Use device readback, configuration identifiers and functional testing because file names or checksums alone may not describe runtime state.
interview.chapter05.q12.step01: Identify the approved SCD revision and generated device configuration.
interview.chapter05.q12.step02: Read back the IED configuration or use vendor comparison tools when supported.
interview.chapter05.q12.step03: Verify IED name, IP, DataSets, RCBs, GOOSE addressing and subscriber references.
interview.chapter05.q12.step04: Test representative status changes, reports and GOOSE inputs under approved test conditions.
interview.chapter05.q12.step05: Document deviations, corrective changes and final configuration backup.
interview.chapter05.q12.scenario: An IED was replaced with a spare: it pings but GOOSE interlocking is unhealthy; read back the installed device configuration and compare with the approved subscriber bindings.
interview.chapter05.q12.takeaway: Commissioning acceptance depends on verified behavior, not just a successful file download.
interview.chapter06.q01.question: Explain the end-to-end SCADA signal path from an IED to an HMI indication.
interview.chapter06.q01.answer: SCADA displays an engineered representation of a field value. The complete path includes the physical signal, IED data object, communication service, SCADA acquisition, database tag and HMI binding. Every stage must preserve value, quality and timestamp where available.
interview.chapter06.q01.step01: Confirm the field contact or measured quantity and IED input using approved test methods.
interview.chapter06.q01.step02: Browse the corresponding IED data object, for example XCBR.Pos.stVal, and inspect quality and timestamp.
interview.chapter06.q01.step03: Verify MMS association, DataSet membership and report delivery, or the project's configured acquisition protocol.
interview.chapter06.q01.step04: Match the received object reference to the SCADA database point, including inversion and quality handling.
interview.chapter06.q01.step05: Check the HMI symbol binding, indication colors, event logging and alarm behavior.
interview.chapter06.q01.step06: Record expected versus actual results in the FAT/SAT test sheet.
interview.chapter06.q01.scenario: Breaker opens physically and the relay shows Open, but HMI remains Closed. Compare the IED value, report capture, SCADA tag and HMI binding to find the first incorrect stage.
interview.chapter06.q01.takeaway: Troubleshoot from field to display; successful ping does not prove point acquisition.
interview.chapter06.q02.question: What is signal mapping in SCADA and how do you validate it?
interview.chapter06.q02.answer: Signal mapping links each source IED data reference or protocol address to a unique SCADA database point and its display, alarm, event and gateway destinations. Mapping must be validated against an approved signal list.
interview.chapter06.q02.step01: Obtain the approved signal list, IED naming conventions and protocol configuration.
interview.chapter06.q02.step02: Identify each source reference, functional constraint, value type and expected engineering unit.
interview.chapter06.q02.step03: Create or import SCADA points with consistent names, descriptions and scaling.
interview.chapter06.q02.step04: Configure status polarity, alarm limits, quality behavior and timestamps as required.
interview.chapter06.q02.step05: Test representative normal, abnormal and communication-failure states.
interview.chapter06.q02.step06: Reconcile exceptions with the signal list and archive test evidence.
interview.chapter06.q02.scenario: Two feeder breaker indications appear swapped on the HMI after a database import. Compare source object references and destination tags before correcting mappings.
interview.chapter06.q02.takeaway: Check both the signal value and its identity; a changing tag may still be the wrong tag.
interview.chapter06.q03.question: How do you configure and test SCADA alarms?
interview.chapter06.q03.answer: An alarm is an engineered condition requiring operator attention. Alarm design includes activation criteria, priority, annunciation, acknowledgement, return-to-normal and historical records.
interview.chapter06.q03.step01: Identify alarm source and operating philosophy from the approved alarm list.
interview.chapter06.q03.step02: Define activation logic, priority, deadband or delay where appropriate.
interview.chapter06.q03.step03: Configure message text, equipment identity and acknowledgment behavior.
interview.chapter06.q03.step04: Generate a safe simulated input or approved test stimulus.
interview.chapter06.q03.step05: Verify activation, timestamp, priority, sound or visual indication, acknowledgment and return-to-normal.
interview.chapter06.q03.step06: Check alarm history and document results.
interview.chapter06.q03.scenario: A transformer temperature alarm appears repeatedly around its threshold. Review analog deadband and delay rather than simply disabling the alarm.
interview.chapter06.q03.takeaway: Alarm acknowledgement is not the same as the condition returning to normal.
interview.chapter06.q04.question: What is SOE and why is time synchronization important?
interview.chapter06.q04.answer: Sequence of Events (SOE) records time-stamped changes to reconstruct the order of operations. Device-originated timestamps can be more useful than server arrival time when network delays vary. Accuracy depends on synchronization and timestamp handling.
interview.chapter06.q04.step01: Check configured time source such as SNTP, NTP, PTP or IRIG-B as supported.
interview.chapter06.q04.step02: Verify time zone and UTC handling across devices and SCADA.
interview.chapter06.q04.step03: Generate controlled events with known order and compare device and SCADA records.
interview.chapter06.q04.step04: Confirm timestamps, quality, event order and millisecond resolution where supported.
interview.chapter06.q04.step05: Investigate clock offsets, unsynchronized quality and delayed reports.
interview.chapter06.q04.scenario: After a trip, the HMI shows breaker open before protection pickup. Compare source timestamps and synchronization status before concluding the sequence is incorrect.
interview.chapter06.q04.takeaway: Distinguish device event time from the time a SCADA server received the event.
interview.chapter06.q05.question: How do you implement breaker Open/Close control from an HMI?
interview.chapter06.q05.answer: Remote breaker control follows the approved authority, interlocking and IEC 61850 control model or the project's other command protocol. A successful command request does not guarantee physical operation.
interview.chapter06.q05.step01: Confirm operator permission, Local/Remote selection and work permit requirements.
interview.chapter06.q05.step02: Check the correct controllable object, such as CSWI.Pos or XCBR.Pos depending on design.
interview.chapter06.q05.step03: Verify interlocks, synchrocheck and other permissives before attempting a test.
interview.chapter06.q05.step04: For select-before-operate, validate select, operate and timeout handling.
interview.chapter06.q05.step05: Observe command response and independently verify physical feedback.
interview.chapter06.q05.step06: Test rejection paths, alarms and audit logs under approved isolated FAT/SAT conditions.
interview.chapter06.q05.scenario: An HMI Close button is enabled but the command fails. Check Local/Remote, interlock permissives, control object, select/operate sequence and device diagnostic response.
interview.chapter06.q05.takeaway: Never bypass electrical interlocks to make an HMI test pass.
interview.chapter06.q06.question: Explain the difference between direct-operate and select-before-operate control.
interview.chapter06.q06.answer: Direct-operate sends an operation without a preceding select stage. Select-before-operate (SBO) requires a selection phase before execution, supporting controlled operation according to the configured IEC 61850 control model.
interview.chapter06.q06.step01: Read the IED control model and SCADA command configuration.
interview.chapter06.q06.step02: Identify select, operate, cancellation and timeout requirements.
interview.chapter06.q06.step03: Verify origin, control number and enhanced-security termination where applicable.
interview.chapter06.q06.step04: Test allowed and rejected commands with approved simulated equipment.
interview.chapter06.q06.step05: Confirm the final state from independent feedback and record logs.
interview.chapter06.q06.scenario: The HMI sends Operate without Select to an SBO-configured IED and receives a rejection. Align the client command workflow with the IED control model.
interview.chapter06.q06.takeaway: Control behavior is configured per object; do not assume every breaker uses SBO.
interview.chapter06.q07.question: How do you configure an HMI single-line diagram and verify dynamic symbols?
