interview.chapter06.q07.answer: An HMI single-line diagram is a graphical view tied to engineered SCADA points. It must show equipment identity, correct state, quality and control permissions without misleading the operator.
interview.chapter06.q07.step01: Build symbols according to approved electrical drawings and equipment naming.
interview.chapter06.q07.step02: Bind each breaker, disconnector and measurement to verified database points.
interview.chapter06.q07.step03: Define normal, open, closed, intermediate, invalid and communication-loss indications.
interview.chapter06.q07.step04: Test each state transition and confirm colors follow the project HMI standard.
interview.chapter06.q07.step05: Verify navigation, popup details, alarms and operator control access.
interview.chapter06.q07.step06: Conduct a point-by-point FAT review with the signal list.
interview.chapter06.q07.scenario: A breaker symbol stays green after the communication link fails. Verify the symbol's quality-state binding, not just its Open/Closed logic.
interview.chapter06.q07.takeaway: Bad quality must be visibly distinguishable from a valid normal state.
interview.chapter06.q08.question: How do you handle analog measurements and scaling in SCADA?
interview.chapter06.q08.answer: SCADA measurements must preserve correct engineering units, sign, magnitude, range and quality. Scaling may occur in an IED, gateway or SCADA database, so duplicate scaling must be avoided.
interview.chapter06.q08.step01: Identify the source data attribute, engineering unit and multiplier.
interview.chapter06.q08.step02: Compare IED native value with expected injected or measured value.
interview.chapter06.q08.step03: Check gateway and SCADA transformations for duplicate factors or sign inversion.
interview.chapter06.q08.step04: Verify display precision, limits, trends and out-of-range handling.
interview.chapter06.q08.step05: Test several points across the operating range and record tolerances.
interview.chapter06.q08.scenario: IED reports 11.0 kV but HMI displays 11000 kV. Inspect engineering-unit multipliers and any extra scaling applied in SCADA.
interview.chapter06.q08.takeaway: Always verify engineering units and sign, not only numeric changes.
interview.chapter06.q09.question: What causes SCADA communication healthy but points not updating?
interview.chapter06.q09.answer: A healthy Ethernet link or MMS association only confirms part of the communication chain. Stale points may result from disabled reporting, wrong DataSet members, RCB ownership, trigger options, point mapping or quality issues.
interview.chapter06.q09.step01: Confirm whether the source IED value changes when the field state changes.
interview.chapter06.q09.step02: Inspect MMS report traffic or polling responses using an approved client/capture.
interview.chapter06.q09.step03: Verify RCB enabled state, reservation, DataSet, trigger options and integrity period.
interview.chapter06.q09.step04: Check whether SCADA receives and decodes the expected object reference.
interview.chapter06.q09.step05: Verify point database mapping, acquisition status, quality and HMI binding.
interview.chapter06.q09.step06: Apply a controlled correction and repeat the test.
interview.chapter06.q09.scenario: All IED points show stale after SCADA restart. Check whether the client re-established association and re-enabled the correct report instances.
interview.chapter06.q09.takeaway: Separate transport connectivity from application-level reporting.
interview.chapter06.q10.question: How do you troubleshoot missing alarms while indications are updating?
interview.chapter06.q10.answer: An indication and its alarm may use different logic, priorities, point configurations or event paths. Working indication alone does not prove alarm engineering is correct.
interview.chapter06.q10.step01: Verify the source condition and current SCADA point value.
interview.chapter06.q10.step02: Check alarm enablement, threshold, polarity, delay and suppression state.
interview.chapter06.q10.step03: Inspect alarm priority, area filters and user display settings.
interview.chapter06.q10.step04: Confirm event processing and alarm server services are healthy.
interview.chapter06.q10.step05: Generate an approved test transition and inspect alarm history.
interview.chapter06.q10.step06: Correct the configuration and verify activation, acknowledgment and clearance.
interview.chapter06.q10.scenario: A protection pickup bit changes on the detail page but no alarm banner appears. The point is mapped correctly, but its alarm class is disabled.
interview.chapter06.q10.takeaway: Trace the alarm rule separately from the raw signal acquisition.
interview.chapter06.q11.question: Explain SCADA database engineering and change management.
interview.chapter06.q11.answer: SCADA database engineering covers naming, point definitions, data acquisition, alarms, events, commands, calculations and HMI associations. Controlled changes prevent unintended effects across multiple displays and interfaces.
interview.chapter06.q11.step01: Back up the approved database and document the change request.
interview.chapter06.q11.step02: Identify affected source references, tags, graphics, alarms, trends and gateway points.
interview.chapter06.q11.step03: Modify the engineering database in a controlled environment.
interview.chapter06.q11.step04: Validate naming, type, scaling, quality and command permissions.
interview.chapter06.q11.step05: Run regression tests on impacted and related points.
interview.chapter06.q11.step06: Record version, reviewer approval, deployment and rollback procedure.
interview.chapter06.q11.scenario: A renamed feeder tag fixes one HMI screen but breaks a gateway export. Use a dependency check before publishing the database change.
interview.chapter06.q11.takeaway: SCADA changes can affect HMI, historian, alarm engine and remote gateway simultaneously.
interview.chapter06.q12.question: How would you perform SCADA/HMI FAT and SAT for a new bay?
interview.chapter06.q12.answer: FAT verifies engineered behavior in a controlled environment; SAT verifies installation, interfaces and approved functionality at site. Testing must cover status, measurements, alarms, events, control, communication loss and recovery.
interview.chapter06.q12.step01: Review approved drawings, signal lists, cause-and-effect logic and test procedures.
interview.chapter06.q12.step02: Verify device communications and time synchronization.
interview.chapter06.q12.step03: Test each digital status and analog measurement with expected value, quality and timestamp.
interview.chapter06.q12.step04: Verify alarms, SOE, trends and HMI symbol behavior.
interview.chapter06.q12.step05: Test authorized commands, interlocks and rejection paths with safe isolation.
interview.chapter06.q12.step06: Simulate approved communication failures and recovery; document defects and retests.
interview.chapter06.q12.scenario: During FAT a bay passes status tests but fails breaker Close due to missing permissive. Record the interlock condition and validate the logic rather than forcing the command.
interview.chapter06.q12.takeaway: Acceptance requires traceable evidence and safe test boundaries.
interview.chapter07.q01.question: Explain the SAS station-bus network architecture and the role of managed Ethernet switches.
interview.chapter07.q01.answer: The station bus interconnects protection IEDs, BCUs, gateways, HMI and engineering stations. Managed industrial switches provide controlled Ethernet forwarding, VLANs, monitoring, redundancy and diagnostics. Network design must follow approved station architecture and traffic requirements.
interview.chapter07.q01.step01: Review the approved network topology and port schedule.
interview.chapter07.q01.step02: Identify IED, SCADA, gateway and time-server connections and their communication protocols.
interview.chapter07.q01.step03: Verify switch port speed, duplex, SFP type and link state.
interview.chapter07.q01.step04: Check VLAN membership, multicast handling and redundancy settings.
interview.chapter07.q01.step05: Test required communication paths and capture evidence before handover.
interview.chapter07.q01.scenario: A new IED is physically connected but cannot communicate with the gateway. Compare its port VLAN, IP configuration and switch MAC learning with the approved design.
interview.chapter07.q01.takeaway: A link LED proves only a physical link, not a correct application path.
interview.chapter07.q02.question: What is PRP and how does it provide zero-recovery-time redundancy?
interview.chapter07.q02.answer: Parallel Redundancy Protocol (IEC 62439-3) allows a dual-attached node to send duplicate Ethernet frames over two independent LANs, LAN A and LAN B. A receiving PRP node accepts the first valid copy and discards duplicates. With both LANs independent, a single LAN failure need not interrupt supported traffic.
interview.chapter07.q02.step01: Confirm the device is a dual-attached node and has two PRP interfaces.
interview.chapter07.q02.step02: Check LAN A and LAN B are physically and logically independent.
interview.chapter07.q02.step03: Verify each PRP interface is connected to the correct LAN and supervision frames are visible.
interview.chapter07.q02.step04: Check duplicate reception and LAN health using vendor diagnostics.
interview.chapter07.q02.step05: Isolate one LAN under an approved test plan and confirm communication continues over the other.
interview.chapter07.q02.scenario: An IED works normally until LAN A is unplugged, then loses SCADA. Investigate whether LAN B is connected, enabled, correctly switched and receiving traffic.
interview.chapter07.q02.takeaway: PRP is not simply two uplinks into the same network; LAN independence matters.
interview.chapter07.q03.question: What is HSR and how is it different from PRP?
interview.chapter07.q03.answer: High-availability Seamless Redundancy (IEC 62439-3) uses a ring of HSR-capable nodes that forward frames in both directions. A destination accepts the first copy and discards duplicates. PRP instead uses two separate parallel LANs. HSR ring nodes require appropriate HSR capability, and non-HSR equipment may connect through a RedBox.
interview.chapter07.q03.step01: Identify whether the approved topology is a PRP dual-LAN or HSR ring design.
interview.chapter07.q03.step02: Check each HSR node has its ring ports correctly wired to its neighbors.
interview.chapter07.q03.step03: Verify ring supervision and duplicate-discard diagnostics.
interview.chapter07.q03.step04: Test a single ring-link failure in a controlled test and check service continuity.
interview.chapter07.q03.step05: Document any RedBox connections and attached conventional Ethernet devices.
interview.chapter07.q03.scenario: A technician connects a conventional Ethernet switch directly as an HSR ring node and traffic fails. Check for an approved RedBox or HSR-capable device.
interview.chapter07.q03.takeaway: PRP and HSR are distinct architectures, not interchangeable switch settings.
interview.chapter07.q04.question: What is RSTP and when is it used in substation networks?
interview.chapter07.q04.answer: Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1w) prevents Layer 2 loops by maintaining a loop-free active topology and reconverging after a change. Unlike PRP and HSR, RSTP generally involves a reconvergence interval and should not be described as zero-recovery redundancy.
interview.chapter07.q04.step01: Review the designed Layer 2 topology and redundant links.
interview.chapter07.q04.step02: Verify the root bridge priority and switch roles are as engineered.
interview.chapter07.q04.step03: Check RSTP is consistently enabled on intended switch ports.
interview.chapter07.q04.step04: Inspect topology-change counters and blocked/forwarding port states.
interview.chapter07.q04.step05: Test an approved link failure and measure the actual application impact.
interview.chapter07.q04.scenario: GOOSE supervision alarms appear for several seconds when a switch uplink fails. Determine whether the topology uses RSTP reconvergence rather than seamless redundancy.
interview.chapter07.q04.takeaway: Never add a redundant Ethernet cable without checking for Layer 2 loops.
interview.chapter07.q05.question: Explain VLAN tagging and why it matters for GOOSE communication.
interview.chapter07.q05.answer: IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tags logically separate Layer 2 traffic and can carry priority information. Conventional IEC 61850 GOOSE is Ethernet multicast; a mismatch in VLAN tagging or port membership can prevent subscriber delivery even when both IEDs have working IP connectivity.
interview.chapter07.q05.step01: Read publisher VLAN ID and priority settings from the approved SCL/IED configuration.
interview.chapter07.q05.step02: Verify switch ingress and egress port mode, permitted VLANs and tagged/untagged behavior.
interview.chapter07.q05.step03: Confirm publisher and subscriber reside in the intended Layer 2 broadcast domain.
interview.chapter07.q05.step04: Capture GOOSE frames at the source and near the subscriber where permitted.
interview.chapter07.q05.step05: Correct the VLAN path and retest subscriber supervision and functional logic.
interview.chapter07.q05.scenario: IED A and IED B respond to ping but the GOOSE subscriber shows timeout. Publisher sends tagged VLAN 100 while the subscriber-facing port only permits VLAN 200.
interview.chapter07.q05.takeaway: Ping is an IP test; it does not validate Layer 2 multicast VLAN forwarding.
interview.chapter07.q06.question: How do multicast MAC addresses, APPID and switch multicast filtering affect GOOSE?
interview.chapter07.q06.answer: GOOSE uses Layer 2 multicast destination MAC addresses and an APPID within its protocol header. Switch multicast filtering and VLAN configuration determine whether frames reach subscribed IEDs. The APPID identifies an application stream for receivers; it is not an IP port.
interview.chapter07.q06.step01: Check destination multicast MAC, APPID and VLAN in the publisher configuration.
interview.chapter07.q06.step02: Confirm subscriber expectations and DataSet/control-block identity.
interview.chapter07.q06.step03: Inspect switch multicast filtering or static forwarding settings where used.
interview.chapter07.q06.step04: Use a permitted SPAN/mirror port to capture GOOSE and verify arrival.
interview.chapter07.q06.step05: Check subscriber diagnostic status and test the configured signal.
interview.chapter07.q06.scenario: Publisher GOOSE frames are visible on one switch but absent at the subscriber port. Investigate multicast forwarding configuration before changing the IED logic.
interview.chapter07.q06.takeaway: GOOSE multicast MAC and APPID must not be confused with TCP/IP addressing.
interview.chapter07.q07.question: How do you plan and troubleshoot IP addressing in a SAS network?
interview.chapter07.q07.answer: IP addresses, subnet masks and gateways determine Layer 3 reachability for MMS, engineering access and remote services. Many station-bus functions use local subnet communication; GOOSE itself does not require an IP address because conventional GOOSE uses Ethernet Layer 2.
interview.chapter07.q07.step01: Compare each device IP address, subnet mask and default gateway with the approved IP schedule.
interview.chapter07.q07.step02: Check for duplicate addresses and wrong subnet masks.
interview.chapter07.q07.step03: Verify switch VLAN and port membership.
interview.chapter07.q07.step04: Test reachability with ping where permitted, then test the actual service such as MMS TCP 102.
interview.chapter07.q07.step05: Inspect ARP, routes and firewall policies if the service crosses network boundaries.
interview.chapter07.q07.scenario: Two IEDs use the same static IP and MMS connections become intermittent. Identify the conflict using ARP tables and switch MAC-port records.
interview.chapter07.q07.takeaway: Separate IP/MMS troubleshooting from Layer 2 GOOSE troubleshooting.
interview.chapter07.q08.question: How do you troubleshoot fibre-optic Ethernet links and SFP modules?
interview.chapter07.q08.answer: Fibre links depend on matching transceiver specifications, correct fibre type, connectors, wavelength, optical power and port settings. Link failures can also result from damaged patch cords or incorrect Tx/Rx connections.
interview.chapter07.q08.step01: Check link LEDs and switch interface counters without disturbing live circuits.
interview.chapter07.q08.step02: Verify SFP speed, wavelength, connector and single-mode/multimode compatibility.
interview.chapter07.q08.step03: Inspect the approved fibre route, patch-panel labels and Tx/Rx cross-connections.
interview.chapter07.q08.step04: Review digital optical monitoring values if supported and compare with transceiver limits.
interview.chapter07.q08.step05: Arrange approved cleaning or optical tests and verify stable link after correction.
interview.chapter07.q08.scenario: A switch reports frequent link flaps after replacing a fibre patch cord. Check connector cleanliness, bend radius and received optical power before replacing the IED.
interview.chapter07.q08.takeaway: Never look into an optical fibre connector; follow site laser-safety procedures.
interview.chapter07.q09.question: How would you use Wireshark to diagnose SAS network communication problems?
interview.chapter07.q09.answer: Wireshark captures packets to distinguish link delivery, protocol negotiation and application issues. Useful filters include goose, mms, arp, icmp and tcp.port == 102, depending on the traffic being investigated. Captures require appropriate switch mirroring and authorization.
interview.chapter07.q09.step01: Define the fault and choose a capture point that can observe the relevant direction.
interview.chapter07.q09.step02: Configure a permitted switch mirror/SPAN port without impacting production forwarding.
interview.chapter07.q09.step03: Capture baseline and fault conditions with synchronized timestamps.
interview.chapter07.q09.step04: Inspect GOOSE APPID, VLAN, stNum, sqNum or MMS association and reporting as applicable.
interview.chapter07.q09.step05: Compare source and destination captures and correlate with device diagnostics.
interview.chapter07.q09.step06: Document packet evidence and validate the correction with a repeat capture.
interview.chapter07.q09.scenario: SCADA connects to an IED but reports stop after a restart. Capture MMS association and report traffic to determine whether the client re-enabled the expected RCB.
interview.chapter07.q09.takeaway: Capturing on a laptop port does not automatically show traffic on every switch port.
interview.chapter07.q10.question: How does time synchronization work in SAS networks?
interview.chapter07.q10.answer: Substation systems may use SNTP/NTP, PTP or IRIG-B depending on accuracy requirements and device capabilities. Consistent time enables meaningful SOE correlation and diagnostics. Network reachability alone does not guarantee synchronized clocks.
interview.chapter07.q10.step01: Identify the approved time source, protocol and required accuracy.
interview.chapter07.q10.step02: Check time-server reachability and configuration on each device.
interview.chapter07.q10.step03: Verify UTC/time-zone handling and daylight-saving policies in display systems.
interview.chapter07.q10.step04: Inspect clock sync status and device time quality.
interview.chapter07.q10.step05: Generate approved test events and compare timestamps across IED and SCADA records.
interview.chapter07.q10.scenario: Two IEDs record the same disturbance several seconds apart. Check each clock synchronization status and source before changing SOE sorting logic.
interview.chapter07.q10.takeaway: Always distinguish event source timestamps from SCADA reception timestamps.
interview.chapter07.q11.question: What is the difference between a network loop, broadcast storm and normal GOOSE retransmission?
interview.chapter07.q11.answer: A Layer 2 loop can cause frames to circulate repeatedly and overload switches; broadcast storms involve excessive broadcast traffic. GOOSE intentionally retransmits state messages with a changing interval, so repeated GOOSE frames alone are not evidence of a loop.
interview.chapter07.q11.step01: Check topology-change and interface utilization counters.
interview.chapter07.q11.step02: Look for MAC address flapping and unexpectedly high broadcast/multicast rates.
interview.chapter07.q11.step03: Verify RSTP or the approved PRP/HSR topology is correctly engineered.
interview.chapter07.q11.step04: Capture traffic and inspect GOOSE stNum/sqNum to distinguish normal retransmission.
interview.chapter07.q11.step05: Isolate the fault only through approved network maintenance procedures.
interview.chapter07.q11.scenario: After connecting an extra patch lead, switch CPU usage spikes and SCADA drops. Investigate a Layer 2 loop rather than disabling GOOSE retransmissions.
interview.chapter07.q11.takeaway: Do not treat every repeated Ethernet frame as a fault.
interview.chapter07.q12.question: How do you perform network FAT/SAT for PRP, VLAN, GOOSE and MMS?
interview.chapter07.q12.answer: Network FAT/SAT validates the approved topology, switch configuration, application connectivity, redundancy and recovery under controlled conditions. It should produce traceable evidence and avoid unapproved live outages or protection operations.
interview.chapter07.q12.step01: Review topology, IP/VLAN schedules, switch configurations and acceptance criteria.
interview.chapter07.q12.step02: Check port labels, SFPs, link state, switch logs and device firmware/configuration versions.
interview.chapter07.q12.step03: Verify MMS and engineering access and confirm GOOSE delivery with approved test signals.
interview.chapter07.q12.step04: Test PRP LAN A/LAN B or HSR ring resilience only as specified in the test procedure.
interview.chapter07.q12.step05: Check time synchronization, alarms and SCADA communication-loss indications.
interview.chapter07.q12.step06: Save captures, diagnostic logs, results, deviations and approved as-built configuration.
interview.chapter07.q12.scenario: During FAT, removing PRP LAN A causes a gateway disconnect. Record the failure, trace LAN B forwarding and repeat the test after the approved correction.
interview.chapter07.q12.takeaway: Prove redundancy by testing failure behavior, not only by looking at two connected cables.
interview.chapter08.q01.question: What is the difference between FAT and SAT in Substation Automation?
interview.chapter08.q01.answer: Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) checks the engineered SAS configuration in a controlled factory or laboratory setup against approved specifications. Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) checks the installed system, actual wiring, communications, interfaces and operational behavior at site. The exact scope depends on the project test plan.
interview.chapter08.q01.step01: Review approved functional design, signal lists, network architecture and acceptance criteria.
interview.chapter08.q01.step02: At FAT, use simulators or connected IEDs to verify mappings, reporting, alarms, controls and redundancy.
interview.chapter08.q01.step03: Record test stimuli, expected outcomes, actual results, screenshots and defect IDs.
interview.chapter08.q01.step04: At SAT, verify installed hardware, wiring, fibre links, IP settings, time synchronization and real interfaces.
interview.chapter08.q01.step05: Repeat required functional and end-to-end tests under approved site safety controls.
interview.chapter08.q01.step06: Close punch-list items and obtain authorized sign-off.
interview.chapter08.q01.scenario: FAT passed with a simulated breaker contact, but SAT shows the wrong HMI state. Trace site wiring, IED input polarity, source object and SCADA tag instead of assuming the factory result covers installation.
interview.chapter08.q01.takeaway: FAT proves engineered functions; SAT proves installed integration.
interview.chapter08.q02.question: How do you prepare an SAS FAT test procedure and checklist?
interview.chapter08.q02.answer: A FAT procedure is a traceable set of tests tied to the approved design and contract requirements. Each test must define prerequisites, test stimulus, expected result, evidence and pass/fail criteria.
interview.chapter08.q02.step01: Collect approved SLDs, architecture drawings, IED signal lists, SCD/CID versions, HMI screenshots and control philosophy.
interview.chapter08.q02.step02: Create a test matrix for statuses, measurements, alarms, SOE, controls, GOOSE, MMS, gateways and network resilience.
interview.chapter08.q02.step03: Define prerequisites, simulated inputs, safe isolation and responsible witnesses.
interview.chapter08.q02.step04: State expected indication, quality, timestamp, command response and recovery behavior.
interview.chapter08.q02.step05: Assign unique test IDs, record actual results and attach captures or screenshots.
interview.chapter08.q02.step06: Track deviations and retest only after approved corrections.
interview.chapter08.q02.scenario: A witness asks how to prove a protection pickup alarm. Show its approved test ID, input method, expected HMI alarm and recorded result.
interview.chapter08.q02.takeaway: A good checklist connects every tested function to an approved requirement.
interview.chapter08.q03.question: How do you test digital status indications from an IED to SCADA?
interview.chapter08.q03.answer: Digital status testing verifies the correct equipment identity, state encoding, polarity, quality, timestamp and HMI presentation through the complete signal chain.
interview.chapter08.q03.step01: Confirm the approved point list and whether the status is single-point or double-point.
interview.chapter08.q03.step02: Apply an authorized simulated contact or IED test input; do not operate live primary equipment without permission.
interview.chapter08.q03.step03: Check the IED binary input and logical data attribute such as XCBR.Pos.stVal when applicable.
interview.chapter08.q03.step04: Confirm MMS report or configured acquisition reaches the SCADA point.
interview.chapter08.q03.step05: Verify HMI Open, Closed, intermediate or invalid states, including quality indication.
interview.chapter08.q03.step06: Record both state transitions and restore the test condition.
interview.chapter08.q03.scenario: A breaker Open input is active in the relay but HMI shows Closed. Check contact inversion, double-point encoding and SCADA mapping.
interview.chapter08.q03.takeaway: Always verify both value and quality, not only a color change.
interview.chapter08.q04.question: How do you perform analog signal testing and scaling verification?
interview.chapter08.q04.answer: Analog testing checks source value, engineering units, multiplier, sign, display precision, alarm limits and trend behavior. Incorrect scaling can create plausible but dangerous values.
interview.chapter08.q04.step01: Identify the source data attribute, CT/VT ratio and engineering unit from approved documents.
interview.chapter08.q04.step02: Use an authorized injection or simulator at several points across the range.
interview.chapter08.q04.step03: Compare IED measured value and quality with expected test values.
interview.chapter08.q04.step04: Check gateway and SCADA conversion factors to avoid double scaling.
interview.chapter08.q04.step05: Verify HMI units, sign, decimal places, trends and alarm thresholds.
interview.chapter08.q04.step06: Document deviations, tolerances and as-left values.
interview.chapter08.q04.scenario: A 110 V simulated secondary value appears as 110 kV instead of the expected engineering value. Verify ratio handling and whether scaling was applied twice.
interview.chapter08.q04.takeaway: Test multiple values, including zero and negative values when applicable.
interview.chapter08.q05.question: How do you test GOOSE publisher and subscriber operation during FAT?
interview.chapter08.q05.answer: GOOSE FAT verifies that the publisher DataSet and GoCB match the subscriber configuration and that approved signal changes are received with correct validity and supervision.
interview.chapter08.q05.step01: Confirm approved SCD and both IED configuration versions.
interview.chapter08.q05.step02: Verify publisher DataSet members, GoCB, APPID, multicast MAC, VLAN and confRev.
interview.chapter08.q05.step03: Check subscriber external references and expected signal order and types.
interview.chapter08.q05.step04: Use an approved test signal and observe the publisher state change.
interview.chapter08.q05.step05: Capture GOOSE traffic and inspect stNum, sqNum, APPID and VLAN information.
interview.chapter08.q05.step06: Verify subscriber input, configured logic response and communication-loss behavior without energizing live trip circuits.
interview.chapter08.q05.scenario: Publisher IED changes its output but subscriber stays unchanged. Inspect VLAN forwarding, subscription mapping and confRev before changing logic.
interview.chapter08.q05.takeaway: GOOSE is Layer 2 multicast; successful ping does not validate it.
interview.chapter08.q06.question: How do you validate MMS reporting and RCB behavior?
interview.chapter08.q06.answer: MMS reporting tests confirm that the client receives correct DataSet changes with quality and timestamps, and that the configured report control blocks are properly enabled and owned.
interview.chapter08.q06.step01: Verify MMS association and access to the correct logical device.
interview.chapter08.q06.step02: Inspect DataSet references and BRCB or URCB configuration.
interview.chapter08.q06.step03: Check RptEna, reservation/ownership, trigger options, BufTm, IntgPd and ConfRev as applicable.
interview.chapter08.q06.step04: Generate approved changes and verify reports at the client and HMI.
interview.chapter08.q06.step05: Test reconnect behavior and buffered delivery when BRCB behavior is in scope.
interview.chapter08.q06.step06: Compare reported values, quality and timestamps to source IED data.
interview.chapter08.q06.scenario: After SCADA restart, values remain stale despite successful ping. Check report reservation and whether the client re-enabled its RCB instance.
interview.chapter08.q06.takeaway: Separate MMS connection testing from report-delivery testing.
interview.chapter08.q07.question: How do you test breaker Open/Close commands safely during FAT and SAT?
interview.chapter08.q07.answer: Breaker command testing validates authorization, control model, interlocks, command response and independent feedback. Live switching must follow site operating rules and approved isolation procedures.
interview.chapter08.q07.step01: Obtain approved switching/test authorization and isolate physical outputs when the procedure requires.
interview.chapter08.q07.step02: Verify Local/Remote status, operator access and correct controllable object.
interview.chapter08.q07.step03: Confirm Direct Operate or Select-Before-Operate configuration and command timeout.
interview.chapter08.q07.step04: Test valid and invalid permissive conditions without bypassing protection interlocks.
interview.chapter08.q07.step05: Issue an authorized simulated command and inspect IED acceptance or rejection diagnostics.
interview.chapter08.q07.step06: Verify independent status feedback, event logs and restoration of the original state.
interview.chapter08.q07.scenario: Close command is rejected while an earth switch is indicated Closed. Confirm the interlock is working and record the expected rejection.
interview.chapter08.q07.takeaway: Never defeat an interlock merely to pass a test.
interview.chapter08.q08.question: How do you verify alarms, SOE and time synchronization during testing?
interview.chapter08.q08.answer: Alarm and SOE testing checks activation logic, priority, acknowledgement, return-to-normal and event chronology. Accurate sequence reconstruction requires trustworthy device timestamps and synchronized clocks.
interview.chapter08.q08.step01: Confirm the approved alarm list, priorities and event sources.
interview.chapter08.q08.step02: Verify IED and SCADA time sources, synchronization status and UTC/time-zone settings.
interview.chapter08.q08.step03: Generate controlled alarm and status transitions in known order.
interview.chapter08.q08.step04: Check HMI banner, alarm history, acknowledgement and clearance behavior.
interview.chapter08.q08.step05: Compare IED event timestamps with SCADA SOE records and quality.
interview.chapter08.q08.step06: Record clock offset or ordering discrepancies and repeat after correction.
interview.chapter08.q08.scenario: Trip appears before pickup in the SOE. Compare source timestamps and clock status before assuming protection logic is wrong.
interview.chapter08.q08.takeaway: Distinguish device event time from SCADA receipt time.
interview.chapter08.q09.question: How do you perform PRP/HSR redundancy and network failover tests?
interview.chapter08.q09.answer: Redundancy testing checks the approved dual-network or ring design under controlled link failures. PRP uses independent LAN A and LAN B paths for dual-attached nodes; HSR forwards frames around a ring.
interview.chapter08.q09.step01: Review approved topology and identify DAN, SAN, RedBox or HSR nodes as applicable.
interview.chapter08.q09.step02: Check switch port, fibre, SFP and redundancy diagnostics in healthy state.
interview.chapter08.q09.step03: Establish baseline MMS/GOOSE traffic and alarms.
interview.chapter08.q09.step04: Disconnect only the approved test link under the authorized procedure.
interview.chapter08.q09.step05: Verify communication continuity, redundancy diagnostics, alarm behavior and recovery.
interview.chapter08.q09.step06: Restore links and archive logs, captures and measured results against project criteria.
interview.chapter08.q09.scenario: MMS disconnects when PRP LAN A is removed. Investigate LAN B configuration, cabling and node redundancy status rather than claiming the topology is redundant.
interview.chapter08.q09.takeaway: Two physical cables alone do not prove fault tolerance.
interview.chapter08.q10.question: How do you verify gateway communication with a remote control centre?
interview.chapter08.q10.answer: Gateway testing validates correct mapping, scaling, cause-of-transmission or event behavior, quality and command handling for the configured external protocol such as IEC 60870-5-104 or DNP3.
interview.chapter08.q10.step01: Review the approved SCADA-to-gateway and gateway-to-control-centre signal lists.
interview.chapter08.q10.step02: Confirm protocol link, addressing, security and time synchronization settings.
interview.chapter08.q10.step03: Generate approved source status and analog changes and compare local and remote values.
interview.chapter08.q10.step04: Check quality, timestamps, spontaneous events, interrogation and scaling as supported.
interview.chapter08.q10.step05: Test authorized remote commands and rejected conditions in an isolated environment.
interview.chapter08.q10.step06: Record all mismatches, resolve mapping issues and retest end to end.
interview.chapter08.q10.scenario: Local SCADA shows a feeder alarm but RCC does not. Trace the source tag, gateway export mapping, protocol event queue and remote point address.
interview.chapter08.q10.takeaway: Remote indication requires its own end-to-end acceptance evidence.
interview.chapter08.q11.question: How do you document and resolve FAT/SAT punch-list defects?
interview.chapter08.q11.answer: A punch list tracks deviations against requirements with evidence, severity, owner, correction and retest status. It supports traceable acceptance and prevents undocumented field changes.
interview.chapter08.q11.step01: Record test ID, equipment identity, software/configuration version and expected result.
interview.chapter08.q11.step02: Capture actual behavior with timestamps, logs, screenshots or packet traces.
interview.chapter08.q11.step03: Classify impact and assign the responsible engineer or vendor.
interview.chapter08.q11.step04: Agree on corrective action through project change control.
interview.chapter08.q11.step05: Apply the approved correction and perform targeted plus regression testing.
interview.chapter08.q11.step06: Update as-built records and obtain witness closure or documented concession.
interview.chapter08.q11.scenario: A GOOSE subscription works after changing confRev-related configuration. Update both configuration baselines and attach the passing retest evidence.
interview.chapter08.q11.takeaway: A defect is closed by verified retest, not by changing its status in a spreadsheet.
interview.chapter08.q12.question: Describe your troubleshooting approach when multiple SAS FAT tests fail at once.
interview.chapter08.q12.answer: Use a structured fault-isolation method to find shared dependencies before changing individual points. Common causes include time source faults, switch VLAN issues, MMS client/report configuration and database imports.
interview.chapter08.q12.step01: List all failed tests and identify common equipment, protocol, network segment or software version.
interview.chapter08.q12.step02: Check recent configuration changes and compare against approved baselines.
interview.chapter08.q12.step03: Verify power, physical links, VLANs, IP addressing and switch diagnostics.
interview.chapter08.q12.step04: Inspect IED values, protocol packets, SCADA acquisition and HMI tags to locate the first failed stage.
interview.chapter08.q12.step05: Apply one approved correction at a time and retest affected and neighboring functions.
interview.chapter08.q12.step06: Document root cause, preventive action and final evidence.
interview.chapter08.q12.scenario: All bay statuses become stale after a database deployment while GOOSE remains healthy. Focus on shared MMS reporting or SCADA acquisition before editing every HMI symbol.
interview.chapter08.q12.takeaway: Find the first failing common layer and preserve evidence before making changes.
interview.chapter09.q01.question: How do you capture IEC 61850 MMS traffic in Wireshark?
interview.chapter09.q01.answer: MMS is normally carried over TCP port 102 using the ISO-on-TCP stack. A capture must be taken at a point where the relevant client/server frames are visible.
interview.chapter09.q01.step01: Confirm IED and SCADA IP addresses
interview.chapter09.q01.step02: configure a switch mirror/SPAN port or approved network TAP
interview.chapter09.q01.step03: start capture before reconnecting the client
interview.chapter09.q01.step05: inspect TCP setup, COTP, MMS association and subsequent services
interview.chapter09.q01.scenario: An IED pings successfully but SCADA stays disconnected. The capture shows TCP SYN retransmissions to port 102, indicating an access, routing or server-listening problem.
interview.chapter09.q01.takeaway: Ping verifies IP reachability, not MMS service availability.
interview.chapter09.q02.question: Which Wireshark filters are useful for SAS troubleshooting?
interview.chapter09.q02.answer: Use display filters to isolate traffic without altering the original capture. The exact filter depends on protocol and Wireshark version.
interview.chapter09.q02.step01: Start with ip.addr == 192.168.1.10 for an example IED
interview.chapter09.q02.step04: sv for sampled values when supported
interview.chapter09.q02.step08: inspect frame details rather than relying on filter counts.
interview.chapter09.q02.scenario: GOOSE status is missing at the subscriber; goose shows no frames at the capture point, so inspect VLAN membership and mirroring configuration.
interview.chapter09.q02.takeaway: A display filter hides packets; it does not prove traffic is absent elsewhere.
interview.chapter09.q03.question: How do you troubleshoot MMS association failures?
interview.chapter09.q03.answer: MMS communication depends on IP connectivity, TCP port 102, protocol negotiation, server access and compatible client configuration.
interview.chapter09.q03.step04: inspect COTP and MMS initiate exchange
interview.chapter09.q03.step05: review server connection limits and authentication or access settings if applicable
interview.chapter09.q03.scenario: TCP handshake completes but MMS initiate is rejected after a firmware update. Compare negotiated parameters and server access settings.
interview.chapter09.q03.takeaway: Identify the exact protocol stage that fails.
interview.chapter09.q04.question: How do you verify that IEC 61850 reports are being received?
interview.chapter09.q04.answer: An active MMS association does not guarantee report delivery. Reporting requires correctly configured and enabled Report Control Blocks and DataSets.
interview.chapter09.q04.step03: verify BRCB/URCB selection, reservation and RptEna
interview.chapter09.q04.step05: check trigger options, BufTm and IntgPd
interview.chapter09.q04.step06: compare report object references, quality and timestamps with SCADA tags.
interview.chapter09.q04.scenario: Breaker status changes in IED but no report reaches SCADA after a restart. Client may not have re-enabled its RCB.
interview.chapter09.q04.takeaway: Check both the RCB configuration and client runtime ownership.
interview.chapter09.q05.question: How do you analyze GOOSE stNum and sqNum?
interview.chapter09.q05.answer: In conventional IEC 61850 GOOSE, stNum advances when the published state changes and sqNum tracks retransmissions within a state. Values must be interpreted with the packet timeline and configuration.
interview.chapter09.q05.step02: isolate the publisher by source MAC or goID
interview.chapter09.q05.step03: inspect stNum and sqNum over time
interview.chapter09.q05.scenario: Publisher stNum changes but subscriber remains stale. Inspect DataSet mapping, confRev and destination VLAN rather than assuming the publisher failed.
interview.chapter09.q05.takeaway: State change and retransmission are different events.
interview.chapter09.q06.question: How do you troubleshoot a GOOSE VLAN mismatch?
interview.chapter09.q06.answer: GOOSE is typically Layer 2 multicast and may carry IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tags. The switching path must carry the configured multicast traffic to the subscriber.
interview.chapter09.q06.step01: Verify publisher VLAN ID and priority
interview.chapter09.q06.step02: inspect tagged packets at the source
interview.chapter09.q06.step03: review ingress/egress switch VLAN settings and trunk/access behavior
interview.chapter09.q06.step06: confirm subscriber accepts the configured GOOSE stream
interview.chapter09.q06.scenario: GOOSE frames are visible on the publisher port but absent at the subscriber port after a switch replacement. Compare switch VLAN and multicast configuration.
interview.chapter09.q06.takeaway: GOOSE can fail even while IP ping works.
interview.chapter09.q07.question: What does confRev mismatch mean in GOOSE troubleshooting?
interview.chapter09.q07.answer: confRev is the configuration revision for a GOOSE control block and helps receivers detect incompatible configuration. A mismatch can occur after changing a published DataSet or its configuration.
interview.chapter09.q07.step01: Read publisher GoCB and subscriber expected confRev
interview.chapter09.q07.step02: compare DataSet member count, order and types
interview.chapter09.q07.step04: regenerate subscriber mapping using the approved engineering workflow
interview.chapter09.q07.scenario: Publisher DataSet gained a new status signal but subscriber still uses old SCD. GOOSE packets arrive, yet subscriber marks them invalid.
interview.chapter09.q07.takeaway: Network delivery alone does not prove application compatibility.
interview.chapter09.q08.question: How do you identify duplicate IP addresses using packet captures?
interview.chapter09.q08.answer: Duplicate IPs may cause intermittent connectivity, ARP changes and communication flapping. Confirm with switch and host evidence before making address changes.
interview.chapter09.q08.step02: observe conflicting MAC addresses claiming the same IP
interview.chapter09.q08.step03: check switch MAC address table and port
interview.chapter09.q08.step04: compare device configuration against the approved IP plan
interview.chapter09.q08.step05: isolate and correct the duplicate under change control
interview.chapter09.q08.step06: clear or refresh ARP as appropriate
interview.chapter09.q08.scenario: Two IEDs are accidentally assigned the same IP and SCADA alternates between connected and disconnected.
interview.chapter09.q08.takeaway: ARP evidence and the approved IP plan establish the root cause.
interview.chapter09.q09.question: How do you troubleshoot TCP retransmissions in MMS traffic?
interview.chapter09.q09.answer: TCP retransmissions indicate segments may not have been acknowledged in time; they can arise from loss, congestion, asymmetric captures or endpoint behavior. They are symptoms, not a diagnosis.
interview.chapter09.q09.step01: Capture at an appropriate network point
interview.chapter09.q09.step02: inspect sequence numbers, RTT and retransmission patterns
interview.chapter09.q09.step03: check interface errors and switch counters
interview.chapter09.q09.step04: compare capture near sender and receiver when possible
interview.chapter09.q09.scenario: MMS reporting is delayed during heavy network traffic. Packet capture shows repeated retransmissions and switch interface drops.
interview.chapter09.q09.takeaway: Correlate packet evidence with switch counters before concluding the network is faulty.
interview.chapter09.q10.question: How do you verify PRP redundancy using Wireshark?
interview.chapter09.q10.answer: PRP sends duplicate frames over independent LAN A and LAN B for doubly attached nodes. Captures and device diagnostics can help verify both paths and duplicate handling.
interview.chapter09.q10.step01: Identify the PRP-capable ports and independent LANs
interview.chapter09.q10.step02: capture at each LAN where permitted
interview.chapter09.q10.step03: inspect PRP trailer and sequence information with a capable decoder
interview.chapter09.q10.step05: isolate one path during approved FAT
interview.chapter09.q10.step06: confirm no unacceptable interruption and monitor duplicate-discard counters.
interview.chapter09.q10.scenario: LAN A fibre is disconnected during FAT and SCADA remains operational through LAN B; diagnostics confirm single-path operation.
interview.chapter09.q10.takeaway: PRP requires two independent networks, not just two cables into one unmanaged path.
interview.chapter09.q11.question: How do you troubleshoot time synchronization issues in event records?
interview.chapter09.q11.answer: SOE analysis depends on synchronized device clocks and correct timestamp interpretation. Packet capture can supplement device time-source diagnostics.
interview.chapter09.q11.step01: Verify device time source and lock/synchronization state
interview.chapter09.q11.step02: capture NTP/SNTP or PTP traffic where relevant
interview.chapter09.q11.step03: inspect network reachability and VLAN path
interview.chapter09.q11.step04: check UTC and time zone conversion in SCADA
interview.chapter09.q11.step05: compare device event timestamps with server receive times
interview.chapter09.q11.scenario: Protection event appears after breaker-open in SCADA despite earlier pickup; device clock is several seconds behind.
interview.chapter09.q11.takeaway: Distinguish source timestamps from SCADA receipt timestamps.
interview.chapter09.q12.question: Describe your systematic workflow for an unknown IEC 61850 communication fault.
interview.chapter09.q12.answer: Troubleshoot layer by layer while preserving evidence and changing one variable at a time. Differentiate physical connectivity, network delivery, application association and point configuration.
interview.chapter09.q12.step01: Record symptoms, affected devices and last known good state
interview.chapter09.q12.step02: verify power, ports, fibre and switch counters
interview.chapter09.q12.step03: check IP and VLAN where applicable
interview.chapter09.q12.step05: compare SCD/CID, RCB/GoCB and subscriber settings
interview.chapter09.q12.step07: apply approved fix, retest and document root cause.
interview.chapter09.q12.scenario: Following a switch configuration change, MMS remains healthy but GOOSE interlocking fails. Packet captures isolate missing multicast forwarding rather than an IED logic fault.
interview.chapter09.q12.takeaway: Avoid random configuration changes; isolate the first failed layer.
interview.chapter10.q01.question: How do you plan integration of Siemens, Schneider, ABB and GE protection IEDs into one SAS?
interview.chapter10.q01.answer: Multi-vendor integration starts with an approved interface matrix. IEC 61850 interoperability is based on services, supported data models and tested configuration, not simply the presence of an Ethernet port. Vendor tools differ in import/export and control behavior.
interview.chapter10.q01.step01: Collect approved signal lists, network diagrams, device models, firmware and ICD/IID/CID files.
interview.chapter10.q01.step02: Confirm each IED supports the required MMS, reporting, GOOSE and control services.
interview.chapter10.q01.step03: Allocate unique IED names, IP addresses, VLANs and time synchronization.
interview.chapter10.q01.step04: Build a common SCD where the engineering workflow supports it; validate vendor-specific imports and exports.
interview.chapter10.q01.step05: Test data acquisition, commands, quality, timestamps and GOOSE subscriptions during FAT.
interview.chapter10.q01.scenario: A new ABB relay is visible in the network but its signals do not appear in a Schneider-based SCADA: validate its actual IEC 61850 object references, reporting and point mapping rather than assuming vendor naming is identical.
interview.chapter10.q01.takeaway: Use an interface matrix and evidence-based point-by-point testing.
interview.chapter10.q02.question: What checks are needed before importing an ICD or IID file from a different vendor?
interview.chapter10.q02.answer: An ICD describes device capability while an IID can represent an instantiated IED configuration. File availability alone does not guarantee compatible engineering features or the latest installed device settings.
interview.chapter10.q02.step01: Verify the exact device type, firmware and SCL edition compatibility.
interview.chapter10.q02.step02: Validate XML structure, namespaces and unique IED names.
interview.chapter10.q02.step03: Inspect logical devices, logical nodes, DataSets and report/GOOSE capabilities.
interview.chapter10.q02.step04: Compare imported object references with the approved signal list.
interview.chapter10.q02.step05: Resolve import warnings, preserve backups and record version changes.
interview.chapter10.q02.scenario: A Siemens device file imports but several logical nodes are missing in the system configurator: compare supported SCL edition, namespaces and exported configuration.
interview.chapter10.q02.takeaway: Treat imported engineering files as configuration inputs requiring verification.
interview.chapter10.q03.question: Why can an MMS connection work while reports from a multi-vendor IED do not arrive?
interview.chapter10.q03.answer: MMS association proves basic application connectivity, but reporting requires a compatible report control block, DataSet, ownership and client configuration. Different devices may implement optional services differently.
interview.chapter10.q03.step01: Confirm the association and browse live values using an IEC 61850 client.
interview.chapter10.q03.step02: Identify the correct BRCB or URCB and DataSet reference.
interview.chapter10.q03.step03: Check reservation or ownership, RptEna, trigger options and integrity period.
interview.chapter10.q03.step04: Check OptFlds, buffer handling and client support for report structure.
interview.chapter10.q03.step05: Capture reports and verify SCADA tag decoding and mapping.
interview.chapter10.q03.scenario: A GE relay responds to MMS reads but the HMI stays stale: the SCADA client is enabling a non-existent RCB instance after a firmware change.
interview.chapter10.q03.takeaway: Distinguish reading data from receiving unsolicited reports.
interview.chapter10.q04.question: How do you configure GOOSE communication between two different vendors?
interview.chapter10.q04.answer: GOOSE interoperability requires the publisher to send a defined DataSet and the subscriber to consume its exact members with correct engineering references and supervision. Publisher and subscriber tools may use different configuration workflows.
interview.chapter10.q04.step01: Define and validate publisher DataSet and GoCB in its vendor tool.
interview.chapter10.q04.step02: Confirm destination multicast MAC, APPID, VLAN ID/priority, GoID and confRev.
interview.chapter10.q04.step03: Import publisher information into the subscriber tool or SCD workflow.
interview.chapter10.q04.step04: Map each subscribed value to the correct external reference and internal logic input.
interview.chapter10.q04.step05: Download approved configurations and verify live reception and quality in a controlled test.
interview.chapter10.q04.scenario: A Schneider IED publishes GOOSE but a Siemens subscriber shows invalid input: compare the DataSet order, type, confRev and subscriber binding.
interview.chapter10.q04.takeaway: GOOSE packets on a switch do not prove the subscriber accepted their contents.
interview.chapter10.q05.question: What is confRev and how can a mismatch affect GOOSE integration?
interview.chapter10.q05.answer: The GOOSE configuration revision identifies the publisher DataSet configuration version. A subscriber may reject or flag messages when its expected revision differs from the transmitted one.
interview.chapter10.q05.step01: Read the current publisher GoCB and DataSet configuration.
interview.chapter10.q05.step02: Capture the GOOSE frame and inspect confRev and DataSet references.
interview.chapter10.q05.step03: Check subscriber expected revision and configured external references.
interview.chapter10.q05.step04: Re-export and re-import the approved publisher description if the DataSet changed.
interview.chapter10.q05.step05: Retest value, quality, communication supervision and logic response.
interview.chapter10.q05.scenario: A relay replacement changes the published DataSet; frames are visible but the subscriber marks the GOOSE input invalid due to revision mismatch.
interview.chapter10.q05.takeaway: Never solve a mismatch by guessing revision values; synchronize engineering configurations.
interview.chapter10.q06.question: How do you handle different logical node naming conventions across vendors?
interview.chapter10.q06.answer: IEC 61850 standardizes logical-node classes and data structures, but logical device names, prefixes, instances and optional data vary by implementation. Integration must use actual object references.
interview.chapter10.q06.step01: Browse each device or inspect its approved SCL file.
interview.chapter10.q06.step02: Record the full object reference and functional constraint for each required point.
interview.chapter10.q06.step03: Map to project-standard SCADA tags without assuming identical naming.
interview.chapter10.q06.step04: Check data type, quality, timestamp and state encoding.
interview.chapter10.q06.step05: Test source-to-HMI behavior for every critical point.
interview.chapter10.q06.scenario: One relay exposes breaker position under a different logical-device path from another relay; a copied tag template silently points to the wrong object.
interview.chapter10.q06.takeaway: Use exact object references rather than memorized vendor-specific paths.
interview.chapter10.q07.question: How do you troubleshoot data type or quality mismatch after an IED replacement?
interview.chapter10.q07.answer: A replacement may change the supported data attribute, quality handling or encoding even when the visible signal name is similar. Incorrect mapping can cause invalid displays or alarms.
interview.chapter10.q07.step01: Compare old and new SCL data models and firmware versions.
interview.chapter10.q07.step02: Inspect actual value, data type, functional constraint, q and t attributes.
interview.chapter10.q07.step03: Check SCADA point type, scaling, status inversion and enum interpretation.
interview.chapter10.q07.step04: Update mapping through approved change control.
interview.chapter10.q07.step05: Test normal, abnormal and bad-quality cases and preserve rollback.
interview.chapter10.q07.scenario: After a relay upgrade, an HMI shows an intermediate breaker state as Closed because the SCADA point treats a double-point status as Boolean.
interview.chapter10.q07.takeaway: IEC 61850 double-point status must not be reduced to Boolean without defined mapping.
interview.chapter10.q08.question: What is the correct way to validate multi-vendor breaker control?
interview.chapter10.q08.answer: Breaker control must honor each IED control model, access authority and interlocks. Vendor implementations may expose different diagnostics or support different control options.
interview.chapter10.q08.step01: Identify the controlled object and configured ctlModel from the device.
interview.chapter10.q08.step02: Verify Local/Remote, authority, interlocks and synchrocheck requirements.
interview.chapter10.q08.step03: Configure direct-operate or select-before-operate according to the actual model.
interview.chapter10.q08.step04: Perform only approved isolated FAT/SAT command tests.
interview.chapter10.q08.step05: Inspect command responses, rejection reasons, event logs and independent position feedback.
interview.chapter10.q08.scenario: SCADA can read a GE breaker status but its Close command fails because the client uses direct operate while the IED requires select-before-operate.
interview.chapter10.q08.takeaway: A successful MMS association does not imply command permission.
interview.chapter10.q09.question: How do you verify interoperability after a firmware upgrade?
interview.chapter10.q09.answer: Firmware can alter supported services, SCL exports, control behavior or reporting details. Interoperability requires impact analysis and regression testing rather than assuming unchanged behavior.
interview.chapter10.q09.step01: Record the old and new firmware, engineering files and configuration backups.
interview.chapter10.q09.step02: Review vendor release notes and compatibility requirements.
interview.chapter10.q09.step03: Compare exported data model, DataSets, RCBs and GoCBs.
interview.chapter10.q09.step04: Check protocol associations, reports, GOOSE subscription and controls.
interview.chapter10.q09.step05: Run targeted FAT regression and approve deployment with rollback readiness.
interview.chapter10.q09.scenario: Following an IED firmware update, the SCADA client cannot reserve its former BRCB instance; investigate service/configuration changes before modifying the production database.
interview.chapter10.q09.takeaway: Always include communication regression tests in firmware change plans.
interview.chapter10.q10.question: What tools would you use to diagnose a Siemens/ABB/Schneider/GE integration issue?
interview.chapter10.q10.answer: Use the vendor engineering tool for device configuration, an independent IEC 61850 client for data browsing, and network capture tools for protocol evidence. Tool names and supported features depend on product generation.
interview.chapter10.q10.step01: Verify device configuration in the appropriate vendor tool such as DIGSI, PCM600, Easergy/related Schneider engineering software or GE EnerVista.
interview.chapter10.q10.step02: Browse the IED using a compatible IEC 61850 test client where permitted.
interview.chapter10.q10.step03: Capture MMS or GOOSE frames with Wireshark at an approved monitoring point.
interview.chapter10.q10.step04: Compare observed object references and packets against the approved SCD and signal list.
interview.chapter10.q10.step05: Document root cause, corrective action and regression tests.
interview.chapter10.q10.scenario: An ABB device looks correct in PCM600 but the station SCADA reports invalid quality: use independent data browsing to separate source quality from client mapping.
interview.chapter10.q10.takeaway: Use independent observations to distinguish IED, network and SCADA faults.
interview.chapter10.q11.question: How do you resolve duplicate IED names or IP addresses during commissioning?
interview.chapter10.q11.answer: Duplicate identities can cause ambiguous SCL references, network connectivity faults and incorrect station mapping. Both IEC 61850 naming and IP planning must be controlled.
interview.chapter10.q11.step01: Check the approved IP and IED naming schedule.
interview.chapter10.q11.step02: Compare installed device identity, IP, subnet and VLAN settings.
interview.chapter10.q11.step03: Inspect ARP tables and switch MAC address tables for conflicts.
interview.chapter10.q11.step04: Correct identities using an approved change request and update SCL/database references.
interview.chapter10.q11.step05: Retest connectivity, reports, GOOSE and HMI mapping.
interview.chapter10.q11.scenario: Two newly installed feeder relays have the same IP address, causing intermittent MMS communication and changing ARP entries.
interview.chapter10.q11.takeaway: Check address uniqueness before investigating complex application faults.
interview.chapter10.q12.question: How do you conduct FAT for a mixed-vendor IEC 61850 SAS?
interview.chapter10.q12.answer: Mixed-vendor FAT should verify interoperability at signal, service and functional levels. Evidence must be traceable to approved specifications, not limited to device ping tests.
interview.chapter10.q12.step01: Approve the interface matrix, SCD, signal list and test procedures.
interview.chapter10.q12.step02: Verify time sync, physical/network configuration and MMS associations.
interview.chapter10.q12.step03: Test each critical indication, measurement, alarm, quality and report behavior.
interview.chapter10.q12.step04: Test GOOSE subscription, supervision, failure and recovery under safe isolation.
interview.chapter10.q12.step05: Verify commands, interlocks and rejection handling with approved test boundaries.
interview.chapter10.q12.step06: Log defects, retest corrective actions and retain captures/screenshots.
interview.chapter10.q12.scenario: During FAT, a subscriber loses GOOSE after a VLAN change while MMS still works; verify switch VLAN membership and multicast forwarding separately.
interview.chapter10.q12.takeaway: Demonstrate end-to-end functions, not only protocol connectivity.
interview.chapter11.q01.question: What is the role of a station gateway in a Substation Automation System?
interview.chapter11.q01.answer: A station gateway collects selected indications, measurements, events and controls from bay-level IEDs and exposes them to a remote control centre through the agreed telecontrol protocol. It is not a substitute for protection logic; its mapping, timestamps, quality and command permissions are engineered separately.
interview.chapter11.q01.step01: Review the approved architecture and signal list, identifying local IEDs and remote masters.
interview.chapter11.q01.step02: Configure upstream IED connections such as IEC 61850 MMS or Modbus according to the project.
interview.chapter11.q01.step03: Create the gateway point database with source references, types, scaling and quality rules.
interview.chapter11.q01.step04: Configure the remote protocol endpoint and permitted command direction.
interview.chapter11.q01.step05: Verify each point from source IED through gateway to the simulated control-centre master.
interview.chapter11.q01.step06: Test communication failure, recovery and event buffering where supported.
interview.chapter11.q01.scenario: The local HMI shows the breaker open but the remote control centre shows closed. Check the IED value, gateway input, telecontrol information-object mapping and master interpretation in that order.
interview.chapter11.q01.takeaway: Gateway integration is end-to-end point engineering, not merely enabling a protocol.
interview.chapter11.q02.question: How does IEC 61850 data map to IEC 60870-5-104 information objects?
interview.chapter11.q02.answer: IEC 61850 uses object references and data attributes such as XCBR1.Pos.stVal, quality and timestamp. IEC 60870-5-104 represents telecontrol information using information-object addresses (IOAs), type identifiers and cause of transmission. The gateway must deliberately map values, quality, timestamps and semantics; there is no universal automatic one-to-one mapping.
interview.chapter11.q02.step01: Obtain the IEC 61850 source reference and expected data type.
interview.chapter11.q02.step02: Choose the IEC 104 type identification appropriate for single-point, double-point or measured value information.
interview.chapter11.q02.step03: Assign a unique IOA within the correct common address of ASDU.
interview.chapter11.q02.step04: Configure value conversion, quality flags and source timestamp handling.
interview.chapter11.q02.step05: Verify spontaneous and interrogation responses at the IEC 104 master.
interview.chapter11.q02.step06: Test abnormal quality and time-invalid conditions.
interview.chapter11.q02.scenario: A double-point breaker indication is configured as a single-point IEC 104 type. The RCC display interprets it incorrectly; correct the semantic mapping and retest both positions.
interview.chapter11.q02.takeaway: Match meaning and quality, not just numeric addresses.
interview.chapter11.q03.question: Explain the difference between IEC 60870-5-101 and IEC 60870-5-104.
interview.chapter11.q03.answer: IEC 101 is a telecontrol protocol commonly carried over serial links, while IEC 104 transports the IEC 101 application information over TCP/IP networks. Both require correct station addressing, information objects, causes of transmission and master/slave or controlling/controlled station behavior.
interview.chapter11.q03.step01: Identify whether the project uses serial IEC 101 or Ethernet IEC 104.
interview.chapter11.q03.step02: For IEC 101 verify baud rate, parity, link addresses and balanced/unbalanced mode as configured.
interview.chapter11.q03.step03: For IEC 104 verify IP connectivity, TCP port 2404, common ASDU address and IOAs.
interview.chapter11.q03.step04: Check interrogation, spontaneous events, time synchronization and command handling.
interview.chapter11.q03.step05: Record master-side and gateway-side traces to isolate a mismatch.
interview.chapter11.q03.scenario: A serial RTU migration to IEC 104 retains the same point semantics but requires new IP/TCP and session settings. Confirm master point addressing rather than assuming the old serial link settings apply.
interview.chapter11.q03.takeaway: IEC 104 is not simply IEC 101 packets tunneled unchanged over Ethernet.
interview.chapter11.q04.question: What are the main IEC 104 connection and session checks?
interview.chapter11.q04.answer: IEC 104 normally uses TCP port 2404 and APCI control frames. The controlling station starts data transfer with STARTDT, and I-format frames carry ASDUs. Sequence counters, acknowledgements, timers and test frames support reliable session operation.
interview.chapter11.q04.step01: Check link state, IP, subnet, route and firewall rules.
interview.chapter11.q04.step02: Verify TCP establishment to the configured IEC 104 server port.
interview.chapter11.q04.step03: Inspect STARTDT activation/confirmation and subsequent I-format data.
interview.chapter11.q04.step04: Check send/receive sequence counters and timer-related disconnects.
interview.chapter11.q04.step05: Verify common address, IOA and type identification in application data.
interview.chapter11.q04.step06: Perform general interrogation and confirm point updates.
interview.chapter11.q04.scenario: TCP connects but the master receives no measurements. Inspect STARTDT state and GI request/response before changing gateway point mapping.
interview.chapter11.q04.takeaway: TCP connected does not necessarily mean IEC 104 data transfer is active.
interview.chapter11.q05.question: What is General Interrogation (GI) in IEC 104?
interview.chapter11.q05.answer: General Interrogation is a request from the controlling station for the current state of configured process information. It complements spontaneous reporting of changes and helps establish a consistent picture after a connection or restart.
interview.chapter11.q05.step01: Establish and start the IEC 104 data-transfer session.
interview.chapter11.q05.step02: Send a GI command with the configured interrogation qualifier.
interview.chapter11.q05.step03: Verify activation confirmation, relevant process ASDUs and activation termination.
interview.chapter11.q05.step04: Compare returned values and quality against gateway source points.
interview.chapter11.q05.step05: Verify spontaneous changes are subsequently reported as configured.
interview.chapter11.q05.scenario: After a control-centre reconnect, the master has blank statuses until a GI is issued. Verify the reconnect sequence and whether the master initiates interrogation.
interview.chapter11.q05.takeaway: GI retrieves current state; it does not replace event/SOE engineering.
interview.chapter11.q06.question: How do you configure Modbus RTU/TCP points in a gateway?
interview.chapter11.q06.answer: Modbus accesses coils, discrete inputs, input registers and holding registers. The engineering task is to map each device address and function code to the correct signal with proper word order, data type, scaling and polling behavior.
interview.chapter11.q06.step01: Review the device Modbus register map and unit/slave ID.
interview.chapter11.q06.step02: Configure RTU serial settings or Modbus TCP IP/port 502 as applicable.
interview.chapter11.q06.step03: Select the correct function code and address offset convention.
interview.chapter11.q06.step04: Interpret 16-bit, 32-bit, signed and floating-point values with correct word/byte order.
interview.chapter11.q06.step05: Apply engineering scaling once and configure scan intervals/timeouts.
interview.chapter11.q06.step06: Compare gateway readings with the source device under several test values.
interview.chapter11.q06.scenario: A power meter displays 12.5 MW locally but the gateway reads an impossible number. Check register offset, float word order and scaling before replacing hardware.
interview.chapter11.q06.takeaway: Modbus register numbering conventions frequently cause off-by-one errors.
interview.chapter11.q07.question: How would you troubleshoot a gateway receiving IEC 61850 MMS but not sending IEC 104 points?
interview.chapter11.q07.answer: The failure may be at the source mapping, gateway point processing, IEC 104 session, information-object configuration or master database. Test each boundary with observed values and protocol traces.
interview.chapter11.q07.step01: Confirm the live IEC 61850 object value, quality and MMS reporting or polling.
interview.chapter11.q07.step02: Check the gateway internal point status and any transform/inversion rules.
interview.chapter11.q07.step03: Verify IEC 104 connection, STARTDT and master interrogation.
interview.chapter11.q07.step04: Inspect transmitted ASDU type, IOA, common address, value and quality.
interview.chapter11.q07.step05: Compare master configuration and event filters with the transmitted object.
interview.chapter11.q07.step06: Retest a controlled change and save logs from both sides.
interview.chapter11.q07.scenario: Gateway diagnostics show breaker status changing, but the RCC point remains static. A mismatched IOA at the master explains the fault despite healthy communications.
interview.chapter11.q07.takeaway: Use protocol captures and gateway internal values to pinpoint the failing stage.
interview.chapter11.q08.question: How do you engineer remote breaker control through a gateway safely?
interview.chapter11.q08.answer: Remote control must preserve authorization, select/execute behavior where configured, local/remote authority, interlocks, feedback and auditability. Mapping a command IOA to an IEC 61850 controllable object is only one part of the safety chain.
interview.chapter11.q08.step01: Confirm approved remote-control philosophy and permitted equipment.
interview.chapter11.q08.step02: Map the IEC 104 command object to the correct IEC 61850 control object and control model.
interview.chapter11.q08.step03: Validate select-before-execute, timeouts, origin and negative responses where applicable.
interview.chapter11.q08.step04: Verify Local/Remote status, electrical interlocks and synchrocheck permissives.
interview.chapter11.q08.step05: Test commands only in approved FAT/SAT isolation or simulation.
interview.chapter11.q08.step06: Confirm independent feedback and log both accepted and rejected commands.
interview.chapter11.q08.scenario: The RCC sends Close but the breaker remains open because the bay is in Local mode. Gateway should return the appropriate failure/status; do not bypass the selector.
interview.chapter11.q08.takeaway: A command acknowledgement is not proof that the breaker physically operated.
interview.chapter11.q09.question: How are quality and timestamps handled during protocol conversion?
interview.chapter11.q09.answer: Source quality and time information must be converted consistently to the destination protocol. IEC 61850 quality details do not always have an exact IEC 104 equivalent, so the project must define a documented mapping and avoid presenting invalid data as healthy.
interview.chapter11.q09.step01: Identify source validity, test, operator-blocked and old-data conditions.
interview.chapter11.q09.step02: Define destination quality bits and invalid/blocked/substituted semantics as supported.
interview.chapter11.q09.step03: Determine whether source or gateway timestamp is transmitted.
interview.chapter11.q09.step04: Verify time synchronization and UTC/local-time conversion.
interview.chapter11.q09.step05: Inject communication-loss and invalid-quality test cases.
interview.chapter11.q09.step06: Check the RCC indication and SOE ordering after conversion.
interview.chapter11.q09.scenario: An IED becomes disconnected but RCC still shows its last good value without an invalid flag. Correct gateway stale-data quality handling and retest.
interview.chapter11.q09.takeaway: Never silently convert bad-quality data into a valid indication.
interview.chapter11.q10.question: What is the difference between spontaneous, cyclic and interrogated data transfer?
interview.chapter11.q10.answer: Spontaneous transfer is triggered by a change or event; cyclic transfer sends data at configured intervals; interrogated transfer responds to a master request. The appropriate behavior depends on point criticality, bandwidth and control-centre requirements.
interview.chapter11.q10.step01: Classify each point according to the approved telecontrol signal list.
interview.chapter11.q10.step02: Configure event triggers and deadbands for spontaneous transmission.
interview.chapter11.q10.step03: Set cyclic periods where required and avoid unnecessary traffic.
interview.chapter11.q10.step04: Verify GI behavior and completeness of current values.
interview.chapter11.q10.step05: Test rapid changes, reconnects and event buffering or loss behavior.
interview.chapter11.q10.scenario: A frequently fluctuating analog signal floods the link with spontaneous events. Review deadband and reporting strategy instead of suppressing the signal without approval.
interview.chapter11.q10.takeaway: Explain why a point is configured for a given reporting mode.
interview.chapter11.q11.question: How do you troubleshoot IEC 104 disconnections or repeated reconnects?
interview.chapter11.q11.answer: Repeated reconnects can result from network loss, firewall/session timeout, duplicate endpoints, application timer settings, sequence problems or gateway resource issues. Use timestamps and captures from both ends to distinguish network and protocol causes.
interview.chapter11.q11.step01: Review link alarms, switch port errors, IP routes and firewall state.
interview.chapter11.q11.step02: Capture TCP SYN/FIN/RST and IEC 104 STARTDT/TESTFR exchanges.
interview.chapter11.q11.step03: Inspect t0/t1/t2/t3 and k/w parameters against the project specification.
interview.chapter11.q11.step04: Check sequence-number handling, master connection limits and duplicate clients.
interview.chapter11.q11.step05: Correlate disconnect times with device logs and network events.
interview.chapter11.q11.step06: Correct the identified mismatch and monitor stability under normal load.
interview.chapter11.q11.scenario: The RCC session drops every idle period while ping stays stable. Inspect TESTFR exchanges and intermediate firewall idle timers before blaming IED data mapping.
interview.chapter11.q11.takeaway: Correlate logs from gateway, network and master rather than relying on ping alone.
interview.chapter11.q12.question: Describe a complete gateway FAT/SAT test plan.
interview.chapter11.q12.answer: Gateway acceptance verifies source acquisition, point mapping, scaling, events, quality, time, controls, redundancy and control-centre communication. FAT uses controlled simulation; SAT confirms installed paths and approved field interfaces.
interview.chapter11.q12.step01: Freeze approved signal list, gateway database and protocol parameters.
interview.chapter11.q12.step02: Verify IEC 61850/Modbus acquisition with controlled status and analog values.
interview.chapter11.q12.step03: Verify IEC 104 addresses, types, GI, spontaneous events and quality.
interview.chapter11.q12.step04: Test time synchronization, communication loss/recovery and event behavior.
interview.chapter11.q12.step05: Test permitted remote controls, rejections and feedback under approved isolation.
interview.chapter11.q12.step06: Record evidence, defects, retests and final configuration versions.
interview.chapter11.q12.scenario: During SAT, one transformer alarm reaches the local HMI but not the RCC. Compare the gateway source mapping, alarm point inclusion and transmitted IOA, then retest with witnessed evidence.
interview.chapter11.q12.takeaway: Point-by-point traceability and negative-path tests are essential to acceptance.
interview.chapter12.q01.question: Explain the complete breaker Close command path from SCADA HMI to the field breaker.
interview.chapter12.q01.answer: A remote Close request begins at an authorized HMI operator and travels through the SCADA client and configured IEC 61850 control object to bay logic and the breaker operating circuit. Depending on the IED design, CSWI represents switching control, XCBR represents breaker status/control, and CILO provides interlocking information. A successful service response is not proof that the breaker physically closed.
interview.chapter12.q01.step01: Check the approved SLD, point list, command path and operator authority.
interview.chapter12.q01.step02: Verify Local/Remote status and relevant permissives before issuing any test command.
interview.chapter12.q01.step03: Confirm the configured control object, control model and HMI-to-IED mapping.
interview.chapter12.q01.step04: Observe Select/Operate exchanges where applicable and capture command diagnostics.
interview.chapter12.q01.step05: Verify the output relay and simulated breaker auxiliary feedback under an approved test arrangement.
interview.chapter12.q01.step06: Confirm HMI status, SOE timestamps, command log and alarms; document evidence.
interview.chapter12.q01.scenario: HMI reports 'command accepted' but breaker remains Open. Trace command termination, output activation, DC supply, interlock status and auxiliary feedback rather than repeating Close commands.
interview.chapter12.q01.takeaway: Separate command acceptance, output operation and actual breaker position.
interview.chapter12.q02.question: What is the difference between Direct Operate and Select-Before-Operate (SBO)?
