interview.chapter12.q02.answer: Direct Operate issues an operate service without a preceding select step. SBO requires the client to select the control object before operating it within a configured timeout. IEC 61850 also defines normal and enhanced security variants; enhanced-security control uses additional termination/feedback semantics. The configured ctlModel determines the permitted sequence.
interview.chapter12.q02.step01: Read ctlModel for the target control object from the IED data model.
interview.chapter12.q02.step02: Identify whether the client must use Select or SelectWithValue before Operate.
interview.chapter12.q02.step03: Confirm client identity, origin, control number and configured select timeout.
interview.chapter12.q02.step04: Test a valid command sequence in an isolated FAT environment.
interview.chapter12.q02.step05: Test invalid sequence, timeout, second-client contention and cancel behavior.
interview.chapter12.q02.step06: Confirm device feedback and operation termination according to the selected control model.
interview.chapter12.q02.scenario: An HMI sends Operate to an SBO-configured IED and receives a negative response. Correct the SCADA control model rather than disabling SBO.
interview.chapter12.q02.takeaway: SBO is a protocol workflow, not a substitute for electrical interlocking.
interview.chapter12.q03.question: What roles do CSWI, XCBR and CILO play in breaker control?
interview.chapter12.q03.answer: CSWI commonly provides the logical switching-control interface, XCBR represents the circuit-breaker function and position, and CILO exposes interlocking conditions. Exact logical-node allocation and wiring depend on the vendor and project. The HMI may control CSWI.Pos or another engineered control object; the displayed position is typically sourced from the configured breaker status.
interview.chapter12.q03.step01: Browse the IED's actual logical nodes and identify control and feedback references.
interview.chapter12.q03.step02: Compare CSWI.Pos, XCBR.Pos and CILO outputs with the approved SCL and logic drawings.
interview.chapter12.q03.step03: Check whether the SCADA command targets the correct controllable object.
interview.chapter12.q03.step04: Verify interlocking logic and feedback using a safe test simulation.
interview.chapter12.q03.step05: Record source references and any vendor-specific mappings.
interview.chapter12.q03.scenario: SCADA reads XCBR.Pos correctly but Close fails because the command was mapped to a non-controllable status attribute. Map the approved controllable object.
interview.chapter12.q03.takeaway: Never assume an object is writable just because it is visible in an IEC 61850 browser.
interview.chapter12.q04.question: Explain Local/Remote selection and command authority.
interview.chapter12.q04.answer: Local/Remote selection determines which operating location or source is permitted to control equipment. Authority may be enforced by hardware selector, IED logic, bay controller, SCADA permissions or a combination. IEC 61850 origin information identifies the command source but does not itself override site control authority.
interview.chapter12.q04.step01: Check selector-switch input and its interpreted IED status.
interview.chapter12.q04.step02: Review approved command-source priority and authorization rules.
interview.chapter12.q04.step03: Verify SCADA user role and command enablement.
interview.chapter12.q04.step04: Attempt approved test commands under both Local and Remote states using isolated equipment.
interview.chapter12.q04.step05: Confirm blocked commands produce the expected rejection and audit trail.
interview.chapter12.q04.step06: Verify return to normal operating authority after testing.
interview.chapter12.q04.scenario: SCADA can monitor a breaker but cannot Close while the bay selector is in Local. Verify authority before investigating network communication.
interview.chapter12.q04.takeaway: Monitoring availability does not imply remote control permission.
interview.chapter12.q05.question: What is interlocking, and how is it different from protection tripping?
interview.chapter12.q05.answer: Interlocking prevents unsafe or prohibited switching operations based on plant conditions such as disconnector positions, earthing-switch state, breaker state or synchrocheck permissives. Protection tripping responds to detected electrical faults. Interlocking logic may be implemented in a BCU, relay or hardwired circuit, with independent safety measures defined by the project.
interview.chapter12.q05.step01: Review the approved switching interlock matrix and cause-and-effect documents.
interview.chapter12.q05.step02: Identify each required input, permissive and block condition.
interview.chapter12.q05.step03: Verify input source, quality and communication supervision.
interview.chapter12.q05.step04: Test each permitted and prohibited state in an isolated FAT setup.
interview.chapter12.q05.step05: Check HMI indications, blocked-command diagnostics and event logging.
interview.chapter12.q05.step06: Document results and obtain approval before field energization.
interview.chapter12.q05.scenario: A breaker Close is blocked because the earthing switch is indicated Closed. Verify the field state and interlock input; do not bypass the condition to pass a test.
interview.chapter12.q05.takeaway: Interlocking must be validated against approved plant logic, not assumptions.
interview.chapter12.q06.question: How do you troubleshoot an HMI Close command rejected by an IED?
interview.chapter12.q06.answer: A rejected command can be caused by incorrect control model, authority, missing select stage, interlock block, object reference mismatch, timeouts, quality or device-specific checks. Diagnosis should start with the actual command response and IED event log.
interview.chapter12.q06.step01: Record exact error, timestamp, operator and target object.
interview.chapter12.q06.step02: Confirm IED association and that the target data attribute is controllable.
interview.chapter12.q06.step03: Read ctlModel and verify Select/Operate sequence and timeout.
interview.chapter12.q06.step04: Check Local/Remote, CILO and other permissives.
interview.chapter12.q06.step05: Review origin, test flag, control number and vendor diagnostics as applicable.
interview.chapter12.q06.step06: Retest once under an approved safe test condition and capture evidence.
interview.chapter12.q06.scenario: HMI says 'Object not selected'. Inspect SBO select timeout and whether a different client reserved the object.
interview.chapter12.q06.takeaway: The precise rejection code is more useful than a generic 'communication failed' message.
interview.chapter12.q07.question: What is synchrocheck and when can it block breaker closing?
interview.chapter12.q07.answer: Synchrocheck is a permissive function used when closing could connect energized systems. It checks configured conditions such as voltage magnitude, phase angle and frequency difference, or approved dead-line/dead-bus conditions. The exact criteria and wiring depend on the scheme.
interview.chapter12.q07.step01: Identify the approved synchrocheck relay/function and closing permissive path.
interview.chapter12.q07.step02: Review voltage inputs, VT supervision and configuration settings.
interview.chapter12.q07.step03: Verify whether the bay is expected to use live-line/live-bus or dead-line/dead-bus logic.
interview.chapter12.q07.step04: Inspect the synchrocheck permit/block indication and event records.
interview.chapter12.q07.step05: Use approved secondary injection or simulator conditions to validate permissives.
interview.chapter12.q07.step06: Confirm the Close command is blocked when conditions are outside approved limits.
interview.chapter12.q07.scenario: SCADA Close fails although communication and Local/Remote are healthy; synchrocheck is blocking due to unacceptable phase angle. Diagnose the permissive, not the MMS link.
interview.chapter12.q07.takeaway: Do not change synchrocheck settings solely to make a remote Close test pass.
interview.chapter12.q08.question: How are GOOSE signals used in interlocking, and what happens on communication failure?
interview.chapter12.q08.answer: GOOSE can carry peer IED states such as disconnector position or interlocking permissives. The subscriber must validate message freshness, quality and configuration consistency. Loss of GOOSE may trigger a configured fail-safe block or another approved fallback; behavior must be verified in the project logic.
interview.chapter12.q08.step01: Identify publisher DataSet, GoCB and subscriber external references.
interview.chapter12.q08.step02: Check multicast/VLAN path, APPID, confRev and subscriber status.
interview.chapter12.q08.step03: Verify the actual received value and quality, not just packet presence.
interview.chapter12.q08.step04: Simulate an approved publisher loss and confirm the specified fail-safe behavior.
interview.chapter12.q08.step05: Restore communication and verify recovery without unintended operations.
interview.chapter12.q08.step06: Record the event sequence and diagnostic alarms.
interview.chapter12.q08.scenario: GOOSE packets are visible but Close remains blocked because the subscriber input is invalid after a confRev mismatch. Correct engineering consistency before retesting.
interview.chapter12.q08.takeaway: Receiving Ethernet frames does not guarantee valid interlocking data.
interview.chapter12.q09.question: What is the difference between command acknowledgment, operation termination and position feedback?
interview.chapter12.q09.answer: A command acknowledgment indicates whether the control service request was accepted or rejected. Enhanced-security control can provide command termination information. Position feedback is an independent measured or calculated breaker state, often derived from auxiliary contacts. These signals should not be conflated.
interview.chapter12.q09.step01: Observe command request and service response in client logs.
interview.chapter12.q09.step02: Check enhanced-security termination indication if the control model supports it.
interview.chapter12.q09.step03: Verify output activation and the physical or simulated switching mechanism.
interview.chapter12.q09.step04: Inspect XCBR.Pos and quality/timestamp after the operation.
interview.chapter12.q09.step05: Check command timeout and mismatch alarms if expected feedback does not arrive.
interview.chapter12.q09.step06: Correlate the sequence using SOE and device records.
interview.chapter12.q09.scenario: The IED accepts Close but the mechanism is blocked; SCADA must show failed or mismatched final position rather than falsely showing Closed.
interview.chapter12.q09.takeaway: Always validate the final field state independently.
interview.chapter12.q10.question: How do you handle intermediate, invalid or bad-quality breaker status?
interview.chapter12.q10.answer: A double-point breaker indication can represent Open, Closed, intermediate and bad/invalid states depending on the data model and mapping. SCADA should distinguish ambiguous or stale information from a confirmed safe state, and control permissives should follow approved engineering logic.
interview.chapter12.q10.step01: Inspect the actual XCBR.Pos.stVal encoding and associated quality.
interview.chapter12.q10.step02: Verify both auxiliary contacts and input logic when double-point indication is used.
interview.chapter12.q10.step03: Test all valid and invalid states through approved simulation.
interview.chapter12.q10.step04: Confirm HMI symbols, alarms and SOE represent intermediate/bad quality correctly.
interview.chapter12.q10.step05: Check communication-loss behavior and command blocking policy.
interview.chapter12.q10.step06: Document discrepancies against the approved point list.
interview.chapter12.q10.scenario: Both 52a and 52b contacts are active after wiring changes. The HMI should indicate an abnormal state rather than a valid Open or Closed position.
interview.chapter12.q10.takeaway: Never treat unknown status as a confirmed safe switching position.
interview.chapter12.q11.question: How do you test breaker Open/Close control during FAT and SAT safely?
interview.chapter12.q11.answer: Control FAT/SAT validates command mapping, permissions, interlocks, protocol workflow, outputs, feedback, alarms and logging. Tests must be conducted under approved isolation and switching procedures; real breaker operation requires site authorization.
interview.chapter12.q11.step01: Review approved test plan, switching procedure, permits and isolation boundaries.
interview.chapter12.q11.step02: Confirm test mode, output isolation and personnel coordination.
interview.chapter12.q11.step03: Verify positive and negative control cases including Local/Remote and interlock blocks.
interview.chapter12.q11.step04: Test Direct Operate or SBO sequence as configured.
interview.chapter12.q11.step05: Check output indication, simulated or authorized physical feedback, alarms and SOE.
interview.chapter12.q11.step06: Restore the original configuration, verify safe state and sign test records.
interview.chapter12.q11.scenario: During FAT a Close command is accepted but the simulator provides no position feedback. Log a feedback-path failure rather than recording a pass.
interview.chapter12.q11.takeaway: Never defeat hardwired interlocks or trip circuits for convenience.
interview.chapter12.q12.question: Describe a systematic troubleshooting workflow when a breaker cannot close remotely.
interview.chapter12.q12.answer: A structured workflow separates SCADA access, protocol/control-service handling, permissives, output circuit and final position feedback. This avoids repeated commands and helps identify the first failed stage.
interview.chapter12.q12.step01: Confirm equipment identity, operating authority and approved safe test conditions.
interview.chapter12.q12.step02: Verify HMI command target and user permissions.
interview.chapter12.q12.step03: Check MMS association and actual control service response.
interview.chapter12.q12.step04: Inspect ctlModel, SBO selection and command timeout.
interview.chapter12.q12.step05: Review Local/Remote, interlocks, synchrocheck, protection lockout and DC supply indications.
interview.chapter12.q12.step06: Check output relay/circuit and independent position feedback under approved testing.
interview.chapter12.q12.step07: Document root cause, corrective action and retest evidence.
interview.chapter12.q12.scenario: An operator reports 'remote Close not working'. Network is healthy and command accepted, but lockout relay 86 is active. Stop at the blocked permissive and escalate per procedure.
interview.chapter12.q12.takeaway: The goal is to identify why control is blocked, not to force the breaker to close.
interview.chapter13.q01.question: What is the difference between protection pickup, trip and breaker-open indication?
interview.chapter13.q01.answer: Pickup indicates that a protection element detected its operating condition. Trip means that protection logic issued a trip request. Breaker-open is the independently measured mechanical position; these events are related but not interchangeable.
interview.chapter13.q01.step01: Identify the protection element and pickup indication in the relay event record.
interview.chapter13.q01.step02: Trace the configured trip logic and master trip output, including PTRC where applicable.
interview.chapter13.q01.step03: Verify the trip circuit and breaker auxiliary contact feedback under an approved test setup.
interview.chapter13.q01.step04: Compare device-originated event timestamps, SCADA mapping and quality.
interview.chapter13.q01.step05: Document whether the issue is detection, trip logic, output wiring or feedback.
interview.chapter13.q01.scenario: Overcurrent pickup is logged but the breaker stays closed. The configured delay may not have elapsed or the trip path may be blocked; do not label pickup as a breaker trip.
interview.chapter13.q01.takeaway: Explain the full chain: detect → trip decision → output → breaker movement → feedback.
interview.chapter13.q02.question: How are PTOC, PDIS, PTRC and RBRF used in IEC 61850?
interview.chapter13.q02.answer: PTOC represents time overcurrent protection, PDIS distance protection, PTRC protection trip conditioning and RBRF breaker failure protection. Actual instantiated logical nodes and their data attributes depend on the relay configuration and edition.
interview.chapter13.q02.step01: Inspect the IED SCL file and actual instantiated logical nodes.
interview.chapter13.q02.step02: Identify configured data attributes for start, operate and trip-related indications.
interview.chapter13.q02.step03: Map required signals into a report DataSet and SCADA points.
interview.chapter13.q02.step04: Check the protection logic and signal-list definitions rather than assuming a generic mapping.
interview.chapter13.q02.step05: Test each relevant event with a relay simulator or approved test method.
interview.chapter13.q02.scenario: The SCADA signal list expects a distance protection start but the relay only publishes configured overcurrent indications. Reconcile the approved engineering design and SCL model.
interview.chapter13.q02.takeaway: Know logical-node purposes, but always verify actual IED data references.
interview.chapter13.q03.question: How do you engineer a protection trip alarm from an IED to SCADA?
interview.chapter13.q03.answer: A protection trip alarm should identify the correct bay, cause and state with reliable event time and quality. Mapping must use the intended protection indication, not a generic breaker position.
interview.chapter13.q03.step01: Review the approved protection and SCADA signal lists.
interview.chapter13.q03.step02: Identify the exact IEC 61850 data object and functional constraint.
interview.chapter13.q03.step03: Verify DataSet and RCB membership or the configured acquisition path.
interview.chapter13.q03.step04: Create the SCADA point with correct polarity, priority and message.
interview.chapter13.q03.step05: Simulate a safe trip indication and confirm HMI banner, SOE and historian records.
interview.chapter13.q03.step06: Verify return-to-normal and acknowledgment behavior separately.
interview.chapter13.q03.scenario: A trip event is visible in IED logs but absent from SCADA alarms. Check reporting, point mapping and alarm enablement in sequence.
interview.chapter13.q03.takeaway: Differentiate alarm source acquisition from alarm annunciation logic.
interview.chapter13.q04.question: What is Sequence of Events (SOE), and how do you verify event order?
interview.chapter13.q04.answer: SOE is a chronological record of operational changes. Reliable sequence analysis requires synchronized source clocks, correct timestamp propagation and awareness of event time versus receipt time.
interview.chapter13.q04.step01: Confirm the time synchronization source and device synchronization status.
interview.chapter13.q04.step02: Generate a controlled series of test events with known order.
interview.chapter13.q04.step03: Read event timestamps in the IED and corresponding SCADA SOE records.
interview.chapter13.q04.step04: Check UTC/time-zone conversion and timestamp resolution.
interview.chapter13.q04.step05: Investigate missing, duplicated or reordered entries and report delays.
interview.chapter13.q04.scenario: A trip appears after breaker open on an HMI event list because one point uses server arrival time and another uses IED time. Compare source timestamps before diagnosing protection logic.
interview.chapter13.q04.takeaway: Never infer physical event order from unsynchronized clocks.
interview.chapter13.q05.question: What are IEC 61850 quality and timestamp attributes, and why do they matter?
interview.chapter13.q05.answer: IEC 61850 data commonly includes status value, quality and timestamp attributes. Quality communicates validity and conditions such as old data, test or operator-blocked states, depending on the applicable data model.
interview.chapter13.q05.step01: Browse the source object and inspect stVal, q and t where available.
interview.chapter13.q05.step02: Confirm SCADA reads and propagates quality and timestamp.
interview.chapter13.q05.step03: Disconnect or simulate a supervised source under safe conditions.
interview.chapter13.q05.step04: Verify that HMI shows bad or stale quality instead of an apparently valid state.
interview.chapter13.q05.step05: Restore communications and check quality recovery and event logging.
interview.chapter13.q05.scenario: A protection alarm stays green during an IED communication outage. The value is cached, but the HMI ignores invalid quality.
interview.chapter13.q05.takeaway: A value without valid quality can mislead an operator.
interview.chapter13.q06.question: How do you configure alarm priorities and acknowledgment?
interview.chapter13.q06.answer: Alarm priority reflects the approved operating philosophy and required operator response. Acknowledgment records operator awareness; it does not clear an active physical condition.
interview.chapter13.q06.step01: Review approved alarm philosophy and signal criticality.
interview.chapter13.q06.step02: Assign priority, message, equipment reference and alarm group.
interview.chapter13.q06.step03: Configure activation, clear, acknowledgment and shelving rules as authorized.
interview.chapter13.q06.step04: Test each alarm transition and user action.
interview.chapter13.q06.step05: Confirm history retains occurrence, acknowledgment and return-to-normal records.
interview.chapter13.q06.scenario: An active transformer protection trip is acknowledged but remains present until the trip condition clears. This is expected when acknowledgment and clearance are separate.
interview.chapter13.q06.takeaway: Avoid treating acknowledgment as a reset of protection or equipment.
interview.chapter13.q07.question: How do you troubleshoot missing SOE entries when alarms are visible?
interview.chapter13.q07.answer: Alarm displays and SOE records may use different processing or storage paths. Missing SOE can result from reporting settings, event ingestion, timestamp handling, filters or historian service issues.
interview.chapter13.q07.step01: Verify the event exists in the source IED log.
interview.chapter13.q07.step02: Inspect report or acquisition traffic and configured trigger options.
interview.chapter13.q07.step03: Check SCADA event processing and SOE database service health.
interview.chapter13.q07.step04: Review event filters, point flags and timestamp acceptance rules.
interview.chapter13.q07.step05: Reproduce the event safely and compare all logging stages.
interview.chapter13.q07.scenario: An alarm banner activates but SOE remains blank because the event-storage service is stopped. The acquisition path is healthy; the historian path is not.
interview.chapter13.q07.takeaway: Follow acquisition, alarm engine and SOE storage as separate paths.
interview.chapter13.q08.question: What causes alarm flooding and how do you troubleshoot it?
interview.chapter13.q08.answer: Alarm flooding occurs when many alarms arrive in a short period, potentially obscuring the initiating event. Root causes include communication flapping, unstable inputs, poor deadbands or cascading equipment conditions.
interview.chapter13.q08.step01: Collect a timestamped alarm list and identify the earliest initiating event.
interview.chapter13.q08.step02: Group alarms by IED, network path and affected equipment.
interview.chapter13.q08.step03: Check communication-loss patterns and time synchronization.
interview.chapter13.q08.step04: Inspect contact chatter, debounce settings and analog deadbands.
interview.chapter13.q08.step05: Apply only approved alarm-rationalization or delay changes.
interview.chapter13.q08.step06: Retest and verify important protection alarms are never masked.
interview.chapter13.q08.scenario: A switch uplink flaps and hundreds of IED communication alarms occur. Restore the link and confirm correlated recovery before changing individual alarms.
interview.chapter13.q08.takeaway: Fix the initiating fault; do not simply suppress high-volume alarms.
interview.chapter13.q09.question: How do you test protection indications during FAT without operating live equipment?
interview.chapter13.q09.answer: FAT uses isolated relay test setups, simulators and controlled digital inputs to verify protection indications and SCADA mapping. Live protection outputs and trip circuits require approved isolation and safety controls.
interview.chapter13.q09.step01: Review test procedure, isolation plan and signal list.
interview.chapter13.q09.step02: Confirm trip outputs cannot unintentionally operate energized equipment.
interview.chapter13.q09.step03: Inject an approved simulated pickup or operate condition.
interview.chapter13.q09.step04: Observe IED event, IEC 61850 report, SCADA alarm and SOE.
interview.chapter13.q09.step05: Check event time, priority, polarity, acknowledgment and reset.
interview.chapter13.q09.step06: Restore normal configuration and attach test evidence.
interview.chapter13.q09.scenario: During FAT a simulated distance protection operate event appears on the wrong feeder alarm. Correct the database source reference and repeat the test.
interview.chapter13.q09.takeaway: State the test isolation and acceptance evidence in your interview answer.
interview.chapter13.q10.question: How do you investigate a protection trip recorded by the relay but not by the station gateway?
interview.chapter13.q10.answer: A missing remote indication may arise in the source DataSet, MMS report acquisition, gateway point mapping, protocol conversion or remote control-centre receiving system.
interview.chapter13.q10.step01: Confirm the trip event and IEC 61850 reference in the relay.
interview.chapter13.q10.step02: Verify the gateway receives the event with correct value, quality and timestamp.
interview.chapter13.q10.step03: Check IEC 61850-to-IEC 104 or other protocol mapping and point enablement.
interview.chapter13.q10.step04: Inspect gateway transmit logs and remote protocol traffic.
interview.chapter13.q10.step05: Validate remote point address, cause of transmission and control-centre database.
interview.chapter13.q10.step06: Perform a safe retest and document the first failing stage.
interview.chapter13.q10.scenario: Local HMI shows a trip but RCC does not. The IEC 104 IOA points to an unused address; correct mapping under change control.
interview.chapter13.q10.takeaway: Local HMI success does not prove gateway or RCC delivery.
interview.chapter13.q11.question: How would you troubleshoot incorrect protection alarm timestamps?
interview.chapter13.q11.answer: Timestamp problems can originate from IED clock drift, time-source loss, UTC conversion, report handling or server-time substitution. Investigate the source timestamp before changing the display.
interview.chapter13.q11.step01: Compare IED clock with the approved master time source.
interview.chapter13.q11.step02: Check synchronization health, time-zone settings and daylight-saving handling.
interview.chapter13.q11.step03: Inspect the timestamp on the original IEC 61850 data/report.
interview.chapter13.q11.step04: Compare gateway, SCADA SOE and historian timestamps.
interview.chapter13.q11.step05: Determine whether a server receipt timestamp replaced the source timestamp.
interview.chapter13.q11.step06: Correct the responsible layer and verify with controlled events.
interview.chapter13.q11.scenario: A relay event is correct in UTC but HMI shows a five-and-a-half-hour offset error due to duplicate local-time conversion.
interview.chapter13.q11.takeaway: Distinguish timestamp source, transport and presentation.
interview.chapter13.q12.question: Explain a systematic approach to a protection alarm that stays active after reset.
interview.chapter13.q12.answer: A persistent alarm may reflect an uncleared physical condition, latched protection indication, reset permission, stale reporting or incorrect SCADA alarm logic. Never force a reset without understanding the cause.
interview.chapter13.q12.step01: Verify equipment is safe and confirm the underlying protection condition is cleared.
interview.chapter13.q12.step02: Read the IED current value and protection latch state.
interview.chapter13.q12.step03: Check authorized reset procedure and whether an active condition blocks reset.
interview.chapter13.q12.step04: Inspect report updates, SCADA tag polarity and alarm clear logic.
interview.chapter13.q12.step05: Review quality, timestamp and communication status.
interview.chapter13.q12.step06: Retest under approved conditions and document root cause.
interview.chapter13.q12.scenario: The relay trip latch clears locally, but SCADA alarm remains active because the reset transition was not reported. Check RCB trigger settings and mapping before restarting services.
interview.chapter13.q12.takeaway: Do not bypass protection latches or interlocks to clear an HMI alarm.
interview.chapter14.q01.question: Why is time synchronization necessary in SAS?
interview.chapter14.q01.answer: Time synchronization aligns IED, gateway and SCADA clocks so SOE, disturbance records and fault investigations can be correlated. Clock accuracy and source timestamp handling must meet project requirements.
interview.chapter14.q01.step01: Identify project accuracy and time-source requirements.
interview.chapter14.q01.step02: Check every device time source and synchronization status.
interview.chapter14.q01.step03: Compare UTC timestamps of controlled events from two IEDs.
interview.chapter14.q01.step04: Confirm SCADA preserves device timestamps and quality.
interview.chapter14.q01.scenario: Two relays report a trip sequence in reverse order; compare synchronization alarms and device-origin timestamps before blaming logic.
interview.chapter14.q01.takeaway: A valid event value with an unsynchronized timestamp can mislead fault analysis.
interview.chapter14.q02.question: What is the difference between NTP and SNTP?
interview.chapter14.q02.answer: NTP is a network time synchronization protocol with algorithms for clock selection and discipline. SNTP is a simpler client implementation often used by industrial devices. Both commonly use UDP port 123, subject to device support.
interview.chapter14.q02.step01: Read device support and time architecture.
interview.chapter14.q02.step02: Configure authorized server addresses and redundancy.
interview.chapter14.q02.step04: Check synchronization state and measured offset.
interview.chapter14.q02.step05: Test failover without changing live protection settings.
interview.chapter14.q02.scenario: An IED points to an obsolete NTP server after network migration and its clock drifts; correct the server and verify lock.
interview.chapter14.q02.takeaway: Do not assume SNTP and NTP provide identical accuracy under all conditions.
interview.chapter14.q03.question: How do you configure SNTP synchronization for an IED?
interview.chapter14.q03.answer: SNTP clients obtain time from configured servers. Vendor menus and support vary, so configuration must follow the approved device manual and site time architecture.
interview.chapter14.q03.step01: Confirm network IP, gateway and VLAN path to time server.
interview.chapter14.q03.step02: Enter primary and secondary time-server IP addresses if supported.
interview.chapter14.q03.step03: Configure UTC/time zone display separately where required.
interview.chapter14.q03.step04: Enable synchronization and verify status diagnostics.
interview.chapter14.q03.step05: Compare IED clock with a trusted reference.
interview.chapter14.q03.step06: Document server failover and recovery test.
interview.chapter14.q03.scenario: IED communicates with SCADA but timestamps drift; discover the SNTP VLAN is blocked and correct switch policy.
interview.chapter14.q03.takeaway: Successful ping to a time server is not proof that UDP 123 exchange works.
interview.chapter14.q04.question: Explain PTP and when it is preferred over SNTP.
interview.chapter14.q04.answer: IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol uses time-aware message exchanges and, where supported, hardware timestamping and suitable network infrastructure for high-accuracy synchronization. Profiles, grandmaster selection and boundary/transparent clocks matter.
interview.chapter14.q04.step01: Identify required PTP profile and accuracy.
interview.chapter14.q04.step03: Check VLAN, multicast and switch PTP features.
interview.chapter14.q04.step04: Confirm grandmaster lock and slave offset diagnostics.
interview.chapter14.q04.step05: Test failover and packet loss according to approved plan.
interview.chapter14.q04.scenario: A merging unit reports loss of synchronization despite network connectivity; inspect grandmaster profile and switch PTP support.
interview.chapter14.q04.takeaway: PTP accuracy depends on the entire timing path, not just enabling a checkbox.
interview.chapter14.q05.question: What is IRIG-B and how does it differ from network time?
interview.chapter14.q05.answer: IRIG-B distributes time using a dedicated electrical or optical signal in supported installations, rather than relying on ordinary IP packet exchange. Encoding, year information and UTC offset handling depend on equipment configuration.
interview.chapter14.q05.step01: Check time source and IRIG-B output format.
interview.chapter14.q05.step02: Verify cabling, signal level and compatible IED input.
interview.chapter14.q05.step03: Configure time code and UTC handling.
interview.chapter14.q05.step04: Inspect lock indication and time accuracy.
interview.chapter14.q05.scenario: An IED shows time input present but wrong year; verify IRIG-B format and year source settings.
interview.chapter14.q05.takeaway: Physical timing signal presence does not guarantee correct decoded time.
interview.chapter14.q06.question: How do you troubleshoot incorrect SOE timestamps?
interview.chapter14.q06.answer: Incorrect event order may result from clock offset, source versus receive timestamp confusion, time zone conversion, reporting delay or bad synchronization quality.
interview.chapter14.q06.step01: Identify which device originated each event.
interview.chapter14.q06.step02: Compare raw IED event time and SCADA stored time.
interview.chapter14.q06.step03: Check clock synchronization state and offset.
interview.chapter14.q06.step05: Inspect event/report buffering and network delay.
interview.chapter14.q06.step06: Repeat a controlled test and document evidence.
interview.chapter14.q06.scenario: Trip and breaker-open events differ by several seconds only on HMI; raw IED logs match, indicating SCADA timestamp conversion error.
interview.chapter14.q06.takeaway: Always compare source timestamps before adjusting alarm delays.
interview.chapter14.q07.question: How do you test redundancy of time servers?
interview.chapter14.q07.answer: Time-source redundancy prevents loss of accurate timing when a primary server or path fails, provided clients support the configured failover mechanism.
interview.chapter14.q07.step02: Record normal synchronization state and offset.
interview.chapter14.q07.step03: Under approved FAT conditions disconnect the primary path.
interview.chapter14.q07.step04: Observe server selection, holdover and alarm behavior.
interview.chapter14.q07.step05: Restore primary and verify recovery without time jumps.
interview.chapter14.q07.scenario: Primary SNTP server is disconnected but some IEDs drift because they were never configured with a secondary address.
interview.chapter14.q07.takeaway: Check each IED individually; a redundant server pair does not imply redundant client configuration.
interview.chapter14.q08.question: What are clock holdover and time-quality indications?
interview.chapter14.q08.answer: Holdover is the clock maintaining estimated time when its reference is unavailable. Accuracy degrades according to oscillator quality and outage duration; status flags indicate unsynchronized or uncertain timing.
interview.chapter14.q08.step02: Check IED sync and quality diagnostics.
interview.chapter14.q08.step04: Measure offset over the required interval.
interview.chapter14.q08.step05: Verify SOE quality flags and alarms.
interview.chapter14.q08.step06: Restore reference and confirm stable resynchronization.
interview.chapter14.q08.scenario: A gateway continues displaying plausible timestamps during a timing outage, but quality shows unsynchronized.
interview.chapter14.q08.takeaway: A plausible clock display is not proof of valid synchronization.
interview.chapter14.q09.question: What is SNMP and what are Manager, Agent, MIB and OID?
interview.chapter14.q09.answer: Simple Network Management Protocol is used to monitor and sometimes manage network equipment. A manager queries agents; MIBs describe managed objects; OIDs identify individual objects or metrics. SNMP does not replace IEC 61850 operational messaging.
interview.chapter14.q09.step01: Identify switch SNMP agent and management station.
interview.chapter14.q09.step02: Review supported MIB and OID list.
interview.chapter14.q09.step03: Enable authorized SNMP access on the management VLAN.
interview.chapter14.q09.step04: Query interface status and counters with a test manager.
interview.chapter14.q09.step05: Map required metrics and alarms into monitoring.
interview.chapter14.q09.scenario: Network monitoring shows a switch port down using ifOperStatus OID while SCADA still shows the last valid relay data.
interview.chapter14.q09.takeaway: SNMP reports network health; it is not a protection trip transport.
interview.chapter14.q10.question: Compare SNMPv2c and SNMPv3 for a substation network.
interview.chapter14.q10.answer: SNMPv2c typically relies on community strings without built-in message confidentiality. SNMPv3 supports authentication and privacy with suitable security levels and is generally preferable where equipment and project policy allow.
interview.chapter14.q10.step01: Check switch and monitoring software versions.
interview.chapter14.q10.step02: Choose approved SNMPv3 security level and users where supported.
interview.chapter14.q10.step03: Limit access with management VLAN and ACLs.
interview.chapter14.q10.step04: Configure secure credentials and permitted managers.
interview.chapter14.q10.step05: Verify polling and traps while checking logs.
interview.chapter14.q10.scenario: A monitoring server can poll a switch with v2c but fails after v3 migration; verify username, auth/privacy algorithms and security level.
interview.chapter14.q10.takeaway: Prefer least privilege and avoid exposing SNMP on untrusted networks.
interview.chapter14.q11.question: What is the difference between SNMP polling, traps and informs?
interview.chapter14.q11.answer: Polling is a manager-initiated request for status or counters. Traps are agent-initiated notifications generally without acknowledgment; informs request acknowledgment and depend on version/device support.
interview.chapter14.q11.step01: List required polled OIDs and notification events.
interview.chapter14.q11.step02: Set appropriate polling interval to avoid excess load.
interview.chapter14.q11.step05: Verify notification reception and event correlation.
interview.chapter14.q11.scenario: Switch port failure is visible during polling but no trap arrives because the destination IP was configured incorrectly.
interview.chapter14.q11.takeaway: Polling and notification delivery are independent checks.
interview.chapter14.q12.question: How do you configure SNMP monitoring on a managed Ethernet switch?
interview.chapter14.q12.answer: SNMP configuration enables approved network health monitoring, including port state, traffic errors, link changes and device status. Exact commands vary by vendor.
interview.chapter14.q12.step01: Confirm management IP, VLAN, ACL and monitoring requirements.
interview.chapter14.q12.step02: Enable supported SNMP version and secure credentials.
interview.chapter14.q12.step03: Configure read-only OID access and trap receiver.
interview.chapter14.q12.step04: Select interface status, error counters and device health OIDs.
interview.chapter14.q12.step05: Test polling and notifications from management station.
interview.chapter14.q12.step06: Save configuration and document backup and security settings.
interview.chapter14.q12.scenario: An industrial switch is reachable by ping but not SNMP; an ACL allows ICMP but blocks UDP 161.
interview.chapter14.q12.takeaway: SNMP polling normally uses UDP 161 and traps typically use UDP 162.
interview.chapter14.q13.question: How do you detect a PRP LAN failure using SNMP?
interview.chapter14.q13.answer: SNMP can expose managed switch port and link status for PRP LAN A and LAN B. PRP redundancy supervision is a separate mechanism; combine switch alarms with DANP/RedBox diagnostics where available.
interview.chapter14.q13.step01: Identify LAN A and LAN B switches and relevant ports.
interview.chapter14.q13.step02: Poll link status and error counters for each independent LAN.
interview.chapter14.q13.step03: Configure link-down traps and device-health alarms.
interview.chapter14.q13.step04: Correlate switch event with PRP supervision diagnostics.
interview.chapter14.q13.step05: Perform an approved single-LAN failure test.
interview.chapter14.q13.step06: Verify communication continuity and correct alarm recovery.
interview.chapter14.q13.scenario: LAN B fibre disconnects; HMI continues receiving MMS over LAN A, while SNMP reports LAN B port down.
interview.chapter14.q13.takeaway: Do not infer PRP health from a single switch alone.
interview.chapter14.q14.question: SNMP traps are not reaching the monitoring server. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.chapter14.q14.answer: Trap loss can arise from wrong receiver IP, routing, VLAN/ACL policy, UDP 162 filtering, version/security mismatch, event configuration or collector processing.
interview.chapter14.q14.step01: Verify that the switch event actually occurred and traps are enabled.
interview.chapter14.q14.step02: Check receiver IP, routing and source interface.
interview.chapter14.q14.step03: Validate management VLAN and firewall rules for UDP 162.
interview.chapter14.q14.step04: Match SNMP version, user/community and security settings.
interview.chapter14.q14.step05: Capture traffic at switch mirror port or collector where permitted.
interview.chapter14.q14.step06: Check collector logs, event rules and duplicate suppression.
interview.chapter14.q14.step07: Retest with an approved port-down event and document results.
interview.chapter14.q14.scenario: A switch sends link-down traps to an old monitoring server address; polling from the new server still works.
interview.chapter14.q14.takeaway: Working SNMP polling does not prove trap delivery.
interview.chapter15.q01.question: How do you approach a new IED configuration task using an engineering tool?
interview.chapter15.q01.answer: Engineering begins with approved drawings, settings, firmware compatibility and an engineering backup. Vendor tools edit device parameters and IEC 61850 models, but configuration must be reviewed and tested before deployment.
interview.chapter15.q01.step01: Confirm device make, model, firmware and tool version.
interview.chapter15.q01.step02: Obtain the approved settings, signal list, network plan and latest project backup.
interview.chapter15.q01.step03: Connect using the approved engineering interface and read the existing device configuration.
interview.chapter15.q01.step04: Compare offline and online settings before making controlled changes.
interview.chapter15.q01.step05: Validate the IEC 61850 model, export the required SCL file and run approved tests.
interview.chapter15.q01.step06: Archive the final project, version, change record and rollback copy.
interview.chapter15.q01.scenario: A replacement relay has a newer firmware revision. Check tool and configuration compatibility before importing the previous relay project.
interview.chapter15.q01.takeaway: Never overwrite an in-service IED without authorization and a verified backup.
interview.chapter15.q02.question: What is Schneider PACiS SCE and how is it used in SAS engineering?
interview.chapter15.q02.answer: PACiS SCE is an engineering environment used in applicable PACiS architectures to configure station automation data and communication relationships. Exact workflows depend on the installed PACiS version and project design.
interview.chapter15.q02.step01: Review the approved PACiS project and engineering database.
interview.chapter15.q02.step02: Identify IEDs, bay objects, signal references and communication configuration.
interview.chapter15.q02.step03: Import or reconcile IED data models and map relevant points.
interview.chapter15.q02.step04: Configure database associations, indications, alarms and required gateway or HMI relationships.
interview.chapter15.q02.step05: Validate database consistency and generate or export project deliverables.
interview.chapter15.q02.step06: Test representative indications, controls and reports in FAT.
interview.chapter15.q02.scenario: An IED status is visible in an IEC 61850 browser but absent from PACiS HMI. Compare source reference, engineering database point and HMI association.
interview.chapter15.q02.takeaway: Describe the engineering workflow without claiming a feature is identical across PACiS versions.
interview.chapter15.q03.question: How do you use Schneider Easergy Studio or Easergy Builder for IED integration?
interview.chapter15.q03.answer: The supported Schneider engineering application is selected according to the IED family and firmware. It can be used for device settings, IEC 61850 configuration and communication validation where supported.
interview.chapter15.q03.step01: Confirm the exact device family, firmware and supported engineering software.
interview.chapter15.q03.step02: Read or import the existing project and verify communication access.
interview.chapter15.q03.step03: Inspect logical devices, logical nodes, DataSets and reporting configuration.
interview.chapter15.q03.step04: Review IP settings, control model and GOOSE settings if supported.
interview.chapter15.q03.step05: Export the supported ICD/CID or other SCL deliverable and validate it.
interview.chapter15.q03.step06: Perform offline checks and approved FAT communication tests.
interview.chapter15.q03.scenario: After importing a relay ICD, the expected breaker status object is missing. Confirm the correct device model and firmware-specific export.
interview.chapter15.q03.takeaway: Avoid assuming every Easergy-family device has the same configuration menus.
interview.chapter15.q04.question: Explain the basic ABB PCM600 engineering workflow.
interview.chapter15.q04.answer: ABB PCM600 is used with supported ABB protection and control IEDs for parameterization and IEC 61850 engineering, with connectivity packages required for the relevant IED types.
interview.chapter15.q04.step01: Install a compatible PCM600 release and IED connectivity package.
interview.chapter15.q04.step02: Create or open the plant structure and add the correct IED type.
interview.chapter15.q04.step03: Read the IED configuration or import approved project data.
interview.chapter15.q04.step04: Review application configuration, communication parameters and signal mapping.
interview.chapter15.q04.step05: Engineer DataSets, reporting and GOOSE as supported by the IED and project.
interview.chapter15.q04.step06: Write approved changes, verify online values and export configuration evidence.
interview.chapter15.q04.scenario: PCM600 connects to a relay but cannot display its complete model. Check connectivity package, device type and firmware compatibility.
interview.chapter15.q04.takeaway: Mention the role of connectivity packages in ABB workflows.
interview.chapter15.q05.question: What do Siemens DIGSI 4 and DIGSI 5 do, and how do you select between them?
interview.chapter15.q05.answer: DIGSI engineering tools configure supported Siemens SIPROTEC protection and control devices. DIGSI 4 and DIGSI 5 support different device generations; selection depends on the exact SIPROTEC family and firmware.
interview.chapter15.q05.step01: Identify the SIPROTEC device model and generation.
interview.chapter15.q05.step02: Confirm the supported DIGSI version and communication interface.
interview.chapter15.q05.step03: Back up the current device settings and project.
interview.chapter15.q05.step04: Inspect protection parameters, communication settings and IEC 61850 configuration.
interview.chapter15.q05.step05: Review report, GOOSE and control engineering in the supported workflow.
interview.chapter15.q05.step06: Test changes and retain the final project and settings report.
interview.chapter15.q05.scenario: An engineer tries to open a SIPROTEC 5 project in DIGSI 4. Identify the tool-generation mismatch rather than troubleshooting Ethernet first.
interview.chapter15.q05.takeaway: Always match engineering tool generation to device generation.
interview.chapter15.q06.question: How is GE EnerVista used for relay configuration and troubleshooting?
interview.chapter15.q06.answer: GE EnerVista is a family of engineering and maintenance tools for supported GE Multilin devices. Capabilities depend on the specific relay and its supported application.
interview.chapter15.q06.step01: Identify the relay model, firmware and appropriate EnerVista application.
interview.chapter15.q06.step02: Establish authorized local or network communication.
interview.chapter15.q06.step03: Read and back up settings and check device health.
interview.chapter15.q06.step04: Inspect digital inputs, outputs, measurements and communication settings.
interview.chapter15.q06.step05: Review supported IEC 61850 objects and reporting configuration.
interview.chapter15.q06.step06: Apply approved changes and verify with controlled test signals.
interview.chapter15.q06.scenario: A GE relay responds over Ethernet but a configured SCADA point is stale. Verify the relay's IEC 61850 reporting and the SCADA mapping independently.
interview.chapter15.q06.takeaway: Avoid presenting all EnerVista products as one identical interface.
interview.chapter15.q07.question: How do you validate an ICD file before importing it into a station project?
interview.chapter15.q07.answer: An ICD file describes an IED's IEC 61850 capabilities. Its content must be compatible with the device version and station engineering requirements; capability descriptions are not proof of final installed configuration.
interview.chapter15.q07.step01: Check file provenance, model, firmware and revision.
interview.chapter15.q07.step02: Validate XML/SCL syntax with an appropriate validator.
interview.chapter15.q07.step03: Inspect logical devices, logical nodes, DataSets and supported services.
interview.chapter15.q07.step04: Check the expected report and GOOSE capabilities.
interview.chapter15.q07.step05: Import into a controlled engineering project and review warnings.
interview.chapter15.q07.step06: Compare the engineered model against the online IED and FAT signal list.
interview.chapter15.q07.scenario: An ICD imports successfully but the intended report DataSet is unavailable. Determine whether the file describes only capabilities and whether final engineering is still required.
interview.chapter15.q07.takeaway: Successful XML import does not prove live IED compatibility.
interview.chapter15.q08.question: How do you troubleshoot a vendor tool that cannot connect to an IED?
interview.chapter15.q08.answer: Connection failure may be caused by physical access, addressing, firewalls, protocol settings, credentials, firmware/tool mismatch or a device-side service restriction.
interview.chapter15.q08.step01: Check engineering authorization and physical port or fibre link.
interview.chapter15.q08.step02: Confirm laptop IP, subnet, route and the intended IED address.
interview.chapter15.q08.step03: Check ARP and ping where applicable; remember some devices block ICMP.
interview.chapter15.q08.step04: Verify required protocol port, service and user credentials.
interview.chapter15.q08.step05: Confirm tool version, driver or connectivity package and firmware support.
interview.chapter15.q08.step06: Capture logs and escalate before changing security or device settings.
interview.chapter15.q08.scenario: A relay responds to ping but the vendor tool times out. Investigate the tool's service port and authentication rather than assuming the network is fully healthy.
interview.chapter15.q08.takeaway: Never disable cybersecurity controls as a shortcut.
interview.chapter15.q09.question: How do you engineer GOOSE across two different vendor tools?
interview.chapter15.q09.answer: Multi-vendor GOOSE requires consistent publisher DataSet and GoCB details plus compatible subscriber signal mapping. Import/export through SCL can assist, but both devices must be independently verified.
interview.chapter15.q09.step01: Export the publisher's correct SCL description.
interview.chapter15.q09.step02: Identify GoCB, DataSet, APPID, multicast MAC, VLAN and configuration revision.
interview.chapter15.q09.step03: Import or map the publisher references in the subscriber engineering tool.
interview.chapter15.q09.step04: Validate data types, member order, quality handling and supervision.
interview.chapter15.q09.step05: Deploy approved configurations to both IEDs.
interview.chapter15.q09.step06: Capture GOOSE traffic and perform isolated functional tests.
interview.chapter15.q09.scenario: Publisher packets appear in Wireshark but the subscriber does not react. Compare subscription mapping, DataSet structure and confRev.
interview.chapter15.q09.takeaway: Packet reception is not equivalent to successful subscriber logic.
interview.chapter15.q10.question: How do you compare an offline engineering project with an online IED?
interview.chapter15.q10.answer: Offline-to-online comparison detects configuration drift between an approved engineering baseline and the installed device. The exact compare feature differs by vendor and tool version.
interview.chapter15.q10.step01: Back up the online configuration before comparison.
interview.chapter15.q10.step02: Verify device identity, firmware and project revision.
interview.chapter15.q10.step03: Read online parameters or supported configuration fingerprint.
interview.chapter15.q10.step04: Compare communication settings, logic, DataSets, RCBs and GOOSE mappings.
interview.chapter15.q10.step05: Classify differences as approved, undocumented or critical.
interview.chapter15.q10.step06: Resolve through change control and repeat targeted FAT/SAT tests.
interview.chapter15.q10.scenario: An SCD file shows a new GOOSE DataSet but the relay still sends the old revision. Confirm whether the updated configuration was downloaded.
interview.chapter15.q10.takeaway: Do not assume exporting a project automatically updates the IED.
interview.chapter15.q11.question: What is the role of IEDScout, IEC 61850 browsers and Wireshark in commissioning?
interview.chapter15.q11.answer: IED browsers and test clients inspect IEC 61850 data and services, while Wireshark analyzes network packets. These tools complement, but do not replace, the vendor engineering software and approved test procedures.
interview.chapter15.q11.step01: Use an IEC 61850 client to establish a permitted MMS association.
interview.chapter15.q11.step02: Browse object references, values, quality and timestamps.
interview.chapter15.q11.step03: Inspect report control attributes and report delivery where permitted.
interview.chapter15.q11.step04: Use Wireshark to verify TCP/MMS and Layer 2 GOOSE packets.
interview.chapter15.q11.step05: Correlate captures with IED diagnostics, SCADA logs and the signal list.
interview.chapter15.q11.step06: Document findings and restore any temporary test configuration.
interview.chapter15.q11.scenario: SCADA misses reports although an IEC 61850 browser reads the current value. Investigate RCB enablement and client ownership.
interview.chapter15.q11.takeaway: A successful MMS read does not prove reporting works.
interview.chapter15.q12.question: How do you manage multi-vendor engineering files during FAT and SAT?
interview.chapter15.q12.answer: Engineering file management ensures that the approved station SCL model, device projects and deployed IED configurations remain traceable. A mismatch can cause difficult-to-diagnose integration faults.
interview.chapter15.q12.step01: Maintain a revision-controlled register of vendor projects and SCL exports.
interview.chapter15.q12.step02: Record IED model, firmware, tool version and IP identity.
interview.chapter15.q12.step03: Validate SCD/IID/CID consistency against the approved station design.
interview.chapter15.q12.step04: Back up deployed configurations before every approved change.
interview.chapter15.q12.step05: Run regression tests for affected reports, GOOSE subscriptions and controls.
interview.chapter15.q12.step06: Store signed test results, deviations and as-built files.
interview.chapter15.q12.scenario: A late firmware upgrade changes an ICD export and a subscriber reports confRev mismatch. Revalidate the SCL integration and retest the affected GOOSE path.
interview.chapter15.q12.takeaway: Treat engineering files as controlled deliverables, not disposable exports.
interview.chapter16.q01.question: An IED responds to ping but SCADA shows communication failure. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.chapter16.q01.answer: ICMP reachability confirms only basic IP connectivity. IEC 61850 MMS requires an operational TCP connection, MMS association, compatible model and configured acquisition. Diagnose each layer independently.
interview.chapter16.q01.step01: Confirm the correct IED IP, VLAN and physical switch port.
interview.chapter16.q01.step02: Check TCP port 102 reachability and review firewall or access-control rules.
interview.chapter16.q01.step03: Use an authorized IEC 61850 client to verify MMS association and browse a known object.
interview.chapter16.q01.step04: Inspect SCADA client logs, IED association limits and authentication or service restrictions.
interview.chapter16.q01.step05: Check SCL object references, DataSets, RCB reservation and report enablement.
interview.chapter16.q01.step06: Retest the affected SCADA points and record the fault cause.
interview.chapter16.q01.scenario: During SAT, ping succeeds but all bay points show bad quality after a SCADA restart. The MMS client fails to re-enable its reserved BRCB. Correct the client configuration and verify reporting.
interview.chapter16.q01.takeaway: Ping success does not establish IEC 61850 application health.
interview.chapter16.q02.question: Breaker status changes in the IED but not on the HMI. What is your method?
interview.chapter16.q02.answer: Trace the signal from physical input through the IEC 61850 object and acquisition chain to the HMI. Check value, quality, timestamps and mapping at each stage.
interview.chapter16.q02.step01: Verify breaker auxiliary contacts and IED binary input safely.
interview.chapter16.q02.step02: Read XCBR.Pos.stVal and its quality and timestamp using an approved client.
interview.chapter16.q02.step03: Check the configured DataSet, RCB and whether reports are reaching SCADA.
interview.chapter16.q02.step04: Compare the SCADA database object reference, inversion and quality processing.
interview.chapter16.q02.step05: Inspect the HMI symbol binding and stale-data handling.
interview.chapter16.q02.step06: Repeat Open/Close indication tests with approved isolation.
interview.chapter16.q02.scenario: IED browser shows Open and reports contain the change, but the HMI still shows Closed. The graphics symbol references a different feeder tag. Fix the HMI binding.
interview.chapter16.q02.takeaway: Always identify the first point in the chain where expected and actual values differ.
interview.chapter16.q03.question: GOOSE frames are visible in Wireshark, but the subscriber does not operate. Why?
interview.chapter16.q03.answer: Packet visibility proves frames reached the capture point, not that the subscriber accepted the message or executed logic. Subscription mapping, DataSet structure, confRev, quality and interlocks may prevent action.
interview.chapter16.q03.step01: Capture GOOSE on the subscriber-facing port or a correctly configured mirror port.
interview.chapter16.q03.step02: Compare APPID, multicast destination MAC, VLAN, GoID and DataSet reference.
interview.chapter16.q03.step03: Verify confRev and DataSet member order and data types against the subscriber configuration.
interview.chapter16.q03.step04: Check subscriber external references, GOOSE supervision and validity diagnostics.
interview.chapter16.q03.step05: Inspect subscriber logic permissives and output blocking conditions.
interview.chapter16.q03.step06: Use isolated FAT signals to verify the subscriber logic without energizing trip outputs.
interview.chapter16.q03.scenario: GOOSE traffic is present but the subscriber reports configuration mismatch after a publisher DataSet change. Re-engineer the subscription and verify the new confRev.
interview.chapter16.q03.takeaway: Separate Ethernet delivery from IEC 61850 subscription and protection logic.
interview.chapter16.q04.question: GOOSE communication stops after changing a switch. What checks do you perform?
interview.chapter16.q04.answer: GOOSE normally uses Layer 2 multicast and may use IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tags. Switch replacement can change VLAN membership, multicast handling and port configuration.
interview.chapter16.q04.step01: Check fibre/SFP link, port speed and error counters.
interview.chapter16.q04.step02: Compare old and new port VLAN membership, tagged/untagged behavior and PVID.
interview.chapter16.q04.step03: Check multicast filtering, storm control and relevant QoS policies.
interview.chapter16.q04.step04: Verify GOOSE frames enter and leave the switch with expected VLAN and destination MAC.
interview.chapter16.q04.step06: Restore approved configuration and perform an isolated functional retest.
interview.chapter16.q04.scenario: An untagged access port is replaced with a tagged trunk port; the subscriber no longer receives expected GOOSE frames. Correct port VLAN configuration.
interview.chapter16.q04.takeaway: GOOSE traffic is not validated by an IP ping test.
interview.chapter16.q05.question: PRP LAN A fails but communications remain healthy. How do you verify redundancy?
interview.chapter16.q05.answer: PRP duplicates eligible frames over two independent LANs. A single LAN failure should not interrupt supported dual-attached communication, but supervision must report the fault.
interview.chapter16.q05.step01: Confirm IEDs and switches are correctly assigned to separate LAN A and LAN B networks.
interview.chapter16.q05.step02: Check PRP supervision, duplicate discard counters and link health.
interview.chapter16.q05.step03: Record baseline MMS and GOOSE operation with both LANs healthy.
interview.chapter16.q05.step04: During an approved test, isolate only LAN A and observe service continuity.
interview.chapter16.q05.step05: Verify alarms, counters and network path behavior; restore LAN A.
interview.chapter16.q05.step06: Repeat for LAN B and document recovery results.
interview.chapter16.q05.scenario: Operators see no loss of indications when LAN A fibre is unplugged, but no redundancy alarm appears. Investigate PRP supervision and alarm mapping.
interview.chapter16.q05.takeaway: Communication continuity and fault annunciation are separate acceptance criteria.
interview.chapter16.q06.question: A SCADA alarm appears with an incorrect timestamp. How do you investigate?
interview.chapter16.q06.answer: Event time can originate at the IED, gateway or SCADA server. Incorrect synchronization, UTC/local conversion or arrival-time substitution can reorder SOE records.
interview.chapter16.q06.step01: Identify the source of the event timestamp and whether it is device-originated.
interview.chapter16.q06.step02: Check IED clock synchronization status, time source and time-quality flags.
interview.chapter16.q06.step03: Verify SNTP/NTP/PTP or IRIG-B settings as applicable.
interview.chapter16.q06.step04: Check UTC, time-zone and daylight-saving conversion at gateway and SCADA.
interview.chapter16.q06.step05: Compare the IED event log with gateway and HMI event records.
interview.chapter16.q06.step06: Generate a controlled event sequence and confirm order and accuracy.
interview.chapter16.q06.scenario: IED event time is correct but HMI SOE is offset by 5 hours 30 minutes. Review UTC-to-local conversion instead of adjusting relay clock blindly.
interview.chapter16.q06.takeaway: Never change time zones to hide a synchronization fault.
interview.chapter16.q07.question: A breaker Close command from HMI is rejected. What is your troubleshooting flow?
interview.chapter16.q07.answer: A command can fail because of user permissions, Local/Remote selection, control model, interlocking, synchrocheck, communication or device diagnostics. A rejection may be the correct safe response.
interview.chapter16.q07.step01: Confirm operating authorization and approved test boundaries.
interview.chapter16.q07.step02: Check operator role and Local/Remote status.
interview.chapter16.q07.step03: Verify the configured control object and Direct Operate or SBO sequence.
interview.chapter16.q07.step04: Read interlock, synchrocheck and other permissive statuses.
interview.chapter16.q07.step05: Inspect IEC 61850 command responses and device diagnostics.
interview.chapter16.q07.step06: Correct the engineering fault and retest without bypassing safety logic.
interview.chapter16.q07.scenario: A breaker closes locally but not from HMI because Local mode is active. Explain the expected command rejection and verify Remote selection only under approved conditions.
interview.chapter16.q07.takeaway: Do not bypass interlocks or force a live breaker to make a test pass.
interview.chapter16.q08.question: MMS reporting stops after an IED configuration download. What might have changed?
interview.chapter16.q08.answer: Downloading an engineered IED configuration may change DataSets, RCB instances, confRev or service settings. SCADA may still expect the earlier model.
interview.chapter16.q08.step01: Compare deployed IED configuration with the approved SCD/CID and prior backup.
interview.chapter16.q08.step02: Check whether the DataSet name, members or RCB references changed.
interview.chapter16.q08.step03: Verify report enablement, reservation, triggers, integrity period and client ownership.
interview.chapter16.q08.step04: Review SCADA SCL import and mapping version.
interview.chapter16.q08.step05: Inspect MMS reports and client logs to locate the mismatch.
interview.chapter16.q08.step06: Align approved configurations and retest reporting after controlled deployment.
interview.chapter16.q08.scenario: A relay update renamed a report DataSet but the SCADA client still references the old RCB. Update engineering references and retest affected points.
interview.chapter16.q08.takeaway: Keep SCADA and IED engineering revisions synchronized.
interview.chapter16.q09.question: The gateway is online but the control centre receives no IEC 104 points. How do you isolate the fault?
interview.chapter16.q09.answer: Gateway network availability is not proof that IEC 60870-5-104 is exchanging application data. Check TCP association, station addressing, mapping, quality and interrogation.
interview.chapter16.q09.step01: Verify gateway health, remote route and TCP port 2404.
interview.chapter16.q09.step02: Check IEC 104 connection state, common address and configuration parameters.
interview.chapter16.q09.step03: Review interrogation requests and corresponding ASDUs in logs or packet captures.
interview.chapter16.q09.step04: Compare IEC 61850 source values with gateway database mappings and IOAs.
interview.chapter16.q09.step05: Check invalid quality flags, blocked transmission and event queues.
interview.chapter16.q09.step06: Test representative points and document the verified end-to-end path.
interview.chapter16.q09.scenario: Gateway pings successfully but the RCC shows blank indications because the IEC 104 common address is mismatched. Correct the approved addressing and retest GI.
interview.chapter16.q09.takeaway: Test protocol-layer data transfer, not just Ethernet connectivity.
interview.chapter16.q10.question: An analog measurement is ten or one thousand times too high on HMI. What do you check?
interview.chapter16.q10.answer: Incorrect scaling usually comes from unit multipliers, CT/VT ratios, gateway conversion or duplicate SCADA scaling. Verify the actual source value and engineering units before changing factors.
interview.chapter16.q10.step01: Record the physical or injected test value and expected engineering unit.
interview.chapter16.q10.step02: Read the raw IED measurement and associated unit/multiplier.
interview.chapter16.q10.step03: Check any gateway transformation and sign convention.
interview.chapter16.q10.step04: Review SCADA tag scaling, display units and decimal precision.
interview.chapter16.q10.step05: Test multiple values across the range, including zero and negative where applicable.
interview.chapter16.q10.step06: Document the corrected scaling and verify trends and alarms.
interview.chapter16.q10.scenario: IED shows 11.0 kV but HMI shows 11000 kV because a factor of 1000 is applied twice. Remove the incorrect SCADA multiplier after approval.
interview.chapter16.q10.takeaway: Scaling fixes must be validated at more than one test point.
interview.chapter16.q11.question: One feeder shows repeated communication-loss alarms while other IEDs are healthy. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.chapter16.q11.answer: A single-IED fault suggests local physical, configuration, resource or device issues, although switch-port and VLAN policies can also affect one device. Use comparative evidence.
interview.chapter16.q11.step01: Check IED diagnostics, reboot logs, CPU load and communication service health.
interview.chapter16.q11.step02: Inspect fibre, SFP, connector cleanliness and switch-port errors.
interview.chapter16.q11.step03: Check IP conflicts, MAC learning, VLAN and ACL configuration.
interview.chapter16.q11.step04: Correlate alarm times with link flaps, MMS session resets and switch logs.
interview.chapter16.q11.step05: Capture packets at the relevant port and compare against a healthy feeder.
interview.chapter16.q11.step06: Correct the confirmed cause and monitor stability during approved tests.
interview.chapter16.q11.scenario: A switch reports intermittent CRC errors on one feeder port and the IED association repeatedly resets. Repair the physical link before modifying SCADA database settings.
interview.chapter16.q11.takeaway: Use fault timestamps and switch counters to avoid random configuration changes.
interview.chapter16.q12.question: How do you handle an intermittent fault during FAT/SAT when it cannot be reproduced immediately?
interview.chapter16.q12.answer: Intermittent faults require evidence collection, controlled reproduction and disciplined change management. Avoid marking the test passed solely because the fault disappeared.
interview.chapter16.q12.step01: Record exact symptoms, affected equipment, timestamps and environmental conditions.
interview.chapter16.q12.step02: Collect IED, SCADA, gateway and switch logs before they roll over.
interview.chapter16.q12.step03: Capture baseline network and device health data.
interview.chapter16.q12.step04: Change one approved variable at a time during safe test conditions.
interview.chapter16.q12.step05: Attempt reproducible test cases and compare with a healthy reference.
interview.chapter16.q12.step06: Document open punch-list item, risk, owner, corrective action and retest criteria.
interview.chapter16.q12.scenario: GOOSE supervision alarm appears once every few hours. Preserve packet capture and switch counters, correlate with network events and track the issue until acceptance criteria are met.
interview.chapter16.q12.takeaway: A temporary recovery is not proof that the root cause is resolved.
interview.chapter17.q01.question: Tell me about yourself for a 2–3 years SAS Engineer interview.
interview.chapter17.q01.answer: I am an Electrical and Electronics Engineering graduate focused on Substation Automation Systems. My technical preparation covers IEC 61850 data models, MMS reporting, GOOSE, SCADA/HMI mapping, station networking and FAT/SAT test procedures. I am comfortable explaining how an IED signal travels through the automation system and how to diagnose faults methodically. I describe my actual project, lab and training exposure accurately and do not claim site commissioning tasks I have not performed.
interview.chapter17.q01.step01: State your education and current role or training background in one sentence.
interview.chapter17.q01.step02: Name three to five relevant skills you can demonstrate.
interview.chapter17.q01.step03: Describe one real task you personally completed, clearly identifying lab versus project work.
interview.chapter17.q01.step04: Explain the type of SAS engineering role you are seeking.
interview.chapter17.q01.step05: Keep the spoken answer to roughly 60–90 seconds.
interview.chapter17.q01.scenario: An interviewer asks for your experience summary. If your practical work was on a simulation laptop, say that it was an engineering lab and explain the actual test results.
interview.chapter17.q01.takeaway: Use your real history; never turn training exercises into invented site experience.
interview.chapter17.q02.question: Explain a SAS project or engineering assignment you worked on.
interview.chapter17.q02.answer: A good project explanation covers scope, architecture, tools, assigned responsibility, test method, outcome and unresolved limitations. It must distinguish your individual contribution from the work of the overall team.
interview.chapter17.q02.step01: Introduce the project or training setup and its purpose.
interview.chapter17.q02.step02: Describe IEDs, station network, SCADA and gateway only where actually present.
interview.chapter17.q02.step03: Identify the exact database, mapping, configuration or testing task you handled.
interview.chapter17.q02.step04: Explain your inputs, actions, validation evidence and results.
interview.chapter17.q02.step05: State challenges and what you learned without exaggerating responsibility.
interview.chapter17.q02.scenario: If you created a simulated breaker HMI, describe the tag mapping and script verification; do not claim physical breaker commissioning.
interview.chapter17.q02.takeaway: Interviewers often ask follow-up questions about every tool and activity you mention.
interview.chapter17.q03.question: What are your main responsibilities as a SAS Engineer?
interview.chapter17.q03.answer: Typical SAS responsibilities can include IED integration, IEC 61850 configuration review, SCADA database mapping, HMI graphics, communication testing, FAT/SAT support, documentation and troubleshooting. The actual scope varies by project and seniority.
interview.chapter17.q03.step01: Start with responsibilities you have personally performed.
interview.chapter17.q03.step02: Separate tasks you independently handled from tasks you assisted or studied.
interview.chapter17.q03.step03: Connect each responsibility to a concrete deliverable, such as a signal list or test record.
interview.chapter17.q03.step04: Explain how you verified work and escalated safety-critical issues.
interview.chapter17.q03.scenario: During a panel interview, the interviewer asks whether you performed SAT. State exactly whether you executed, observed, assisted or only studied the SAT procedure.
interview.chapter17.q03.takeaway: Describe typical role scope, but label your own exposure precisely.
interview.chapter17.q04.question: Describe an IEC 61850 issue and how you would troubleshoot it.
interview.chapter17.q04.answer: An IEC 61850 problem should be investigated in layers: physical connection, network reachability, service association, IED data model, reporting or GOOSE subscription, SCADA mapping and application behavior. Evidence should determine the root cause.
interview.chapter17.q04.step01: Define the symptom and identify affected devices and points.
interview.chapter17.q04.step02: Check physical link, IP connectivity where applicable and switch diagnostics.
interview.chapter17.q04.step03: Verify MMS association or Layer 2 GOOSE packet presence as appropriate.
interview.chapter17.q04.step04: Inspect DataSet, RCB, GoCB, confRev, quality and object references.
interview.chapter17.q04.step05: Compare IED source value with SCADA or subscriber behavior.
interview.chapter17.q04.step06: Document the fault, correction and repeat test.
interview.chapter17.q04.scenario: Breaker indication is visible in an IED browser but not on the HMI. Inspect the RCB and SCADA tag mapping before changing network configuration.
interview.chapter17.q04.takeaway: Give a repeatable diagnostic sequence instead of guessing one cause.
interview.chapter17.q05.question: How would you explain GOOSE communication to an interviewer?
interview.chapter17.q05.answer: GOOSE is an IEC 61850 event messaging mechanism commonly used for fast IED-to-IED signal exchange. Conventional GOOSE uses Ethernet Layer 2 multicast with publisher and subscriber engineering; it does not depend on TCP or IP routing.
interview.chapter17.q05.step01: Identify the publisher IED and its DataSet.
interview.chapter17.q05.step02: Describe the GoCB, multicast MAC, APPID, VLAN and confRev.
interview.chapter17.q05.step05: Explain how to verify packets and subscriber logic safely.
interview.chapter17.q05.scenario: A protection IED publishes an interlock permissive but a bay controller does not update. Verify subscription configuration and packet capture.
interview.chapter17.q05.takeaway: Clearly distinguish GOOSE from MMS client-server reporting.
interview.chapter17.q06.question: How do you explain your FAT or SAT testing approach?
interview.chapter17.q06.answer: FAT validates engineered functionality in a controlled test environment; SAT validates installed interfaces and approved functionality on site. Both require traceable procedures, expected results and recorded evidence.
interview.chapter17.q06.step01: Review drawings, signal lists, control philosophy and approved test procedures.
interview.chapter17.q06.step02: Confirm test isolation and safety authorization.
interview.chapter17.q06.step03: Check communications, status, measurements, alarms and event timestamps.
interview.chapter17.q06.step04: Test controls and interlocks only under approved conditions.
interview.chapter17.q06.step05: Log defects, corrective actions and retest evidence.
interview.chapter17.q06.scenario: An HMI Close command fails during FAT because an interlock is active. Record the expected rejection and investigate permissives rather than bypassing the interlock.
interview.chapter17.q06.takeaway: Never imply you personally conducted site tests if you only practiced FAT simulations.
interview.chapter17.q07.question: What would you do if a senior engineer asks you to change a live relay setting urgently?
interview.chapter17.q07.answer: Changes to protection or control settings can affect equipment safety and service continuity. I would follow authorization, change management, backup and testing procedures rather than make an undocumented live change.
interview.chapter17.q07.step01: Confirm the request, affected device and operational risk.
interview.chapter17.q07.step02: Check work permit, approved settings and responsible authority.
interview.chapter17.q07.step03: Back up the current configuration and record the existing revision.
interview.chapter17.q07.step04: Prepare a reviewed change and rollback plan.
interview.chapter17.q07.step05: Implement only with required authorization and safe operating conditions.
