interview.chapter17.q07.step06: Validate results and document the final as-built configuration.
interview.chapter17.q07.scenario: A request arrives to disable an interlock to complete a test. Escalate and use an approved isolated test arrangement instead.
interview.chapter17.q07.takeaway: Safety and traceability are stronger answers than speed.
interview.chapter17.q08.question: How do you work with protection, SCADA and networking teams?
interview.chapter17.q08.answer: SAS integration crosses disciplines. Clear interface definitions, approved signal lists, coordinated test windows and defect ownership reduce integration errors.
interview.chapter17.q08.step01: Confirm the responsible team for each IED, switch, gateway and HMI function.
interview.chapter17.q08.step02: Use shared interface documents and configuration revisions.
interview.chapter17.q08.step03: Communicate exact object references, IP/VLAN details and test expectations.
interview.chapter17.q08.step05: Track ownership, corrective actions and retest results.
interview.chapter17.q08.scenario: A GOOSE subscription fails. Share the publisher capture and subscriber configuration evidence with the protection and network teams rather than assigning blame.
interview.chapter17.q08.takeaway: Explain technical collaboration using artifacts and test evidence.
interview.chapter17.q09.question: How do you handle an unfamiliar engineering tool?
interview.chapter17.q09.answer: I first confirm the supported device and tool version, read vendor documentation, work on a backed-up offline project, and validate any change in a safe test environment. I ask for review before touching production configurations.
interview.chapter17.q09.step01: Identify the tool, device model, firmware and required license or package.
interview.chapter17.q09.step02: Study the relevant engineering workflow and safety notes.
interview.chapter17.q09.step03: Open a training project or backed-up configuration.
interview.chapter17.q09.step04: Practice read, compare, export and validation functions.
interview.chapter17.q09.step05: Record results and request peer review.
interview.chapter17.q09.step06: Move to live systems only after authorization and competency checks.
interview.chapter17.q09.scenario: Asked about a tool you have only seen in training, explain what you practiced and what you would need to learn for deployment.
interview.chapter17.q09.takeaway: An accurate limitation plus a structured learning plan is better than a false claim.
interview.chapter17.q10.question: Describe a difficult troubleshooting situation and what you learned.
interview.chapter17.q10.answer: Use a clear Situation–Task–Action–Result structure. The result should be measurable or observable, and the description should be based on a genuine project or lab exercise.
interview.chapter17.q10.step01: State the symptom and operational impact.
interview.chapter17.q10.step02: Explain your assigned task and the initial evidence.
interview.chapter17.q10.step03: Describe the checks in the order you performed them.
interview.chapter17.q10.step04: Identify the actual root cause, or say if it remained unresolved.
interview.chapter17.q10.step05: Report the observed result and a preventive lesson.
interview.chapter17.q10.scenario: In a training lab, an HMI breaker symbol failed to change after a script edit. Explain the tag binding, script test, correction and verified outcome if that is what actually happened.
interview.chapter17.q10.takeaway: Never invent an outage, site incident or customer project to make the story impressive.
interview.chapter17.q11.question: What is the difference between your knowledge and your hands-on experience?
interview.chapter17.q11.answer: Knowledge means I can explain a concept and its configuration principles; hands-on experience means I personally used the relevant tools or equipment and verified results. Site commissioning, factory testing and laptop simulation are different types of exposure.
interview.chapter17.q11.step01: List concepts you can explain confidently.
interview.chapter17.q11.step02: List tools you actually operated and what you did with them.
interview.chapter17.q11.step03: Separate simulated tests from physical equipment testing.
interview.chapter17.q11.step04: Identify gaps you are actively closing.
interview.chapter17.q11.step05: Offer to walk through a real configuration or troubleshooting exercise.
interview.chapter17.q11.scenario: If asked whether you commissioned a relay on site, answer directly and then explain your related offline configuration and test practice.
interview.chapter17.q11.takeaway: Precise experience claims help the interviewer assess your readiness fairly.
interview.chapter17.q12.question: Why should we hire you for a 2–3 years SAS engineering role?
interview.chapter17.q12.answer: My strengths are structured IEC 61850 and SCADA fundamentals, careful troubleshooting, documentation discipline and willingness to learn vendor-specific workflows. I can contribute to engineering support and testing tasks appropriate to my demonstrated skills, and I will escalate unfamiliar or safety-critical work.
interview.chapter17.q12.step01: Match your verified skills to the job description.
interview.chapter17.q12.step03: Emphasize evidence-based testing and safe change management.
interview.chapter17.q12.step04: Show willingness to learn the employer's engineering tools.
interview.chapter17.q12.step05: Avoid unsupported promises about independent commissioning experience.
interview.chapter17.q12.scenario: For a multi-vendor integration role, highlight a real GOOSE mapping or MMS reporting exercise you completed and describe its limitations.
interview.chapter17.q12.takeaway: Confidence comes from specific verifiable examples, not overstated experience.
interview.chapter18.q01.question: Explain a typical SAS architecture from process level to station level.
interview.chapter18.q01.answer: A SAS integrates process equipment and IEDs with station-level SCADA, engineering workstations, gateways, and time sources. Bay-level protection and control functions remain engineered independently of the operator display. IEC 61850 MMS commonly supports supervision and control; GOOSE supports fast peer-to-peer event exchange.
interview.chapter18.q01.step02: Identify process interfaces and bay ieds.
interview.chapter18.q01.step06: Validate one signal end to end.
interview.chapter18.q01.scenario: An HMI loses one bay while other bays remain healthy. Trace that bay IED, switch path, MMS session, report and SCADA mapping.
interview.chapter18.q01.takeaway: Explain functional layers and actual interfaces, not only a block diagram.
interview.chapter18.q02.question: How does redundant SCADA server architecture work?
interview.chapter18.q02.answer: Two servers may operate as primary/standby or in another vendor-specific redundancy model. Redundancy involves application state, acquisition ownership, historian/event synchronization, and operator connectivity, not simply two PCs on a network.
interview.chapter18.q02.step01: Identify the redundancy design and active roles.
interview.chapter18.q02.step03: Verify acquisition ownership and report reservations.
interview.chapter18.q02.step05: Confirm hmi values and soe continuity.
interview.chapter18.q02.scenario: Primary SCADA fails and the standby becomes active but some IED reports stop. Check RCB reservation and report re-enablement by the new client.
interview.chapter18.q02.takeaway: Never assume failover is seamless without functional tests.
interview.chapter18.q03.question: What is gateway redundancy and how would you test it?
interview.chapter18.q03.answer: Station gateways may use active/standby or other supported redundancy schemes to maintain remote control center communication. The mechanism, addressing, state replication and command authority depend on the gateway vendor and protocol configuration.
interview.chapter18.q03.step03: Check downstream iec 104 or other interface.
interview.chapter18.q03.step06: Check gi, indications, events and commands.
interview.chapter18.q03.scenario: Remote control center stops receiving events after gateway switchover although the standby TCP session is established. Verify event queues, interrogation and mapping.
interview.chapter18.q03.takeaway: Distinguish a healthy TCP connection from healthy application data.
interview.chapter18.q04.question: Compare PRP and HSR in a redundant substation network.
interview.chapter18.q04.answer: PRP sends duplicate frames over independent LAN A and LAN B; a dual-attached node accepts the first valid copy and discards duplicates. HSR uses a ring where participating nodes forward frames around both directions. RedBoxes can interface singly attached equipment with a redundant domain where supported.
interview.chapter18.q04.step02: Verify prp lan independence or hsr ring connections.
interview.chapter18.q04.scenario: An IED continues MMS on PRP LAN A failure but raises a redundancy alarm. That may be expected continuity with degraded redundancy; investigate the failed path.
interview.chapter18.q04.takeaway: PRP and HSR are distinct designs, not interchangeable switch settings.
interview.chapter18.q05.question: How do you integrate single-attached devices into a redundant station network?
interview.chapter18.q05.answer: A single-attached node does not natively provide PRP or HSR redundancy. Depending on the architecture, a RedBox or supported infrastructure can connect it to a redundant network, but the device-side link can remain a single point of failure.
interview.chapter18.q05.step01: Identify san, danp or danh device capabilities.
interview.chapter18.q05.step04: Validate mac learning and duplicate handling.
interview.chapter18.q05.step06: Document residual single points of failure.
interview.chapter18.q05.scenario: A legacy gateway connects through a RedBox and loses service when its only copper cable is unplugged. Explain why network redundancy does not protect that single device link.
interview.chapter18.q05.takeaway: State the limits of redundancy clearly.
interview.chapter18.q06.question: How do you design VLANs for MMS and GOOSE traffic?
interview.chapter18.q06.answer: VLANs can segment traffic and support engineering control of multicast forwarding. MMS generally uses TCP/IP while conventional GOOSE is Ethernet Layer 2 multicast. VLAN IDs, tagging, priorities and port membership must match the approved station design.
interview.chapter18.q06.step04: Check multicast forwarding and subscriber port membership.
interview.chapter18.q06.step06: Test controlled changes and restore baseline.
interview.chapter18.q06.scenario: GOOSE is visible on the publisher switch port but not at the subscriber. Check VLAN membership and multicast filtering before editing the relay DataSet.
interview.chapter18.q06.takeaway: GOOSE is not made routable by adding an IP address.
interview.chapter18.q07.question: What is IEC 61850 interoperability and how is it validated?
interview.chapter18.q07.answer: Interoperability means independently engineered devices and clients exchange required services and data correctly. Standards compliance helps but does not guarantee every optional service, control model or vendor interpretation will match the station requirements.
interview.chapter18.q07.step01: Compare device capability and conformance information.
interview.chapter18.q07.step02: Validate scl versions and data models.
interview.chapter18.q07.step04: Confirm control model and quality handling.
interview.chapter18.q07.scenario: A SCADA client can read values from a third-party IED but cannot operate a breaker. Verify control model, authority, origin and command sequence.
interview.chapter18.q07.takeaway: Test each required service rather than claiming interoperability from a successful ping.
interview.chapter18.q08.question: How do you manage SCD revisions across multiple vendors?
interview.chapter18.q08.answer: The SCD is the coordinated station configuration description. Engineering changes may affect IED subscriptions, reports, naming and communication parameters; updates need controlled distribution and device-level validation.
interview.chapter18.q08.step01: Back up approved scd and vendor projects.
interview.chapter18.q08.step03: Validate scl syntax and object references.
interview.chapter18.q08.scenario: A publisher DataSet changes after an SCD revision but subscriber configuration is not updated. GOOSE frames arrive while the subscriber rejects the new configuration.
interview.chapter18.q08.takeaway: An SCD update is not automatically downloaded to all devices.
interview.chapter18.q09.question: How do you isolate a system-wide communication fault?
interview.chapter18.q09.answer: System-wide faults require determining the scope and common dependencies before changing individual devices. Possible shared causes include switch uplinks, VLAN changes, time source failures, server acquisition faults and gateway configuration.
interview.chapter18.q09.step02: Identify common network paths and services.
interview.chapter18.q09.step03: Check switch health and recent changes.
interview.chapter18.q09.scenario: Multiple bays become stale simultaneously after a core switch maintenance window. Compare affected VLANs and uplink counters rather than changing every relay.
interview.chapter18.q09.takeaway: Use a fault-domain approach to avoid unnecessary changes.
interview.chapter18.q10.question: How do you test time synchronization in a redundant SAS?
interview.chapter18.q10.answer: Accurate event sequence depends on source clock health, protocol configuration, device support and timestamp handling. Redundant time servers may provide resilience, but failover behavior and accuracy must be verified.
interview.chapter18.q10.step01: Identify supported ntp/sntp, ptp or irig-b sources.
interview.chapter18.q10.step05: Isolate the primary source in a controlled test.
interview.chapter18.q10.scenario: After a time-server failure, SOE order appears inconsistent across bays. Inspect clock offset, synchronization flags and source timestamps.
interview.chapter18.q10.takeaway: Do not infer event order solely from server arrival time.
interview.chapter18.q11.question: How would you plan a full-system FAT for a redundant SAS?
interview.chapter18.q11.answer: A system FAT should validate integrated functions and failure recovery using approved architecture, signal lists, control philosophy and acceptance criteria. Tests must include negative and degraded-mode behavior, not only nominal indications.
interview.chapter18.q11.step01: Review approved test scope and safety isolation.
interview.chapter18.q11.step03: Test representative mms reports and goose.
interview.chapter18.q11.step05: Test server, gateway and network failover.
interview.chapter18.q11.step06: Check control rejection and alarm handling.
interview.chapter18.q11.scenario: The HMI remains responsive during server failover but breaker controls time out. Record the failed control path and examine active-server command ownership.
interview.chapter18.q11.takeaway: Include restoration and regression tests after each simulated fault.
interview.chapter18.q12.question: How do you approach cybersecurity and change control in SAS integration?
interview.chapter18.q12.answer: Substation automation changes must preserve availability, integrity and operational safety. Access permissions, network segmentation, backups, logging and reviewed change windows help prevent unplanned outages. Exact controls depend on the project security policy.
interview.chapter18.q12.step01: Identify assets and approved access paths.
interview.chapter18.q12.step03: Assess impact on protection and control.
interview.chapter18.q12.step05: Apply changes in an authorized window.
interview.chapter18.q12.scenario: A new switch ACL blocks TCP 102 and SCADA reports become stale. Validate the rule against approved traffic requirements rather than disabling all security controls.
interview.chapter18.q12.takeaway: Never bypass protections or security rules just to complete a test.
interview.chapter19.q01.question: How do you plan system-level SAS commissioning before energization?
interview.chapter19.q01.answer: Commissioning is a controlled verification of the complete SAS, from IEDs and networks through SCADA and the gateway. The plan must define scope, responsibilities, safety boundaries, prerequisites and acceptance evidence.
interview.chapter19.q01.step01: Review approved drawings, signal lists, SCD files, network design and test procedures.
interview.chapter19.q01.step02: Confirm IED firmware, configuration revisions, IP/VLAN plan and time source.
interview.chapter19.q01.step03: Agree isolation boundaries, work permits, control authority and rollback plans.
interview.chapter19.q01.step04: Verify communication and point mapping before any functional control test.
interview.chapter19.q01.step05: Execute approved test cases and record expected/actual values, quality and timestamps.
interview.chapter19.q01.step06: Close punch-list items with retest evidence and obtain sign-off.
interview.chapter19.q01.scenario: During pre-energization checks, a bay has correct MMS communication but an unverified close interlock. Hold the affected control test until the permissive logic is reviewed and safe isolation is confirmed.
interview.chapter19.q01.takeaway: Acceptance is evidence-based; a green communication indicator is not commissioning sign-off.
interview.chapter19.q02.question: An entire bay disappears from SCADA after a switch replacement. How do you isolate the fault?
interview.chapter19.q02.answer: A complete bay outage suggests a shared communication path or configuration issue, but it should not be assumed. Compare switch port status, VLAN membership, addressing and IEC 61850 services with the approved baseline.
interview.chapter19.q02.step01: Define the scope: one IED, one bay, or multiple bays.
interview.chapter19.q02.step02: Check power, fibre/SFP link, port errors and switch logs.
interview.chapter19.q02.step03: Compare replacement switch VLAN tagging, port membership and trunk settings.
interview.chapter19.q02.step04: Verify IP/ARP connectivity and TCP 102 access for MMS where permitted.
interview.chapter19.q02.step05: Inspect SCADA association and reporting status after connectivity is restored.
interview.chapter19.q02.step06: Recheck alarms, status, controls and redundancy; record the root cause.
interview.chapter19.q02.scenario: The new switch has the correct physical links but the bay VLAN is not permitted on its uplink. Correct the approved switch configuration and repeat point tests.
interview.chapter19.q02.takeaway: Do not change IED settings until the shared network path is understood.
interview.chapter19.q03.question: GOOSE packets are visible, but an interlocking permissive is not updating. What is your approach?
interview.chapter19.q03.answer: GOOSE reception at a capture point does not prove successful subscription or application logic. Check publisher configuration, subscriber mapping, supervision and quality before interpreting the permissive.
interview.chapter19.q03.step01: Confirm the publisher DataSet value changes and GoCB is enabled.
interview.chapter19.q03.step02: Inspect APPID, destination MAC, VLAN, confRev, stNum and sqNum in capture.
interview.chapter19.q03.step03: Verify the subscriber expects the correct publisher reference and DataSet member order/types.
interview.chapter19.q03.step04: Inspect subscriber GOOSE supervision, quality and validity diagnostics.
interview.chapter19.q03.step05: Check the mapped internal signal and interlocking logic.
interview.chapter19.q03.step06: Use approved isolated tests and verify the final permissive without bypassing safety logic.
interview.chapter19.q03.scenario: A firmware update changed the publisher DataSet revision; the subscriber sees frames but rejects the configuration. Update engineering consistently and retest.
interview.chapter19.q03.takeaway: Separate Ethernet delivery, subscription acceptance and protection logic.
interview.chapter19.q04.question: What would you do if MMS reports stop after a SCADA server failover?
interview.chapter19.q04.answer: Server failover may change the MMS client identity, associations and RCB ownership. Buffered and unbuffered reporting behavior depends on IED capabilities and client configuration.
interview.chapter19.q04.step01: Confirm which SCADA server is active and whether the standby took over.
interview.chapter19.q04.step02: Check network reachability and MMS association from the new active server.
interview.chapter19.q04.step03: Inspect report control reservation, enablement and configured client identity.
interview.chapter19.q04.step04: Verify DataSet, trigger options, GI and buffered entry handling as applicable.
interview.chapter19.q04.step05: Compare received report traffic with SCADA point status and timestamps.
interview.chapter19.q04.step06: Test failback and record expected report continuity and any gaps.
interview.chapter19.q04.scenario: After failover, the new active server establishes MMS but does not enable the assigned BRCB. Restore the approved client/RCB workflow and retest.
interview.chapter19.q04.takeaway: A successful failover ping is not proof of report recovery.
interview.chapter19.q05.question: How do you test PRP redundancy without interrupting SAS functions?
interview.chapter19.q05.answer: PRP dual-attached nodes use independent LAN A and LAN B paths. A valid redundancy test demonstrates continued communication after an approved single-LAN failure while preserving diagnostics and service quality.
interview.chapter19.q05.step01: Confirm DANP connections to physically independent LAN A and LAN B.
interview.chapter19.q05.step02: Record baseline link status, PRP diagnostics and normal MMS/GOOSE behavior.
interview.chapter19.q05.step03: Obtain authorization for a controlled single-path interruption.
interview.chapter19.q05.step04: Disable or disconnect one approved test path while monitoring point updates and packet counters.
interview.chapter19.q05.step05: Verify traffic continuity, loss diagnostics and recovery after restoring the path.
interview.chapter19.q05.step06: Repeat for the other LAN only if the approved procedure allows it.
interview.chapter19.q05.scenario: A station remains operational when LAN A is disconnected but an IED reports PRP duplicate discard errors after reconnection. Inspect LAN separation and topology.
interview.chapter19.q05.takeaway: Do not disconnect both PRP LANs or treat two ports on one switch as independent redundancy.
interview.chapter19.q06.question: How do you investigate an incorrect SOE sequence during a trip event?
interview.chapter19.q06.answer: SOE ordering depends on source timestamps, time synchronization, timestamp quality and event buffering. SCADA arrival order can differ from the actual event order.
interview.chapter19.q06.step01: Collect IED event records and SCADA SOE exports for the same incident.
interview.chapter19.q06.step02: Check UTC/time zone handling and whether devices were synchronized.
interview.chapter19.q06.step03: Compare source timestamps, timestamp quality and server receive times.
interview.chapter19.q06.step04: Inspect SNTP/PTP/IRIG-B source status, offsets and holdover alarms.
interview.chapter19.q06.step05: Check event buffering, gateway translation and report delay.
interview.chapter19.q06.step06: Correct the verified cause and perform a controlled multi-event test.
interview.chapter19.q06.scenario: SCADA shows breaker open before protection trip, but the relay clock is several seconds ahead of the BCU. Repair synchronization and retest ordering.
interview.chapter19.q06.takeaway: Do not reorder records manually to make an event sequence appear correct.
interview.chapter19.q07.question: A breaker close command is rejected even though the HMI shows all permissives healthy. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.chapter19.q07.answer: The HMI display may not reflect every IED-level permissive or the configured control model. Control failures require examination of authority, interlocking, SBO sequence and device response.
interview.chapter19.q07.step01: Confirm the equipment is in an approved isolated test state and remote control is permitted.
interview.chapter19.q07.step02: Check Local/Remote, operator authority and command object reference.
interview.chapter19.q07.step03: Inspect CILO, synchrocheck, spring charge and other required permissives.
interview.chapter19.q07.step04: Verify direct-operate or SBO workflow, select timeout and origin attributes.
interview.chapter19.q07.step05: Read the device command response and event log, not just the HMI message.
interview.chapter19.q07.step06: Correct the underlying configuration or condition and repeat the approved test.
interview.chapter19.q07.scenario: The HMI permissive tag is stale while CILO reports blocked. Fix acquisition/quality handling rather than bypassing the interlock.
interview.chapter19.q07.takeaway: Never force a breaker close to demonstrate successful commissioning.
interview.chapter19.q08.question: IEC 104 gateway is connected to RCC but some indications are wrong. What is your troubleshooting method?
interview.chapter19.q08.answer: IEC 104 link health does not prove correct information-object mapping, quality, timestamps or command handling. Diagnose source-to-gateway-to-master mapping point by point.
interview.chapter19.q08.step01: Identify affected IOAs, types and common address from the approved point list.
interview.chapter19.q08.step02: Verify corresponding IED/SCADA source values and quality.
interview.chapter19.q08.step03: Inspect gateway mapping, inversion, timestamp conversion and scaling.
interview.chapter19.q08.step04: Check IEC 104 spontaneous transmission and General Interrogation behavior.
interview.chapter19.q08.step05: Compare gateway transmit capture with RCC received values.
interview.chapter19.q08.step06: Retest corrected points and ensure other mapped points remain unaffected.
interview.chapter19.q08.scenario: RCC shows a feeder disconnector open when it is closed because the gateway point polarity was inverted. Correct the mapping and document the test.
interview.chapter19.q08.takeaway: Use source, gateway and control-centre evidence to isolate the first wrong stage.
interview.chapter19.q09.question: How do you diagnose intermittent MMS disconnections across multiple IEDs?
interview.chapter19.q09.answer: Intermittent outages may originate from congestion, switch errors, routing, duplicated addresses, server resource exhaustion or session timeouts. A time-correlated evidence set is essential.
interview.chapter19.q09.step01: Build a timeline from SCADA logs and IED communication alarms.
interview.chapter19.q09.step02: Check switch port errors, interface utilization, MAC flapping and redundancy events.
interview.chapter19.q09.step03: Inspect duplicate IP/ARP anomalies and TCP retransmissions in captures.
interview.chapter19.q09.step04: Review server CPU, memory, connection limits and MMS client behavior.
interview.chapter19.q09.step05: Correlate disconnects with backups, network changes or traffic bursts.
interview.chapter19.q09.step06: Apply one controlled correction and verify stability over an agreed observation period.
interview.chapter19.q09.scenario: Multiple relays disconnect at the same minute during a scheduled network scan. Confirm correlation and review authorized scan scope with the cybersecurity team.
interview.chapter19.q09.takeaway: Avoid restarting all IEDs before collecting evidence.
interview.chapter19.q10.question: What is your process for a multi-vendor SCD or firmware change during SAT?
interview.chapter19.q10.answer: A late SCD or firmware change can affect object references, DataSets, GOOSE subscriptions, report control settings and vendor project compatibility. Changes require impact assessment and regression testing.
interview.chapter19.q10.step01: Identify the exact devices, firmware and SCL revisions affected.
interview.chapter19.q10.step02: Back up vendor projects and installed configurations.
interview.chapter19.q10.step03: Run SCL validation and compare the approved station model with new exports.
interview.chapter19.q10.step04: Review MMS references, RCBs, GoCBs, confRev and subscriber mapping.
interview.chapter19.q10.step05: Deploy only under approved change control and maintain rollback artifacts.
interview.chapter19.q10.step06: Run targeted regression tests and update as-built documentation.
interview.chapter19.q10.scenario: An updated publisher firmware changes GOOSE DataSet structure. Retest every subscriber that depends on the publisher before SAT sign-off.
interview.chapter19.q10.takeaway: A successful configuration download is not proof of system interoperability.
interview.chapter19.q11.question: How do you handle a critical FAT/SAT defect that cannot be resolved immediately?
interview.chapter19.q11.answer: Critical defects require a clear risk assessment, containment, ownership and formal disposition. Testing may continue only where safe and authorized; acceptance should not hide unresolved functions.
interview.chapter19.q11.step01: Log the defect with equipment ID, reproducible steps and expected/actual results.
interview.chapter19.q11.step02: Capture logs, screenshots, packet traces and configuration versions.
interview.chapter19.q11.step03: Classify severity and operational or safety impact with responsible engineers.
interview.chapter19.q11.step04: Define containment and stop affected tests if needed.
interview.chapter19.q11.step05: Assign corrective action, retest criteria and due date.
interview.chapter19.q11.step06: Obtain formal review of residual risk and acceptance status.
interview.chapter19.q11.scenario: An interlocking signal remains unreliable before energization. Keep the function open as a blocking defect rather than marking the test passed.
interview.chapter19.q11.takeaway: A punch-list item is not closed until its fix is verified.
interview.chapter19.q12.question: Explain a structured root-cause analysis after a SAS integration failure.
interview.chapter19.q12.answer: Root-cause analysis should distinguish symptoms from the underlying defect and establish evidence linking the cause to the failure. Corrective actions should include prevention and regression checks.
interview.chapter19.q12.step01: State the failure, affected scope and impact in precise terms.
interview.chapter19.q12.step02: Build a timeline using device logs, SCADA events and network captures.
interview.chapter19.q12.step03: List plausible causes across field, IED, network, protocol, database and HMI layers.
interview.chapter19.q12.step04: Test hypotheses against observations without making unsafe changes.
interview.chapter19.q12.step05: Document the confirmed cause, correction and verification results.
interview.chapter19.q12.step06: Update engineering checklists, baselines or tests to prevent recurrence.
interview.chapter19.q12.scenario: A GOOSE subscriber fails after a switch replacement. Evidence shows the switch port dropped the required VLAN; revise the switch acceptance checklist.
interview.chapter19.q12.takeaway: An interview answer is stronger when it explains why other suspected causes were ruled out.
interview.chapter20.q01.question: In two minutes, explain the complete SAS signal path from a breaker to the control centre.
interview.chapter20.q01.answer: Start with the breaker auxiliary contact, IED input and IEC 61850 data object. The station SCADA acquires the value using its configured MMS reporting or other acquisition service, then maps it to a database point and HMI symbol. A station gateway separately maps approved signals to the control-centre protocol, commonly IEC 60870-5-104. The status, quality and event timestamp must remain consistent throughout.
interview.chapter20.q01.step01: Identify the physical contact and IED terminal.
interview.chapter20.q01.step02: Verify the IED data reference, such as XCBR.Pos.stVal, quality and timestamp.
interview.chapter20.q01.step03: Confirm DataSet, RCB and MMS report delivery to SCADA.
interview.chapter20.q01.step04: Verify SCADA point mapping, alarm/SOE and HMI symbol.
interview.chapter20.q01.step05: Check gateway point address, type, quality mapping and control-centre receipt.
interview.chapter20.q01.scenario: IED shows breaker Open, local HMI shows Open, but RCC shows Closed. Isolate the fault at gateway mapping, IEC 104 transfer or RCC database rather than changing the relay.
interview.chapter20.q01.takeaway: Give the path in order and identify the first stage with incorrect data.
interview.chapter20.q02.question: An IED responds to ping, but the SCADA server cannot establish MMS communication. What do you check?
interview.chapter20.q02.answer: Ping proves only that ICMP reachability may exist. MMS uses TCP port 102 and application association services, so firewall policy, TCP connectivity, service availability and client/server compatibility must be verified separately.
interview.chapter20.q02.step01: Confirm correct IP, subnet, VLAN and physical link.
interview.chapter20.q02.step02: Test TCP port 102 reachability from the actual SCADA host.
interview.chapter20.q02.step03: Check IED MMS server enablement and allowed client connections.
interview.chapter20.q02.step04: Inspect association attempts and error messages in SCADA logs or Wireshark.
interview.chapter20.q02.step05: Check supported services, configuration revisions and server capacity.
interview.chapter20.q02.step06: Retest association and confirm a valid data read or report.
interview.chapter20.q02.scenario: A laptop pings the relay but SCADA shows connection refused on TCP 102. Check IED service and access restrictions before altering RCB settings.
interview.chapter20.q02.takeaway: Ping success does not prove IEC 61850 application connectivity.
interview.chapter20.q03.question: MMS association is healthy, but breaker status is not updating. Explain your troubleshooting sequence.
interview.chapter20.q03.answer: A live MMS association is not the same as correct report delivery. The source object, DataSet, Report Control Block and SCADA mapping must all be consistent. For polling systems, inspect the polling request and response instead.
interview.chapter20.q03.step01: Confirm the IED source value changes and has valid quality.
interview.chapter20.q03.step02: Check the expected DataSet member and functional constraint.
interview.chapter20.q03.step03: Inspect RCB enabled state, reservation, trigger options and report identifier.
interview.chapter20.q03.step04: Capture report traffic and verify the object reference and value.
interview.chapter20.q03.step05: Check SCADA acquisition status, tag mapping and HMI binding.
interview.chapter20.q03.step06: Correct the first failed stage and repeat the controlled test.
interview.chapter20.q03.scenario: After a SCADA restart, indications freeze although the association returns. Verify that the client re-enables the intended RCB instance.
interview.chapter20.q04.question: GOOSE packets are visible in Wireshark but the subscriber output does not operate. Why?
interview.chapter20.q04.answer: GOOSE packet visibility proves network delivery at the capture point, not that the subscriber accepts the message or its application logic operates. Subscription matching, DataSet structure, configuration revision, quality and interlocks can all block the intended action.
interview.chapter20.q04.step01: Verify publisher GoCB, DataSet and actual transmitted values.
interview.chapter20.q04.step02: Compare APPID, multicast MAC, VLAN and confRev with subscriber engineering.
interview.chapter20.q04.step03: Confirm expected DataSet member order, types and external references.
interview.chapter20.q04.step04: Inspect subscriber communication supervision and quality checks.
interview.chapter20.q04.step05: Verify downstream logic, permissives and output mapping.
interview.chapter20.q04.step06: Perform an isolated, approved functional test with trip outputs controlled.
interview.chapter20.q04.scenario: Publisher changes a permissive, stNum increments, but subscriber does not respond after an SCD update. Compare confRev and imported subscriber mapping.
interview.chapter20.q04.takeaway: Do not bypass protection or interlocks to make a GOOSE test pass.
interview.chapter20.q05.question: How do you prove PRP redundancy during FAT without causing an outage?
interview.chapter20.q05.answer: PRP dual-attached nodes send duplicate frames over independent LAN A and LAN B. A valid redundancy test verifies communication continuity during an approved single-LAN failure and restores both paths afterward.
interview.chapter20.q05.step01: Review topology and confirm the two LANs are independent.
interview.chapter20.q05.step02: Check DANP ports, switch links and redundancy diagnostics.
interview.chapter20.q05.step03: Establish baseline MMS, GOOSE and alarm behavior.
interview.chapter20.q05.step04: Under an approved FAT procedure, isolate one LAN path.
interview.chapter20.q05.step05: Verify continuity, packet loss indicators and device alarms.
interview.chapter20.q05.step06: Restore the LAN, repeat for the other path if authorized, and record evidence.
interview.chapter20.q05.scenario: SCADA stays online when LAN A is disconnected, but a switch alarm appears. This can be expected; investigate if any required data path actually fails.
interview.chapter20.q05.takeaway: Do not confuse PRP with RSTP or HSR.
interview.chapter20.q06.question: A breaker Close command from HMI is rejected. How do you diagnose it safely?
interview.chapter20.q06.answer: Breaker control depends on operator authority, Local/Remote status, the IEC 61850 control model, device permissives and the physical switching circuit. A rejected command can be correct behavior when an interlock is not satisfied.
interview.chapter20.q06.step01: Confirm authorization and equipment test isolation.
interview.chapter20.q06.step02: Verify the selected breaker and HMI command mapping.
interview.chapter20.q06.step03: Check Local/Remote mode and operator access rights.
interview.chapter20.q06.step04: Inspect CSWI/CILO permissives, synchrocheck and interlocking logic.
interview.chapter20.q06.step05: Check Direct Operate or SBO select/operate sequence and diagnostic response.
interview.chapter20.q06.step06: Verify command outcome using independent XCBR feedback; record rejection reason.
interview.chapter20.q06.scenario: Close is rejected because an earthing switch is closed. Confirm the interlock and report the expected rejection; never force the close.
interview.chapter20.q06.takeaway: A safe refusal is not automatically a software defect.
interview.chapter20.q07.question: SOE event order is incorrect after commissioning. What could cause it?
interview.chapter20.q07.answer: Incorrect SOE order may come from clock drift, unsynchronized IEDs, UTC/time-zone conversion, different timestamp sources, delayed reporting or SCADA sorting by arrival time rather than event time.
interview.chapter20.q07.step01: Compare IED clock against the approved time source.
interview.chapter20.q07.step03: Inspect event timestamp, time-quality flags and server arrival time.
interview.chapter20.q07.step04: Confirm UTC and local time conversions across systems.
interview.chapter20.q07.step05: Generate two safe test events in known order.
interview.chapter20.q07.step06: Correct synchronization or display processing and repeat the SOE test.
interview.chapter20.q07.scenario: A trip appears before protection pickup in SCADA although relay logs show the opposite. Compare source timestamps and time-quality before blaming logic.
interview.chapter20.q07.takeaway: Always distinguish event time from receipt time.
interview.chapter20.q08.question: The control centre receives IEC 104 indications but remote commands fail. Where do you look?
interview.chapter20.q08.answer: IEC 104 monitoring and control can use different mappings, permissions and command semantics. Successful indications do not prove that command addresses, select/execute sequences and interlocks are configured correctly.
interview.chapter20.q08.step01: Check gateway IEC 104 connection and command permissions.
interview.chapter20.q08.step02: Verify command Type ID, common address and information object address.
interview.chapter20.q08.step03: Check select/execute behavior and cause-of-transmission handling.
interview.chapter20.q08.step04: Trace gateway-to-IED control mapping and IEC 61850 control model.
interview.chapter20.q08.step06: Use an approved isolated command test and review confirmations.
interview.chapter20.q08.scenario: RCC sees breaker status but receives negative confirmation for Close. Inspect IEC 104 command mapping and IED rejection reason.
interview.chapter20.q08.takeaway: Treat remote commands as safety-critical; do not test on live equipment without authorization.
interview.chapter20.q09.question: What is your method for diagnosing a multi-vendor IED integration issue?
interview.chapter20.q09.answer: First verify the device's actual IEC 61850 capabilities and deployed configuration, then compare the station SCL engineering model with online behavior. Different vendor tools may express similar services differently, so packet evidence and object references are useful neutral references.
interview.chapter20.q09.step01: Record device model, firmware, vendor tool and SCL file revisions.
interview.chapter20.q09.step02: Validate ICD/IID/CID/SCD consistency and actual online model.
interview.chapter20.q09.step03: Compare DataSets, RCBs, GoCBs, confRev and data types.
interview.chapter20.q09.step04: Verify IP/VLAN and network transport separately.
interview.chapter20.q09.step05: Use IEC 61850 browser and Wireshark captures for independent evidence.
interview.chapter20.q09.step06: Document correction, approval and regression test.
interview.chapter20.q09.scenario: After replacing an IED, SCADA reports work but a GOOSE subscriber flags configuration mismatch. Compare the new device's publisher confRev and DataSet.
interview.chapter20.q09.takeaway: Do not assume an imported ICD represents the installed configuration.
interview.chapter20.q10.question: During FAT you discover 15 unmapped alarms. How do you manage the defect?
interview.chapter20.q10.answer: FAT issues should be documented with traceable references, severity, responsible owner, corrective action and retest evidence. The goal is controlled closure, not hiding exceptions to achieve sign-off.
interview.chapter20.q10.step01: Record each alarm with signal-list ID, expected result and observed result.
interview.chapter20.q10.step02: Capture source values, screenshots and relevant logs.
interview.chapter20.q10.step03: Classify impact and assign the appropriate engineering owner.
interview.chapter20.q10.step04: Correct mapping or alarm logic through change control.
interview.chapter20.q10.step05: Retest each affected point and related functionality.
interview.chapter20.q10.step06: Update punch list and obtain required acceptance approval.
interview.chapter20.q10.scenario: A new HMI database import removes alarm priorities for several feeder points. Restore the approved configuration and regression-test all affected alarms.
interview.chapter20.q10.takeaway: Explain defect tracking as well as technical diagnosis.
interview.chapter20.q11.question: Explain the difference between SNMP and SNTP in a substation network.
interview.chapter20.q11.answer: SNMP monitors managed network devices using manager/agent polling, MIB/OID values and notifications such as traps. SNTP is a simpler time synchronization protocol based on NTP messaging. They solve different problems and may both be used in an SAS network.
interview.chapter20.q11.step01: Identify which switches and servers support SNMP monitoring.
interview.chapter20.q11.step02: Check SNMP version, credentials, polling reachability and trap destinations.
interview.chapter20.q11.step03: Verify interface/link alarms and relevant redundancy diagnostics.
interview.chapter20.q11.step04: Identify the configured time source and clients for SNTP/NTP.
interview.chapter20.q11.step05: Compare clock status and SOE timestamps separately from SNMP alarms.
interview.chapter20.q11.scenario: A switch reports a fibre-port-down SNMP trap while relay clocks remain synchronized. Network monitoring and time synchronization are independent functions.
interview.chapter20.q11.takeaway: SNMP is monitoring; SNTP is time synchronization.
interview.chapter20.q12.question: How do you answer a question about work you have studied but not performed on site?
interview.chapter20.q12.answer: Be precise about the level of exposure. Explain what you actually configured or tested in training, which steps you understand conceptually, and which site tasks would require supervision. Technical accuracy and transparency matter more than claiming unsupported commissioning experience.
interview.chapter20.q12.step01: State the actual context: project, FAT lab, simulation or study.
interview.chapter20.q12.step02: Describe the exact device, tool, configuration and result you personally handled.
interview.chapter20.q12.step03: Explain the correct engineering procedure and safety controls.
interview.chapter20.q12.step04: Identify what you have not yet done independently.
interview.chapter20.q12.step05: Offer a relevant troubleshooting walkthrough or demonstration.
interview.chapter20.q12.scenario: If asked whether you independently commissioned a PRP network, describe your genuine lab or observation experience rather than inventing a site commissioning claim.
interview.chapter20.q12.takeaway: An interviewer can probe details; accurate experience descriptions build credibility.

iec61850.chapter08.l01.title: Introduction to Manufacturing Message Specification
iec61850.chapter08.l01.p01: Manufacturing Message Specification (MMS) defines services for exchanging named, typed information between applications. IEC 61850 uses a mapping to MMS for much of its client-server communication; MMS itself is not a protection function or a relay configuration language.
iec61850.chapter08.l01.p02: An IED exposes a server model while a gateway or station HMI acts as a client. Reads obtain current information, reports deliver configured updates, and control services request actions subject to the server's control model. A successful network connection proves none of these application functions by itself.
iec61850.chapter08.l01.wf01: Identify the required monitoring and control services
iec61850.chapter08.l01.wf02: Check the server and client capability statements
iec61850.chapter08.l01.wf03: Allocate point references and test each service independently
iec61850.chapter08.l01.example: For 33-F01, the gateway reads XCBR1.Pos and receives breaker events through a configured report. Fault tripping remains a protection application with its own operating path.
iec61850.chapter08.l01.check: Explain which device initiates the association and which publishes a report; neither role is determined by the equipment's physical size.
iec61850.chapter08.l02.title: MMS in IEC 61850 Architecture
iec61850.chapter08.l02.p01: IEC 61850 separates information models, abstract services and communication mappings. Parts 7-3 and 7-4 describe common data structures and logical nodes; Part 7-2 describes abstract services; Part 8-1 maps relevant services to MMS and Ethernet communication.
iec61850.chapter08.l02.p02: The same breaker position has a semantic identity regardless of how an engineering tool displays it. The network transports an encoded representation of that identity. GOOSE and Sampled Values use different mappings and operating patterns, so a functioning MMS association does not establish that either multicast service works.
iec61850.chapter08.l02.wf01: Trace a physical input to its logical node
iec61850.chapter08.l02.wf02: Identify its functional constraint and data type
iec61850.chapter08.l02.wf03: Follow the configured service to the consuming application
iec61850.chapter08.l02.example: 52a/52b feedback becomes the illustrative object IED_33_F01LD0/XCBR1.Pos. The HMI must interpret its double-point state and quality, not simply turn any nonzero value green.
iec61850.chapter08.l02.check: Keep model naming, abstract service and Ethernet transport as separate columns in the engineering schedule.
iec61850.chapter08.l03.title: IEC 61850 Client-Server Communication
iec61850.chapter08.l03.p01: Client-server communication is association-oriented: the client requests a relationship with the server, then exchanges supported services within that relationship. The server may send unsolicited reports once the relevant RCB is correctly configured and enabled.
iec61850.chapter08.l03.p02: One physical computer can run several clients, and one IED may accept several associations within documented limits. Client identity, server resources and access rights matter. A reporting client is not automatically authorized to operate equipment or edit settings, even when it can browse the entire model.
iec61850.chapter08.l03.wf01: List each gateway, HMI and engineering client
iec61850.chapter08.l03.wf02: Assign a purpose and access level
iec61850.chapter08.l03.wf03: Test simultaneous connections and resource allocation
iec61850.chapter08.l03.example: Gateway A and a maintenance laptop connect to 33-F01. Both can read approved measurements, but their report resources and control authority are engineered separately.
iec61850.chapter08.l03.check: Record association and report-instance limits from the exact firmware documentation rather than assuming unlimited clients.
iec61850.chapter08.l04.title: MMS Protocol Stack and TCP/IP
iec61850.chapter08.l04.p01: In the conventional IEC 61850-8-1 TCP mapping, MMS uses association, presentation and session services above an ISO transport mapping carried over TCP/IP. RFC 1006 provides the TPKT framing used with COTP over TCP. Ethernet carries the resulting IP packets on the station network.
iec61850.chapter08.l04.p02: TCP is a byte stream. One MMS message may span several TCP segments, while a packet may contain more than one higher-layer unit. Packet count therefore cannot be treated as report count. Reassembly and complete capture are essential when diagnosing an apparent malformed message.
iec61850.chapter08.l04.wf02: Confirm TCP connection and TPKT/COTP decoding
iec61850.chapter08.l04.example: An oversized DataSet report from the 132 kV line relay spans multiple TCP segments. The SCADA client processes one reconstructed report, not independent values from each segment.
iec61850.chapter08.l04.check: Do not place ordinary GOOSE or SV inside the MMS/TCP stack in a network diagram.
iec61850.chapter08.l05.title: MMS Association Establishment
iec61850.chapter08.l05.p01: Association establishment progresses beyond the TCP three-way handshake. COTP connection setup and application association negotiation must also succeed; MMS initiation negotiates relevant capabilities and message handling parameters. A TCP socket marked connected may still have no usable IEC 61850 association.
iec61850.chapter08.l05.p02: Association selectors, application identifiers, access policy and supported services can differ between implementations. Diagnose the last successful exchange before changing configuration. Repeatedly increasing timeouts will not repair an explicitly rejected association or a mismatched selector.
iec61850.chapter08.l05.wf02: Identify TCP, COTP and association responses
iec61850.chapter08.l05.wf03: Compare rejected parameters with the approved client/server settings
iec61850.chapter08.l05.example: The 33-F01 server accepts TCP port 102 but rejects the gateway association. The test record distinguishes this application rejection from a firewall silently dropping the TCP SYN.
iec61850.chapter08.l05.check: Preserve the rejection response and both device logs; an HMI's generic communication alarm is insufficient evidence.
iec61850.chapter08.l06.title: IEC 61850 Server Data Model Discovery
iec61850.chapter08.l06.p01: Model discovery allows a client to enumerate available logical devices, logical nodes, data objects and supported data structures. Discovery services are useful for confirming the running model against the approved SCL configuration and for locating exact object references.
iec61850.chapter08.l06.p02: Browsing is evidence about the connected device, not permission to rewrite the engineering database automatically. Firmware changes, optional functions and naming prefixes can alter the exposed model. A client that silently accepts every discovered change can hide configuration drift and map the wrong physical equipment.
iec61850.chapter08.l06.wf02: Browse the relevant logical device and types
iec61850.chapter08.l06.wf03: Compare the model against the controlled signal schedule
iec61850.chapter08.l06.example: For 33-F01, confirm whether the actual logical device domain is IED_33_F01LD0 and whether MMXU1 exists before importing illustrative references into the gateway.
iec61850.chapter08.l06.check: Compare types and functional constraints as well as names; matching text labels alone do not prove compatibility.
iec61850.chapter08.l07.title: MMS Read Services
iec61850.chapter08.l07.p01: Read services retrieve a present value or structure from the server. A read is useful for commissioning, initial display and targeted diagnostics, but cyclic reading alone does not guarantee collection of every intermediate event between polls.
iec61850.chapter08.l07.p02: Read the correct functional constraint and preserve quality and time where the selected structure includes them. A successful read can return invalid or questionable application data. Also distinguish a source timestamp from the workstation time at which the response arrived.
iec61850.chapter08.l07.wf01: Select the exact object and functional constraint
iec61850.chapter08.l07.wf02: Read value, quality and source time as supported
iec61850.chapter08.l07.wf03: Compare the response with an injected state or measurement
iec61850.chapter08.l07.example: Polling XCBR1.Pos once per second can miss an open-close sequence completed between polls. Reporting and suitable event retention are required when that sequence must be recorded.
iec61850.chapter08.l07.check: Document polling intervals and stale-data rules; a continuously visible last value is not proof of a healthy source.
iec61850.chapter08.l08.title: MMS Write Services and Access Control
iec61850.chapter08.l08.p01: Write services change only attributes that the server permits to be written under the current conditions. IEC 61850 status attributes are generally produced by the application and should not be treated as editable process commands.
iec61850.chapter08.l08.p02: Access depends on the service, attribute, device mode and security policy. Writing an RCB parameter is different from issuing a breaker operation. A denied write may be correct behavior because the report is enabled, another client owns a resource, or the account lacks permission.
iec61850.chapter08.l08.wf01: Confirm the attribute is writable and the test is approved
iec61850.chapter08.l08.wf02: Read and record its original value
iec61850.chapter08.l08.wf03: Apply the change and verify both acceptance and resulting behavior
iec61850.chapter08.l08.example: During an isolated FAT, adjust an assigned RCB's IntgPd using the documented sequence. Restore the approved interval and prove that another client's reporting was unaffected.
iec61850.chapter08.l08.check: Never test breaker control by trying to overwrite XCBR1.Pos.stVal; use the supported control service and authorized procedure.
iec61850.chapter08.l09.title: MMS Reporting Services
iec61850.chapter08.l09.p01: MMS reports carry data selected through a DataSet and governed by a Report Control Block. The client enables the appropriate RCB and interprets the report's inclusion information, trigger reason and optional fields according to the configured structure.
iec61850.chapter08.l09.p02: An event report may contain only changed members. A general interrogation or integrity report provides a current-state snapshot; neither reconstructs every past transition. Buffered reporting offers conditional recovery of retained entries, subject to finite capacity and correct resynchronization.
iec61850.chapter08.l09.wf01: Verify ordered DataSet members and ConfRev
iec61850.chapter08.l09.wf02: Allocate and enable the assigned RCB
iec61850.chapter08.l09.wf03: Exercise data change, quality change, GI and reconnect
iec61850.chapter08.l09.example: 33-F01 sends a breaker event to Gateway A. If stVal, q and t are separate scalar members, confirm their inclusion rather than assuming every event repeats all three.
iec61850.chapter08.l09.check: Check RptEna, ownership and event triggers before blaming the Ethernet network for missing reports.
iec61850.chapter08.l10.title: MMS Control Services
iec61850.chapter08.l10.p01: IEC 61850 control services manage requests to controllable data objects, including direct and select-before-operate models. Normal and enhanced security models have different service behavior; enhanced control can provide command termination information.
iec61850.chapter08.l10.p02: Communication acceptance, command execution and physical breaker feedback are distinct outcomes. The client must follow the object's ctlModel, preserve command context and observe application interlocks. A timeout leaves an uncertain result until actual position and relevant logs are checked.
iec61850.chapter08.l10.wf03: Execute the required sequence and independently inspect position feedback
iec61850.chapter08.l10.example: An HMI operates the approved CSWI1.Pos control point for 33-F01 and monitors XCBR1.Pos feedback. The two references have related functions but are not interchangeable writable variables.
iec61850.chapter08.l10.check: After a timeout, reconcile physical state before any retry; do not blindly repeat a close command.
iec61850.chapter08.l11.title: MMS Communication over Station Ethernet
iec61850.chapter08.l11.p01: Station Ethernet carries MMS together with other engineered traffic. MMS normally uses unicast IP communication, while Layer-2 GOOSE and SV have different addressing and forwarding requirements. Sharing switches does not make their performance requirements identical.
iec61850.chapter08.l11.p02: Design paths for availability, bandwidth and controlled access. Excessive multicast flooding or oversubscribed uplinks can affect TCP performance, but giving every packet the highest priority merely moves the congestion problem. Switch monitoring should expose errors, discards and queue pressure.
iec61850.chapter08.l11.wf03: Verify switch policies under representative loading
iec61850.chapter08.l11.example: The 33 kV gateway reads several feeder IEDs across station VLAN 100. Process-bus SV is confined to its approved distribution paths so monitoring traffic remains predictable.
iec61850.chapter08.l11.check: Check both directions of a TCP path and the actual switch port membership, not only the logical network drawing.
iec61850.chapter08.l12.title: TCP Port 102 and Network Requirements
iec61850.chapter08.l12.p01: TCP port 102 is the conventional listener used by the RFC 1006-based MMS mapping. The client normally uses an ephemeral source port and connects to the IED's configured server address. The reply must return through the permitted network path.
iec61850.chapter08.l12.p02: An open port only proves a transport endpoint answered. Firewalls, routing, duplicate IP addresses, selectors and application policies remain separate checks. Any security-enabled alternative must follow the project's IEC 62351 and product implementation requirements rather than a guessed port change.
iec61850.chapter08.l12.wf01: Confirm server address, mask and route
iec61850.chapter08.l12.wf03: Test association and application exchange after transport connectivity
iec61850.chapter08.l12.example: For Gateway A at 192.168.100.10 and 33-F01 at 192.168.100.31, verify the intended same-subnet path and TCP 102 policy before investigating RCB behavior.
iec61850.chapter08.l12.check: Avoid exposing the station MMS service directly to the public Internet; use the approved station access architecture.
iec61850.chapter08.l13.title: MMS Communication Between IED and SCADA
iec61850.chapter08.l13.p01: SCADA integration converts the IED model into an operational point database. The client must acquire the correct values, interpret their types and quality, and present source time and communication health in a useful operator view.
iec61850.chapter08.l13.p02: The communication driver and HMI database are separate configuration layers. A correct MMS report can reach the driver while an incorrect database reference, scale or state conversion produces the wrong display. Test from the field stimulus through the final HMI indication.
iec61850.chapter08.l13.wf01: Bind each SCADA tag to a controlled reference
iec61850.chapter08.l13.wf02: Configure quality, time and scaling rules
iec61850.chapter08.l13.wf03: Inject representative values and compare every layer
iec61850.chapter08.l13.example: IED_33_F01LD0/MMXU1.A.phsA.cVal.mag.f is an illustrative phase-current reference. Check the actual model, unit and ratio before displaying it as primary amperes.
iec61850.chapter08.l13.check: Do not declare a point tested from the driver's online value alone; inspect the operator screen and event list.
iec61850.chapter08.l14.title: Multiple MMS Clients and Server Limitations
iec61850.chapter08.l14.p01: Server resources include associations, outstanding requests, DataSet capacity and RCB instances. These limits are implementation-specific and can be shared across services. A maintenance client can consume resources needed by a redundant gateway if no capacity is reserved.
iec61850.chapter08.l14.p02: An RCB instance is not a general broadcast channel for arbitrary clients. Engineer independent instances or a documented redundancy strategy, and verify reservation and reconnection behavior. Conflicting clients can repeatedly enable, disable or reconfigure a resource without any physical network fault.
iec61850.chapter08.l14.wf03: Test startup, failover and maintenance access together
iec61850.chapter08.l14.example: Gateway A, Gateway B and the engineering laptop connect during FAT. Confirm each intended report stream remains stable and rejected extra connections produce a clear diagnostic.
iec61850.chapter08.l14.check: Record maximum tested load separately from a manufacturer's advertised maximum; both depend on the actual configuration.
iec61850.chapter08.l15.title: MMS Connection Loss and Recovery
iec61850.chapter08.l15.p01: Connection loss breaks the active association and requires an explicit client recovery process. The client detects failure, reconnects, confirms the model and report configuration, and restores data acquisition without presenting stale values as healthy live information.
iec61850.chapter08.l15.p02: Buffered recovery depends on retained entries and a valid recovery position. A changed configuration, buffer overflow or device restart may prevent complete replay. A GI or read restores current state but must not erase evidence of an unrecoverable event gap.
iec61850.chapter08.l15.wf01: Break the communication path under test control
iec61850.chapter08.l15.wf03: Reconcile retained events, current values and any recorded gap
iec61850.chapter08.l15.example: After a station-switch outage, Gateway A reconnects to 33-F01 and requests eligible BRCB entries. It marks any discontinuity and refreshes the present breaker state.
iec61850.chapter08.l15.check: Test both short and long interruptions; a successful short outage does not prove buffer capacity for an extended failure.
iec61850.chapter08.l16.title: MMS Communication Configuration
iec61850.chapter08.l16.p01: MMS configuration combines network settings, the server model and client service allocation. Start with the approved SCD and signal list, then translate them into the settings supported by each device and gateway tool.
iec61850.chapter08.l16.p02: The sequence matters: model changes can invalidate DataSet membership, and DataSet changes can invalidate report decoding. Commission a controlled configuration revision rather than editing both endpoints independently until communication happens to work.
iec61850.chapter08.l16.wf02: Import and verify the model and point schedule
iec61850.chapter08.l16.wf03: Allocate DataSets/RCBs, enable acquisition and archive the tested revision
iec61850.chapter08.l16.example: For 33-F01, use station address 192.168.100.31, Gateway A .10 and a project-assigned buffered status report. Timing values are engineering examples, not mandatory IEC defaults.
iec61850.chapter08.l16.check: Store exported configurations with firmware versions and checksums so the tested state can be restored exactly.
iec61850.chapter08.l17.title: Practical Example — 33 kV Feeder Monitoring
iec61850.chapter08.l17.p01: A feeder monitoring application combines breaker position, current, voltage, protection operation and device health. Group signals by engineering purpose and update behavior rather than creating one oversized DataSet containing the entire model.
iec61850.chapter08.l17.p02: Use event reporting for status changes and suitable deadbands or acquisition intervals for measurements. Preserve invalid quality and distinguish a fault operation from a breaker position change. Protection may operate without the breaker opening if the trip circuit or mechanism fails.
iec61850.chapter08.l17.wf03: Inject current, operate the test breaker model and inspect HMI/SOE
iec61850.chapter08.l17.example: 33-F01 uses XCBR1.Pos for position, PTOC1.Op for an available overcurrent indication and MMXU1 for measurements. Actual prefixes, instances and phase structure come from its exported model.
iec61850.chapter08.l17.check: Include a failed-breaker-feedback scenario; a protection trip indication is not physical proof that the primary circuit opened.
iec61850.chapter08.l18.title: MMS Packet Analysis Using Wireshark
iec61850.chapter08.l18.p01: Packet analysis shows what crossed the capture point. For MMS, identify the TCP stream, association setup, confirmed requests/responses and report traffic. Use reassembly and preserve capture timing before interpreting a missing or malformed message.
iec61850.chapter08.l18.p02: Capture placement limits conclusions. A mirrored switch port may omit traffic or drop packets under load, and capture timestamps are workstation observations rather than IED event times. Correlate packet evidence with device and client logs.
iec61850.chapter08.l18.wf01: Capture startup and one known event
iec61850.chapter08.l18.wf03: Follow the TCP stream and compare the decoded report with the point schedule
iec61850.chapter08.l18.example: Toggle the isolated 33-F01 test input once and locate its report. Record inclusion, value and source time where present, then compare the HMI event without inventing a packet latency budget.
iec61850.chapter08.l18.check: TCP retransmission indicates transport recovery; it is different from an IED sending another application report.
iec61850.chapter08.l19.title: MMS FAT/SAT Testing
iec61850.chapter08.l19.p01: MMS acceptance testing verifies the delivered application, not merely a successful ping. Define expected values, quality transitions, timestamps, permitted controls and recovery behavior before applying test stimuli.
iec61850.chapter08.l19.p02: FAT can use an isolated simulator and representative IEDs; SAT confirms the installed addresses, ports, wiring and operational interfaces. Pass criteria must refer to the project requirements and the tested client/server versions.
iec61850.chapter08.l19.wf02: Test reporting, access restrictions and approved controls
iec61850.chapter08.l19.wf03: Interrupt communication, reconnect and retain traceable evidence
iec61850.chapter08.l19.example: For 33-F01, record the injected breaker state, reported value, source timestamp, HMI display and alarm result. Repeat with invalid quality and with the assigned RCB unavailable.
iec61850.chapter08.l19.check: Keep an expected/actual record for each point and failure mode; screenshots without a known stimulus are weak acceptance evidence.
iec61850.chapter08.l20.title: MMS Troubleshooting
iec61850.chapter08.l20.p01: Troubleshoot MMS in layers: physical link, Ethernet/VLAN, IP, TCP, association, model reference, report configuration and client presentation. Stop at the first failed layer rather than changing unrelated settings simultaneously.
iec61850.chapter08.l20.p02: Different symptoms require different evidence. No TCP response suggests reachability or service availability; association rejection suggests application parameters or policy; successful reads with no reports suggest RCB ownership, triggers or DataSet configuration. Correct packets with wrong HMI values point toward mapping.
iec61850.chapter08.l20.wf02: Compare a working and failing path
iec61850.chapter08.l20.wf03: Change one cause, repeat the same test and archive the result
iec61850.chapter08.l20.example: If 33-F01 reads work but status events do not, inspect RptEna and the assigned DataSet before altering VLANs. If reports arrive correctly, inspect the gateway database next.
iec61850.chapter08.l20.check: End with a cause-and-evidence statement, not simply 'reboot fixed it'; verify that recovery survives the original failure scenario.
iec61850.chapter09.l01.title: Introduction to GOOSE
iec61850.chapter09.l01.p01: Generic Object Oriented Substation Event (GOOSE) communication distributes an ordered set of application data from a publisher to configured subscribers. Conventional station-LAN GOOSE uses Ethernet multicast without a TCP connection or per-subscriber acknowledgment.
iec61850.chapter09.l01.p02: The publisher repeats state information so a subscriber can receive updates despite occasional frame loss. Correct reception still depends on addressing, configuration agreement, network delivery and application supervision. GOOSE does not automatically make an arbitrary protection scheme dependable or secure.
iec61850.chapter09.l01.wf03: Specify supervision and the consequence of missing or invalid data
iec61850.chapter09.l01.example: A 33 kV feeder IED publishes a protection operation to a designated receiving IED. The receiver maps the relevant member into its approved application logic.
iec61850.chapter09.l01.check: Distinguish GOOSE service availability from complete protection performance, which includes sensing, logic, output and breaker operation.
iec61850.chapter09.l02.title: Why GOOSE Is Used in Substations
iec61850.chapter09.l02.p01: GOOSE can replace selected inter-panel signal wiring with engineered data exchange. It supports protection coordination, interlocking, blocking and status distribution where the required timing, dependability and supervision have been demonstrated.
iec61850.chapter09.l02.p02: Removing a copper connection transfers part of the engineering responsibility into DataSet design, network paths and subscriber logic. It does not remove the need for signal ownership, cause-and-effect documentation or failure analysis. Communication health becomes an application input that must have a defined response.
iec61850.chapter09.l02.wf01: Compare the existing hardwired function with its networked equivalent
iec61850.chapter09.l02.wf03: Prove the complete signal path under normal and degraded conditions
iec61850.chapter09.l02.example: An upstream 33 kV protection function receives a downstream blocking signal. The project specifies how loss of that signal affects coordination rather than assuming all lost signals should become false.
iec61850.chapter09.l02.check: Choose a communication-failure response from the protection study; a universal fail-open or fail-closed rule is inappropriate.
iec61850.chapter09.l03.title: Publisher and Subscriber Architecture
iec61850.chapter09.l03.p01: A publisher sends one multicast stream that multiple subscribers can receive. Subscription is configured by engineering tools and application mapping; the publisher does not establish a separate TCP session with every recipient.
iec61850.chapter09.l03.p02: Subscriber matching involves the engineered identity and structure of the stream. Destination MAC, APPID, control-block reference, configuration revision and ordered data types have different roles. Matching only one field can admit the wrong stream or reject a valid update.
iec61850.chapter09.l03.wf02: Map every DataSet member to a subscriber input
iec61850.chapter09.l03.wf03: Verify reception and application use at each destination
iec61850.chapter09.l03.example: 33-F01 may publish one stream to a bay controller and a station test device. Each consumer interprets only the members assigned to its function and supervises the stream independently.
iec61850.chapter09.l03.check: A packet visible on a mirrored port does not prove that the subscriber application has accepted it.
iec61850.chapter09.l04.title: GOOSE Communication over Ethernet
iec61850.chapter09.l04.p01: Conventional GOOSE frames use EtherType 0x88B8 and are forwarded within the engineered Layer-2 network. They do not use an IP destination, TCP port or ordinary IP multicast subscription mechanism.
iec61850.chapter09.l04.p02: An optional IEEE 802.1Q tag carries VLAN identity and priority. Ethernet switches must deliver the multicast frame along intended paths while avoiding excessive flooding. Routable GOOSE is a separate architecture and should not be inferred from a standard station-LAN example.
iec61850.chapter09.l04.wf02: Trace VLAN and multicast forwarding through each switch
iec61850.chapter09.l04.wf03: Capture at the receiving port and check stream identity
iec61850.chapter09.l04.example: Two IEDs with reachable IP addresses can still fail to exchange GOOSE if their Layer-2 VLAN membership differs. A successful ping is therefore not an acceptance test for subscription.
iec61850.chapter09.l04.check: Do not troubleshoot a conventional GOOSE failure by opening TCP port 102; that port belongs to the MMS transport mapping.
iec61850.chapter09.l05.title: GOOSE DataSet Configuration
iec61850.chapter09.l05.p01: A GOOSE DataSet defines the ordered application values in a stream. Subscribers rely on the member order, encoded types and intended meaning. Reordering members can be just as disruptive as removing one.
iec61850.chapter09.l05.p02: Include quality or other supervision information according to the engineered application and supported model. Do not assume each scalar value implicitly carries a separate quality and timestamp field. Changing the DataSet requires coordinated configuration and revision handling across publisher and consumers.
iec61850.chapter09.l05.wf01: Select exact model references and functional constraints
iec61850.chapter09.l05.wf03: Update publisher and subscriber configurations as one controlled change
iec61850.chapter09.l05.example: An illustrative trip DataSet selects PTRC1.Tr.general and PTRC1.Tr.q as separate supported members. The receiver maps the Boolean trip and quality to different application inputs.
iec61850.chapter09.l05.check: Verify the actual IED exposes those attributes; do not manufacture missing logical nodes or rely on an undocumented member position.
iec61850.chapter09.l06.title: GOOSE Control Block Configuration
iec61850.chapter09.l06.p01: The GOOSE Control Block associates the publisher's DataSet with a stream identity and configuration revision. Network addressing is represented in the associated SCL communication configuration, while application logic determines the values being published.
iec61850.chapter09.l06.p02: Parameters such as GoCBRef, DatSet, GoID and ConfRev are not interchangeable. A configuration revision identifies a relevant configuration change; it is not the current event number. Enabling publication does not prove that any subscriber has accepted the configuration.
iec61850.chapter09.l06.wf01: Bind the control block to the approved DataSet
iec61850.chapter09.l06.wf02: Assign stream identity and network parameters
iec61850.chapter09.l06.wf03: Export SCL and verify the live frame against that configuration
iec61850.chapter09.l06.example: For 33-F01, an illustrative gcbTrip references dsTrip. The project records its APPID, multicast address and VLAN separately so addressing changes cannot silently alter the signal definition.
iec61850.chapter09.l06.check: Check ConfRev and ordered types at every subscriber after a DataSet edit, then repeat functional tests.
iec61850.chapter09.l07.title: APPID, MAC Address and VLAN Parameters
iec61850.chapter09.l07.p01: APPID identifies an application stream within the configured Ethernet service context; the multicast destination MAC controls Ethernet delivery. VLAN ID identifies the broadcast domain and priority code point influences switch queue treatment where configured.
iec61850.chapter09.l07.p02: These fields must be coordinated in a station allocation register. Different tools may display APPID and VLAN values in decimal or hexadecimal. SCL encodings and engineering interfaces must be interpreted explicitly rather than copying a number without its base.
iec61850.chapter09.l07.wf02: Record numeric value and display format
iec61850.chapter09.l07.wf03: Compare the exported SCL with live frame fields
iec61850.chapter09.l07.example: Use illustrative GOOSE APPID 0x1001, destination 01-0C-CD-01-00-01 and VLAN decimal 200 for one approved stream. In an SCL VLAN-ID field, hexadecimal 0C8 represents decimal 200.
iec61850.chapter09.l07.check: Priority 4 is an example, not a universal performance guarantee; verify the switch policy and device support.
iec61850.chapter09.l08.title: GOOSE State Number and Sequence Number
iec61850.chapter09.l08.p01: stNum identifies a new GOOSE state, while sqNum distinguishes transmissions associated with that state. A state change advances stNum and starts a new transmission sequence; retransmissions of the same state advance sqNum.
iec61850.chapter09.l08.p02: Do not treat these counters as permanent event IDs across device restarts, wraparound or reconfiguration. Evaluate the event timestamp, configuration revision, publisher identity and subscriber supervision together. A repeated state with increasing sqNum is normal behavior, not automatically an event storm.
iec61850.chapter09.l08.wf03: Compare state, sequence, timestamp and payload before and after the change
iec61850.chapter09.l08.example: An illustrative capture shows stNum 17/sqNum 6 before a trip, then stNum 18/sqNum 0 followed by 18/1 and 18/2. Exact observed startup behavior must match the implementation.
iec61850.chapter09.l08.check: Differentiate an application state change from packet duplication introduced by PRP or HSR capture placement.
iec61850.chapter09.l09.title: GOOSE Retransmission Mechanism
iec61850.chapter09.l09.p01: After a state change, GOOSE typically repeats quickly and then increases the interval toward a steady-state heartbeat. This repetition supports delivery without acknowledgments, but the exact schedule is implementation- and configuration-dependent.
iec61850.chapter09.l09.p02: timeAllowedtoLive tells a receiver how long the received state remains valid for communication supervision. It is not a guaranteed end-to-end trip time or a permanent DataSet retention period. A subscriber must detect expiry and apply its engineered loss-of-communication behavior.
iec61850.chapter09.l09.wf01: Measure the event burst and steady heartbeat
iec61850.chapter09.l09.wf02: Remove the stream under test control
iec61850.chapter09.l09.wf03: Verify expiry indication and application response
