iec61850.chapter12.l17.example: 33-F01's breaker position, current, protection operation and device health appear on the feeder HMI. A communication outage must mark those values appropriately rather than leave them looking live indefinitely.
iec61850.chapter12.l17.check: Keep command and indication references separate in the mapping sheet and verify the correct bay identity at the operator interface.
iec61850.chapter12.l18.title: Practical Example — 33 kV Feeder IED
iec61850.chapter12.l18.p01: The practical feeder configuration begins with approved hardware, settings and a signal schedule for 33-F01. It combines physical I/O, measurements, protection indications, MMS reporting and any authorized GOOSE exchange.
iec61850.chapter12.l18.p02: Use one controlled revision through engineering and testing. Configure a representative feeder completely before cloning settings to other bays, because copied addresses, stream identifiers and equipment names can create duplicate identities.
iec61850.chapter12.l18.wf03: Execute a full stimulus-to-display/output test and archive the result
iec61850.chapter12.l18.example: The example uses address 192.168.100.31, illustrative LD0 references and gcbTrip APPID 0x1001. Another feeder receives its own approved names and allocations rather than an unchanged clone.
iec61850.chapter12.l18.check: Compare every copied bay's unique identifiers, ratios and protection settings before energization or release.
iec61850.chapter12.l19.title: IED FAT/SAT Testing
iec61850.chapter12.l19.p01: IED FAT verifies the configured device against the requirements in a controlled environment. SAT confirms the installed terminals, network paths, time source and station interfaces match the tested design.
iec61850.chapter12.l19.p02: Test scope includes protection and control functions as well as communication. Negative cases reveal incorrect authority, stale inputs and resource conflicts that normal operation can conceal. Record configuration checksums and the exact stimulus for each result.
iec61850.chapter12.l19.wf02: Test I/O, measurements, reports, GOOSE and approved controls
iec61850.chapter12.l19.wf03: Exercise failure/recovery and reconcile site changes
iec61850.chapter12.l19.example: For 33-F01, retain point-test sheets, protection test results, network evidence and the final exported project. Any site correction triggers the affected repeat tests.
iec61850.chapter12.l19.check: Do not present a passed communication test as proof of protection coordination or primary-equipment condition.
iec61850.chapter12.l20.title: IED Troubleshooting
iec61850.chapter12.l20.p01: IED troubleshooting separates hardware, application, communication and integration faults. Establish whether the local device sees the expected input before investigating how it publishes that information.
iec61850.chapter12.l20.p02: Use diagnostics at each boundary: terminal state, internal logic, exposed model, transmitted message and receiving application. A correct network packet with an incorrect source value points upstream, while a correct source and packet with a wrong display points downstream.
iec61850.chapter12.l20.wf02: Trace the signal through each boundary
iec61850.chapter12.l20.wf03: Correct one cause and repeat the original test
iec61850.chapter12.l20.example: If 33-F01's HMI says closed while the relay model says open, inspect gateway state mapping. If both say closed despite open test contacts, inspect input polarity and position logic first.
iec61850.chapter12.l20.check: Archive the cause, changed settings and verification evidence; an unexplained factory reset is not a controlled engineering resolution.
iec61850.chapter13.l01.title: Introduction to Substation Communication Networks
iec61850.chapter13.l01.p01: Substation communication networks connect protection, control, monitoring and engineering systems with different performance and availability requirements. The design must account for traffic paths and failure consequences rather than merely provide enough Ethernet sockets.
iec61850.chapter13.l01.p02: MMS, GOOSE, SV and time synchronization use different service mechanisms. Their coexistence requires capacity planning, appropriate forwarding and observable diagnostics. IEC TR 61850-90-4 provides a network-engineering framework where applicable to the project.
iec61850.chapter13.l01.wf03: Draw normal and degraded traffic paths
iec61850.chapter13.l01.example: The 132/33 kV station has feeder IEDs, gateways, operator stations and timing equipment. Process-bus traffic is included only where the selected architecture actually uses it.
iec61850.chapter13.l01.check: Record what each network failure means to protection, control and operator visibility; a single generic availability target can hide important differences.
iec61850.chapter13.l02.title: Station Bus Architecture
iec61850.chapter13.l02.p01: The station bus links bay devices with station-level functions and may carry inter-IED GOOSE. Its physical topology, VLAN design and redundancy arrangement must support the actual application exchanges.
iec61850.chapter13.l02.p02: Station bus is a functional architecture, not necessarily one physical switch or one flat VLAN. Separate management and process paths where required, while keeping necessary service connectivity explicit. Unplanned routing or filtering can break a valid logical design.
iec61850.chapter13.l02.wf01: Place each station and bay endpoint
iec61850.chapter13.l02.wf02: Mark MMS, GOOSE and time paths
iec61850.chapter13.l02.example: Gateway A acquires 33-F01 over station VLAN 100. Approved GOOSE uses VLAN 200 on the engineered ports, with no assumption that an IP route transfers that Layer-2 stream.
iec61850.chapter13.l02.check: Compare the as-built port schedule with the logical drawing before commissioning; mismatched patching can invalidate both addressing and redundancy assumptions.
iec61850.chapter13.l03.title: Industrial Ethernet Switches
iec61850.chapter13.l03.p01: Industrial Ethernet switches provide forwarding plus features suited to the specified environment and network design. Relevant capabilities may include VLANs, priority queues, multicast filtering, redundancy support, diagnostics and precise-time functions.
iec61850.chapter13.l03.p02: Feature names alone are insufficient. Check exact firmware behavior, port speed, optical compatibility, environmental ratings and whether the required PTP profile or redundancy role is supported. A switch with two power inputs can still share other single points of failure.
iec61850.chapter13.l03.wf01: Match switch capabilities to the network specification
iec61850.chapter13.l03.wf02: Verify optics, power and port allocation
iec61850.chapter13.l03.wf03: Test configured forwarding and diagnostics under load
iec61850.chapter13.l03.example: The station switch serving 33-F01 must forward its approved GOOSE stream and MMS traffic while exposing link errors and discards to maintenance staff.
iec61850.chapter13.l03.check: Do not assume all managed switches implement PRP, HSR or transparent-clock behavior; those functions need explicit support.
iec61850.chapter13.l04.title: Ethernet Network Topologies
iec61850.chapter13.l04.p01: Star, ring, dual-LAN and mesh arrangements have different failure and maintenance properties. A drawing should show actual links, forwarding behavior and device roles rather than use the word ring as a substitute for a redundancy protocol.
iec61850.chapter13.l04.p02: A physical ring requires a mechanism that prevents uncontrolled loops or deliberately handles duplicates. RSTP, HSR and proprietary ring protocols are not interchangeable. End-device capabilities and recovery requirements determine which architecture is appropriate.
iec61850.chapter13.l04.wf02: Identify the loop-control or duplication mechanism
iec61850.chapter13.l04.wf03: Evaluate each link and node failure
iec61850.chapter13.l04.example: A dual-star PRP station uses two separate switched LANs, while an HSR bay ring connects compatible two-port nodes around a closed loop.
iec61850.chapter13.l04.check: Keep physical topology and protocol behavior separate in documentation so maintenance staff do not bridge paths that must remain independent.
iec61850.chapter13.l05.title: Network Redundancy Requirements
iec61850.chapter13.l05.p01: Redundancy requirements follow the permitted interruption and failure consequences of each application. Monitoring may tolerate a different outage from a high-speed protection exchange or synchronized measurement path.
iec61850.chapter13.l05.p02: Identify common dependencies such as power, cable route, switch chassis, timing source and end device. Two visible cables do not provide independent paths if both pass through the same failed component. Define the fault set the design is intended to survive.
iec61850.chapter13.l05.wf03: Allocate independent resources and acceptance tests
iec61850.chapter13.l05.example: For 33-F01 reporting, the project may require continued acquisition after one LAN failure. That requirement does not automatically cover failure of the feeder IED itself.
iec61850.chapter13.l05.check: State the failure assumptions explicitly; 'zero downtime' without a defined fault model cannot be verified.
iec61850.chapter13.l06.title: Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP)
iec61850.chapter13.l06.p01: Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP), standardized in IEC 62439-3, sends duplicate frames through two separate LANs. A compatible receiving node accepts the useful copy and discards the duplicate.
iec61850.chapter13.l06.p02: LAN A and LAN B remain independent networks. They must not be joined through an ordinary bridge or switch. PRP provides seamless communication for covered network-path failures but does not protect a failed application, shared supply or incorrectly configured endpoint.
iec61850.chapter13.l06.wf01: Connect each PRP port to its assigned LAN
iec61850.chapter13.l06.wf03: Interrupt LAN A and LAN B separately while observing the application
iec61850.chapter13.l06.example: 33-F01 and Gateway A are PRP-capable nodes in the illustrative dual-LAN station. Both LANs carry the required service, with independent switches and power paths as specified.
iec61850.chapter13.l06.check: Do not assign PRP behavior to two ordinary NICs without the supported redundancy implementation.
iec61850.chapter13.l07.title: High-availability Seamless Redundancy (HSR)
iec61850.chapter13.l07.p01: High-availability Seamless Redundancy (HSR) uses compatible nodes that forward duplicate traffic along opposite ring directions in a typical ring arrangement. The receiver processes the first valid copy and removes the duplicate.
iec61850.chapter13.l07.p02: HSR is not two independent switched LANs. Ring nodes and RedBoxes have defined forwarding responsibilities, and ring loading depends on the traffic and topology. A single ring break can leave a surviving path, while multiple breaks can partition the network.
iec61850.chapter13.l07.wf01: Confirm every ring node's HSR role
iec61850.chapter13.l07.wf03: Test each link break and observe forwarding, duplicates and application continuity
iec61850.chapter13.l07.example: Four compatible bay devices form an illustrative HSR ring. Opening one link changes the available path without requiring the same convergence mechanism as RSTP.
iec61850.chapter13.l07.check: Never replace an HSR ring node with an ordinary two-port device unless the documented architecture explicitly supports that connection.
iec61850.chapter13.l08.title: PRP vs HSR Comparison
iec61850.chapter13.l08.p01: PRP and HSR both use duplicate transmission to avoid recovery delay for covered failures, but their physical arrangements differ. PRP uses independent LANs; a typical HSR ring threads compatible two-port nodes around a ring.
iec61850.chapter13.l08.p02: Selection affects device requirements, traffic loading, maintenance and expansion. Neither protocol eliminates all common-mode failures or guarantees a correct application configuration. Choose from the station's failure model and supported equipment rather than visual preference.
iec61850.chapter13.l08.wf03: Test the selected architecture with representative devices
iec61850.chapter13.l08.example: The practical station project selects PRP for its station bus. An HSR ring is taught as a separate alternative and is not drawn as a renamed second PRP LAN.
iec61850.chapter13.l08.check: Keep the comparison focused on tested requirements; seamless network delivery does not guarantee zero application delay or unlimited fault tolerance.
iec61850.chapter13.l09.title: RedBox and Single-Attached Nodes
iec61850.chapter13.l09.p01: A RedBox connects suitable single-attached equipment to a redundant network according to its supported PRP or HSR role. It handles the redundancy functions that the ordinary attached device lacks.
iec61850.chapter13.l09.p02: A directly single-attached node on one PRP LAN has only that path. A RedBox can improve network access availability, but its own power, connection to the attached node and hardware remain dependencies. RedBox roles for connecting HSR rings or networks must follow the supported design.
iec61850.chapter13.l09.wf02: Select the appropriate documented RedBox arrangement
iec61850.chapter13.l09.wf03: Test path loss and RedBox-related failure cases
iec61850.chapter13.l09.example: A maintenance server connects through a supported RedBox to the station's PRP networks. Its single cable to the RedBox remains a visible failure point in the availability assessment.
iec61850.chapter13.l09.check: Do not describe every device with two Ethernet ports as a RedBox; verify the implemented protocol and topology role.
iec61850.chapter13.l10.title: RSTP and Network Recovery
iec61850.chapter13.l10.p01: Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol maintains a loop-free active topology and can activate alternate paths after a change. Unlike duplicate-transmission schemes, it involves convergence and can produce an interruption.
iec61850.chapter13.l10.p02: Actual recovery depends on topology, settings, link detection and connected equipment. Protection and control applications must tolerate the measured interruption or use another architecture. Incorrect edge-port settings or unmanaged loops can create severe instability.
iec61850.chapter13.l10.wf01: Identify the intended root and alternate paths
iec61850.chapter13.l10.wf03: Measure application recovery during representative failures
iec61850.chapter13.l10.example: A station monitoring network uses an RSTP ring only if its measured outage meets the project requirement. That result does not automatically qualify the same design for a time-critical protection exchange.
iec61850.chapter13.l10.check: Do not quote one universal RSTP recovery time; measure the delivered topology and verify the application's response.
iec61850.chapter13.l11.title: VLAN Fundamentals
iec61850.chapter13.l11.p01: A VLAN partitions Ethernet forwarding into logical broadcast domains. IEEE 802.1Q tagging carries a VLAN identifier and priority information where used, while access-port classification can assign untagged frames to a configured VLAN.
iec61850.chapter13.l11.p02: VLAN separation controls traffic reachability but is not, by itself, complete cybersecurity. Port membership, trunk allowances and routing policy determine which endpoints can exchange information. A missing tag in a capture may reflect NIC offload or switch mirror behavior.
iec61850.chapter13.l11.wf02: Configure ingress classification and egress tagging
iec61850.chapter13.l11.wf03: Verify permitted and prohibited traffic paths
iec61850.chapter13.l11.example: Station MMS uses VLAN 100 and a selected protection GOOSE group uses VLAN 200 in the tutorial. These numbers are project examples, not IEC-mandated allocations.
iec61850.chapter13.l11.check: Keep VLAN ID and priority code point separate; changing priority does not move traffic into another VLAN.
iec61850.chapter13.l12.title: VLAN Configuration for GOOSE and MMS
iec61850.chapter13.l12.p01: MMS and GOOSE can be carried through engineered VLAN arrangements, but their forwarding needs differ. MMS uses the configured IP path; conventional GOOSE requires Layer-2 delivery to its subscribers.
iec61850.chapter13.l12.p02: An access/trunk mismatch can allow one service and block another. Define which devices send tagged frames and which rely on switch ingress classification. Maintain consistent numeric representation between SCL, device tools and switch configuration.
iec61850.chapter13.l12.wf01: Map each service to a VLAN and endpoint
iec61850.chapter13.l12.wf03: Test live frames at the publisher and receiving port
iec61850.chapter13.l12.example: 33-F01 can communicate with Gateway A on VLAN 100 while its GOOSE VLAN 200 is blocked at an uplink. The repair is a reviewed port policy change, followed by subscriber tests.
iec61850.chapter13.l12.check: Do not assume an IP router forwards conventional GOOSE between VLANs; any alternate architecture needs explicit design support.
iec61850.chapter13.l13.title: Ethernet Multicast and Filtering
iec61850.chapter13.l13.p01: Ethernet multicast delivers one frame toward multiple recipients. GOOSE and SV require an engineered distribution plan so necessary consumers receive traffic without flooding every unrelated port.
iec61850.chapter13.l13.p02: IGMP snooping concerns IP multicast and does not automatically discover conventional Layer-2 GOOSE/SV subscriptions. Industrial switches may provide static multicast tables or other supported filtering mechanisms. Verify actual behavior rather than relying on a checkbox label.
iec61850.chapter13.l13.wf01: List stream destinations and subscriber ports
iec61850.chapter13.l13.wf03: Measure reception and unwanted traffic under normal and failure conditions
iec61850.chapter13.l13.example: The 132 kV MU stream is forwarded only to its approved protection subscribers and test access point. Station HMIs do not need every high-rate SV frame.
iec61850.chapter13.l13.check: Check failover paths as well as normal paths; a filter that works on one LAN can silently block the redundant copy.
iec61850.chapter13.l14.title: IP Addressing and Subnet Planning
iec61850.chapter13.l14.p01: IP planning allocates unique addresses, subnet masks and routes for services that use IP. The plan should distinguish station applications, management interfaces and remote-access boundaries.
iec61850.chapter13.l14.p02: An address identifies an IP endpoint, not a GOOSE subscription or physical bay by itself. Document names and roles alongside addresses. Duplicate assignments, incorrect masks and unintended default gateways can create intermittent or asymmetric communication.
iec61850.chapter13.l14.wf03: Test same-subnet and routed paths with the approved access policy
iec61850.chapter13.l14.example: The example uses Gateway A 192.168.100.10, Gateway B .11 and 33-F01 .31 on /24. Switch management uses a separately documented management subnet.
iec61850.chapter13.l14.check: Check the actual device address and MAC before reconnecting a replacement IED; cloned configurations can introduce duplicates.
iec61850.chapter13.l15.title: Fibre-Optic Communication
iec61850.chapter13.l15.p01: Fibre links provide electrical isolation and support substation distances when the correct optical components are selected. Fibre type, wavelength, connector, transceiver compatibility and optical budget must agree at both ends.
iec61850.chapter13.l15.p02: A link LED does not prove adequate margin or a clean path. Dirty connectors, excessive bends, incorrect patching and marginal receive power can cause intermittent errors. Redundant fibres also need physically diverse routes where the availability design requires them.
iec61850.chapter13.l15.wf02: Inspect and test the installed path
iec61850.chapter13.l15.wf03: Record optical levels, port errors and route identity
iec61850.chapter13.l15.example: PRP LAN A and LAN B fibres to 33-F01 follow the approved separate routes. Placing both in one vulnerable tray may defeat the intended common-cause protection.
iec61850.chapter13.l15.check: Use approved fibre inspection practices and equipment; do not look into an active optical connector.
iec61850.chapter13.l16.title: Network Switch Configuration and Monitoring
iec61850.chapter13.l16.p01: Switch configuration includes port roles, VLANs, multicast forwarding, redundancy, timing features and management access. Monitoring provides evidence of link state, errors, discards and topology changes.
iec61850.chapter13.l16.p02: Save a controlled configuration after testing and verify it survives restart. An unsaved running configuration can make a station work during FAT and fail after a power cycle. Alarm thresholds and log retention should support useful diagnosis without overwhelming operators.
iec61850.chapter13.l16.wf03: Save, restart under test conditions and compare the restored configuration
iec61850.chapter13.l16.example: The switch serving 33-F01 exposes loss of either PRP-facing network path to station maintenance. The alarm identifies the actual port and LAN rather than a generic communication fault.
iec61850.chapter13.l16.check: Keep switch backups linked to the SCD/network revision; switch settings are not fully represented by the SCD alone.
iec61850.chapter13.l17.title: Practical Example — 132/33 kV Station Bus
iec61850.chapter13.l17.p01: The practical station-bus example uses dual PRP LANs with compatible IEDs and gateways. Each LAN has its own switched path, and every required service is verified independently on both.
iec61850.chapter13.l17.p02: The architecture includes station acquisition, approved GOOSE exchanges and time distribution. Single-attached maintenance equipment is documented explicitly. Device power, switch power and fibre route independence are reviewed alongside logical connectivity.
iec61850.chapter13.l17.wf01: Prepare the dual-LAN port and address schedules
iec61850.chapter13.l17.wf03: Test normal operation and each single-path interruption
iec61850.chapter13.l17.example: 33-F01 at 192.168.100.31 communicates with Gateway A at .10 through PRP. The example uses one logical endpoint identity per PRP node, not unrelated A/B application addresses by default.
iec61850.chapter13.l17.check: Verify the device's documented PRP addressing behavior and capture placement before interpreting duplicate frames as a fault.
iec61850.chapter13.l18.title: PRP/HSR Failure Scenarios
iec61850.chapter13.l18.p01: Failure analysis asks what remains connected after a specified fault. In PRP, one failed LAN path can leave the other available; in a typical HSR ring, one break can leave an alternate direction.
iec61850.chapter13.l18.p02: Multiple faults, shared power loss or endpoint failure can exceed the design's protection. Tests should include diagnostics and recovery, not just whether the HMI stayed green. The application must detect degraded redundancy before the second fault removes service.
iec61850.chapter13.l18.wf01: Enumerate link, switch, supply and endpoint failures
iec61850.chapter13.l18.wf03: Apply controlled failures and compare observed behavior
iec61850.chapter13.l18.example: Disconnect LAN A from 33-F01 and confirm acquisition continues through B with a redundancy alarm. Restore A and verify supervision clears without duplicate application events.
iec61850.chapter13.l18.check: State which failures were tested and which were only analyzed; do not generalize one cable-pull result to every network failure.
iec61850.chapter13.l19.title: Network FAT/SAT Testing
iec61850.chapter13.l19.p01: Network FAT verifies the designed topology and configuration under representative traffic. SAT confirms installed ports, optics, fibre routes, power supplies and management access match the accepted design.
iec61850.chapter13.l19.p02: Test both service delivery and failure behavior. Capture loss at a mirror port must be separated from actual network loss. Acceptance criteria should include relevant latency, availability and diagnostic requirements from the project specification.
iec61850.chapter13.l19.wf01: Verify addresses, VLANs and multicast paths
iec61850.chapter13.l19.wf02: Load the network with intended services
iec61850.chapter13.l19.wf03: Test each redundancy path and restore the baseline
iec61850.chapter13.l19.example: For the 132/33 kV station, record MMS continuity, GOOSE reception and timing health during each planned failure. Include configuration backups and as-built port labels in the evidence pack.
iec61850.chapter13.l19.check: Do not certify protection transfer performance from an unsynchronized laptop capture alone; use a suitable measurement method.
iec61850.chapter13.l20.title: Network Troubleshooting
iec61850.chapter13.l20.p01: Network troubleshooting follows the actual packet path. Start with power, optical/link status and port identity, then inspect VLANs, forwarding, addressing, transport and the application service.
iec61850.chapter13.l20.p02: Use port counters and captures to locate where traffic disappears or becomes corrupted. Avoid disabling all filtering as a permanent fix; that can mask the original fault and overload unrelated devices. Preserve the failing configuration for comparison.
iec61850.chapter13.l20.wf02: Compare ingress and egress evidence at each hop
iec61850.chapter13.l20.wf03: Correct the specific mismatch and repeat normal/failure tests
iec61850.chapter13.l20.example: If 33-F01 GOOSE is visible at the source switch but absent at the receiving port, inspect VLAN and multicast policy on the intervening path before editing relay logic.
iec61850.chapter13.l20.check: Finish with an updated drawing, saved switch configuration and reproducible test result, not only a restored green link indicator.
iec61850.chapter14.l01.title: Introduction to Time Synchronization
iec61850.chapter14.l01.p01: Time synchronization establishes a common time reference for events, measurements and distributed applications. Its required accuracy depends on what the station must correlate or control, not simply whether clocks display the same minute.
iec61850.chapter14.l01.p02: Source time, server processing time and message arrival time are different observations. A network delay can make an event arrive late without changing when it occurred. Conversely, a fast network cannot repair an incorrect source clock.
iec61850.chapter14.l01.wf02: Define application accuracy and availability requirements
iec61850.chapter14.l01.wf03: Select and test the complete timing chain
iec61850.chapter14.l01.example: 33-F01 timestamps a breaker transition locally. The HMI preserves that source time and separately records acquisition health, allowing an engineer to distinguish delayed delivery from incorrect event timing.
iec61850.chapter14.l01.check: Specify how unsynchronized time is indicated; hiding bad time quality can produce convincing but incorrect event sequences.
iec61850.chapter14.l02.title: Importance of Accurate Time in SAS
iec61850.chapter14.l02.p01: Accurate time supports sequence-of-events analysis, disturbance correlation and synchronized sampling where required. Different applications tolerate different uncertainty, so one timing method may not satisfy all station functions.
iec61850.chapter14.l02.p02: An SOE study needs enough accuracy to distinguish relevant events across IEDs. A protection function comparing samples from different merging units may require tighter alignment. Do not infer either requirement from the visible number of decimal places on a display.
iec61850.chapter14.l02.wf01: List the events and measurements to be correlated
iec61850.chapter14.l02.wf03: Allocate a timing method and verification method to each device class
iec61850.chapter14.l02.example: The 132 kV process bay uses its specified precision timing profile, while a station monitoring application may use a separately justified SNTP arrangement.
iec61850.chapter14.l02.check: Record accuracy, resolution and synchronization status separately; millisecond formatting does not prove millisecond accuracy.
iec61850.chapter14.l03.title: Sequence of Events and Timestamping
iec61850.chapter14.l03.p01: Sequence of events relies on timestamps assigned at the appropriate source. The event list must retain the original time, state, quality and equipment identity rather than reorder everything solely by arrival at the gateway.
iec61850.chapter14.l03.p02: Buffered reports can deliver older events after reconnection. Equal or near-equal timestamps may not establish a unique physical order when uncertainty overlaps. Clock steps, invalid time quality and device restart must remain visible to investigators.
iec61850.chapter14.l03.wf01: Inject a known sequence at the source
iec61850.chapter14.l03.wf02: Compare IED, gateway and HMI times
iec61850.chapter14.l03.wf03: Repeat during communication delay and timing degradation
iec61850.chapter14.l03.example: 33-F01's protection operation precedes breaker-open feedback. A late buffered report should retain its source time instead of appearing as a new physical operation at the reconnection instant.
iec61850.chapter14.l03.check: Do not infer causation from timestamp order alone; consider measurement uncertainty, input filtering and application processing delays.
iec61850.chapter14.l04.title: GPS and GNSS Time Sources
iec61850.chapter14.l04.p01: GNSS receivers derive time from satellite systems and can discipline a station time server or grandmaster. Antenna placement, cable delay, receiver health and the selected equipment affect the quality delivered to the station.
iec61850.chapter14.l04.p02: Loss of satellite reception does not necessarily stop the clock immediately; the oscillator may enter holdover with growing uncertainty. The station must monitor that condition and know how long the selected equipment can meet the application's requirement under specified conditions.
iec61850.chapter14.l04.wf02: Confirm reference lock and timing outputs
iec61850.chapter14.l04.wf03: Test loss of reference and the resulting alarms/holdover behavior
iec61850.chapter14.l04.example: The station time server distributes time to 33 kV IEDs and a compatible PTP domain. A GNSS alarm is mapped to SCADA so degradation is visible before event timing becomes unreliable.
iec61850.chapter14.l04.check: Use the manufacturer's holdover specification and test evidence; do not promise indefinite accuracy from a disconnected antenna.
iec61850.chapter14.l05.title: SNTP Fundamentals
iec61850.chapter14.l05.p01: SNTP provides a simplified means of obtaining time using the NTP message format, commonly through UDP port 123. An IED client exchanges timestamps with an approved server and adjusts its local clock according to its implementation.
iec61850.chapter14.l05.p02: Accuracy depends on clock behavior, network delay and asymmetry, polling and the device's timestamping method. SNTP is useful where its demonstrated performance meets the requirement, but it should not be assumed adequate for every process-bus application.
iec61850.chapter14.l05.wf02: Confirm successful exchanges and clock status
iec61850.chapter14.l05.wf03: Measure offset and test server loss/recovery
iec61850.chapter14.l05.example: 33-F01 obtains station time from a designated server. During FAT, a known input event is compared against a suitable reference rather than judging synchronization from a ping response.
iec61850.chapter14.l05.check: Verify the IED's supported redundancy and polling behavior; specifying two servers does not prove automatic correct failover.
iec61850.chapter14.l06.title: NTP vs SNTP
iec61850.chapter14.l06.p01: NTP provides mechanisms for clock synchronization and source selection; SNTP uses a simpler subset of the approach for appropriate clients. Both are distinct from the precise hardware-assisted timing architectures often used with PTP.
iec61850.chapter14.l06.p02: Product behavior matters more than a generic label. Check supported versions, server selection, authentication where implemented, holdover and diagnostic visibility. A device called an NTP client may expose only limited configuration, while a time server can support several client types.
iec61850.chapter14.l06.wf01: Review the implemented protocol and features
iec61850.chapter14.l06.wf02: Match them to the timing requirement
iec61850.chapter14.l06.wf03: Test source change, offset and unhealthy-source behavior
iec61850.chapter14.l06.example: The station server can serve multiple monitoring devices while the process-bus system uses a separate compatible PTP profile. The design documents how both relate to the same reference.
iec61850.chapter14.l06.check: Do not claim SNTP and NTP have a fixed universal accuracy difference; assess the complete implementation and network.
iec61850.chapter14.l07.title: SNTP Client-Server Architecture
iec61850.chapter14.l07.p01: An SNTP architecture consists of approved time servers and configured clients connected through permitted IP paths. The design includes source health, client reachability and monitoring of synchronization status.
iec61850.chapter14.l07.p02: Time traffic must traverse the intended VLANs and routing policy. A working MMS connection does not prove UDP timing traffic is permitted. Server redundancy also needs client support and a test of actual selection behavior.
iec61850.chapter14.l07.wf03: Verify every client and test the loss of its preferred source
iec61850.chapter14.l07.example: 33-F01 uses the station time-server address in its configuration. The gateway records a time-synchronization alarm separately from the general IED communication alarm.
iec61850.chapter14.l07.check: Check both server health and client offset; a healthy server cannot guarantee a client is actually using it.
iec61850.chapter14.l08.title: Precision Time Protocol (PTP)
iec61850.chapter14.l08.p01: Precision Time Protocol synchronizes clocks through timestamped message exchanges and a defined clock hierarchy. Hardware timestamping and compatible network clock functions can reduce uncertainty compared with software-only timing paths.
iec61850.chapter14.l08.p02: PTP interoperability depends on the selected profile, transport, delay mechanism, domain and supported message behavior. Matching the word PTP in two datasheets is insufficient. Network asymmetry and incorrect profile combinations can produce persistent offset despite visible packets.
iec61850.chapter14.l08.wf02: Verify grandmaster, switch and endpoint compatibility
iec61850.chapter14.l08.wf03: Measure endpoint offset and behavior during reference/path changes
iec61850.chapter14.l08.example: MU_132_L01 uses a supported power-utility PTP profile to align sample timing. The protection test checks synchronized measurement behavior as well as the merging unit's clock diagnostic.
iec61850.chapter14.l08.check: Do not equate a PTP link indicator with verified application accuracy; measure at the relevant endpoint.
iec61850.chapter14.l09.title: IEEE 1588 and IEC/IEEE 61850-9-3
iec61850.chapter14.l09.p01: IEEE 1588 defines the PTP framework, while profiles constrain choices for particular applications. IEC/IEEE 61850-9-3 defines a precision-time profile for power utility automation where selected by the project.
iec61850.chapter14.l09.p02: Profiles help interoperability but do not make unsupported hardware compatible. Edition, transport and peer-delay behavior must align. Avoid combining arbitrary settings from different telecom, industrial or power profiles simply because each device accepts them individually.
iec61850.chapter14.l09.wf01: Record the required profile and edition
iec61850.chapter14.l09.wf03: Validate the selected configuration on the complete path
iec61850.chapter14.l09.example: The process-bus specification names its power-utility profile explicitly. Switches and merging units are checked against that requirement rather than using a vendor's unspecified PTP default.
iec61850.chapter14.l09.check: Keep profile compliance, measured accuracy and application acceptance as separate evidence items.
iec61850.chapter14.l10.title: PTP Grandmaster Clock
iec61850.chapter14.l10.p01: A PTP grandmaster supplies the selected time reference to its domain. Selection mechanisms compare advertised clock properties according to the profile, and engineered priorities can influence which suitable source is preferred.
iec61850.chapter14.l10.p02: The best advertised clock is only useful if the time source and configured properties are trustworthy. Monitor reference lock, clock quality and changes in grandmaster identity. Redundant grandmasters need a controlled failover test, not merely duplicate hardware installation.
iec61850.chapter14.l10.wf01: Configure approved master priorities and domain
iec61850.chapter14.l10.wf03: Remove the preferred source and measure transition/recovery
iec61850.chapter14.l10.example: The 132 kV process-bus endpoints select the station's intended grandmaster. During a controlled loss, the test records any offset excursion and resulting sample synchronization indication.
iec61850.chapter14.l10.check: Do not hard-code an unsupported accuracy class or priority to force selection; use the documented profile and device behavior.
iec61850.chapter14.l11.title: Boundary Clock and Transparent Clock
iec61850.chapter14.l11.p01: A boundary clock synchronizes through one port and serves time through other ports, creating timing domains within the hierarchy. A transparent clock measures relevant transit behavior and contributes correction information rather than acting as a new master in the same way.
iec61850.chapter14.l11.p02: The supported delay mechanism and profile determine how these functions operate. An ordinary switch can carry PTP frames yet add variable delay without the required compensation. Verify the exact switch mode and endpoint compatibility.
iec61850.chapter14.l11.wf01: Identify each network device's clock role
iec61850.chapter14.l11.wf03: Measure the complete path under load and after topology changes
iec61850.chapter14.l11.example: The process network uses compatible transparent-clock switches or an approved boundary-clock design. These roles are drawn differently so maintenance staff do not confuse forwarding with clock regeneration.
iec61850.chapter14.l11.check: Do not enable unrelated PTP modes on adjacent switches and assume correction fields will remain meaningful.
iec61850.chapter14.l12.title: PTP Synchronization Mechanism
iec61850.chapter14.l12.p01: PTP estimates clock offset using timing exchanges and a model of path delay. Sync and, in two-step operation, Follow_Up convey timing information; the selected profile's delay mechanism supplies the needed path-delay observations.
iec61850.chapter14.l12.p02: End-to-end Delay_Req/Delay_Resp and peer-delay exchanges are different mechanisms. The power-utility profile must be implemented as specified rather than mixing these sequences. Asymmetric delay remains an important source of error even when message exchange succeeds.
iec61850.chapter14.l12.wf01: Inspect profile, domain and message sequence
iec61850.chapter14.l12.wf02: Compare measured offset and path-delay diagnostics
iec61850.chapter14.l12.wf03: Test loading and path changes against the accuracy requirement
iec61850.chapter14.l12.example: For the power-utility example, verify the supported peer-delay behavior between adjacent devices and the expected Sync/Follow_Up handling at the endpoint.
iec61850.chapter14.l12.check: An educational sequence diagram simplifies message timing; it is not a substitute for the selected profile's exact state machines.
iec61850.chapter14.l13.title: SNTP vs PTP Comparison
iec61850.chapter14.l13.p01: SNTP and PTP serve different engineering needs and implementations. SNTP is commonly used for suitable station-event timing, while compatible PTP designs support tighter timing requirements such as synchronized process-bus measurements.
iec61850.chapter14.l13.p02: Selection depends on demonstrated accuracy, availability, device support and maintenance complexity. Neither protocol name guarantees a fixed result. PTP also requires correct profile and network-clock behavior; adding a grandmaster alone may not achieve the required accuracy.
iec61850.chapter14.l13.wf03: Select the method and prove it with an appropriate measurement
iec61850.chapter14.l13.example: The station can use one GNSS reference to support an SNTP service and a compatible PTP system, while monitoring both independently.
iec61850.chapter14.l13.check: Keep actual test limits in the project specification; do not teach one universal accuracy number for every SNTP or PTP deployment.
iec61850.chapter14.l14.title: Time Synchronization for Process Bus
iec61850.chapter14.l14.p01: Process-bus synchronization aligns sample acquisition where protection algorithms require consistent timing across sources. The timing chain includes the reference, distribution network, merging-unit clock and sampling behavior.
iec61850.chapter14.l14.p02: Clock health must propagate into useful diagnostics and application supervision. A grandmaster failure may first cause holdover, then unacceptable uncertainty; the receiving protection response depends on the selected design and supported quality indications.
iec61850.chapter14.l14.wf02: Verify timing at each merging unit
iec61850.chapter14.l14.wf03: Test reference loss, path change and restoration with the subscriber operating
iec61850.chapter14.l14.example: Two measurement sources used by a 132 kV protection application are compared using suitable synchronized test equipment. A common source name in their configuration is not enough to prove alignment.
iec61850.chapter14.l14.check: Test the protection application's documented degraded-time response rather than assuming every device immediately stops publishing samples.
iec61850.chapter14.l15.title: IED Time Configuration
iec61850.chapter14.l15.p01: IED time configuration sets the supported timing source, related network parameters and display conventions. The device's internal timestamp basis should be distinguished from local time-zone formatting at an HMI or engineering workstation.
iec61850.chapter14.l15.p02: UTC-based event handling avoids ambiguous daylight-saving transitions, while operator displays can convert time according to the site policy. Incorrect time-zone configuration can produce a fixed offset even when the underlying clock is synchronized.
iec61850.chapter14.l15.wf01: Select the approved source and profile/server
iec61850.chapter14.l15.wf02: Verify source time and time quality
iec61850.chapter14.l15.wf03: Check display conversion, restart and loss-of-reference behavior
iec61850.chapter14.l15.example: 33-F01 event timestamps are preserved through the gateway, with local display conversion applied consistently for the station. A 5:30 difference is investigated as a possible display-zone issue before altering the clock.
iec61850.chapter14.l15.check: Do not compensate a display conversion error by deliberately offsetting the IED's reference time.
iec61850.chapter14.l16.title: SCADA and Gateway Time Synchronization
iec61850.chapter14.l16.p01: Gateways and SCADA servers need their own synchronized clocks for logs, communication diagnostics and locally generated events. They must also preserve source timestamps from IEDs instead of replacing every event with gateway arrival time.
iec61850.chapter14.l16.p02: Redundant servers can disagree if their clock sources or time-zone settings differ. During failover, check event ordering and duplicate handling as well as data continuity. Distinguish source-time quality from the health of the gateway's own clock.
iec61850.chapter14.l16.wf02: Configure timestamp preservation and display policy
iec61850.chapter14.l16.wf03: Test delayed reports and server failover
iec61850.chapter14.l16.example: A buffered 33-F01 event arrives after reconnection. The SOE shows its original source time and the system can still record when it was received for diagnostics.
iec61850.chapter14.l16.check: Verify exported logs retain enough timezone/UTC context to compare records from different devices without guesswork.
iec61850.chapter14.l17.title: Time Quality and Clock Failure
iec61850.chapter14.l17.p01: Time quality communicates whether a timestamp can be trusted to the degree required by the application. Relevant flags and accuracy indications depend on the service, edition and device implementation.
iec61850.chapter14.l17.p02: Clock failure, loss of synchronization and uncertain accuracy are not identical conditions. Holdover may preserve useful time temporarily while uncertainty grows. The HMI should make degraded time visible without confusing it with invalid process value quality.
iec61850.chapter14.l17.wf02: Map them to alarms and investigation rules
iec61850.chapter14.l17.wf03: Test reference failure and recovery at source and consumer
iec61850.chapter14.l17.example: 33-F01 continues reporting breaker state during a time-source outage, but its event timing is marked according to the device's supported status. The operator can distinguish a valid position from uncertain event time.
iec61850.chapter14.l17.check: Do not silently sort uncertain events into a definitive causal sequence; preserve the quality evidence.
iec61850.chapter14.l18.title: Practical Example — 132/33 kV Substation
iec61850.chapter14.l18.p01: The practical timing design serves a 132/33 kV station with monitored reference equipment, configured clients and compatible process-bus timing where used. It documents every source and the applications that depend on it.
iec61850.chapter14.l18.p02: Redundancy is assessed across antenna, receiver, power and network paths. The design also states what happens during holdover and how operators recognize degradation. A second server sharing all the same failure points may provide less resilience than expected.
iec61850.chapter14.l18.wf03: Test source/path failures and compare application outcomes
iec61850.chapter14.l18.example: 33-F01 event timing and MU_132_L01 sample timing are tested separately against their specified requirements. Both contribute health indications to station monitoring.
iec61850.chapter14.l18.check: Maintain one consistent time-zone/display policy and retain reference-quality evidence with the acceptance records.
iec61850.chapter14.l19.title: Time Synchronization FAT/SAT Testing
iec61850.chapter14.l19.p01: Timing FAT verifies compatible profiles, source selection, endpoint accuracy and failure behavior in a controlled arrangement. SAT adds installed antenna, cable, switch and network-path verification.
iec61850.chapter14.l19.p02: Use suitable reference equipment and a defined measurement method. Comparing two unsynchronized laptop clocks cannot establish microsecond performance. Record uncertainty, loading conditions and the exact device configuration used for every result.
iec61850.chapter14.l19.wf01: Verify normal synchronization and source identity
iec61850.chapter14.l19.wf02: Measure endpoint timing against the required limit
iec61850.chapter14.l19.wf03: Test reference loss, holdover, failover and restoration
iec61850.chapter14.l19.example: For the process bay, observe sample alignment and subscriber health during a grandmaster transition. For SOE, inject known events and compare source timestamps and quality through the HMI.
iec61850.chapter14.l19.check: State the measurement method and uncertainty with the pass result; precision in a screenshot is not accuracy evidence.
iec61850.chapter14.l20.title: Time Synchronization Troubleshooting
iec61850.chapter14.l20.p01: Time troubleshooting distinguishes source failure, network transport failure, profile mismatch, offset error and display conversion. Begin by checking which source the endpoint actually uses and whether its quality is acceptable.
iec61850.chapter14.l20.p02: Stable fixed offsets often suggest time-zone, UTC-offset or configuration issues; variable offsets may indicate delay, load or synchronization problems. These are diagnostic hypotheses, not proofs. Confirm them with source, network and endpoint evidence.
iec61850.chapter14.l20.wf02: Inspect timing messages and selected profile
iec61850.chapter14.l20.wf03: Correct one cause and repeat normal/failure measurements
iec61850.chapter14.l20.example: If 33-F01 events are consistently shifted only in the HMI, inspect gateway/display conversion. If the IED itself reports unsynchronized time, trace its configured server or PTP path.
iec61850.chapter14.l20.check: Do not hide a timing fault by increasing alarm thresholds without proving the application still meets its requirement.
iec61850.chapter15.l01.title: Introduction to Substation SCADA
iec61850.chapter15.l01.p01: Substation SCADA acquires operational information, presents alarms and supports authorized control. It brings together equipment identity, current values, quality and time so operators can understand the station state.
iec61850.chapter15.l01.p02: SCADA is not the primary protection algorithm. A healthy screen does not prove protection is correctly configured, and a lost HMI should not be confused with loss of every local protection function. Define the monitoring and control scope clearly.
iec61850.chapter15.l01.wf01: Identify operator information and control requirements
iec61850.chapter15.l01.wf02: Build the point and alarm schedules
iec61850.chapter15.l01.wf03: Test each function from source to final presentation
iec61850.chapter15.l01.example: The 132/33/11 kV station displays line, transformer and feeder status with measurements and alarms. Each displayed value is traceable to an actual source reference.
iec61850.chapter15.l01.check: Avoid creating attractive but unbound symbols; every operational indication needs a defined source, quality policy and test case.
iec61850.chapter15.l02.title: Station Gateway Architecture
iec61850.chapter15.l02.p01: A station gateway aggregates data from IEDs and exposes selected information to station or remote systems. It may translate protocols, manage point databases and provide redundancy functions according to its supported implementation.
iec61850.chapter15.l02.p02: Protocol conversion is semantic engineering, not just changing packet headers. Data types, quality, timestamps and command behavior must be mapped deliberately. Unsupported features must be identified rather than silently discarded.
iec61850.chapter15.l02.wf03: Test normal, invalid and communication-failure cases end to end
iec61850.chapter15.l02.example: Gateway A acquires 33-F01 over MMS and sends selected points to the control centre using the approved IEC 60870-5-104 configuration.
iec61850.chapter15.l02.check: Document any loss of quality or timestamp detail during conversion so operators and engineers understand the resulting limitation.
iec61850.chapter15.l03.title: SCADA Server and HMI Workstation
iec61850.chapter15.l03.p01: SCADA servers manage acquisition, alarms, history and control services, while HMI workstations present operator views. The exact division depends on the product architecture and redundancy design.
iec61850.chapter15.l03.p02: Separate server health from process quality. A workstation can display cached values while the acquisition server is disconnected. Operator permissions, session state and control ownership also need testing across server changes.
iec61850.chapter15.l03.wf02: Configure data sources and access rights
iec61850.chapter15.l03.wf03: Test workstation loss, server loss and reconnection
iec61850.chapter15.l03.example: The station operator can inspect 33-F01 on a redundant HMI arrangement where specified. The display marks stale acquisition and does not retain an apparently live green status after its source is unavailable.
iec61850.chapter15.l03.check: Verify the actual failover behavior; installing two computers does not automatically create redundant acquisition or command arbitration.
iec61850.chapter15.l04.title: IEC 61850 MMS Client Configuration
iec61850.chapter15.l04.p01: An IEC 61850 MMS client needs the correct endpoint, supported association parameters, model references and service configuration. Reporting also requires assigned RCB resources and compatible DataSet interpretation.
iec61850.chapter15.l04.p02: Importing an SCD can accelerate engineering, but imported points still need review. Optional model objects, firmware changes and client limitations may require explicit selection. Keep control permissions separate from read/report access.
iec61850.chapter15.l04.wf01: Verify server identity and online model
iec61850.chapter15.l04.wf02: Allocate reports and map required points
iec61850.chapter15.l04.wf03: Test acquisition, reconnect and approved control behavior
iec61850.chapter15.l04.example: Gateway A connects to 33-F01 at 192.168.100.31 and enables its assigned buffered status report. Its point database retains the actual reference and functional constraint.
iec61850.chapter15.l04.check: Do not treat an association-success message as proof that the client's report blocks, data types and alarm mappings are correct.
iec61850.chapter15.l05.title: Gateway Data Acquisition
iec61850.chapter15.l05.p01: Gateway acquisition can use reads, reports or other supported services according to the source protocol and application. The engineering choice affects update latency, network load and event retention.
iec61850.chapter15.l05.p02: Polling obtains snapshots; reporting can convey transitions and quality changes. Both need stale-data detection and recovery logic. Redundant acquisition must avoid conflicting resource ownership or duplicate operator events.
iec61850.chapter15.l05.wf01: Classify status, measurement and event requirements
iec61850.chapter15.l05.wf03: Test changes, loss and restoration with realistic load
iec61850.chapter15.l05.example: 33-F01 breaker transitions use reporting, while appropriate measurement updates follow the configured deadband or acquisition strategy. The gateway records a data gap if recovery cannot restore all required events.
iec61850.chapter15.l05.check: Do not use a periodic current-state refresh as proof that no events were lost during an outage.
iec61850.chapter15.l06.title: IEC 61850 Signal Mapping
iec61850.chapter15.l06.p01: Signal mapping links a source reference to an engineering tag and destination representation. A useful mapping record includes equipment, logical device/node, object/attribute, functional constraint, type, unit, quality and timestamp policy.
iec61850.chapter15.l06.p02: Names alone are insufficient because different devices can expose similar labels for different functions. Preserve the original reference and document any conversion. Review mappings whenever the model or SCD revision changes.
iec61850.chapter15.l06.wf03: Inject known values and verify the final tag
iec61850.chapter15.l06.example: The tag 33_F01_CB_POS maps to the actual XCBR1.Pos source for that feeder. A separate control tag targets the approved controllable object.
iec61850.chapter15.l06.check: Never map a command acknowledgment into the breaker-position tag; physical feedback remains the authoritative indication of position.
iec61850.chapter15.l07.title: Digital Status Mapping
iec61850.chapter15.l07.p01: Digital status mapping must preserve the source's state semantics. Single-point status is Boolean-like, while double-point position can represent intermediate and bad states in addition to open and closed.
iec61850.chapter15.l07.p02: Contact inversion and encoded values must be handled explicitly. Mapping every nonzero double-point value to closed loses important abnormal conditions. Quality and stale-data behavior should remain visible in the HMI symbol and alarm logic.
iec61850.chapter15.l07.wf02: Define destination labels and abnormal-state behavior
iec61850.chapter15.l07.wf03: Test every supported state and invalid quality
iec61850.chapter15.l07.example: For XCBR1.Pos.stVal, the illustrative double-point mapping uses 1=open/off, 2=closed/on, 0=intermediate and 3=bad-state according to the applicable model semantics.
iec61850.chapter15.l07.check: Confirm the device and destination protocol encoding; a Boolean control request is not encoded the same way as this double-point status.
iec61850.chapter15.l08.title: Analog Measurement Mapping
iec61850.chapter15.l08.p01: Analog mapping converts a source quantity into the intended engineering unit and range. The source may already represent primary values, so ratio conversion must be located explicitly in the chain.
iec61850.chapter15.l08.p02: Check units, multiplier, signedness, floating-point representation, phase identity and deadband. A single correct nominal value can hide an offset or scaling error. Alarm thresholds must use the same engineering basis as the displayed measurement.
iec61850.chapter15.l08.wf02: Test zero and several representative values
iec61850.chapter15.l08.wf03: Verify display, history and alarm thresholds
iec61850.chapter15.l08.example: 33-F01 phase current is displayed in primary amperes. If the relay already applies the CT ratio, the gateway uses that value without multiplying the ratio again.
iec61850.chapter15.l08.check: Test negative power or reverse flow where relevant; unsigned conversion can hide direction or produce an extreme positive value.
iec61850.chapter15.l09.title: Alarm and Event Mapping
iec61850.chapter15.l09.p01: Alarms identify conditions requiring attention, while events record changes for analysis. The same source may contribute to both, but priority, acknowledgment and return-to-normal behavior belong to the operator philosophy.
iec61850.chapter15.l09.p02: Alarm acknowledgment means the operator has recognized the alarm; it does not repair the condition. Preserve source time and quality, and avoid creating repeated alarms from every retransmission of the same state.
iec61850.chapter15.l09.wf03: Test transitions, persistent conditions and communication failures
iec61850.chapter15.l09.example: 33-F01 protection operation appears in SOE and may generate a configured alarm. Breaker-open feedback is recorded separately so the operator can distinguish trip initiation from successful opening.
iec61850.chapter15.l09.check: Ensure an invalid source is not interpreted as a normal cleared alarm merely because the last received Boolean was false.
iec61850.chapter15.l10.title: Circuit Breaker Control Mapping
iec61850.chapter15.l10.p01: Breaker control mapping connects an authorized operator request to the correct IEC 61850 control object and model. It also binds independent feedback and command-result information to the operator workflow.
iec61850.chapter15.l10.p02: The command must respect selection, authority, interlocks and timeout behavior supported by the server. A positive service response does not prove the mechanism moved. Controls should be labeled unambiguously with equipment identity and intended action.
iec61850.chapter15.l10.wf01: Verify the control reference and ctlModel
iec61850.chapter15.l10.wf02: Map command result and physical feedback separately
iec61850.chapter15.l10.wf03: Test allowed, rejected and uncertain-result cases in isolation
iec61850.chapter15.l10.example: The HMI issues an approved close request to 33-F01's supported CSWI1.Pos control object and watches XCBR1.Pos for actual position.
iec61850.chapter15.l10.check: After a timeout, reconcile state before retrying; never implement automatic repeated close requests based solely on missing acknowledgment.
iec61850.chapter15.l11.title: IEC 61850 to IEC 60870-5-104 Mapping
iec61850.chapter15.l11.p01: IEC 61850 to IEC 60870-5-104 mapping assigns source information to destination types, common addresses and information object addresses. Quality, timestamps and control semantics require deliberate conversion according to the selected interoperability profile.
iec61850.chapter15.l11.p02: There is no universal IOA derived automatically from a logical-node name. The project signal schedule defines stable addresses and types. Verify single/double-point selection, measurement format, cause of transmission and time-tag handling as supported.
iec61850.chapter15.l11.wf03: Test point values and controls through the remote master
iec61850.chapter15.l11.example: 33-F01 breaker position uses an agreed double-point indication type, such as a compatible time-tagged form where specified. Its IOA is a project allocation, not an IEC 61850 object number.
iec61850.chapter15.l11.check: Document unsupported source detail and verify command select/execute behavior at both protocol boundaries.
iec61850.chapter15.l12.title: IEC 61850 to Modbus Mapping
iec61850.chapter15.l12.p01: Modbus exposes coils and registers rather than the full IEC 61850 object and service model. Mapping therefore requires explicit addresses, data representation, word order, scaling and separate handling for status or quality that does not fit the chosen register.
iec61850.chapter15.l12.p02: A 32-bit floating-point value spans two 16-bit registers, but word order varies by implementation. Register numbering conventions can also differ between documentation and protocol offsets. Control through registers needs an approved gateway implementation and cannot simply mimic IEC 61850 SBO semantics.
iec61850.chapter15.l12.wf03: Test boundary values and read/write permissions
iec61850.chapter15.l12.example: 33-F01 current can be exported as an agreed two-register float with a separate validity register. The worksheet states the exact word order and zero-based offset convention.
iec61850.chapter15.l12.check: Do not assume Modbus inherently preserves source timestamps, quality or IEC 61850 control security behavior.
iec61850.chapter15.l13.title: SCADA Single-Line Diagram Engineering
iec61850.chapter15.l13.p01: An HMI single-line diagram presents the station's electrical connectivity and equipment states. Its symbols must reflect the approved primary drawing and be bound to verified source tags.
iec61850.chapter15.l13.p02: Visual color is an operator convention, not a universal electrical meaning. Show intermediate, bad and unavailable states distinctly. Navigation and equipment labels should prevent a command intended for one bay from being applied to another.
iec61850.chapter15.l13.wf01: Build the SLD from the approved topology
iec61850.chapter15.l13.wf03: Test state changes, invalid data and equipment selection
iec61850.chapter15.l13.example: The practical station's 11 kV bus is supplied through its 33/11 kV transformer, not drawn directly off the 33 kV bus. Feeder labels remain identical to the signal schedule.
iec61850.chapter15.l13.check: Verify electrical connectivity independently of screen appearance; a polished graphic can still contain a wrong bus connection.
iec61850.chapter15.l14.title: Alarm and SOE Configuration
iec61850.chapter15.l14.p01: Alarm and SOE configuration defines priorities, timestamp policy, acknowledgment and event retention. These settings should help operators distinguish first causes, consequences and communication degradation.
iec61850.chapter15.l14.p02: Avoid event floods caused by unstable contacts, excessive measurement updates or duplicate acquisition. Deadbands and debounce must follow the application requirement and must not hide meaningful operations. Buffered replay should retain original event time and be distinguishable from a new occurrence.
iec61850.chapter15.l14.wf03: Test bursts, reconnect and acknowledgment behavior
iec61850.chapter15.l14.example: During a feeder fault, the HMI records protection operation and breaker feedback separately. A subsequent communication alarm does not overwrite the original event chronology.
iec61850.chapter15.l14.check: Measure event handling under representative bursts, including recovery after an outage, rather than testing one slow transition at a time.
iec61850.chapter15.l15.title: SCADA Database Engineering
iec61850.chapter15.l15.p01: The SCADA database is an engineering deliverable containing point identities, acquisition, conversions, alarms, history and controls. Its structure should support traceability from physical equipment to source and destination references.
iec61850.chapter15.l15.p02: Bulk import is useful only when templates preserve unique identifiers and validated transformations. Duplicate tags or copied addresses can silently bind several symbols to one feeder. Use reviewable revisions and comparison reports for changes.
iec61850.chapter15.l15.wf02: Import from the controlled signal schedule
iec61850.chapter15.l15.wf03: Validate uniqueness and perform point-by-point tests
iec61850.chapter15.l15.example: 33_F01_CB_POS and 33_F02_CB_POS have distinct source references and destination addresses. A template creates consistent structure but never reuses the same source accidentally.
iec61850.chapter15.l15.check: Archive the tested database with the SCD and gateway configuration; a spreadsheet alone may not represent the deployed system.
iec61850.chapter15.l16.title: Redundant SCADA and Gateway Architecture
iec61850.chapter15.l16.p01: Redundant SCADA and gateways maintain service through selected component failures. The design must specify active/standby or other supported roles, data synchronization and command ownership.
iec61850.chapter15.l16.p02: Dual hardware can introduce duplicate alarms, competing RCB reservations or simultaneous control if coordination is incomplete. Test acquisition and command behavior separately during failover and restoration. Shared power, storage or network paths remain possible common failures.
iec61850.chapter15.l16.wf01: Define role selection and resource allocation
iec61850.chapter15.l16.wf03: Test failure, switchover, restart and split-connectivity cases
iec61850.chapter15.l16.example: Gateway A and B acquire 33-F01 using their approved reporting strategy. Only the authorized control path issues a command, and failover does not replay an old pending close request.
iec61850.chapter15.l16.check: Verify recovery to the normal role as carefully as initial failover; unstable role switching can be worse than a clear single failure.
iec61850.chapter15.l17.title: Remote Control Centre Communication
iec61850.chapter15.l17.p01: Remote control-centre communication exposes selected station information and authorized operations through the approved telecontrol interface. The station gateway separates source models from the remote protocol and addressing scheme.
iec61850.chapter15.l17.p02: Network security, command authority and outage behavior belong to the system design. The control centre should see communication and data-quality changes, not just cached values. Remote operations still depend on local interlocks and the station's authority policy.
iec61850.chapter15.l17.wf03: Test indications, controls and link failure with both ends participating
iec61850.chapter15.l17.example: The control centre receives 33-F01 position and measurements through Gateway A. Local/remote authority and command rejection are tested at the station and visible remotely.
iec61850.chapter15.l17.check: Do not bypass station interlocks during protocol conversion; an accepted remote packet is not permission to ignore local operating conditions.
iec61850.chapter15.l18.title: Practical Example — 132/33/11 kV Substation
iec61850.chapter15.l18.p01: The practical mapping exercise follows the 132/33/11 kV project from IEDs through gateways to station HMI and remote control centre. It uses one controlled equipment and signal schedule throughout.
iec61850.chapter15.l18.p02: Separate source references, engineering tags and destination protocol addresses. A correction at one layer must be reviewed for effects on the others. Test measurements, states, alarms and controls with invalid and unavailable cases as well as normal values.
iec61850.chapter15.l18.wf03: Execute witnessed point-to-point tests and archive the final database
iec61850.chapter15.l18.example: 33-F01 at 192.168.100.31 maps breaker position to tag 33_F01_CB_POS. The 11-F01 feeder uses its own IED and tag rather than a duplicated 33 kV reference.
iec61850.chapter15.l18.check: Verify that every displayed voltage level and bay identity matches the actual source, especially when reusing HMI templates.
iec61850.chapter15.l19.title: SCADA FAT/SAT Testing
iec61850.chapter15.l19.p01: SCADA FAT verifies configured acquisition, mapping, alarms, history and authorized control before site installation. SAT proves the installed field-to-screen and remote-control-centre paths.
iec61850.chapter15.l19.p02: Expected results must include quality, source time, scaling and failure behavior. A test that checks only the displayed number can miss invalid data, wrong event timing or unsafe command retry. Record the source stimulus and destination observation together.
iec61850.chapter15.l19.wf02: Test approved controls and rejected requests
iec61850.chapter15.l19.wf03: Interrupt IED, server and remote links and verify recovery
iec61850.chapter15.l19.example: For 33-F01, the witness records injected current, local relay value, gateway value, HMI display and remote indication. Control tests include physical feedback and a deliberately rejected permissive case.
iec61850.chapter15.l19.check: Close database changes with repeat tests; a corrected tag invalidates the earlier result for that affected point.
iec61850.chapter15.l20.title: SCADA and Gateway Troubleshooting
iec61850.chapter15.l20.p01: SCADA troubleshooting follows the information chain from source to acquisition driver, database transformation and operator presentation. Confirm whether the source itself is correct before editing HMI graphics.
iec61850.chapter15.l20.p02: A correct driver value with a wrong display suggests mapping or visualization; a stale driver value with healthy association suggests reporting or polling; incorrect source data requires IED/application investigation. Use one known stimulus and compare timestamps across layers.
iec61850.chapter15.l20.wf01: Identify the failing point and expected state
iec61850.chapter15.l20.wf02: Compare source, driver, tag and display
iec61850.chapter15.l20.wf03: Correct the specific layer and repeat related failure tests
iec61850.chapter15.l20.example: If 33-F01 current is ten times too high only after gateway conversion, inspect scaling and CT-ratio handling. If all layers agree incorrectly, inspect the measurement source first.
iec61850.chapter15.l20.check: Preserve logs and the previous database revision so the correction is explainable and reversible.
iec61850.chapter16.l01.title: Introduction to Substation Control Functions
iec61850.chapter16.l01.p01: Substation control functions turn authorized requests into equipment actions under defined conditions. They include authority selection, interlocking, command sequencing, output operation and independent feedback.
iec61850.chapter16.l01.p02: Protection tripping and operator switching are related but different applications. Their permissives and priorities must follow the approved design. Communication services provide the request mechanism; they do not determine every electrical or operational condition for safe switching.
iec61850.chapter16.l01.wf01: Identify the equipment and permitted actions
iec61850.chapter16.l01.example: 33-F01 supports an approved remote close/open function while its protection trip path retains the required independence. Both paths are documented rather than represented by one generic HMI button.
iec61850.chapter16.l01.check: Do not assume every condition that blocks closing should also block protection tripping; evaluate the actual scheme.
iec61850.chapter16.l02.title: Circuit Breaker Operating Mechanism
iec61850.chapter16.l02.p01: A circuit breaker mechanism converts electrical control energy into mechanical opening or closing. Auxiliary contacts provide position feedback, while stored-energy, trip-circuit and other supervision signals depend on the installed equipment.
iec61850.chapter16.l02.p02: An energized coil does not guarantee the main contacts reached the intended position. Mechanical failure, supply loss or wiring faults can interrupt the action. Control engineering therefore monitors both command results and physical feedback within specified timing.
iec61850.chapter16.l02.wf02: Identify command outputs and auxiliary feedback
iec61850.chapter16.l02.wf03: Test the isolated mechanism or simulator with expected timing
iec61850.chapter16.l02.example: For 33-F01, a close output is followed by verified XCBR1.Pos feedback. If feedback does not change, the HMI reports failure or uncertainty according to the project design.
iec61850.chapter16.l02.check: A teaching block diagram is not a terminal-level wiring instruction; actual coils, contacts and supply ratings come from approved drawings.
iec61850.chapter16.l03.title: Local and Remote Control
iec61850.chapter16.l03.p01: Local/remote control establishes where switching authority resides. Authority may involve physical selectors, device modes, station roles and remote-control-centre permissions according to the station philosophy.
iec61850.chapter16.l03.p02: A local selector can block an otherwise valid network command. The rejection should be visible and understandable rather than bypassed. Changing authority must not accidentally suppress required protection functions or leave an old selection active indefinitely.
iec61850.chapter16.l03.wf02: Map their status and command checks
iec61850.chapter16.l03.wf03: Test each permitted and prohibited operating location
iec61850.chapter16.l03.example: 33-F01 in local mode rejects an HMI close request while allowing the authorized local procedure. The HMI shows the authority state so the operator can understand the rejection.
iec61850.chapter16.l03.check: Verify authority again at execution time where required; an earlier screen indication may be stale.
iec61850.chapter16.l04.title: Direct Control vs Select-Before-Operate
iec61850.chapter16.l04.p01: Direct control sends an operation request without a separate selection phase. Select-before-operate reserves or selects the controllable object before an operation under the supported control model.
iec61850.chapter16.l04.p02: SBO helps coordinate access and request context but does not replace electrical interlocks, authorization or physical feedback. Normal and enhanced security variants differ in service behavior. The client must use the object's actual ctlModel rather than a generic preferred sequence.
iec61850.chapter16.l04.wf03: Test acceptance, rejection, cancellation and timeout
iec61850.chapter16.l04.example: 33-F01's approved control point may use an SBO model, while another device uses direct control. The gateway stores those differences explicitly instead of forcing every breaker through the same driver behavior.
iec61850.chapter16.l04.check: Do not label enhanced control security as equivalent to encrypted transport; those are different concepts.
iec61850.chapter16.l05.title: Select-Before-Operate (SBO) Sequence
iec61850.chapter16.l05.p01: An SBO transaction includes selection, an operation while selection remains valid, and result handling. Depending on the control model, selection can use the normal or enhanced service form, with supported cancellation and timeout behavior.
iec61850.chapter16.l05.p02: Selection is not a guarantee that a later operation will succeed. Authority, interlocks or equipment state can change before execution. The client must preserve the required command context and treat rejection or timeout as an explicit outcome.
iec61850.chapter16.l05.wf02: Select using the supported service and then operate within its validity
iec61850.chapter16.l05.wf03: Evaluate service result, termination where applicable and independent feedback
iec61850.chapter16.l05.example: For isolated 33-F01 closing, select the approved object, issue close and confirm breaker feedback. A deliberately expired selection must not execute as if still valid.
iec61850.chapter16.l05.check: After uncertainty, reconcile the actual position before another attempt; never retry an old operation automatically.
iec61850.chapter16.l06.title: IEC 61850 Control Models
iec61850.chapter16.l06.p01: IEC 61850 control models distinguish status-only, direct and SBO behavior, with normal or enhanced security variants for controllable objects. The model is represented through ctlModel where applicable.
iec61850.chapter16.l06.p02: Enhanced control provides additional command-result handling such as command termination according to the service model. That response still differs from independent physical feedback and does not prove every external mechanism condition. Exact supported options must come from the device model and manual.
iec61850.chapter16.l06.wf01: Inspect ctlModel and supported control structure
iec61850.chapter16.l06.wf03: Test the required sequence and error/result handling
iec61850.chapter16.l06.example: The tutorial compares direct-normal, SBO-normal, direct-enhanced and SBO-enhanced behavior without assigning a universal model to every XCBR or CSWI instance.
iec61850.chapter16.l06.check: Do not write a new ctlModel value in service merely to satisfy a client limitation; any change requires supported engineering and retesting.
iec61850.chapter16.l07.title: CSWI Logical Node
iec61850.chapter16.l07.p01: CSWI represents switching-control functionality in the IEC 61850 model. It commonly provides an application interface for requests that are evaluated with authority and interlocking logic before driving equipment.
iec61850.chapter16.l07.p02: The exact relationship between CSWI, physical outputs and breaker feedback is implementation-specific. A supported controllable object must be identified from the actual IED model. Naming a logical node CSWI1 does not create an operating circuit by itself.
iec61850.chapter16.l07.wf02: Trace its authority and permissive inputs
iec61850.chapter16.l07.wf03: Verify output action and feedback association
iec61850.chapter16.l07.example: The illustrative HMI request targets IED_33_F01LD0/CSWI1.Pos where supported. The resulting action is checked against the actual 33-F01 breaker feedback source.
iec61850.chapter16.l07.check: Keep command intent separate from measured position; the CSWI request value is not evidence that the breaker moved.
iec61850.chapter16.l08.title: XCBR Logical Node
iec61850.chapter16.l08.p01: XCBR models circuit-breaker information and associated functionality. Its position object represents the breaker state according to the configured application and available feedback.
iec61850.chapter16.l08.p02: Use the correct double-point interpretation and preserve quality. Intermediate or inconsistent auxiliary-contact combinations should not be forced into a healthy open or closed display. Some implementations expose control through different supported objects, so follow the actual model.
iec61850.chapter16.l08.wf01: Trace auxiliary contacts into position logic
iec61850.chapter16.l08.wf02: Verify the exposed Pos structure and quality
iec61850.chapter16.l08.wf03: Test open, closed, transition and abnormal cases
iec61850.chapter16.l08.example: 33-F01's 52a/52b inputs update XCBR1.Pos. The HMI uses this feedback to confirm a requested close independently of the command-service response.
iec61850.chapter16.l08.check: An object name alone does not prove which physical breaker it represents; verify the equipment association and signal schedule.
iec61850.chapter16.l09.title: CILO Interlocking Logical Node
iec61850.chapter16.l09.p01: CILO models interlocking-related information. Supported objects can communicate whether switching actions are permitted, while the detailed logic behind those indications belongs to the engineered application.
iec61850.chapter16.l09.p02: Interlocking must reflect the actual bus arrangement, equipment capabilities and operating policy. A permissive should be based on valid and sufficiently fresh inputs. CILO is a standardized model concept, not a universal built-in interlocking program for every substation.
