iec61850.chapter20.l01.p02: 33-F01 serves a 33 kV load from 33-B1. 33-F02 leaves 33-B2 and supplies T2; T2 feeds 11-B1 and feeders 11-F01/11-F02. This teaching project uses conventional analogue inputs and a PRP station bus; detailed protection ratings and additional independent schemes require the project study.
iec61850.chapter20.l01.wf01: Freeze the equipment and interface schedule
iec61850.chapter20.l01.wf02: Allocate models, networks and operator functions
iec61850.chapter20.l01.wf03: Test the complete chain and retain as-built records
iec61850.chapter20.l01.example: 33-BC01 is normally open in the stated baseline, leaving the B2/T2/11 kV branch de-energized until an approved operating condition and procedure permits energization.
iec61850.chapter20.l01.check: These are consistent teaching assumptions, not a construction design or a recommended operating arrangement for every station.
iec61850.chapter20.l02.title: 132/33/11 kV Substation Architecture
iec61850.chapter20.l02.p01: The project separates process equipment, bay IEDs and station systems. Conventional CT/VT and binary wiring connect equipment to its assigned protection/control application, while station Ethernet carries MMS, approved GOOSE and timing services.
iec61850.chapter20.l02.p02: PRP provides two independent network paths between compatible nodes. Gateway A/B and HMI provide acquisition and authorized control with a documented redundancy strategy. This project does not add an SV process bus implicitly; the process-bus chapter remains a separate architecture study.
iec61850.chapter20.l02.wf01: Draw physical equipment and IED boundaries
iec61850.chapter20.l02.wf03: Review common power, network and timing dependencies
iec61850.chapter20.l02.example: 132-L01 and T1 supply 33-B1. 33-BC01 connects B1 to B2 when permitted, and 33-F02/T2 then supplies the 11 kV system.
iec61850.chapter20.l02.check: Keep the electrical power path distinct from the Ethernet communication paths; a network arrow is not a primary conductor.
iec61850.chapter20.l03.title: Single-Line Diagram and Equipment
iec61850.chapter20.l03.p01: The single-line diagram is the electrical source of truth for this exercise. It contains 132-B1, T1, 33-B1/33-B2, 33-BC01, 33-F01/33-F02, T2, 11-B1 and 11-F01/11-F02 with the connections defined in the project scope.
iec61850.chapter20.l03.p02: Show breaker and transformer symbols consistently and distinguish normal position from commanded state. Detailed disconnectors, earth switches and instrument-transformer locations belong to approved bay drawings; the compact training SLD explicitly simplifies them rather than inventing a complete switchyard arrangement.
iec61850.chapter20.l03.wf01: Verify every voltage boundary and connection
iec61850.chapter20.l03.wf02: Match names to the equipment schedule
iec61850.chapter20.l03.wf03: Bind operational symbols to tested feedback tags
iec61850.chapter20.l03.example: The 11 kV bus is supplied through T2, never directly connected to the 33 kV bus. Opening 33-BC01 isolates the B2 branch from the sole illustrated source.
iec61850.chapter20.l03.check: Do not infer that a de-energized display proves safe isolation; operating and earthing procedures require the actual approved scheme.
iec61850.chapter20.l04.title: 132 kV Line Bays
iec61850.chapter20.l04.p01: The single incoming bay 132-L01 connects the external 132 kV source to 132-B1. Its protection and control functions are allocated according to a separate protection study, including any required independent main and backup systems.
iec61850.chapter20.l04.p02: For course mapping, IED_132_L01 at 192.168.100.21 represents the documented bay information interface. This address allocation does not assert that one IED alone is sufficient for a real 132 kV line scheme. Measurements, breaker status and protection indications are selected from the actual supported model.
iec61850.chapter20.l04.wf01: Review line protection and control requirements
iec61850.chapter20.l04.wf02: Allocate the supported bay model and physical interfaces
iec61850.chapter20.l04.wf03: Test indications, trip paths and station integration separately
iec61850.chapter20.l04.example: The HMI displays 132-L01 position and measurements from its verified source, while protection test results establish the relevant operating behavior independently of MMS reporting.
iec61850.chapter20.l04.check: Do not choose distance, differential or backup settings from this tutorial; they require the line and system studies.
iec61850.chapter20.l05.title: 132/33 kV Power Transformers
iec61850.chapter20.l05.p01: T1 is the project's single 132/33 kV transformer connecting 132-B1 to 33-B1. Transformer protection, cooling, tap control and mechanical indications are included only as supported and specified by the actual design.
iec61850.chapter20.l05.p02: IED_T1 at 192.168.100.22 is the illustrative protection-information interface. HV and LV measurements and breaker associations must be distinguished, including ratios and vector-group considerations for protection engineering. Generic point names cannot replace a winding-specific signal schedule.
iec61850.chapter20.l05.wf01: Review transformer data and protection requirements
iec61850.chapter20.l05.wf02: Allocate winding measurements and equipment indications
iec61850.chapter20.l05.wf03: Verify source identity, scaling and trip destinations
iec61850.chapter20.l05.example: T1 status and alarms reach the gateway through controlled DataSets. A transformer protection operation and each associated breaker feedback are recorded separately.
iec61850.chapter20.l05.check: Transformer ratings, differential compensation and trip matrix are project-specific; this exercise does not invent mandatory settings or assume every mechanical alarm is available digitally.
iec61850.chapter20.l06.title: 33 kV Feeder Bays
iec61850.chapter20.l06.p01: The project has exactly two 33 kV outgoing circuits. 33-F01 leaves 33-B1 for an external 33 kV load; 33-F02 leaves 33-B2 and supplies the HV side of transformer T2.
iec61850.chapter20.l06.p02: IED_33_F01 uses 192.168.100.31 and IED_33_F02 uses .32. Each has its own model references, reports and physical feedback. A copied feeder template must change equipment identity, ratios, protection settings and stream allocations as required.
iec61850.chapter20.l06.wf01: Create separate F01 and F02 signal schedules
iec61850.chapter20.l06.wf02: Configure each IED from its approved circuit data
iec61850.chapter20.l06.wf03: Test every point against the correct physical bay
iec61850.chapter20.l06.example: F01's illustrative status object is IED_33_F01LD0/XCBR1.Pos. F02 uses its own IED_33_F02LD0 domain under the stated naming assumption.
iec61850.chapter20.l06.check: Do not label F02 as a second generic load feeder in later drawings; it is consistently the T2 supply circuit.
iec61850.chapter20.l07.title: 11 kV Distribution Feeders
iec61850.chapter20.l07.p01: The 11 kV system contains one bus 11-B1 and two outgoing feeders, 11-F01 and 11-F02. T2 at 33/11 kV supplies the bus from the 33-F02 circuit; no direct 132/11 kV transformer is introduced.
iec61850.chapter20.l07.p02: IED_11_F01 uses 192.168.100.41 and IED_11_F02 uses .42. T2's illustrative interface IED_T2 uses .34. The LV incomer feedback is associated with the T2 application where supported, with exact object allocation documented in the real design.
iec61850.chapter20.l07.wf02: Allocate distinct feeder references and tags
iec61850.chapter20.l07.wf03: Test measurements and status at the correct voltage level
iec61850.chapter20.l07.example: The HMI tags 11_F01_CB_POS and 11_F02_CB_POS bind to their respective IEDs, not copied 33 kV sources.
iec61850.chapter20.l07.check: Confirm transformer and feeder ratios independently; identical screen templates do not imply identical electrical scaling or protection settings.
iec61850.chapter20.l08.title: Bus Coupler and Bus Section
iec61850.chapter20.l08.p01: 33-BC01 connects bus sections 33-B1 and 33-B2. IED_33_BC01 at 192.168.100.33 represents its illustrative control/status interface. The stated normal baseline leaves the coupler open.
iec61850.chapter20.l08.p02: With the single illustrated source feeding B1 through T1, B2 and its T2 branch are not energized until the approved operating conditions allow the connection. The control philosophy must address actual source states, equipment positions and required checks; future sources would require revisiting the matrix.
iec61850.chapter20.l08.wf01: Define the coupler's electrical role and normal position
iec61850.chapter20.l08.wf03: Test allowed and rejected cases with independent feedback
iec61850.chapter20.l08.example: The training HMI shows the B1/B2 separation and coupler state explicitly. It does not imply that a command acknowledgment proves the B2 bus is energized.
iec61850.chapter20.l08.check: Do not apply this single-source example's logic to a station with parallel independent sources without a new engineering study.
iec61850.chapter20.l09.title: Protection IED Selection and Allocation
iec61850.chapter20.l09.p01: IED selection starts from protection, control, measurement, environmental and availability requirements. Communication support is one selection dimension alongside input ratings, output duties, hardware redundancy and application capability.
iec61850.chapter20.l09.p02: The course schedule assigns one illustrative information interface per listed bay/function. Real projects may require additional independent protection IEDs, merging units or controllers; those must be allocated by the approved scheme rather than inferred from a vendor image.
iec61850.chapter20.l09.wf03: Record the selected interfaces and required acceptance tests
iec61850.chapter20.l09.example: The fixed interface schedule assigns 132-L01 to .21, T1 to .22, 33-F01 to .31, 33-F02 to .32, 33-BC01 to .33, T2 to .34, 11-F01 to .41 and 11-F02 to .42.
iec61850.chapter20.l09.check: Use the address table as the unambiguous allocation record; product choice does not authorize unsupported functions or replace protection coordination.
iec61850.chapter20.l10.title: Station Bus Network Design
iec61850.chapter20.l10.p01: The station bus uses PRP with independent LAN A and LAN B for compatible IEDs and gateway nodes. Each logical PRP endpoint retains the addressing behavior documented by its implementation; the example schedule lists one logical station address per node.
iec61850.chapter20.l10.p02: Both LANs carry the required MMS, approved GOOSE and timing paths. They are not connected by an ordinary bridge. Switch power and fibre routes are reviewed for common failures, and single-attached equipment uses an explicitly documented arrangement.
iec61850.chapter20.l10.wf02: Configure matching required service delivery without cross-bridging
iec61850.chapter20.l10.wf03: Test each path and redundancy supervision
iec61850.chapter20.l10.example: 33-F01 communicates with Gateway A .10 and Gateway B .11 through the supported PRP arrangement. The HMI server uses .12 in the station schedule.
iec61850.chapter20.l10.check: Network redundancy does not duplicate an IED's application or analogue inputs; document those remaining dependencies separately.
iec61850.chapter20.l11.title: IP Addressing and VLAN Planning
iec61850.chapter20.l11.p01: The project station subnet is 192.168.100.0/24 on VLAN 100. Gateway A/B use .10/.11, HMI uses .12 and the station time service uses .20. Bay interfaces use the fixed addresses in the project allocation table.
iec61850.chapter20.l11.p02: Selected GOOSE uses VLAN 200 with project-assigned multicast identities. Switch management has a separate 192.168.99.0/24 plan whose individual addresses are allocated in the switch schedule. VLAN numbers and example addresses are engineering choices, not IEC defaults.
iec61850.chapter20.l11.wf01: Reserve the complete address and stream register
iec61850.chapter20.l11.wf03: Verify exported configuration and live traffic
iec61850.chapter20.l11.example: 33-F01 gcbTrip uses APPID 0x1001 and MAC 01-0C-CD-01-00-01. VLAN 200 appears as hexadecimal 0C8 in the relevant SCL address field.
iec61850.chapter20.l11.check: Do not assign the same illustrative GOOSE identity to every copied feeder; allocate each additional stream explicitly.
iec61850.chapter20.l12.title: IEC 61850 Logical Node Engineering
iec61850.chapter20.l12.p01: Logical-node engineering links each physical function to a supported model. For the tutorial, LD0 is the illustrative logical-device instance and the exposed domain follows the stated IED-name-plus-LD0 convention, subject to actual device verification.
iec61850.chapter20.l12.p02: XCBR represents breaker information, CSWI switching control, MMXU measurements and protection nodes the supported protection functions. Optional attributes and naming prefixes are never assumed universally. Equipment association remains essential when one IED hosts several functions.
iec61850.chapter20.l12.wf01: Map equipment/functions to actual logical nodes
iec61850.chapter20.l12.wf02: Record exact references, types and functional constraints
iec61850.chapter20.l12.wf03: Compare the exported and online models
iec61850.chapter20.l12.example: For 33-F01, position is IED_33_F01LD0/XCBR1.Pos, an available control point may be CSWI1.Pos, and phase current may use MMXU1.A.phsA.cVal.mag.f.
iec61850.chapter20.l12.check: These references are coherent examples, not evidence that every selected vendor model exposes those exact names or attributes.
iec61850.chapter20.l13.title: DataSet and Report Configuration
iec61850.chapter20.l13.p01: The project groups required station status into controlled DataSets and assigns compatible report resources to gateways. The 33-F01 example uses dsStatus and brcbStatus with supported event triggers and optional fields.
iec61850.chapter20.l13.p02: Separate client allocation and recovery behavior must be defined for Gateway A/B. Buffered retention is finite, and a GI restores current state rather than missing historical transitions. Measurement deadbands and update policies are chosen from operator needs and device capability.
iec61850.chapter20.l13.wf02: Allocate report instances and client ownership
iec61850.chapter20.l13.wf03: Test data/quality changes, GI, integrity and reconnect
iec61850.chapter20.l13.example: An object-level XCBR1.Pos [ST] selection carries the supported structure, while separate scalar selections need explicit inclusion handling. The gateway database matches the actual chosen DataSet layout.
iec61850.chapter20.l13.check: Do not reuse a tested report decoder after changing member order without coordinating ConfRev and repeating the affected tests.
iec61850.chapter20.l14.title: GOOSE Communication Engineering
iec61850.chapter20.l14.p01: The project demonstrates one explicitly allocated GOOSE exchange: 33-F01 publishes a supported trip indication through dsTrip/gcbTrip to a designated receiving application in IED_33_BC01 for a supervised indication/test function.
iec61850.chapter20.l14.p02: This teaching exchange does not automatically trip or close the bus coupler. Any operational protection or interlocking use requires the approved cause-and-effect matrix. The subscriber verifies identity, types, quality and expiry and maps the signal to its documented internal input.
iec61850.chapter20.l14.wf02: Resolve the coupler IED's external reference and internal binding
iec61850.chapter20.l14.wf03: Test indication, invalid quality and stream timeout in isolation
iec61850.chapter20.l14.example: Use APPID 0x1001, MAC 01-0C-CD-01-00-01 and VLAN 200 consistently. The receiving test indication is separate from the coupler command output.
iec61850.chapter20.l14.check: Never turn a training subscription into an operational trip path without the required protection design and acceptance evidence.
iec61850.chapter20.l15.title: SCL/SCD Engineering Workflow
iec61850.chapter20.l15.p01: The project SCD coordinates the fixed equipment names, IED instances, addresses, reports and approved GOOSE exchange. Vendor projects retain protection logic, hardware settings and any internal bindings not fully represented in the system file.
iec61850.chapter20.l15.p02: Engineering changes follow one revision owner and a reviewed exchange process. A corrected publisher DataSet may affect the subscriber, gateway and test sheets. Keep all affected exports synchronized rather than distributing a mixture of old and new files.
iec61850.chapter20.l15.wf02: Build and validate the coordinated SCD
iec61850.chapter20.l15.wf03: Export device configurations, deploy through supported tools and compare online behavior
iec61850.chapter20.l15.example: The final 33-F01 and 33-BC01 configurations reference the same gcbTrip definition and ordered members. Gateway reports match the final dsStatus layout.
iec61850.chapter20.l15.check: Archive the as-built SCD with tool versions, device firmware and complete vendor projects so the tested system can be reproduced.
iec61850.chapter20.l16.title: Gateway and SCADA Signal Mapping
iec61850.chapter20.l16.p01: The signal matrix connects each project source to a station tag and any remote protocol destination. It records value type, unit, quality, source-time policy and control semantics, preventing silent meaning changes during conversion.
iec61850.chapter20.l16.p02: Use consistent bay prefixes throughout the HMI and gateway. Distinguish T1 HV/LV measurements and T2/11 kV incomer information where represented. Command references remain separate from position feedback and protocol acknowledgments.
iec61850.chapter20.l16.wf03: Perform point-to-point tests through every required destination
iec61850.chapter20.l16.example: 33_F01_CB_POS maps to IED_33_F01LD0/XCBR1.Pos. A project-allocated remote IOA such as 1001 is documented separately and does not derive from the logical-node name.
iec61850.chapter20.l16.check: Verify all abnormal double-point states and invalid quality; a two-color open/closed display alone is incomplete.
iec61850.chapter20.l17.title: HMI Single-Line Diagram Development
iec61850.chapter20.l17.p01: The project HMI follows the fixed electrical SLD and uses verified source tags for all operational symbols. Voltage levels, equipment names and bus connections stay consistent with the drawings and point schedule.
iec61850.chapter20.l17.p02: Show unavailable or invalid information distinctly and provide useful alarm context. The normal-open coupler baseline must not make the B2 branch appear energized merely because a communication link is healthy. Electrical-state inference requires the approved logic and measurements.
iec61850.chapter20.l17.wf01: Create the SLD from the fixed project topology
iec61850.chapter20.l17.wf03: Test normal, abnormal and stale indications with the operator
iec61850.chapter20.l17.example: The screen shows T1 between 132-B1 and 33-B1, then 33-BC01 toward 33-B2 and 33-F02/T2 toward 11-B1. The two 11 kV feeders retain their own tags.
iec61850.chapter20.l17.check: Do not infer safe isolation or voltage absence solely from color; site operating procedures govern those determinations.
iec61850.chapter20.l18.title: Breaker Control and Interlocking
iec61850.chapter20.l18.p01: Project controls use supported IEC 61850 control models with explicit authority, interlocks and feedback. Feeder and coupler requirements are derived separately from their electrical roles and actual equipment.
iec61850.chapter20.l18.p02: The example does not prescribe a universal switching sequence. 33-F01 closing and 33-BC01 energization have different condition sets, and missing/invalid remote states require defined responses. Protection trip paths retain the behavior specified by the protection design.
iec61850.chapter20.l18.wf03: Test permitted, rejected and uncertain-result cases under isolation
iec61850.chapter20.l18.example: The 33-F01 HMI request uses its supported CSWI1.Pos control point and checks XCBR1.Pos. The coupler's control input is never driven directly by the training GOOSE trip indication.
iec61850.chapter20.l18.check: After timeout or missing feedback, reconcile actual state before another authorized operation; do not automatically retry closing.
iec61850.chapter20.l19.title: Complete FAT/SAT Testing Procedure
iec61850.chapter20.l19.p01: The project FAT/SAT plan covers documents, device configurations, I/O, measurements, network services, timing, SCADA and authorized controls. Each requirement has a test ID, known stimulus and observable expected result.
iec61850.chapter20.l19.p02: FAT proves the engineered combination using declared simulation and isolated equipment. SAT confirms installed wiring, fibre routes, power and final station interfaces. Changes after FAT are incorporated into the baseline and trigger relevant repeat tests.
iec61850.chapter20.l19.wf01: Execute the bay point and service matrix
iec61850.chapter20.l19.wf02: Test PRP paths, timing loss and acquisition recovery
iec61850.chapter20.l19.wf03: Resolve punch points and verify normal-state restoration
iec61850.chapter20.l19.example: 33-F01 receives a full stimulus-to-HMI test, while 33-F02/T2/11 kV identities and scaling are verified independently. Coupler tests confirm the approved rejection and permitted cases.
iec61850.chapter20.l19.check: Do not prefill pass results in the example checklist; actual witnessed measurements and observations determine acceptance.
iec61850.chapter20.l20.title: Project Commissioning and Troubleshooting
iec61850.chapter20.l20.p01: Commissioning closes the gap between tested design and maintainable operation. The final package includes as-built drawings, SCD, vendor projects, gateway database, switch backups, timing configuration and accepted test records.
iec61850.chapter20.l20.p02: Troubleshooting follows the same source-to-destination boundaries used during testing. Record unresolved limitations and any operating restrictions explicitly. Remove temporary simulations, test streams and overrides, then verify normal modes before the authorized handover.
iec61850.chapter20.l20.wf01: Reconcile every punch point and revision
iec61850.chapter20.l20.wf02: Verify restored physical and logical boundaries
iec61850.chapter20.l20.wf03: Deliver backups, evidence and operating/maintenance information
iec61850.chapter20.l20.example: The final project record keeps the fixed 132-L01/T1/33-F01/33-F02/T2/11-F01/11-F02 topology and 33-BC01 baseline consistent across all artifacts. A replacement device is checked against that record before connection.
iec61850.chapter20.l20.check: This course supplies an illustrative engineering workflow; construction settings and energization authorization require the responsible project's approved studies, procedures and acceptance.

site.content.00873: Before PC1 (192.168.10.10) can send an ICMP Echo Request to PC2 (192.168.10.11), it broadcasts an ARP Request (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) to discover PC2's MAC address.

site.content.00887: SW1 learns PC2's MAC on Fa0/2 and forwards the unicast ARP Reply exclusively out Fa0/1 to PC1. PC1 updates `arp -a` and immediately transmits the queued ICMP ping.

site.content.00889: Demonstrates how a Cisco Catalyst Layer 2 switch builds its Content Addressable Memory (CAM) table from Source MACs and forwards frames using Destination MACs.
site.content.00891: Frame enters SW1 Fa0/1. SW1 inspects the Source MAC (000A.F311.1010) and adds/refreshes the 300-second aging timer for `VLAN 1 | 000A.F311.1010 | DYNAMIC | Fa0/1`.
site.content.00893: SW1 looks up Destination MAC 000B.E422.2020 in `show mac address-table`, finds match on Fa0/2, and switches the frame directly out Fa0/2 (PC3 on Fa0/3 sees zero traffic).
site.content.00895: PC2 replies. SW1 refreshes Fa0/2's MAC timer and switches the reply frame directly to Fa0/1 at wire speed with zero collisions.

site.content.00906: Router1 strips the LAN-10 Ethernet header, decrements IPv4 TTL from 128 to 127, recalculates the IP header checksum, and matches `C 192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1`.
site.content.00911: Router1 encapsulates the packet in a brand-new Ethernet frame with Source MAC = R1 Gi0/1 (00E0.R100.0002) and Destination MAC = PC2 (000B.2020.0002) while keeping IP 192.168.10.10 → 192.168.20.10 intact.

site.content.01303: Why Two Separate Subnets Are Used: LAN-10 (192.168.10.0/24) and LAN-20 (192.168.20.0/24) are separate broadcast domains. A router refuses overlapping subnets on two routed ports.
site.content.01304: Why the Router Requires Two Interfaces: GigabitEthernet0/0 serves as the Default Gateway (192.168.10.1) for LAN-10, and GigabitEthernet0/1 serves as the Default Gateway (192.168.20.1) for LAN-20.
site.content.01305: How PC1 Chooses Its Default Gateway: PC1 compares 192.168.10.10/24 with destination 192.168.20.10/24. Because the third octet differs (10 ≠ 20), PC1 knows the destination is remote and sends the frame to its Default Gateway MAC (192.168.10.1).
site.content.01306: How ARP Works on Each LAN: PC1 broadcasts an ARP Request on LAN-10 for 192.168.10.1 (Router1 G0/0 replies with its MAC). Router1 broadcasts an ARP Request on LAN-20 for 192.168.20.10 (PC2 replies with its MAC).
site.content.01307: How Router1 Forwards the Packet & Why No Static Route Is Required: Both 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.20.0/24 are directly connected ('C' routes in `show ip route`). Router1 strips the LAN-10 L2 header, decrements TTL from 128 to 127, and adds a new LAN-20 L2 header.
site.content.01308: How the Return Packet Reaches PC1: PC2 sends its ICMP Echo Reply (192.168.20.10 → 192.168.10.10) to its gateway 192.168.20.1 (Router1 G0/1), which routes it back out G0/0 to PC1.
site.content.01309: First ping shows `.!!!!` (80% due to initial ARP resolution on LAN-20) and subsequent pings show `!!!!!` (100%). PC1 `tracert 192.168.20.10` shows Hop 1 = `192.168.10.1` and Hop 2 = `192.168.20.10`.

site.content.03450: Manufacturer lineage and matching data model
site.content.03456: UR version; other families may use other tools
site.content.03459: Correct source reaches intended internal input
site.content.03460: Wrong revision, invalid quality and stream loss
site.content.03462: Ownership conflict, reconnect and event gap
site.content.03464: Local mode, expired selection, missing feedback
site.content.03481: F01: B1 → load; F02: B2 → T2
site.content.03503: Supported trip indication, not breaker-open proof
site.content.03508: Fixed equipment, addresses and SCD agree
site.content.03511: Every F01/F02 point belongs to its actual voltage level
site.content.03513: A failure and B failure separately
site.content.03516: F01 indication reaches coupler test input only
site.content.03520: No simulations, overrides or temporary links remain
site.content.03523: The IEC 61850 data model describes information by its engineering meaning. A breaker position, a phase current and a protection operation have recognizable structures instead of being identified only by an unexplained register number. This shared vocabulary helps the IED manufacturer, protection engineer and SCADA integrator describe the same function consistently.
site.content.03524: The usual hierarchy is server → logical device → logical node → data object → data attribute. The physical IED hosts the server; the remaining levels organize information inside that server. Data attributes carry values and supporting information such as quality and time. The hierarchy describes information, while communication services determine how clients read it, receive reports or request permitted controls.
site.content.03525: A standardized model does not mean every relay contains identical functions or identical names. Implementations differ in logical-device organization, node instances, optional objects and supported services. Engineering therefore combines the standard vocabulary with the actual device model and the project signal list.
site.content.03526: For feeder 33-F01, the HMI needs breaker position, phase currents and an overcurrent trip indication. First identify the relevant XCBR, MMXU and protection logical nodes in the IED. Then record their complete references and the attributes needed to interpret each signal. Only after that should the communication and display mappings be configured.
site.content.03527: Explain the difference between the meaning of a signal, its full object reference and the service that transports it. A successful network connection proves none of these mappings by itself.
site.content.03529: IEC 61850 groups related information into objects representing equipment and automation functions. A logical-node class defines a recognizable function; an instance represents one occurrence of that function in a particular device. XCBR is a circuit-breaker class, while XCBR1 and XCBR2 can represent two distinct breaker functions. Instance numbers identify instances, not voltage levels or universal bay numbers.
site.content.03530: Within a logical node, a data object represents a specific aspect of the function. A Common Data Class (CDC) defines the structure and semantics of that object. For example, breaker position uses DPC, a controllable double-point structure. Reusable classes make the model consistent while allowing separate instances to hold different live values.
site.content.03531: Think of a class as a specification and an instance as the configured occurrence. This analogy helps explain reuse, but it does not imply that the relay is programmed in any particular object-oriented language. The communication model exposes agreed information, not the internal source code of the protection algorithm.
site.content.03532: A bus-coupler controller may expose two XCBR instances. Both contain position information, but one belongs to the first breaker and the other to the second. Mapping both HMI symbols to XCBR1 would produce two plausible displays with only one actual source.
site.content.03533: Record class, instance, equipment association and CDC separately. Verify each instance against drawings and configuration instead of inferring its purpose from its number.
site.content.03535: An Intelligent Electronic Device is the equipment performing protection, control, measurement or another automation task. Its IEC 61850 server is the communication-side model through which supported information and services are exposed. A single protection relay can perform several functions and organize them into multiple logical devices under its server.
site.content.03536: An IP address identifies a network endpoint; it is not the complete identity of a measurement or breaker indication. After reaching the endpoint, a client must use the correct logical-device name, logical-node instance, data path and functional constraint. Changing an IED name or importing a different configuration can change references even when the IP address stays unchanged.
site.content.03537: The model available online should agree with the configuration and firmware used for engineering. An ICD describes capabilities, whereas project and device configuration files describe configured instances within their respective scopes. Use the deployed configuration and vendor documentation to resolve differences between what a file advertises and what a running server exposes.
site.content.03538: Two identical feeder relays have different station IP addresses and IED names. Importing the first relay into a client and changing only the IP address may still leave object references pointing to the first relay’s logical-device domain. Browse the second relay and compare the complete names.
site.content.03539: Confirm the physical device, network endpoint, IED identity, firmware and deployed configuration revision before diagnosing individual data points.
site.content.03540: A logical device groups related logical nodes within the server model. A manufacturer might separate protection, measurements and control into different LDs, or combine several functions in one LD. The grouping is an engineering organization; an LD is not automatically a separate hardware module or an independently addressed Ethernet device.
site.content.03541: Each logical device contains LLN0, the logical node for information and services common to that logical device. LPHD represents physical-device information within the applicable model; inspect its actual placement rather than assuming one universal arrangement. Application nodes such as XCBR and PTOC then describe particular functions.
site.content.03542: The SCL LDevice instance identifier and the exposed logical-device name must be distinguished. In common naming, an IED name and LD instance are combined; an explicit ldName can affect the resulting reference where supported. Always use the configured or browsed name rather than constructing it from a guessed naming rule.
site.content.03543: An illustrative IED named FDR01 with LD instance LD0 may expose the domain FDR01LD0. A second LD may contain protection functions. Finding XCBR1 in one LD does not mean PTOC1 is necessarily beside it.
site.content.03544: List every LD and its function. Confirm the actual exposed LD name and LLN0 information before building datasets or SCADA tags.
site.content.03545: A logical node is a standardized grouping of data associated with a function. IEC 61850-7-4 defines many commonly used logical-node classes and their data objects. The four-letter class conveys the type of function, while a prefix and instance number distinguish configured occurrences. Prefixes and instances are part of the reference and must be retained exactly.
site.content.03546: Equipment functions and automation functions can be represented by different nodes even when they interact. XCBR represents circuit-breaker information; CSWI represents switching control. PTOC describes time-overcurrent protection information, and PTRC describes protection trip conditioning. The presence of these classes does not describe every connection in the relay’s internal logic.
site.content.03547: Standard class names improve discoverability, but not all optional objects or services are implemented. Some project signals use generic input/output nodes such as GGIO when no appropriate dedicated mapping is exposed. In those cases, descriptions and signal documentation become particularly important.
site.content.03552: Which physical breaker does this instance represent?
site.content.03554: Which command path and control model are configured?
site.content.03556: Which measurement location and ratios apply?
site.content.03558: Which stage and characteristic are represented?
site.content.03560: Which protection functions feed this trip logic?
site.content.03561: A feeder relay may contain PTOC1, PTOC2 and PTOC3 for separate overcurrent stages. The project engineer must associate each with the configured protection stage before naming alarms in SCADA.
site.content.03562: Compare the LN prefix, class and instance with the vendor signal list. Never treat the instance number as a guaranteed protection-stage definition.
site.content.03564: A data object describes one aspect of a logical-node function. In XCBR1.Pos, XCBR1 identifies the node and Pos identifies its position object. The object is a structured collection, so reading its name alone is not the same as selecting a particular scalar value for an HMI tag.
site.content.03565: The Common Data Class gives the object its expected organization. DPC combines double-point status with control-related information where supported; MV describes a measured value; structured measurement classes organize multi-phase or vector quantities. The CDC tells an engineer what kinds of attributes to expect, while the actual device description tells which applicable optional attributes exist.
site.content.03566: Objects may contain sub-data objects before reaching attributes. For example, a phase measurement can require selecting a phase component and then its magnitude. Do not flatten all objects into a single Boolean or number: doing so can lose phase identity, units, quality or control semantics.
site.content.03567: A request to “map breaker Pos” is incomplete. For indication, select the status value and preserve its quality and timestamp. For a control request, identify the supported controllable object and service path separately.
site.content.03568: For each required DO, record its CDC, subordinate structure, supported attributes and intended use. Confirm that the chosen object represents the required equipment function.
site.content.03570: A data attribute holds a particular value or property within a data object. Familiar names include stVal for a status value, q for quality and t for a timestamp. Attributes have defined types: a Boolean alarm, a coded double-point state and a floating-point measurement cannot be interpreted interchangeably.
site.content.03571: Some attributes are structured. A measurement path may pass through cVal and mag before reaching the floating-point component f. Engineers must distinguish a structured attribute from its basic components. A client can display a whole structure, but a scalar HMI tag usually needs the correct basic value together with associated quality and time handling.
site.content.03572: Attribute availability and update behavior depend on the CDC, supported services and configuration. A timestamp is not necessarily refreshed continuously; its semantics follow the modeled data and event rules. A value that has not changed may therefore legitimately retain an older data timestamp.
site.content.03573: A client that imports stVal as Boolean may display both “on” and “bad-state” as true. Selecting the correct data type prevents a contact discrepancy from appearing as a normal closed breaker.
site.content.03574: Inspect the attribute type and full structure in the online browser. Preserve associated quality and timestamp rather than importing the numerical value alone.
site.content.03576: A functional constraint groups data attributes according to their role. It is a classification used in access and service modeling, not another physical level between the IED and logical node. Attributes belonging to one data object can have different functional constraints because status, settings and controls serve different purposes.
site.content.03577: ST commonly identifies status attributes and MX measurements. CF covers configuration, DC descriptive information and CO control-related information. SG and SE relate to setting groups and their editing where supported. SV denotes substitution in this context; it must not be confused with the abbreviation SV used for Sampled Values communication.
site.content.03578: Some tools present an FC as a separate selection, while MMS-oriented displays may include it in a dollar-separated item identifier. A correct data path with the wrong FC can fail to resolve or select the wrong group. An FC also does not grant permission: control models, access rules and device operating conditions still apply.
site.content.03584: Operate structures of supported controllable objects
site.content.03589: A model browser may show XCBR1 → ST → Pos. Another tool may show Pos and ask for ST in a separate field. Both can refer to the same functional grouping.
site.content.03590: Record the FC alongside every mapped data reference and confirm the client’s naming convention. Do not use the control FC to read an indication.
site.content.03592: A readable object reference identifies the logical device, logical node and nested data path. The slash separates the LD name from the LN; dots separate data objects, sub-objects and attributes. Exact spelling, capitalization, prefixes and instance numbers matter. A short name such as XCBR1.Pos is useful in discussion but is incomplete when several LDs or IEDs contain that node.
site.content.03593: ACSI-style references and MMS item names are different presentations of related information. With MMS, the logical-device name is commonly the domain, and an item identifier uses dollar separators with an FC grouping. A client may accept the readable path and FC independently, or it may require the mapped domain/item form. Follow that client’s documented interface.
site.content.03594: SCL references can identify components through separate XML attributes rather than one concatenated string. This is why copying a name from a screenshot is less reliable than importing the deployed SCL and validating against the online directory. Renaming an IED or LD can invalidate previously configured client references.
site.content.03595: If the live server exposes CBXCBR1 but the HMI requests XCBR1, the reference is wrong even though the class and attribute look familiar. The CB prefix cannot be silently omitted.
site.content.03596: Copy the reference from the authoritative model and verify it online. Keep the readable object reference, FC and client-specific address fields in the mapping sheet.
site.content.03598: The structural view answers “where does this information belong?” It follows the hierarchy from LD to LN to DO and DA. The functional view answers “which part of this information is required for this service?” It groups attributes using functional constraints. These are complementary views of the same model.
site.content.03599: A functionally constrained data object (FCD) selects the attributes of an object for a particular FC. A functionally constrained data attribute (FCDA) identifies a particular attribute with its FC. A dataset can therefore select a suitable group or an individual attribute according to the implementation and configuration. The selected level affects the structure received by a client.
site.content.03600: Dataset order and nesting are operationally important. A consumer expecting a scalar must not silently treat a received structure as a scalar, and an index-based decoder must agree with the configured dataset order. Changing members may also require corresponding configuration-revision handling and client configuration updates.
site.content.03601: Including XCBR1.Pos with FC ST can provide a status structure with value, quality and time. Including only XCBR1.Pos.stVal selects a narrower value. Confirm the actual member and decoded structure before deciding that an HMI will automatically receive q and t.
site.content.03602: Inspect dataset membership, FC, ordering and the received structure. Verify quality and timestamp coverage explicitly rather than assuming they accompany every scalar selection.
site.content.03604: Status information describes a condition such as breaker position, trip operation or an equipment alarm. A single-point indication has two logical states; double-point indication distinguishes valid positions from intermediate and bad states. Each must be interpreted using its data class and project meaning.
site.content.03605: Measurements describe quantities such as current, voltage, power and frequency. Correct integration requires the unit, multiplier, phase or phase-pair, sign convention and conversion settings. A believable number is not proof of correct scaling: 1.0 may represent a secondary quantity, a primary quantity or a value displayed with a multiplier depending on the model and configuration.
site.content.03606: Control data requests an action through a defined service and control model. Writing an observed status attribute is not a valid substitute for operating a controllable object. Direct control and select-before-operate workflows, local/remote state, interlocks and command feedback must be considered separately from the monitoring path.
site.content.03607: For one breaker, the HMI may display XCBR position, trend MMXU feeder current and issue an authorized command through the configured CSWI or XCBR control object. These paths interact in the application but must remain separately documented.
site.content.03608: Classify each signal as indication, measurement, setting or control. Verify data type, unit or state mapping and the required service before connecting it to an HMI element.
site.content.03610: Quality tells a receiving application how much confidence to place in a value. It includes validity and, where applicable, detail indicators such as old data, out of range or failure, together with source, test and operator-blocked information. Collapsing all quality into a normal-looking number hides distinctions that operators and automation logic may need.
site.content.03611: The data timestamp t describes the modeled event or update according to the relevant data semantics. It is distinct from a report creation time, network arrival time or HMI display time. Time quality also matters: a device can supply a timestamp while indicating a clock problem or lack of synchronization. Displaying many decimal places does not establish corresponding time accuracy.
site.content.03612: The client must handle both source quality and communication health. After a connection loss, a last-known good value can remain visible; the HMI should identify its stale communication state according to the project policy. A valid process value, a synchronized event time and a healthy reporting connection are three separate checks.
site.content.03613: A feeder current remains at 245 A after communication is interrupted. The number alone looks reasonable, but the client should mark the point stale or unavailable. For event analysis, retain the original device timestamp and distinguish it from the time the client noticed the outage.
site.content.03614: Exercise invalid/questionable quality, test/substitution indications, loss of communication and clock-unsynchronized conditions in the approved test environment. Verify the HMI behavior for each.
site.content.03616: XCBR.Pos describes circuit-breaker position using the DPC data class. Its status value is double-point information, not a plain Boolean. The model distinguishes intermediate-state, off, on and bad-state. For a normal breaker display, off and on are generally interpreted as open and closed; the project must verify that interpretation against the actual equipment and IED logic.
site.content.03617: The IED typically derives the indication from configured auxiliary contacts and processing logic. Contact polarity, input inversion, filtering and discrepancy supervision affect the result. An invalid contact combination must not be forced into an apparently healthy open or closed indication just to simplify an HMI symbol.
site.content.03618: Position confirmation is distinct from a command request or a protection trip indication. A trip command may be issued without the breaker reaching open position. Conversely, a breaker can open for another reason. Troubleshooting therefore compares command, protection event, auxiliary feedback and timing rather than treating one signal as proof of the others.
site.content.03633: During an approved simulated opening test, observe the trip request, the change in auxiliary inputs, Pos.stVal, q and t, and the HMI update. If PTRC shows a trip but Pos remains on, investigate the feedback and operating path instead of declaring the breaker open.
site.content.03634: Test all four decoded states and quality handling using an isolated simulator or approved commissioning procedure. Raw wire encodings and driver representations may differ from the decoded numbers shown here.
site.content.03636: MMXU provides a model for electrical measurements such as phase currents, voltages, power and frequency where implemented. Multi-phase quantities are structured: A can contain phsA, phsB and phsC, with a complex measured value under each phase. Magnitude and angle are different components and must not be confused.
site.content.03637: An illustrative current magnitude path is MMXU1.A.phsA.cVal.mag.f with FC MX. Its associated quality and timestamp are found at the corresponding measured-value structure, not necessarily by appending q or t to the final floating-point leaf. Browse the complete structure to establish the correct paths.
site.content.03638: Measurement verification includes units, multipliers, CT/VT ratios, phase identity, direction and deadband configuration. Reports may send changes based on configured triggers and thresholds, so a constant displayed value does not automatically indicate a broken link. Conversely, applying an extra CT ratio in the HMI to a value already expressed in primary amperes produces a large scaling error.
site.content.03639: For a training case with a 600/1 A CT, a 0.5 A secondary injection corresponds to 300 A primary. Compare the expected primary value with the IED display and exposed measurement, then confirm whether the HMI needs any conversion. The conversion is determined by configuration, not by the path name alone.
site.content.03640: Use at least two known test points and verify each phase, unit and multiplier. Check zero, sign/direction where relevant, quality and report deadband behavior.
site.content.03642: PTOC represents time-overcurrent protection information. Common data objects include Str for start and Op for operation, with structured attributes such as general where present. A start indicates that the relevant protection logic has picked up; operation indicates that the function’s operating criteria have been met. They should not share an indistinguishable alarm label.
site.content.03643: PTRC represents protection trip conditioning and exposes trip-related information, commonly through Tr. It can aggregate or condition results from protection functions according to the relay’s application logic. A PTOC operation and a PTRC trip therefore describe related but different points in the protection chain.
site.content.03644: The complete sequence depends on the configured relay logic, output circuits and breaker behavior. IEC 61850 node names do not reveal every blocking input, latch, reset rule or trip matrix. Use the application configuration and event records to interpret which stage operated and how its result reached the trip output.
site.content.03645: In a simulated fault, the start may precede operation by the configured protection delay. PTRC may then assert, followed by breaker opening feedback. Use the individual timestamps and time-quality indications to analyze the sequence rather than measuring it from screen refreshes.
site.content.03646: Verify the actual stage-to-node association, trip matrix and reset/latching behavior. Confirm that the SCADA labels distinguish pickup, operation, trip and breaker position.
site.content.03648: A data model browser helps inspect the server directory, logical devices, logical nodes and data structures exposed by an IED. Use it to establish what the device actually presents, then compare that model with the SCL and signal list. Browsing names is only the first step; reading types and values and inspecting supported services provide additional evidence.
site.content.03649: Start with the intended endpoint and confirm the IED identity. Expand the relevant LD and LN, inspect the object and FC, then read the required value, quality and timestamp. For report-based integration, inspect configured datasets and report control blocks as supported by the tool and device.
site.content.03650: Keep passive inspection separate from commissioning operations. Some browser tools expose write, control and report-configuration functions beside read functions. A connection used for inspection should follow the site’s access policy, and active tests should use a simulator or an authorized commissioning arrangement.
site.content.03651: If the HMI cannot find a breaker point, browse the IED and search the applicable XCBR instance. Compare the complete name and type. If the browser reads the correct point but the HMI remains wrong, focus next on the HMI address, dataset/report subscription and state conversion.
site.content.03652: Save a model export or inspection record with device identity and configuration revision. A cached offline tree must not be mistaken for a confirmed online model.
site.content.03653: Mapping Physical Signals to Data Objects
site.content.03654: Physical-to-model mapping connects an equipment signal to its IEC 61850 meaning. For a hardwired status, the chain may include an auxiliary contact, terminal number, IED binary input, input logic, application signal and model attribute. For a network-sourced input, document the publisher, subscribed dataset member and consuming application logic instead of a copper terminal.
site.content.03655: A useful mapping sheet preserves both the physical source and the modeled destination. Record contact polarity or active state, filtering, logic inversion, equipment identity and the complete reference with FC. For measurements, record the measurement location, CT/VT data, units and conversion settings.
site.content.03656: Choose a dedicated standardized object when the device and application expose an appropriate one. If a generic indication is used, give it an unambiguous description and document its semantics. A generic node name alone cannot tell a future engineer whether true means healthy, alarm, permissive or blocked.
site.content.03660: Both stable positions and discrepancy states
site.content.03667: If the field breaker is open but the online model shows on, changing the HMI color mapping would conceal the underlying input or model error. Trace the chain from contact state through the relay logic to the published value first.
site.content.03668: Verify one signal end to end and retain the evidence. Do not compensate for an upstream mapping error with an undocumented downstream inversion.
site.content.03669: Data Model to SCADA/HMI Signal Mapping
site.content.03670: SCADA integration associates a modeled point with an operator tag, symbol, alarm or trend. The mapping must include the full reference, FC, data type, state or unit conversion, quality policy and timestamp source. A tag name should identify the bay and equipment clearly while the engineering record retains the exact underlying reference.
site.content.03671: For MMS reporting, confirm that the intended data is present in a supported dataset and that the relevant report control block is correctly configured and enabled for the client. A successful direct read does not prove that change reporting is working. Trigger options, client association, buffering and dataset interpretation all influence the delivery path.
site.content.03672: A gateway may transform the point into another protocol for a control center. Preserve the meaning of valid states, quality and event time through that conversion. Test reconnection and initialization so that old values are not presented as fresh observations and a missing report does not silently freeze a healthy-looking breaker symbol.
site.content.03673: Map FDR01LD0/XCBR1.Pos.stVal [ST] to tag 33_F01_CB_POSITION, with explicit open, closed, intermediate and bad-state display rules. Associate its source quality and timestamp, then verify both the initial state and a simulated change delivered by the reporting path.
site.content.03674: Compare the live IED value, received report and displayed HMI state. Include quality-only changes, connection loss, recovery and the project’s event-time requirements in acceptance tests.
site.content.03675: Consider training feeder 33-F01 with one circuit breaker, a feeder protection IED, a station HMI and a gateway. Assume the illustrative LD name FDR01LD0. The actual project may place the same functions in several LDs, so the following names are a worked mapping example rather than a device import file.
site.content.03676: Define four information groups: breaker position from XCBR, electrical measurements from MMXU, overcurrent indications from PTOC and conditioned trip information from PTRC. For each group, retain the relevant quality and timestamp. Build the reporting configuration from the required signals and supported dataset structures, then associate the received information with the HMI display.
site.content.03677: In an isolated simulator or approved test setup, begin with a closed breaker and stable current. Apply the simulated fault condition, observe protection start and operation, inspect the trip indication, and verify that breaker feedback changes after the simulated operating delay. Protection execution belongs to the approved protection scheme; the HMI receives indications and must not be a prerequisite for tripping.
site.content.03683: Acceptance evidence should show the simulated source condition, correct online value, received report, HMI indication and event timestamp for each point. Repeat with a quality problem and a communication interruption to verify that the display communicates uncertainty instead of merely keeping the last value.
site.content.03684: Use the mapping sheet to verify every path and the recovery behavior. Treat command acceptance, protection trip indication and confirmed breaker opening as separate outcomes.
site.content.03686: Troubleshoot in layers: physical/application source, online data model, dataset/report service, client decoding and HMI mapping. Establish where the first disagreement appears. If the source and online value disagree, investigate the IED mapping; if the online value is right but the HMI is wrong, move toward transport, decoding and display configuration.
site.content.03687: Configuration changes can produce subtle failures. Renamed LDs or LNs break references, revised dataset members change decoded structures, and firmware changes can alter optional model elements. Compare the deployed configuration, engineering files and client import rather than assuming all copies are synchronized.
site.content.03688: Close testing with recorded evidence: device and configuration identity, point references, expected and observed states, quality behavior, event-time behavior and recovery results. Correcting one point is insufficient if the same naming or type assumption was applied to an entire bay. Review the affected mapping group after fixing the root cause.
site.content.03692: LD/LN spelling, prefix, instance and FC
site.content.03693: Compare online directory with deployed SCL
site.content.03695: Wrong instance, phase, ratio or unit
site.content.03696: Trace from the known physical/test source
site.content.03698: Dataset, RCB, client ownership and triggers
site.content.03699: Inspect actual report delivery and decoding
site.content.03702: Test all states and quality indications
site.content.03704: Source timestamps, clock status and receipt-time use
site.content.03705: Compare device events with client records
site.content.03709: A breaker point works before an SCL update and disappears afterward. Compare old and new LD/LN names first. Once the reference is corrected, recheck dataset membership and the HMI’s state, quality and timestamp mapping; a successful read alone does not complete the repair.
site.content.03710: Final review: all 20 lessons understood, actual references verified, value/q/t handled, state and unit conversions tested, reporting confirmed and configuration revisions recorded.
site.content.03712: One physical protection IED can host an IEC 61850 server with several logical devices and many logical nodes. A feeder relay may expose XCBR for breaker information, MMXU for measurements, PTOC for overcurrent protection and PTRC for trip conditioning. These are functions within an engineered model, not necessarily separate processors, Ethernet ports or physical boxes.
site.content.03713: A logical-node class is a reusable definition, while an instance identifies a particular occurrence. Two feeders may each have an XCBR1, distinguished by their logical-device names. Within one device, prefixes and instance numbers distinguish multiple functions. Correct integration therefore requires both the standard function meaning and the complete configured reference.
site.content.03714: At a 132/33/11 kV station, the 33-F01 feeder IED supplies position, current and protection events to the station HMI. Instead of treating them as unrelated register addresses, the engineer identifies their LN instances, selects the required attributes and documents how each instance is associated with the feeder.
site.content.03715: Browse the actual IED and identify one equipment LN, one measurement LN and one protection LN. Confirm their physical/application associations using the project drawings and deployed configuration.
site.content.03716: Purpose and Structure of Logical Nodes
site.content.03717: Logical nodes organize functions into discoverable information structures. A node contains data objects, and each object is structured according to a Common Data Class (CDC). In CTRLXCBR1.Pos.stVal, CTRLXCBR1 is the LN instance, Pos is the position data object and stVal is one status attribute. Pos also contains other information defined by its CDC and implemented by the device.
site.content.03718: Common LN information can describe operating mode, behavior, health or identification according to the applicable class and edition. Application-specific objects then express the function: breaker position differs from a protection start or a phase-current measurement. Never infer that every node implements every familiar object or every optional component of a CDC.
site.content.03719: The information model, service model and application logic must be considered together. A data object may exist but be exposed as status-only, or its control service may be restricted by configuration. Similarly, showing a protection start in the model does not establish which output contact or GOOSE publication is driven by that start. Those connections belong to the engineered application.
site.content.03731: An HMI request for “breaker Pos” should be expanded into the indication value, its quality, timestamp and state mapping. A separate command specification identifies the controllable object and supported control model. This avoids confusing command requests with measured breaker feedback.
site.content.03732: For each required point, record LN class, instance, DO, CDC, DA, functional constraint and supported service. Inspect the actual type definitions before importing tags.
site.content.03734: A typical application LN name is formed from a configured prefix, a four-letter LN class and an instance identifier. In CTRLXCBR1, CTRL is the prefix, XCBR is the circuit-breaker class and 1 is the instance. The prefix is project or vendor engineering information; it is not a universal keyword that all devices must use. Special nodes such as LLN0 follow their defined naming rules.
site.content.03735: The examples below assume IED_33_F01 is the actual exposed logical-device name. In a complete IEC 61850 object reference, the part before the slash is the LD name, not merely the physical IED label. Real LD names may be formed from an IED name and LD instance, or use an explicitly configured name where supported. If IED_33_F01 is only the physical device name in your project, replace it with the server’s actual LD name.
site.content.03736: A slash separates LD from LN. Dots separate the object and attribute path. Case, prefix and instance identifiers must match the server. Functional constraint ST is normally supplied separately in readable references; a client using MMS domain/item notation may present the same information with dollar-separated components.
site.content.03737: If the online directory shows LD name IED_33_F01CTRL and LN name CBXCBR1, the correct point starts IED_33_F01CTRL/CBXCBR1. Copying the tutorial reference unchanged would fail even though both models represent a circuit breaker.
site.content.03738: Compare names in the deployed SCL and live browser. Keep physical IED name, LD instance, exposed LD name, LN prefix, class and instance in separate mapping-sheet fields.
site.content.03740: The first letter of an LN class identifies its group. This helps an engineer navigate a large model: X classes describe switchgear, M classes describe metering or measurement, P classes describe protection functions and C classes describe supervisory control. The group provides orientation, but the complete class determines the specific function.
site.content.03741: A relay generally contains nodes from several groups because it performs several related tasks. For example, a feeder protection IED can contain XCBR, CSWI, CILO, MMXU, PTOC and PTRC. A protection-related class may belong to a different group than a primary protection function; use the actual standard classification rather than grouping solely by an English description.
site.content.03742: Generic nodes can expose signals for which the device has no dedicated application mapping. They should not erase useful semantics: a generic alarm requires a clear description, active-state definition, source and testing record. The table is a practical subset for this course, not an exhaustive catalogue of all IEC 61850 application domains or later extensions.
site.content.03751: A 132 kV line bay might expose PDIS for distance protection and RREC for autoreclosing, while an 11 kV outgoing feeder might use PTOC. Voltage level alone does not determine which nodes must exist; the protection and control design does.
site.content.03752: Identify the supported class and namespace in the IED documentation. Do not rename vendor extensions to standard objects without verifying that their meaning and structure match.
site.content.03754: XCBR models circuit-breaker information. Its Pos data object uses CDC DPC, which includes double-point position status and control-related structure according to the implemented control model. Typical indication attributes are Pos.stVal, Pos.q and Pos.t with FC ST. Other objects, such as operation count or blocking information, must be checked against the device model rather than assumed universally available.
site.content.03755: A common physical indication arrangement uses 52a and 52b auxiliary contacts connected to IED digital inputs. Conventionally, 52a follows the closed breaker and 52b follows the open breaker. Input inversion, contact wiring, debounce and discrepancy logic determine how the relay interprets the contact combination. The example diagram represents information flow and is not a terminal-wiring drawing.
site.content.03756: The decoded double-point states are intermediate-state, off, on and bad-state. Open and closed HMI states must be mapped deliberately; intermediate or inconsistent states must remain distinguishable. A trip request is not position confirmation: a failed mechanism or feedback problem can leave Pos indicating closed after protection has operated.
site.content.03763: Both feedback channels and HMI state
site.content.03766: For 33-F01, trace auxiliary contacts through the relay input logic to IED_33_F01/CTRLXCBR1.Pos.stVal, then to a configured MMS report and the SCADA symbol. Retain q and t alongside the value so an invalid or stale indication remains visible to the operator.
site.content.03767: Using an isolated test setup, exercise open, closed, intermediate and discrepancy conditions; record relay input states, model values, quality, timestamps and HMI interpretation. Driver wire encodings may differ from the decoded numbers in this table.
site.content.03768: XSWI — Disconnector and Switch Logical Node
site.content.03769: XSWI models switching equipment such as a disconnector or earthing switch. Like XCBR, its position information commonly uses Pos with CDC DPC. The similar data structure does not imply the same electrical interrupting capability. A disconnector must be operated within its equipment rating and the approved switching sequence; its IEC 61850 class does not authorize load interruption.
site.content.03770: The IED obtains position feedback from the configured physical inputs or application interface. Equipment identity, switch type and operating capability may be described by supported model objects, but optional data and extensions differ between implementations. Two XSWI instances may represent an isolator and an earth switch; their instance numbers alone do not identify which is which.
site.content.03771: SCADA needs clear open, closed, intermediate and discrepancy indications for each switch. The control path may be represented through a CSWI instance with interlocking information associated with CILO. These relationships are configured in the IED application and station engineering, rather than created automatically by placing matching LN names in an SCL file.
site.content.03772: In a 132 kV bay, document the line disconnector and earthing switch as separate equipment functions with separate references. In a 33 kV switchgear lineup, confirm how the supplied product models its disconnecting and earthing mechanisms instead of forcing the 132 kV naming scheme onto it.
site.content.03773: Verify each switch against the single-line diagram, equipment tag and feedback contacts. Test approved permissive and blocking conditions with simulated inputs before any authorized operating test.
site.content.03775: The control model determines whether the client operates directly or performs select-before-operate, and whether normal or enhanced security behavior is supported. In this terminology, enhanced security refers to control-service supervision and command completion behavior; it does not by itself mean network encryption or user authentication.
site.content.03776: An accepted command request is not proof of completed mechanical movement. The application evaluates relevant permissions and conditions, drives its configured output and supervises the result as implemented. The HMI should distinguish selection, request acceptance, command termination where applicable, and actual XCBR or XSWI feedback. Writing Pos.stVal is not a substitute for the control service.
site.content.03777: During FAT, a permitted simulated close command is issued through the configured CSWI object. The test records the service response and independently checks breaker feedback. A second test removes a required permissive and verifies that the request is rejected without an unintended output.
site.content.03778: Verify local/remote state, supported control model, selection timeout where relevant, command feedback and independent position indication. Perform active controls only within the approved test arrangement.
site.content.03780: CILO represents interlocking information used to determine whether an operation is permitted. EnaOpn and EnaCls are standard-defined enable-open and enable-close objects using single-point status information. Their values are the modeled results of interlocking evaluation; the class name does not define the complete interlocking logic or the project switching rules.
site.content.03781: Inputs may include breaker and disconnector positions, earthing-switch position, local/remote conditions and information received from other IEDs. The engineered application evaluates those inputs and applies its control checks. If a required remote input becomes invalid or stale, the resulting behavior must follow the approved design and be verified; it must not be guessed from the last Boolean value.
site.content.03782: An HMI can display the permissive and, where separately available, the reason for a block. CILO does not guarantee that a detailed cause string exists. A displayed permissive is also not blanket authority to operate equipment: the command path, control mode and operating procedure still apply. Supervisory switching permissives must not be casually inserted into or used to bypass the independent protection-trip scheme.
site.content.03783: For 33-F01, the approved closing logic may require an open earth switch and valid relevant position inputs. Simulate each prerequisite independently and verify the permissive, client response and output behavior. This is an example test method, not a universal interlocking equation.
site.content.03784: Test the permitted state, every specified blocking condition, invalid/stale remote information and recovery. Confirm the actual link from interlocking evaluation to the controlled object.
site.content.03786: MMXU organizes electrical measurements such as currents, voltages, power and frequency where implemented. Objects can be structured: phase currents under A can contain phsA, phsB and phsC, and each complex measured-value structure can expose magnitude and angle. Select the required phase and component rather than treating the whole A object as one floating-point value.
site.content.03787: For an illustrative phase-A current, A.phsA.cVal.mag.f is a possible floating-point magnitude path with FC MX. Associated quality and timestamp belong to the measured-value structure, for example A.phsA.q and A.phsA.t. Units, multipliers and supported components must be obtained from the actual model; not every quantity is expressed through the same path.
site.content.03788: CT/VT scaling, primary-versus-secondary presentation, phase order and power direction are essential integration details. Measurement reporting can use deadbands and configured triggers, so a small change may not immediately produce a new report. MMXU information is distinct from the raw sampled-value stream used by a process bus; seeing MMXU does not establish that the IED publishes or subscribes to SV.
site.content.03789: With a training 600/1 A CT ratio, 0.5 A secondary corresponds to 300 A primary. Compare the injected value, relay display, model value and HMI. Apply the ratio only where required by the configured representation; applying it twice causes a major scaling error.
site.content.03790: Verify at least two known measurement points, all phases, units and sign conventions. Check deadband response, quality propagation and the client’s stale-data behavior.
site.content.03792: PTOC models time-overcurrent protection information. The protection function evaluates current against its configured criteria and timing characteristic. Pickup, intentional delay, directional supervision where part of the implemented function and blocking conditions belong to the actual protection application. The LN model exposes information about that function without prescribing one universal algorithm.
site.content.03793: Commonly used objects include Str for start and Op for operation. These use protection-specific structures, commonly ACD for starting information and ACT for activation information; they should not automatically be imported as simple SPS objects. A general Boolean component can be available alongside phase-specific components according to the model.
site.content.03794: Multiple PTOC instances may represent different stages or functions. Map each one to the vendor’s protection configuration before naming it “low set” or “high set.” A start indicates pickup, while operation indicates that the relevant operating criteria have been met. Neither alone proves that the breaker has opened.
site.content.03795: For 33-F01, an approved secondary-injection test applies a current above a configured pickup setting and records start and operation times. Test values and expected delays come from the approved setting file and relay characteristic, not from the tutorial. Reported events are compared with the test equipment and relay event record.
site.content.03796: Verify stage identity, pickup/dropout behavior, timing at specified test points, blocking inputs and reset/latching behavior. Separate relay operate time from reporting and HMI update delay.
site.content.03798: PDIS models distance-protection information. Distance protection uses voltage and current to evaluate an apparent impedance for selected fault loops and compares that result with configured operating characteristics. Reach, direction, timing and supervision depend on the relay application. A simple V/I explanation is introductory; actual fault-loop calculations can include phase selection and compensation.
site.content.03799: Distance zones can be represented through one or several configured instances and associated objects depending on the implementation. Starting and operation information, commonly Str and Op, may include general, phase or directional components where supported. An instance named PDIS2 must not automatically be labelled Zone 2 without checking the vendor mapping.
site.content.03800: This function is a useful example for the 132 kV line bays of a 132/33/11 kV station. The 33-F01 outgoing feeder need not contain PDIS if its protection design does not use distance protection. Adding a node to a training signal list does not add the corresponding protection capability to an IED.
site.content.03801: For a 132 kV line relay, FAT uses approved impedance test points inside and outside each configured zone and verifies the relevant start, operation and trip indications. The HMI labels identify the actual zone and function. Voltage-transformer failure supervision and other specified blocks are tested according to the relay application.
site.content.03802: Confirm the zone-to-instance mapping, fault-loop meaning, configured reach/delay and applicable supervision. Use relay-specific test procedures; this lesson supplies no operational distance-protection settings.
site.content.03804: PTRC represents protection trip-conditioning information. It relates protection results to a conditioned trip output according to the engineered application. Possible application behavior includes combining selected function outputs, applying specified latching or pulse behavior, and routing trip indications. These details are configuration dependent; the presence of PTRC does not guarantee any particular timer, latch or wiring arrangement.
site.content.03805: Tr is a commonly used trip data object with activation information, often including Tr.general and supported phase components. It describes the trip function’s state, not the physical breaker position. A PTOC.Op indication, PTRC.Tr indication, relay output contact operation and XCBR.Pos change are distinct verification points.
site.content.03806: The diagram shows an illustrative internal signal chain from current evaluation through PTOC and PTRC to a trip output. It does not mean that each arrow is an MMS or GOOSE message. A project may use hardwired outputs, engineered GOOSE exchanges or a combination. The actual protection path must satisfy its design independently of whether the HMI is available.
site.content.03807: A 33-F01 test produces a configured overcurrent operation. Verify the PTOC indication, its intended trip-matrix association, PTRC trip state, assigned output and simulated breaker feedback. If the trip indication appears but feedback remains closed, investigate the output/mechanical/feedback chain instead of changing the HMI to show open.
site.content.03808: Compare the approved trip matrix with the configured application. Verify each input path, output assignment, pulse or latch behavior, reset conditions and independent breaker feedback.
site.content.03809: LLN0 and LPHD — Common Logical Nodes
site.content.03810: LLN0 is the logical node for information and services common to a logical device. Each LD has its LLN0. It is a familiar location for engineered datasets and report or GOOSE control blocks according to the relevant service and configuration rules. Do not assume that every dataset or service in every product is available at one hard-coded location.
site.content.03811: LPHD represents physical-device information. Its supported identification and health information helps distinguish a device-level issue from a particular application-function issue. Objects such as PhyNam and PhyHealth should be interpreted using the actual model and supported attributes. Verify how LPHD is placed and instantiated in the device rather than treating its location as universal.
