site.content.03812: System and application health must be interpreted separately. A healthy physical device does not prove that all field inputs are valid or that every GOOSE subscription is healthy. Likewise, an application function may be blocked or in test mode while the device remains operational. The HMI should retain these distinctions instead of using one green “IED OK” lamp as evidence for every function.
site.content.03813: During 33-F01 integration, inspect LLN0 to locate the configured reporting objects and inspect supported LPHD information to confirm device identity and health. If breaker status is missing, compare those results with XCBR quality and the reporting configuration before deciding that the whole relay has failed.
site.content.03814: Record the actual LD/LLN0 organization and supported LPHD references. Validate device identification, available health indications and report-control configuration without changing unrelated settings.
site.content.03816: A Common Data Class is a reusable structure for a type of information. IEC 61850-7-3 defines CDCs and constructed attribute classes; IEC 61850-7-4 associates data objects with those structures in logical-node definitions. The LN answers “which function?”, the DO answers “which aspect of that function?”, and the CDC answers “how is that information organized and interpreted?”
site.content.03817: For example, XCBR.Pos is a position object whose CDC is DPC. DPC is the type definition, not another path component to insert between Pos and stVal. The class defines relevant status, control and supporting attributes with conditions and functional constraints. The device’s instantiated type determines the supported members for that configuration.
site.content.03818: The nine CDCs shown here provide an introduction to status, measurement and control information. They are not the complete IEC 61850 catalogue: protection structures such as ACD and ACT and enumerated classes such as ENS and ENC also matter. Choosing a CDC only because it has a convenient primitive value can lose important semantics.
site.content.03819: In SCL, an LN instance refers to an LNodeType; its DO definition refers to a DOType whose cdc identifies the class. Nested structures can reference additional type definitions. Inspect the whole type chain and the applicable edition rather than declaring every attribute seen in one vendor file mandatory everywhere.
site.content.03820: For a model review, locate the actual LNodeType for CTRLXCBR1, follow its Pos type to the DOType and verify cdc="DPC". Then inspect the instantiated status and control attributes. This establishes the modeled type without assuming that all control services are enabled.
site.content.03821: Verify the standard-defined semantics, supported instance structure and client decoding together. Keep custom namespaces and vendor extensions identifiable in the engineering record.
site.content.03822: SPS, DPS, INS — Status Data Classes
site.content.03823: SPS represents single-point status, typically with a Boolean stVal and associated quality and timestamp. A Boolean has two values but its application meaning must still be documented: true could mean alarm present, device healthy or a permissive asserted. Tag descriptions and alarm polarity must come from the engineered signal definition.
site.content.03824: DPS represents double-point status. It distinguishes intermediate-state, off, on and bad-state, allowing a receiver to show uncertainty or inconsistency instead of collapsing all nonzero values into true. DPC has a related double-point status representation but adds controllable semantics; DPS and DPC should not be treated as identical classes.
site.content.03825: INS represents integer status. The number may be a count or another integer-valued state according to the data object, with associated quality/time where defined. An integer data type does not by itself provide an enumeration dictionary. In editions and models using ENS for enumerated status, preserve that class distinction and obtain the allowed meanings from the type definition.
site.content.03829: Document active polarity and alarm meaning
site.content.03833: Confirm range, unit/count meaning and reset behavior
site.content.03834: For a station HMI, a permissive may use SPS, a status-only switching indication may use DPS and a supported operation count may use INS. These are illustrative uses; the actual DO’s declared CDC controls the mapping. A count must not be displayed as a binary alarm.
site.content.03835: Test both SPS states, all DPS states and representative INS values including boundaries. Verify quality-only changes and event timestamps without assuming every integer is an enumerated state.
site.content.03836: MV, CMV, SAV — Measurement Data Classes
site.content.03837: MV represents a measured quantity, commonly exposing a magnitude through mag and related measurement metadata. The magnitude structure may provide an integer or floating-point component according to the type. Instantaneous and deadband-related attributes have defined roles; optional instantaneous members must not be invented just because a client expects them.
site.content.03838: CMV represents a complex measured value, with a vector structure such as cVal containing magnitude and angle components. In a multi-phase measurement object, each phase can contain its own CMV structure. Units, angle convention, phase association and the availability of optional components must be checked. An angle and a magnitude cannot be combined into one scalar tag without a deliberate representation.
site.content.03839: SAV represents a sampled analogue value, using an instantaneous-magnitude structure such as instMag according to the model. It is a data class, not the Ethernet Sampled Values transport itself. Do not assume that SAV has the same per-value timestamp layout as MV or CMV; in an SV application, sample counts, synchronization indications and stream timing also matter.
site.content.03840: Measurements should be validated with known inputs and end-to-end scaling checks. A report deadband affects when a change is sent, while a CT ratio or multiplier affects the numerical meaning. These are different causes of apparently incorrect HMI behavior and require different diagnostic tests.
site.content.03841: Illustrative value path within a DO
site.content.03844: Scalar magnitude; verify unit and deadband
site.content.03848: Sampled analogue structure; inspect time handling separately
site.content.03849: Use a known three-phase test source to compare phase magnitudes and angles with the relay model. For a process-bus test, additionally verify the configured SV stream and timing indicators; an accurate MMXU display alone does not validate the sampled-value communication path.
site.content.03850: Confirm the actual DOType/DAType structure, numerical representation, units, q/t availability and transport context. Never append “.t” blindly to every measurement leaf.
site.content.03851: SPC, DPC, INC — Control Data Classes
site.content.03852: SPC is controllable single point, DPC is controllable double point and INC is controllable integer status. These classes combine applicable status information with control-related structures. The presence of a controllable CDC does not guarantee that a particular device instance accepts remote operations; the configured control model can be status-only or otherwise restricted.
site.content.03853: For DPC, the observed stVal has double-point states, while a supported command’s ctlVal is typically Boolean for off/on. The command value is therefore not the same four-state code used for feedback. SPC uses single-point control/status semantics, and INC handles an integer control/status value according to the modeled object. Do not replace INC with a floating-point setpoint or assume an enumerated control is INC rather than ENC.
site.content.03854: Control execution uses the defined control service and applicable structures, such as Oper and selection-related objects where supported. The client must honor direct versus select-before-operate behavior, permitted origin and check fields, and command completion rules. An ad hoc write to the status attribute bypasses the intended model and is not the correct implementation.
site.content.03855: A complete test observes request handling and process feedback separately. A rejected operation, expired selection, interlock block or unsuccessful movement should produce the correct client behavior and operator indication without changing unrelated status information.
site.content.03857: Single-point status and supported Boolean control
site.content.03858: What action and feedback does true represent?
site.content.03860: Which object is commandable and which gives feedback?
site.content.03861: Integer status and supported integer control
site.content.03862: What range and operation are permitted?
site.content.03863: For a simulated feeder breaker, inspect the configured CSWI.Pos control model, perform the required client workflow and verify the independent XCBR.Pos response. Do not send the double-point “bad-state” code as a close command.
site.content.03864: Verify supported control services, command data types, limits, selection/termination behavior and negative cases. Use an authorized simulator or FAT setup for active operations.
site.content.03866: Quality is part of the meaning of a measurement or status. It can communicate validity, detailed problems, substitution, test state and operator blocking according to the relevant structure. The HMI must not convert an invalid but numerically plausible value into a healthy display. Communication loss also requires client-side stale-data handling even if the last received source quality was good.
site.content.03867: A data timestamp t describes the modeled data event or update according to its CDC semantics. It is different from report creation time, message arrival time and HMI refresh time. Time quality can indicate clock problems or lack of synchronization. An unchanged signal may retain an old data timestamp legitimately, so age alone must be interpreted in its service and quality context.
site.content.03868: Functional constraints classify attributes by role. ST is used for status, MX for measurements, CO for control, CF for configuration and DC for descriptions. Setting-group and substitution constraints apply where supported. FC is not a physical hierarchy level or an access permission. Some clients require it in a separate field, while an MMS item name may embed it.
site.content.03869: A dataset can select a functionally constrained object or a narrower attribute. Confirm the actual member structure and whether value, quality and time are included. Selecting only stVal must not be assumed to deliver every sibling attribute automatically.
site.content.03870: A 33-F01 breaker report changes quality while position remains on. The HMI should reflect the quality change even though the breaker symbol’s state value is unchanged. After a connection interruption, verify that the client distinguishes stale information from a newly confirmed closed position.
site.content.03871: Exercise data changes, quality-only changes, test/substituted values where supported, unsynchronized time, communication loss and recovery. Compare source event time with receipt time explicitly.
site.content.03872: Practical Example — 33 kV Feeder Protection IED
site.content.03873: Consider outgoing feeder 33-F01 at a 132/33/11 kV substation. Its protection IED receives current/voltage inputs and breaker feedback, evaluates protection and interlocking logic, exposes IEC 61850 information and drives its configured outputs. For this worked example, assume the server exposes LD name IED_33_F01. All prefixes, instances and paths below are illustrative and must be replaced by the deployed model.
site.content.03874: Separate three application paths. Monitoring exposes measurements through MMXU and breaker feedback through XCBR to SCADA. Supervisory control accepts a command through CSWI subject to configured checks, including relevant CILO permissives. Protection evaluates the fault through PTOC and the configured PTRC/output chain. Supervisory close permissives do not define whether the independent protection scheme is allowed to trip.
site.content.03875: Start FAT with configuration identity and a complete signal mapping sheet. Verify the physical/application source against the live model, then inspect the configured dataset/report delivery and HMI interpretation. During a simulated fault, compare start, operation, trip output and breaker feedback as separate events. Timing expectations come from the approved protection design and test plan.
site.content.03876: During SAT, verify the installed terminal associations, device identities, communication paths and time synchronization against the accepted configuration. Active output and switching tests require the project’s isolation and authorization procedures. Preserve the as-left configuration and signed test evidence so later troubleshooting can distinguish a configuration change from a field problem.
site.content.03886: Acceptance sequence: confirm identity → read baseline values → simulate each indication → verify report and HMI → test approved control permissions → simulate protection operation → verify independent breaker feedback → test quality/time and communication recovery → archive the final mapping and configuration.
site.content.03887: For every test, record stimulus, expected response, observed model value, q/t interpretation, client response and pass/fail evidence. Never equate a successful MMS connection with completed feeder commissioning.
site.content.03889: Begin with the authoritative device identity and configuration. Compare the online LD/LN directory with the deployed SCL and vendor MICS. Inspect the LN prefix/class/instance, DO type, CDC, nested attribute type and FC. A cached browser tree or an old ICD can look convincing while describing a different model than the device currently exposes.
site.content.03890: Trace faults from the source toward the display. If the physical/test source disagrees with the online value, inspect input mapping and application logic. If the online value is correct but direct client access fails, inspect the reference, FC and type. If a direct read works but reporting fails, inspect the dataset, report-control configuration and client association. If received data is correct but the HMI is wrong, inspect conversion, quality handling and tag mapping.
site.content.03891: After firmware, SCL or application changes, recheck affected names, optional attributes, datasets and control models. A renamed prefix can break many points; a changed dataset structure can break a decoder that relied on member order. Fixing the first visible symptom should be followed by a review of every point sharing the same assumption.
site.content.03892: Close the investigation with repeatable evidence and the final configuration revision. Retest normal operation and the failure case that exposed the issue. Keep standard-defined behavior separate from vendor implementation details and project settings in the handover notes.
site.content.03895: LD/LN name, prefix, FC or optional support
site.content.03896: Compare live directory and current SCL/MICS
site.content.03899: Trace actual input and equipment tag
site.content.03901: Unit, multiplier, CT/VT or phase mapping
site.content.03902: Compare known injection and source value
site.content.03904: Dataset, RCB, triggers or client association
site.content.03905: Inspect actual report contents and delivery
site.content.03907: Control model, local/remote, selection or permissive
site.content.03908: Inspect service response and approved logic
site.content.03909: Data time versus arrival time; clock quality
site.content.03910: Compare relay record and synchronized test source
site.content.03913: Interrupt and restore the approved test link
site.content.03914: After an IED update, CTRLXCBR1 becomes CBXCBR1. The HMI loses position while current measurements continue working. Compare the directory, correct the affected references through the normal engineering workflow, then verify dataset delivery, all four position states, quality and event time.
site.content.03915: Completion criteria: correct LN/CDC mappings, all required attributes resolved, six functional paths understood, negative tests passed, old configuration assumptions removed and FAT/SAT evidence retained.
site.content.03917: An IEC 61850 DataSet is an ordered collection of references to modeled information. Its members identify the data that a service can read, report or publish. The members refer to information already present in the server model; creating a DataSet does not create new protection functions or new physical measurements. A member can select a functionally constrained data object or a particular data attribute, subject to the supported service and implementation.
site.content.03918: A DataSet is passive configuration. It does not automatically transmit when a value changes. Reporting requires a configured Report Control Block, appropriate triggers and a functioning client/server reporting arrangement. GOOSE requires its own GOOSE control block and publisher configuration. These services may use the DataSet concept, but their transport, delivery behavior and engineering rules differ.
site.content.03919: For reporting, think of the DataSet as the ordered content definition and the RCB as the reporting controller. The RCB refers to a DataSet through DatSet and controls when and how reports are produced. SCADA must interpret the received member values using the correct order, structure and configuration revision, not only a convenient tag label.
site.content.03920: For feeder 33-F01, an engineer selects breaker position and overcurrent operation for a status DataSet. A BRCB references that collection and reports relevant changes to the station HMI. The relay continues to perform its protection function independently of whether the HMI subscribes to those reports.
site.content.03921: Locate the DataSet and its ordered members online, then locate the service control block that actually uses it. A visible DataSet alone is not evidence of live reporting.
site.content.03923: DataSets provide a reusable, structured selection of application information. Instead of configuring an unrelated transaction for every point, an engineer can group signals according to purpose, update behavior and consumer requirements. Reporting can then identify which configured members are included in a particular event report, while an integrity or GI report can provide the whole collection.
site.content.03924: Grouping is an engineering decision. Fast-changing measurements and occasional status changes may benefit from different DataSets and report settings. Very large collections consume server resources, increase payloads and can require segmentation. Excessively fragmented collections can consume scarce RCB instances and complicate client management. Supported member counts and report sizes must be checked in the device and client documentation.
site.content.03925: A reporting DataSet supplies a client/server report service. A GOOSE DataSet supplies a publisher/subscriber exchange controlled by a GOOSE control block, with its own state-change and retransmission behavior. Sharing the same members between services, where permitted, does not make the services interchangeable or guarantee that one configuration is appropriate for both. RptEna does not enable GOOSE, and a GOOSE retransmission is not a buffered MMS report.
site.content.03939: Current publisher state; not BRCB event-history replay
site.content.03940: Use a reporting collection for 33-F01 breaker status and operator alarms, and separately engineer any protection/interlocking GOOSE exchange. Even if both contain a trip indication, their performance criteria, receiver configuration and failure tests remain different.
site.content.03941: Document each DataSet’s consumers and services. Confirm capacity, update rates and payload structure rather than grouping every available point into one collection.
site.content.03943: The usual expansion of FCDA is functionally constrained data attribute. It identifies an attribute together with its Functional Constraint. ST groups status information, MX measurements and other constraints distinguish roles such as configuration or control. FC is part of the selection semantics; it is not another piece of physical equipment and does not grant access permission.
site.content.03944: In SCL, the element named FCDA can describe an attribute-level selection or an object-level functionally constrained data selection. An element with doName and fc but no daName selects the relevant object information for that FC. Supplying daName selects the specified attribute. The resulting received value may therefore be a structure or a scalar, and the client must decode the actual member type.
site.content.03945: Selecting XCBR1.Pos with ST commonly provides a status structure containing stVal, q and t, plus any other applicable members in that structure. Selecting Pos.stVal alone does not automatically include its sibling quality and timestamp. Even if stVal, q and t are three separate DataSet members, an event report may include only members selected by its inclusion rules. Do not assume an unchanged q or a non-triggering t is automatically carried alongside a changed scalar.
site.content.03946: For reliable breaker-event interpretation, inspect whether the client receives an entire Pos[ST] structure or separate scalar members. Verify how it obtains the source timestamp for each position event, rather than relying on the fact that a t member exists somewhere in the DataSet.
site.content.03947: Verify LD instance, LN prefix/class/instance, DO, DA when present, FC and decoded member structure. Inspect actual reports to confirm value, quality and timestamp coverage.
site.content.03949: A DataSet has a name within its owning logical-node context and an ordered membership list. LLN0 is a common location, but do not hard-code it as the only possible location. The references and permitted scope depend on the service and implementation. Reordering members can break a consumer that uses positional mapping even when all the same signals remain present.
site.content.03950: This chapter uses an illustrative physical IED name IED_33_F01 and an LD instance LD0, assuming the exposed LD name is IED_33_F01LD0. The readable DataSet reference is IED_33_F01LD0/LLN0.dsStatus. A mapped MMS/client representation may use LLN0$dsStatus or a domain plus item name. Use the notation expected by the particular client API; do not mix them blindly.
site.content.03951: The SCL name, runtime reference and HMI tag are related but different identifiers. An SCL FCDA uses ldInst="LD0" to identify the LD instance rather than inserting the entire exposed LD name. Prefixes and LN instances must match the engineered model. Association-specific or dynamically created DataSets have additional lifecycle and service restrictions; they must not be assumed suitable for buffered recovery.
site.content.03952: A client imports member 0 as breaker position and member 1 as protection operation. If engineering reverses those members, a positional decoder may misinterpret them. Configuration revision and type checks should expose the mismatch before the HMI uses the data.
site.content.03953: Export and compare ordered membership, not just the DataSet name. Preserve a versioned mapping sheet and verify the associated RCB’s ConfRev after engineering changes.
site.content.03955: Start from the approved signal list and the actual device capabilities. Identify the physical/application source, LN instance, DO/DA, FC and required quality/time behavior for each point. Choose status and measurement groupings that fit the reporting and client requirements. Confirm the supported number of DataSets, members and RCB instances before configuring the collection.
site.content.03956: In an engineering tool, select the owning logical node, create a meaningful DataSet name and add the required members in a documented order. Inspect the exported SCL to confirm that the tool selected an object-level FCD or an individual FCDA as intended. A visual tree selection is not sufficient evidence of the resulting payload structure.
site.content.03957: Next assign the collection to a compatible RCB, configure supported trigger/optional-field choices and engineer client allocation. Static and dynamic configuration capabilities differ between products. Follow the vendor workflow for validation, export, deployment and restart requirements; editing an SCD file on a workstation does not itself update the running IED.
site.content.03958: After deployment, compare the live directory, membership and RCB configuration with the accepted engineering output. A device can still serve an earlier configuration while the latest file on the laptop looks correct. Maintain revision control through the IED tool, system configuration and client import stages.
site.content.03959: Verify the resulting SCL, live member order, supported member types and value/q/t delivery. Record the deployed IED configuration identity and the matching client import revision.
site.content.03961: A Report Control Block controls reporting for an associated DataSet. IEC 61850-7-2 defines the abstract service behavior, IEC 61850-6 represents engineering configuration, and IEC 61850-8-1 maps the relevant communication to MMS. A report is information sent by the server over the client association after the reporting arrangement has been established; it is not simply a periodic sequence of client reads.
site.content.03962: The RCB identifies its DataSet through DatSet, reports a configuration revision through ConfRev and uses TrgOps to select supported triggering conditions. OptFlds controls optional report metadata. RptEna enables transmission for the client arrangement. RptID identifies the report stream, while other attributes govern timing, reservation and buffered recovery as applicable.
site.content.03963: BufTm is an event-coalescing interval, conventionally represented in milliseconds. It allows eligible events occurring close together to be assembled according to the report rules. It is not the amount of historical outage storage and does not define how long a BRCB can retain events. Repeated changes, service rules and implementation details can affect report assembly; do not assume every event experiences one exact fixed delay.
site.content.03964: A report can contain only a subset of the DataSet. Its inclusion bitstring identifies included member positions, and optional reason information explains why members were included. Large reports may require segmentation, which the client must reassemble correctly. A visible RCB is therefore only the starting point for end-to-end reporting verification.
site.content.03978: For 33-F01, a correctly configured dsStatus remains silent if the client has not enabled the appropriate RCB, or if no configured trigger occurs. Reading the same values directly can still work, so successful reads alone do not prove reporting.
site.content.03979: Inspect the runtime RCB values, its association/ownership and actual MMS reports. Separate content-selection, trigger, transport and client-decoding failures.
site.content.03981: A BRCB supports retention of report entries so eligible information can be delivered after an interruption. The buffer is finite. Retention depends on the server’s supported buffering state, valid configuration, available capacity and lifecycle behavior. Merely creating an RCB in SCL does not establish unlimited history or prove that every event before client initialization is retained.
site.content.03982: After an association loss, the client must reconnect, regain access to the intended instance and perform the supported resynchronization/enable sequence. EntryID is an opaque identifier for a buffered entry and can be used to resume after a retained entry. It is not a timestamp, member index or counter that the client should invent. Persist the last accepted report identifier according to the client design and validate the server’s response during recovery.
site.content.03983: TimeOfEntry relates to the report handler’s entry time and the EntryID exposed by the BRCB. It is distinct from each data object’s t and from packet arrival time. Buffer survival across power loss and detailed capacity limits are implementation properties that require documentation and testing, not assumptions from the word “buffered.”
site.content.03984: Initialize the 33-F01 BRCB, confirm reporting, disconnect the test client, produce a known sequence of position changes and reconnect using the client’s supported recovery method. Compare the recovered entries with the test sequence and inspect overflow/gap indications.
site.content.03985: Verify initialized buffering, capacity limits, EntryID handling, reservation after disconnect, overflow and restart behavior. Do not claim lossless recovery unless the tested conditions and retention evidence support it.
site.content.03987: A URCB provides event-driven reporting to its active client without a retained event queue for later replay after disconnection. While the reporting association is active and enabled, it can deliver the configured change reports. It can also support integrity and GI reporting according to the device’s services and configuration.
site.content.03988: When the association is lost, the client must establish the reporting arrangement again. Events that occurred during the disconnected interval are not recovered as a historical URCB sequence. A subsequent read or GI can establish current values, but a point that changed twice and returned to its original state cannot have its missing transitions reconstructed from that snapshot.
site.content.03989: The lack of a historical replay queue does not mean every report is instantaneous or that BufTm has no role. URCBs can still use the configured event-coalescing behavior. Distinguish report assembly from retained outage storage. Reservation and enablement use the appropriate unbuffered service model, commonly involving Resv where supported.
site.content.03990: URCB suitability depends on the application’s tolerance for missing transitions and its separate event-recording arrangements. It can be appropriate for some monitoring uses, but should not be selected solely because its initial connection appears simpler. The client must clearly mark communication loss and avoid presenting the last received value as freshly confirmed.
site.content.03991: If a training alarm turns on and then off while a URCB client is disconnected, a later GI may show only the current off state. The station cannot infer the alarm’s occurrence or duration from that one value.
site.content.03992: Test normal event delivery, loss of association, re-enablement and current-state refresh. Confirm that the HMI does not claim historical completeness for the disconnected interval.
site.content.03994: BRCB and URCB both report configured DataSet information to a client; the key distinction is retained-entry recovery. A BRCB offers a mechanism to recover eligible buffered entries, whereas a URCB does not keep an outage replay queue. Neither choice removes the need to configure triggers, client access, member interpretation and quality handling.
site.content.03995: Buffered reporting introduces additional engineering responsibilities: capacity assessment, EntryID persistence and resynchronization, overflow awareness, buffer lifecycle and reservation behavior. The recovery requirement should define the expected outage duration and event rate, then verify the implementation under that load. A vendor buffer expressed in bytes cannot be translated into a fixed number of events without knowing report sizes and storage behavior.
site.content.03996: A client may still need a current-state synchronization strategy after either type reconnects. That strategy must coexist with BRCB recovery and event ordering rather than accidentally purging history or treating a GI snapshot as a replayed event. Select the service based on operational requirements and supported interoperability, not a belief that buffered means permanent archival storage.
site.content.04001: No retained queue for later replay
site.content.04006: Finite buffer; overflow and purge matter
site.content.04013: Flag gap and restore current state
site.content.04014: Restore current state; missed history unavailable
site.content.04015: Run the same known event sequence during a disconnection against separate test BRCB and URCB instances. Compare recovered events, the current-state refresh and HMI gap indications. Use the result to validate the client design rather than merely noting that both clients reconnect.
site.content.04016: Document the tested buffer limits, reconnect procedure and information-loss policy. Retain evidence for the expected failure duration and event load.
site.content.04017: Report Trigger Options — dchg, qchg, dupd
site.content.04018: dupd concerns a supported data-update notification and can cause reporting without a change in the value. It is not a command to poll every attribute continuously, and enabling it does not manufacture update events for attributes that do not provide that trigger behavior. Verify the CDC/model trigger properties and the device’s supported implementation.
site.content.04019: Measurement change detection may involve deadband behavior defined by the data model and configuration. Small input variations do not necessarily cause a report for every sample. A large dchg threshold, an absent qchg selection or an unsupported dupd expectation can all produce “missing report” symptoms for different reasons.
site.content.04020: Event reports often carry a subset of members. Optional reason-for-inclusion information distinguishes a data change from quality change, data update, integrity or GI. Multiple eligible reasons may apply. Decode the included member positions and reasons rather than assuming every received report is a new process event.
site.content.04024: Correct eligible value change and member inclusion
site.content.04025: Position quality changes while stVal stays fixed
site.content.04026: Quality event reaches client and HMI
site.content.04027: Supported source updates the same value
site.content.04028: Attribute supports update notification; reason decoded
site.content.04032: Whole-DataSet response; not a recovered event history
site.content.04033: For 33-F01, test one position change and one quality-only change separately. Confirm that the client reports their different causes. Use a specifically supported test attribute for dupd rather than repeatedly reading a normal status point and expecting an update report.
site.content.04034: Compare model trigger properties, runtime TrgOps and the report’s reason fields. Verify measurement deadbands before treating quiet traffic as a communications failure.
site.content.04036: Integrity reporting provides a periodic report of the DataSet’s current information when the integrity trigger and interval are configured. IntgPd is the integrity period, conventionally represented in milliseconds. It is a server reporting timer, not a requirement for the client to poll each point. An interval value of zero disables the periodic integrity timer; a useful nonzero interval still needs the corresponding trigger/service configuration.
site.content.04037: General Interrogation requests a current DataSet report through the GI mechanism when supported and permitted by the enabled reporting arrangement. It is commonly used to establish a known current view, but it does not ask the server to invent missed historical events. The request has defined service behavior rather than acting as a permanently latched “send everything” mode.
site.content.04038: Integrity and GI select the whole DataSet rather than only members that triggered a change. A large snapshot may be segmented. The included information is a reported view of the collection; do not automatically treat all member source timestamps as equal or assume that the entire physical process was sampled atomically at one instant.
site.content.04039: Choose intervals with traffic and operator requirements in mind. A short period applied to many large DataSets can dominate bandwidth and client processing. A long period is not an acceptable substitute for correctly configured event triggers where prompt indications are required. Reconnection logic must coordinate snapshots with buffered replay and gap detection.
site.content.04040: An illustrative IntgPd of 60000 ms produces a nominal one-minute integrity cycle when enabled. A separate GI test requests a snapshot immediately through the client workflow. These values are training settings, not universal defaults or timing guarantees.
site.content.04041: Verify integrity enablement and interval, GI response, member completeness, segmentation and reason codes. Confirm that event logs distinguish snapshots from newly occurring process events.
site.content.04043: OptFlds selects additional metadata in reports. The best choices depend on the service, edition, server and client requirements. Optional does not mean operationally unimportant: a client may require particular fields for mapping, recovery or diagnostics. Confirm support and compatibility instead of enabling a copied bitmask from another product.
site.content.04044: SqNum helps follow a report sequence, but it can wrap or reset according to the service lifecycle. It is not a globally unique event identifier. ConfRev identifies the relevant configuration revision and helps detect a mismatched content definition. DataSet name and data references can make decoding more explicit, while reason-for-inclusion explains why a member was sent.
site.content.04045: For buffered reporting, EntryID and buffer-overflow information support recovery and loss detection. Report time relates to report-entry formation; each data object’s t describes its own modeled event/update. They are different clocks in the information chain. TimeOfEntry is a BRCB attribute; do not infer that a URCB exposes the same control-block attribute merely because a report can carry timestamp metadata.
site.content.04046: The inclusion bitstring is fundamental to interpreting a partial report and is not a user-selected substitute for a known DataSet. If a report is segmented, sequence/subsequence and continuation information must be handled by the client as required. The application should use the reassembled report, not mistakenly treat every fragment as a complete snapshot.
site.content.04049: Treating it as a permanent unique event ID
site.content.04052: Logging every snapshot as a new alarm
site.content.04055: Using old member order after a change
site.content.04066: Processing one segment as the complete DataSet
site.content.04067: A recovered BRCB report has a later network arrival time than its entry time and its source event timestamp. Retain these distinctions when reconstructing the 33-F01 event sequence. A correct breaker symbol alone does not validate the event log.
site.content.04068: Match required optional fields with the client manual. Inspect a change report, a snapshot and a recovered/segmented report where supported, and verify metadata decoding.
site.content.04069: Report Enable, Reservation and Client Association
site.content.04070: MMS reporting operates within an established client/server association. The client must gain appropriate access to an RCB instance, verify its settings and enable reporting with RptEna. RptEna is a service state, not a physical input or a universal instruction to start every reporting instance in the IED.
site.content.04071: Reservation prevents competing clients from reconfiguring or taking over the same instance improperly. URCBs commonly use Resv, while BRCBs can expose ResvTms according to supported edition and implementation. A positive ResvTms value represents a reservation period associated with recovery after association loss, in seconds; zero indicates no reservation and a configured -1 value has a predefined reservation meaning. Do not assume the field exists on every device or write a negative value as a generic takeover technique.
site.content.04072: Read the existing state and ownership first. Make only supported, necessary configuration changes while the RCB is in the required state, then enable it and read back the result. Many reporting configuration attributes cannot be changed while enabled. Some changes can purge buffered entries, so repeatedly rewriting a saved configuration during reconnect can undermine recovery.
site.content.04073: A communication connection, successful reservation and successful enable operation are separate outcomes. A maintenance browser can unintentionally occupy an RCB needed by SCADA. Ownership and authorization must therefore be coordinated through the engineering plan rather than solved by forcibly clearing another client’s reporting arrangement.
site.content.04074: SCADA A reconnects before its BRCB reservation expires and resumes using its configured instance. If SCADA B tries to reserve that same instance, rejection may be correct behavior. Inspect ownership and the intended client allocation before declaring the IED faulty.
site.content.04075: Verify association, supported reservation mechanism, ownership, RptEna response/readback and disconnect/reconnect behavior. Keep ResvTms seconds distinct from BufTm and IntgPd milliseconds.
site.content.04076: RCB Instances and Multiple SCADA Clients
site.content.04077: Each independently reporting client needs an appropriate reporting arrangement and available RCB instance. Two clients cannot be assumed to independently control the same enabled instance. One DataSet can be referenced by multiple supported RCB instances, allowing the same information to be delivered through separately managed client streams.
site.content.04078: SCL ReportControl configuration and RptEnabled capacity describe engineered reporting resources. With indexed reporting, engineering tools commonly create instance-specific names. The exact suffix, naming and available instance count must be verified online. Setting max="2" in a teaching fragment does not prove that the target product supports two additional active clients or sufficient memory for their buffered traffic.
site.content.04079: A station may have an HMI, redundant gateways and an engineering client. Allocate their reporting instances and recovery responsibilities explicitly. Redundant systems may use independent instances or a supported coordinated failover arrangement; they should not compete blindly for the same reservation. Confirm how the client software persists EntryID and handles duplicate or late events across failover.
site.content.04080: Resource planning also includes association limits, report bandwidth, event rates and buffer allocation. Multiple clients receiving the same point increase traffic and can increase storage requirements. A quiet laboratory test with one client does not demonstrate capacity for the complete station configuration.
site.content.04088: Does not take over production client instance
site.content.04089: For 33-F01, both HMI and gateway require status information. They reference the same dsStatus through separate supported RCB instances. During FAT, disconnect each client independently and confirm that the other stream continues and the returning client follows its own recovery procedure.
site.content.04090: Inventory all clients and RCB instances. Test simultaneous operation, failover, reservation expiry and reconnect load using the actual supported allocation.
site.content.04091: DataSet and RCB Configuration Using SCL Files
site.content.04092: IEC 61850-6 provides SCL elements describing DataSets and report controls. The fragment below is intended to sit within a properly defined IED/server/LD model, here assumed to use IED name IED_33_F01 and LDevice inst="LD0". ExampleLLN0, XCBR1 and PTOC1 must exist with compatible type definitions in the full document. This is a teaching fragment, not a ready-to-import complete SCD or CID.
site.content.04093: Both FCDA members omit daName, selecting the objects’ ST information rather than only a single leaf. ReportControl datSet="dsStatus" binds the report control to that local DataSet name. buffered="true" chooses a BRCB configuration. The example confRev is an initial illustration; the engineering workflow and server must manage revision changes correctly. Do not manually force a revision merely to conceal a client mismatch.
site.content.04094: SCL spelling differs from runtime terminology: bufTime maps to BufTm, intgPd to IntgPd, TrgOps period selects integrity reporting, and OptFields configRef requests configuration-revision information. The configured 50 ms buffer time and 60000 ms integrity period are illustrative values. Runtime writable fields, ranges and constraints must be checked with the actual device.
site.content.04095: RptEnabled max="2" illustrates capacity for two indexed instances where supported; it is not a declaration that two clients are already connected or that RptEna is true. The complete system may also engineer ClientLN associations. Validate the full document against the project’s SCL schema and vendor tools, deploy through the approved workflow and compare the live directory afterward.
site.content.04096: After importing the final configuration, browse the live DataSet, verify XCBR1.Pos[ST] and PTOC1.Op[ST] in that order, identify the actual generated RCB instance names and read ConfRev. Then configure each client using the deployed values rather than guessed suffixes.
site.content.04097: Validate the full SCL schema/type references and vendor capability limits. Verify the deployed model and runtime service behavior; well-formed XML alone does not establish valid or working IED configuration.
site.content.04099: The server updates its modeled information from the IED application. The selected DataSet members identify the relevant information, and the RCB evaluates configured reporting conditions. Eligible notifications are assembled according to the service rules, including event coalescing, member inclusion and buffering where applicable. The resulting report travels over the established MMS client/server association.
site.content.04100: Under the commonly used IEC 61850-8-1 TCP/IP mapping, MMS uses the ISO communication stack over TCP, commonly on port 102. A working Ethernet link or reachable IP address is only a prerequisite. Association negotiation, access permissions, RCB ownership, enablement, triggers and client handling must also be correct. Reporting is not a GOOSE multicast exchange.
site.content.04101: MMS reports are InformationReport messages sent by the server; the client does not issue a separate read for each event. Transport reliability helps deliver bytes within a live connection but does not establish unlimited report history, successful HMI processing or correct application mapping. BRCB recovery addresses eligible retained entries after interruption through its own service mechanism.
site.content.04102: For diagnostics, inspect the actual association and report traffic using an authorized capture method. A switched network may require an appropriate mirrored port or tap; the engineering laptop will not necessarily see other devices’ unicast traffic by merely sharing the station switch. Protected traffic may require approved endpoint diagnostics instead of readable packet payloads.
site.content.04103: Verify the source value, MMS association, actual report contents and client result. Inspect inclusion bits, reason codes, sequence/revision and source time rather than relying only on packet counts.
site.content.04104: Practical Example — 33 kV Feeder Breaker Status
site.content.04105: Use feeder 33-F01 with an illustrative exposed LD name IED_33_F01LD0 and breaker LN XCBR1. The physical breaker moves from closed to open. Its auxiliary contacts change the IED’s digital-input states, and the configured input logic updates XCBR1.Pos. The double-point stVal is interpreted with its quality q and data timestamp t; open/closed, intermediate and bad-state meanings must match the project.
site.content.04106: The reporting DataSet includes the required position information, preferably an appropriate object-level ST structure when supported by the client design. A configured, enabled RCB evaluates the eligible dchg notification and applies its report assembly rules. The server sends the MMS report to the associated SCADA client. No report should be expected solely because the DataSet exists.
site.content.04107: SCADA decodes the included member against the correct DataSet structure and ConfRev, updates the breaker symbol and records the source event time and quality. Alarms follow the configured project logic: a normal commanded opening may be an event without being a fault alarm. Invalid position, unexpected operation or stale communication can have separate alarm policies.
site.content.04108: If only a scalar stVal is selected, explicitly verify how source quality and time accompany each event. A report-level timestamp is not an automatic replacement for Pos.t. During a disconnect, distinguish BRCB replay of retained transitions from a current-state GI snapshot. A closed-to-open-to-closed sequence can be invisible in a final snapshot alone.
site.content.04109: FAT sequence: set a simulated closed input → confirm model and HMI → change auxiliary-input simulation to open → inspect Pos value/q/t → capture the resulting report → compare the HMI symbol and event record. Repeat for quality-only change and a known disconnect/reconnect sequence.
site.content.04110: Record evidence at all seven stages: breaker condition, auxiliary inputs, model update, DataSet member, RCB trigger, MMS report and SCADA result. Do not infer mechanical position from a command or trip indication alone.
site.content.04111: Practical Example — Protection Trip and Alarm Reporting
site.content.04112: Protection reporting describes events produced by the configured protection application. PTOC.Str, PTOC.Op and PTRC.Tr represent different stages: start, protection operation and trip conditioning. Their structured data can include general and phase components according to the actual model. Reporting them does not implement the trip scheme or establish the physical breaker’s position.
site.content.04113: A protection/alarm DataSet can select the required ST structures and quality/time information. Different events may be assembled into one report or separate reports depending on timing and BufTm rules. Use each source timestamp and the defined signal semantics to analyze the sequence; report order or one common entry time alone may not capture the exact protection chronology.
site.content.04114: A trip is often followed by breaker feedback and alarm processing. Keep command output, protection indication, position confirmation and operator alarm distinct in the mapping sheet. A buffered report arriving late after reconnect should retain its historical meaning rather than being presented as a newly occurring live fault solely because its network arrival time is recent.
site.content.04115: Alarm latching, acknowledgment and reset are application functions. An RCB does not automatically retain an HMI alarm acknowledgment or reset the relay’s protection latch. Likewise, repeated integrity/GI snapshots of an asserted trip should not create a fresh alarm occurrence every time. The client needs defined state and event handling.
site.content.04116: An isolated test produces pickup, delayed overcurrent operation, conditioned trip and simulated breaker opening. Compare test-equipment timing, relay event records, reported source timestamps and the HMI log. Repeat with reporting interrupted while ensuring the protection test remains governed by the approved scheme.
site.content.04117: Validate start/operate/trip labels, phase/general mapping, q/t delivery, delayed replay, duplicate handling and reset behavior. Protection execution must not depend on SCADA report receipt.
site.content.04118: FAT/SAT Testing of DataSets and RCBs
site.content.04119: FAT verifies the engineered model and reporting behavior in a controlled environment before installation. Start with the IED firmware/configuration identity, SCL revision, client version and approved signal list. Confirm DataSet order and member types, assigned RCB instances, optional fields and client mappings. Record expected results before applying stimuli.
site.content.04120: Exercise value changes, quality-only changes, supported data updates, integrity and GI separately. Verify member inclusion, reason codes, source timestamps, report metadata and HMI results. Test structured values and segmentation where relevant. Include negative conditions such as an unavailable RCB instance, invalid reference or unsupported setting without disturbing other clients.
site.content.04121: For BRCB recovery, initialize reporting, disconnect the designated test client and generate a known event sequence within the expected retention envelope. Reconnect and compare retained entries and current state. A separate controlled capacity test checks overflow/gap handling. Do not deliberately flood a live operational IED or purge its buffer merely to demonstrate an overflow condition.
site.content.04122: SAT confirms the installed configuration, network paths, client allocations, time synchronization and actual field-to-model associations. Apply the site’s isolation and authorization procedure for input simulation and any active equipment tests. After restoration, verify the as-left reporting settings and normal client associations; a temporary engineering client must not remain in possession of production RCBs.
site.content.04125: Correct reference, type, value, q/t and HMI
site.content.04130: Complete current DataSet; proper event handling
site.content.04133: EntryID recovery, retained events and gap status
site.content.04135: Documented loss indication and current-state recovery
site.content.04138: No unintended takeover or impact on other streams
site.content.04139: Known event time and synchronization condition
site.content.04140: Source t, report time and arrival time distinguished
site.content.04141: The acceptance sheet for 33-F01 records the stimulus, model value, RCB identity, report metadata, HMI result and pass/fail evidence for every point. A screenshot of an open breaker is insufficient to prove quality, source time and recovery behavior.
site.content.04142: Retain configuration exports, decoded captures or logs, timing evidence and signed results. Restore normal settings and verify that all intended clients are reporting after the test.
site.content.04144: Troubleshoot from source to display: physical/application update → model → DataSet → RCB → association/transport → client decoding → HMI. Establish the first point of disagreement. If a direct read is correct but reporting is silent, inspect member selection, trigger eligibility, RptEna and client ownership before changing the physical wiring or rewriting the entire SCL.
site.content.04145: After a configuration change, compare the deployed member order/types and ConfRev with the client import. A report with valid transport can still be interpreted incorrectly by stale application mapping. During reconnect failures, inspect the requested instance, reservation state, retained EntryID availability and any configuration writes that may have purged the buffer.
site.content.04146: Interview question: “Does a DataSet send data by itself?” No; a service uses it. “Does BufTm define outage retention?” No; it concerns event assembly. “Does GI recover missed history?” No; it requests a current snapshot. “Does BRCB guarantee every event survives a long outage or restart?” No; capacity, state, retention and recovery conditions must be evaluated.
site.content.04147: Further questions: “Can a qchg report occur with unchanged stVal?” Yes, when the modeled notification and RCB trigger apply. “Why can two SCADA clients conflict?” They may be competing for one RCB instance or reservation. “Why compare source t with report time?” They describe different stages. Strong answers connect the standard concepts to actual model inspection and test evidence.
site.content.04150: RCB binding, RptEna, ownership and TrgOps
site.content.04151: Generate an eligible test event and inspect traffic
site.content.04154: Compare full runtime DataSet with client mapping
site.content.04157: Test unchanged value with changed quality
site.content.04159: Buffer capacity/state, purge, EntryID and reservation
site.content.04160: Compare known sequence and overflow/gap metadata
site.content.04162: Replay, GI/integrity and client event handling
site.content.04165: Source t versus entry/arrival time; clock status
site.content.04166: Compare synchronized source and device log
site.content.04169: Use the engineered independent client resource
site.content.04170: An HMI works before an SCL update, then displays mismatched status values. Compare the revised DataSet order and ConfRev with the client’s cached mapping. Correct the mismatch through the engineering workflow, then retest changes, snapshots, quality and recovery for every affected member.
site.content.04171: Close the fault only after normal operation and the original failure scenario both pass. Record the root cause, final revisions, client allocation and evidence rather than relying on a temporary successful connection.
site.content.04173: Voltage-rated conductor / busbar or power cable, including auxiliary AC feeders. Voltage is shown on the connection; this is not a communication link.
site.content.04176: Multicore copper control wiring through terminal blocks. Trip, close and status use separate circuits; arrows summarize a circuit, not individual conductors.
site.content.04179: Dedicated instrument-transformer secondary wiring. CT current and VT voltage circuits are separate; no Ethernet or fiber is implied.

site.content.04319: Conventional bay: analog measurement and binary control remain copper. The protection IED and bay controller exchange station information over Ethernet.
site.content.04343: Station bus carries MMS reporting and control alongside engineered GOOSE exchanges. GOOSE multicast remains within its configured Layer 2 domain.
site.content.04352: The MU streams sampled measurements over process-bus Ethernet. The relay consumes SV and publishes trip GOOSE to the PIU. PTP is a separate synchronization service.
site.content.04363: GOOSE to bay PIU; copper to coils
site.content.04365: PRP sends duplicate frames over two independent LANs. A DANP has one logical network identity; LAN A and LAN B must not be bridged together. A RedBox can attach a single-attached node.
site.content.04369: Two PRP ports · one logical identity
site.content.04384: HSR nodes forward duplicate frames in opposite directions around a closed ring. Every ring device must support HSR; the images identify roles, not a claim that the pictured model supports HSR.
site.content.04393: Optical channel: active SFP → patch cord → LIU → trunk fiber → remote LIU → patch cord → SFP. Select single-mode/multimode, optics and optical budget together.
site.content.04403: The relay is physical; LD, LN, DO and DA are logical data objects inside its IEC 61850 server. Dashed relationships below are not communication cables.
site.content.04410: MMS reports travel from an IED server to an associated client over TCP 102. Buffered reports can retain configured events across a client interruption, subject to device buffer capacity.
site.content.04426: GOOSE is Layer 2 multicast (0x88B8); MMS is TCP/IP (port 102). A state change causes rapid GOOSE retransmission followed by a longer heartbeat interval. Actual performance depends on engineering.
site.content.04434: Two independent services are shown: an MMS select-before-operate control path, and a sampled-value measurement path. SV does not carry the operator control command.
site.content.04445: SCL files describe engineering information. ICD and SSD feed system configuration, SCD captures the integrated design, and a device-specific CID may be deployed using the vendor workflow.
site.content.04460: A field indication changes an IED data attribute, becomes a station event and can be mapped onward through a gateway. Signal identity, quality and timestamps must be preserved in the mapping.

site.content.05101: Why do we use 132/33/11 kV voltage levels in a substation, and what is the functional difference between a Circuit Breaker (52), a Disconnector (89), and an Earth Switch (89E)?
site.content.05102: High transmission voltage (132 kV) minimizes I²R line losses over long distances, while 33 kV and 11 kV distribute power safely to industrial and local distribution transformers.

site.content.05413: Two-Section Busbar with Bus Coupler (CB-132, CB-33, CB-11)
site.content.05414: Dividing the busbar into Section A and Section B via a Bus Coupler breaker allows half the substation to remain in service during maintenance or busbar faults. Normally, Incomer 1 feeds Bus A, Incomer 2 feeds Bus B, and the Bus Coupler remains OPEN (2-out-of-3 scheme) to limit short-circuit fault current.
site.content.05415: Never parallel two independent incoming transformers through a closed Bus Coupler unless permitted by short-circuit MVA rating and synch-check (CSWI25).
site.content.05417: Circuit Breakers (XCBR) interrupt fault and load current. Disconnectors/Isolators (XSWI Q1/Q9) provide visible off-load isolation and must only operate when the breaker is OPEN. Earth Switches (Q8) safely ground de-energized line or feeder sections for maintenance.
site.content.05418: Interlocking (CILO1) strictly prevents closing Earth Switch Q8 when Q1/Q9 or CB is CLOSED.

site.content.05422: To reduce auxiliary DC battery consumption
site.content.05423: To prevent paralleling two 50 MVA transformers and exceeding the 33 kV switchgear short-circuit breaking capacity
site.content.05424: Because IEC 61850 does not support three closed breakers on a busbar
site.content.05425: To disable OLTC automatic voltage regulation
site.content.05426: Paralleling T1 and T2 halves the equivalent source impedance, nearly doubling the 33 kV fault current beyond the switchgear kA rating.
site.content.05427: What is the switching sequence to isolate a 132 kV Line Bay for maintenance?
site.content.05428: 1) Verify remote end breaker open or transfer load. 2) Open local Circuit Breaker (52). 3) Visually/electrically confirm CB is OPEN. 4) Open Busbar Disconnector (89B/Q1) then Line Disconnector (89L/Q9). 5) Verify line is dead via CVT voltage indication, then close Line Earth Switch (89E/Q8).

site.content.05432: Differential protection compares HV and LV currents compensated for transformer ratio and vector group (YNyn0d1 / Dyn11). Second-harmonic restraint prevents mal-operation during magnetizing inrush, while 5th-harmonic restraint blocks tripping during over-excitation.
site.content.05433: When 87T or Buchholz/PRD operates, both HV and LV circuit breakers must trip simultaneously via hardwired 86T and GOOSE intertrip.
site.content.05435: If a protection trip (`PTRC1.Tr.general`) is issued but current continues flowing above threshold after 60 ms, `RBRF1.OpIn` issues a retrip to the local breaker; if still un-cleared at 150 ms, `RBRF1.OpEx` publishes a high-priority GOOSE trip to all adjacent breakers on that bus section.
site.content.05436: RBRF relies on high-speed GOOSE (< 4 ms transmission) for busbar zone tripping.

site.content.05441: What is the difference between Protection Pickup (Str / ACD) and Protection Operate (Op / ACT)?
site.content.05442: Pickup (`Str`, Common Data Class `ACD`) asserts immediately when fault current exceeds the threshold and includes directionality (`dirGeneral`). Operate (`Op`, Common Data Class `ACT`) asserts only after the configured time-delay curve (IDMT or definite time) expires to trip the breaker.
site.content.05443: IEC 61850 Data Modelling (IED → LD → LN → DO → DA → FC)
site.content.05444: Decode the hierarchical object model of IEC 61850-7-4 and 7-3: Logical Devices, Logical Nodes, Data Objects, Common Data Classes (CDC), Data Attributes, and Functional Constraints.
site.content.05446: Consider `IED_33_F01Application/XCBR1.Pos.stVal [ST]`. Here `IED_33_F01` is the IED name, `Application` is the Logical Device (`ldInst`), `XCBR1` is the Logical Node, `Pos` is the Data Object (CDC = `DPC`), and `stVal` is the Data Attribute with Functional Constraint `ST` (Status).
site.content.05447: Never confuse a Data Object (`Pos`) with a leaf Data Attribute (`stVal`, `q`, `t`).
site.content.05448: Functional Constraints (ST, MX, CO, CF, DC, SP)
site.content.05449: Functional Constraints filter which attributes belong to a service or dataset: `ST` = Status, `MX` = Measurands (analog), `CO` = Control operations (`SBOw`, `Oper`, `Cancel`), `CF` = Configuration (`ctlModel`, `sboTimeout`), `DC` = Description.
site.content.05450: A Dataset FCDA always specifies the Functional Constraint (`fc="ST"` or `fc="MX"`) so the report/GOOSE includes only the intended attributes.
site.content.05451: Open the IED Explorer tab, select any relay, and inspect its Logical Devices, Logical Nodes, Data Objects, and leaf attributes.
site.content.05452: IED Explorer → Select IED_132_L1 → Logical Nodes tab.
site.content.05453: In IEC 61850-7-3, what is the Common Data Class (CDC) of `MMXU1.A.phsA` (Phase A Current)?
site.content.05458: Phase currents and voltages in MMXU are Complex Measured Values (CMV) with magnitude (`cVal.mag.f`) and angle (`cVal.ang.f`).
site.content.05459: Why should circuit breaker OPEN and CLOSED indications not be modelled as two independent XCBR nodes?
site.content.05460: One physical 3-pole circuit breaker corresponds to one `XCBR` instance (`XCBR1`). Its position is a 2-bit Double-Point status (`XCBR1.Pos.stVal` of type `Dbpos`: `00` intermediate, `01` open, `10` closed, `11` bad). Single-point open/closed tags in legacy SCADA are derived from this `Dbpos` or auxiliary `GGIO` contacts.
site.content.05462: Contrast Layer-2 multicast GOOSE (Ethertype 0x88B8) for < 4 ms peer-to-peer protection/interlocking with TCP/IP Port 102 Client/Server MMS for SCADA reporting and SBO control.
site.content.05463: GOOSE State Machine (`stNum` & `sqNum`) and Retransmission Curve
site.content.05464: GOOSE maps directly onto Ethernet Layer 2 bypassing TCP/IP overhead. During steady state, frames repeat at `MaxTime` (e.g. 1000 ms) with `sqNum` incrementing. On a data change in the linked DataSet, `stNum` increments by 1, `sqNum` resets to 0, and frames burst at `MinTime` (e.g. 4 ms → 8 ms → 16 ms → 1000 ms).
site.content.05465: Subscribers detect lost or stale GOOSE streams using `timeAllowedToLive` (TAL) and `confRev` validation.
site.content.05466: Buffered (BRCB) vs Unbuffered (URCB) MMS Report Control Blocks
site.content.05467: Buffered RCBs (`BRCB`) store Sequence-of-Events (`dchg`, `qchg`) in relay RAM during a SCADA connection loss and replay them via `EntryID` upon reconnection. Unbuffered RCBs (`URCB`) stream cyclic analog measurements (`MMXU`) without buffering.
site.content.05468: Always assign status/protection datasets to BRCBs and cyclic metering datasets to URCBs.

site.content.05471: What happens to `stNum` and `sqNum` in a GOOSE frame immediately when a circuit breaker trips?
site.content.05472: stNum resets to 0 and sqNum increments by 1
site.content.05473: stNum increments by 1 and sqNum resets to 0
site.content.05474: Both stNum and sqNum increment by 1
site.content.05476: A state change in any FCDA of the GOOSE dataset increments stNum (State Number) by 1 and resets sqNum (Sequence Number) to 0.
site.content.05477: Why does GOOSE use multicast MAC addresses in the range 01-0C-CD-01-00-00 to 01-0C-CD-01-01-FF?
site.content.05478: IEC 61850-8-1 Annex A reserves the IEEE OUI prefix `01-0C-CD` with `01` for GOOSE, `02` for GSSE, and `04` for Sampled Values (SV), allowing Ethernet switches and NIC hardware filters to identify and prioritize Layer-2 substation multicast frames.

site.content.05482: Each relay starts as an unconfigured `.icd` template. In the vendor tool, engineers configure protection settings and export an `.iid`. The System Configurator imports all `.iid`/`.icd` files, binds GOOSE `<Inputs><ExtRef>` and IP/VLAN parameters, and exports the station master `.scd`, from which individual `.cid` files are loaded into each IED.

site.content.05488: What is an `<ExtRef>` element in an SCL file?
site.content.05489: `<ExtRef>` (External Reference) inside a subscriber IED’s `<Inputs>` section binds an external publisher’s GOOSE or SV data attribute (`iedName`, `ldInst`, `lnClass`, `doName`, `daName`, `srcCBName`) to an internal logical node input (`intAddr`).
