site.content.05491: Design zero-recovery-time redundant station buses using IEC 62439-3 Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP) and High-availability Seamless Redundancy (HSR).
site.content.05492: PRP (LAN A + LAN B) vs HSR Ring Topology
site.content.05493: In PRP, each Dual Attached Node (DANP) sends duplicate frames with a Redundancy Control Trailer (RCT) simultaneously onto two independent switches (LAN A and LAN B). In HSR, DANH relays form a daisy-chain ring without dedicated switches, forwarding frames in both directions.
site.content.05494: Single Attached Nodes (SAN) require a RedBox to participate on a PRP or HSR network.
site.content.05495: Open Network Topology tab, switch between PRP, HSR, Dual LAN, and Single LAN modes, and simulate a LAN-A switch outage.
site.content.05496: Network & Redundancy → Toggle PRP/HSR & test link diagnostic drawer.
site.content.05497: What is the worst-case network recovery time of IEC 62439-3 PRP or HSR during a single fiber link break?
site.content.05499: Because every frame is transmitted simultaneously over two independent paths, the receiver simply uses the surviving path with 0 ms recovery time.
site.content.05500: Why is SNTP insufficient for IEC 61850 Sampled Values and high-precision SOE compared to IEEE 1588v2 PTP?
site.content.05501: SNTP provides millisecond accuracy (~1–10 ms), whereas IEEE 1588v2 PTP with hardware timestamping and Transparent/Boundary Clocks (IEC/IEEE 61850-9-3 Power Profile) achieves sub-microsecond (< 1 µs) synchronization required for synchrophasors and SV.
site.content.05502: Industrial Communication Protocols for Substation Automation (MMS, GOOSE, Modbus TCP, IEC-104, OPC UA, PTP/SNTP)
site.content.05503: Complete Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced engineering guide to all six protocols in this 132/33/11 kV substation: IEC 61850 MMS (TCP/102), IEC 61850 GOOSE (0x88B8), Modbus TCP (TCP/502), IEC 60870-5-104 (TCP/2404), OPC UA (TCP/4840), and SNTP/PTP Time Sync.
site.content.05504: 1. Beginner Level — What, Why & Where Each Protocol is Used
site.content.05505: • IEC 61850 MMS (TCP Port 102): Client/Server protocol between Bay IEDs (MMS Servers) and SCADA Server A (MMS Client) for BRCB/URCB reporting, measurements, and SBO breaker control. • IEC 61850 GOOSE (EtherType 0x88B8): High-speed (< 3 ms) Layer-2 Ethernet multicast between IEDs for protection trips (PTRC), breaker failure (50BF), and bay interlocking (CILO). • Modbus TCP (TCP Port 502): Client/Server register polling between 33/11 kV Feeder Energy Meters (Servers, Unit ID 1–14) and the Station Gateway / SCADA. • IEC 60870-5-104 (TCP Port 2404): Wide-area telecontrol protocol linking the Station Gateway (Controlled Station, COA=132) to the Remote Control Center (SLDC / RCC Controlling Station). • OPC UA (opc.tcp://10.132.10.200:4840): Secure architecture linking SCADA Server A (OPC UA Server) to the Enterprise Historian & Analytics engine. • SNTP / NTP / PTP (UDP/123 & L2 0x88F7): Distributes GPS/GLONASS time from the Meinberg LANTIME M400 Grandmaster to all IEDs and switches.
site.content.05506: Each protocol serves a specific tier: Process/Bay (GOOSE), Station Bus (MMS, Modbus TCP, PTP/SNTP), WAN Telecontrol (IEC-104), and Enterprise Historian (OPC UA).
site.content.05507: 2. Intermediate Level — Roles, Packet Flow & Configuration Parameters
site.content.05508: • MMS Flow: SCADA Client opens TCP:102 ISO COTP association → enables BRCB (RptEna=TRUE) → triggers General Interrogation (GI) → receives spontaneous InformationReports. • GOOSE Flow: Publisher IED multicasts Layer-2 802.1Q VLAN 20 frames (01-0C-CD-01-00-xx); on state change, stNum increments, sqNum resets to 0, and MinTime (4 ms) burst retransmission starts. • Modbus TCP Flow: Client sends 7-byte MBAP Header + 5-byte PDU (FC 03/04, Start Register, Word Count) → Meter replies with raw 16/32-bit registers scaled to engineering units. • IEC-104 Flow: RCC sends STARTDT ACT (U-Frame) → Gateway replies STARTDT CON → I-Frames carry ASDUs (TypeID 31 M_DP_TB_1 for breaker pos, TypeID 36 M_ME_TF_1 for MW, TypeID 46 C_DC_NA_1 for commands) identified by COA=132 and IOA. • OPC UA Flow: Client validates X.509v3 certificate → opens SecureChannel & Session → browses Namespace ns=2 → creates Subscription & MonitoredItems for DataChange callbacks.
site.content.05509: Never confuse Layer-2 GOOSE multicast (0x88B8) with TCP/IP client-server protocols (MMS 102, Modbus 502, IEC-104 2404, OPC UA 4840).
site.content.05510: 3. Advanced Level — Cross-Protocol Translation, Troubleshooting & FAT/SAT
site.content.05511: • End-to-End Trace: Field 52a/52b Contact → IED DI Ch.1 → XCBR1.Pos.stVal → IEC 61850 MMS (TCP/102) → SCADA / Station Gateway → IEC-104 IOA 1001 (TypeID 31, TCP/2404) → RCC HMI (and OPC UA ns=2 NodeId → Historian). • Troubleshooting Checklist: 1. MMS Disconnected: Check IP reachability, TCP Port 102, OSI-AP-Title, and BRCB RptEna state. 2. GOOSE Not Received: Check switch VLAN 20 trunking, Multicast MAC, APPID, confRev, and TAL expiration. 3. Modbus Exception 0x02: Check 0-based vs 1-based register offset and Unit ID. 4. IEC-104 No Data: Check STARTDT CON state, COA=132 match, and IOA mapping table. 5. OPC UA BadSecurityChecksFailed: Trust the X.509v3 certificate on both client and server.
site.content.05512: During FAT/SAT, always verify end-to-end timestamp preservation (CP56Time2a in IEC-104 and SourceTimestamp in OPC UA) from the originating IED.
site.content.05513: Open Modbus TCP Lab (Port 502), IEC-104 Lab (Port 2404), and OPC UA Lab (Port 4840) to test live register polling, RCC remote breaker commands, and Historian subscriptions.
site.content.05514: Sidebar → Modbus TCP Lab / IEC-104 Lab / OPC UA Lab
site.content.05515: Which protocol and port are used between the Station Gateway (COA 132) and the Remote Control Center (RCC / SLDC)?
site.content.05519: IEC 60870-5-104 over TCP Port 2404 is the standard wide-area telecontrol protocol connecting the Station Gateway to the RCC.
site.content.05520: Why is IEC 61850 GOOSE (0x88B8) mapped directly onto Layer-2 Ethernet rather than TCP/IP?
site.content.05521: To achieve deterministic sub-3 ms protection trip delivery without TCP handshake/acknowledgment overhead
site.content.05522: To poll energy meter holding registers
site.content.05525: GOOSE bypasses TCP/IP network/transport layers and uses IEEE 802.1Q Priority 4 multicast to deliver protection trips in under 3–4 ms.
site.content.05526: Explain the complete path of a 132 kV breaker status change from the switchyard to both the local SCADA HMI and the Remote Control Center (RCC).
site.content.05527: The 52a/52b auxiliary contacts wire to the bay IED DI card (debounced & PTP-timestamped). The IED maps the double-point status to XCBR1.Pos.stVal [ST, DPC] and transmits it via IEC 61850 MMS (TCP/102 BRCB) to SCADA Server A and the Station Gateway (and via Layer-2 GOOSE 0x88B8 to peer IEDs). The Station Gateway translates XCBR1.Pos.stVal to IEC 60870-5-104 TypeID 31 (M_DP_TB_1, COA=132, IOA=1001) and transmits a spontaneous I-Frame (COT=3) over TCP Port 2404 to the RCC, while SCADA Server A exposes the tag via OPC UA (opc.tcp://10.132.10.200:4840) to the Historian.
site.content.05530: What information is needed, and which service exchanges it? The Application layer defines the communication services used by applications, not merely the SCADA display.
site.content.05531: IEC 61850 ACSI defines abstract services for reading, reporting, and control. Client-server services are mapped to MMS. The Logical Device → Logical Node → Data Object → Data Attribute hierarchy gives signals standardized meaning.
site.content.05532: In a 33 kV feeder IED, XCBR1.Pos.stVal represents breaker position. A configured DataSet and enabled Report Control Block can report changes to SCADA. The complete object reference must use the correct Logical Device and functional constraint.
site.content.05533: SCADA client, station gateway, IED server; MMS, ACSI, reports, controls.
site.content.05534: If the MMS association is healthy but the indication is stale, inspect DataSet membership, RCB reservation, RptEna, trigger options, object reference, quality, and timestamp. For control, verify the control model, permissions, local/remote state, and interlocks.
site.content.05535: GOOSE and SV also carry application information. Calling them Layer 2 protocols describes their direct Ethernet mapping, not an absence of application semantics.
site.content.05538: Devices must interpret exchanged information consistently. Presentation functions support data representation, syntax negotiation, and encoding.
site.content.05539: ASN.1 describes data structures; BER specifies how values are encoded as bytes. Conventional MMS associations use ISO presentation contexts and negotiated syntax. Encoding is not the same as encryption.
site.content.05540: An IED sends structured breaker position, quality, and timestamp values. The client must decode the correct types before showing OPEN/CLOSED; it must not assume an arbitrary byte is a Boolean.
site.content.05541: IED / SCADA protocol libraries; ISO presentation, ASN.1 and BER.
site.content.05542: For decoding errors, inspect TCP reassembly, capture completeness, negotiated contexts, device compatibility, and data types. Do not immediately mistake truncated captures for device protocol defects.
site.content.05543: Encryption is not universally a Layer 6 function. Its placement depends on the actual protocol and security profile.
site.content.05546: Session functions help establish, manage, and release conversations between applications. An established TCP connection does not mean the MMS association is ready.
site.content.05547: The conventional MMS stack includes ISO session functions. Association establishment also involves presentation context, ACSE, and MMS Initiate negotiation. ACSE is an application-layer association control service, not exclusively a Session-layer function.
site.content.05548: After a station gateway restarts, TCP is followed by COTP, session/presentation, and ACSE/MMS negotiation. The client must restore the required RCB state for reports to resume.
site.content.05549: Client/server protocol stacks; ISO session. ACSE and MMS association functions cooperate above it.
site.content.05550: If TCP connects but the association is rejected, inspect configured selectors, association limits, access permissions, presentation context, and the rejection reason.
site.content.05551: A session is not identical to a TCP socket. Never assume reporting automatically resumes after an association is lost.
site.content.05554: TCP provides an ordered byte stream with sequence numbers, acknowledgements, and retransmissions. UDP datagrams have no equivalent built-in delivery guarantees.
site.content.05555: Conventional MMS uses ISO transport over TCP: COTP over TPKT (RFC 1006), followed by TCP. Servers commonly listen on TCP port 102, while client source ports are usually ephemeral. TPKT frames protocol messages over the TCP byte stream.
site.content.05556: SCADA 192.168.10.10 connects to IED 192.168.10.101:102. Even after SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK, upper-layer association negotiation remains necessary. SNTP commonly uses UDP 123; conventional GOOSE and SV use neither TCP nor UDP.
site.content.05557: Host TCP stack, server listener, firewall transport rules; TCP, UDP, COTP / TPKT adaptation.
site.content.05558: For repeated SYNs, check network paths, firewalls, and the server listener. For RSTs, investigate endpoint rejection. Correlate retransmissions, resets, and timeouts on established connections.
site.content.05559: TCP reliability does not guarantee a fixed protection deadline. An open TCP 102 port does not guarantee available MMS reports.
site.content.05562: IP addresses and subnet masks identify logical endpoints. Communication between different subnets requires suitable routing through a router or Layer 3 switch.
site.content.05563: On the same IPv4 subnet, ARP resolves the destination MAC. For a remote subnet, the host sends an Ethernet frame to the next-hop gateway MAC. Ethernet destination addresses may change at each hop while the routed IP endpoint remains the same, unless translation is used.
site.content.05564: SCADA 192.168.10.10/24 and IED 192.168.10.101/24 share a subnet. Reaching IED 192.168.20.101/24 requires approved routing and a return path. These addresses are training examples.
site.content.05565: IED IP interface, engineering PC, router / Layer 3 switch; IPv4/IPv6, ICMP, routing.
site.content.05566: Verify IP address, mask, duplicate addresses, gateway, routes, and return path. Ping demonstrates ICMP reachability only, not MMS association or GOOSE subscription. MMS can still work when ICMP is blocked.
site.content.05567: Conventional Ethernet GOOSE and SV are not routed like IP packets. R-GOOSE and R-SV are separate routable profiles.
site.content.05571: Ethernet frames are forwarded using MAC addresses within the local network. VLANs, multicast forwarding, priority tagging, and frame error detection belong to this layer.
site.content.05572: GOOSE uses EtherType 0x88B8 and SV uses 0x88BA. Conventional profiles carry their application payload directly in Ethernet frames. IEEE 802.1Q VLAN IDs and PCP priorities are Layer 2 fields; tagging depends on the engineered profile and port configuration.
site.content.05573: Between a feeder IED publisher and subscriber, verify VLAN membership, multicast forwarding, and APPID/subscription configuration. APPID is a protocol identifier, not an IP address or TCP port.
site.content.05574: Industrial Ethernet switches, NICs; Ethernet, VLAN, PCP, PRP / HSR.
site.content.05575: Compare captures at publisher egress and subscriber ingress. Check VLAN tags/PVID, allowed VLANs, multicast filters, port counters, and subscriber diagnostics. IGMP snooping alone does not configure non-IP GOOSE/SV multicast.
site.content.05576: PRP/HSR provide path redundancy; they do not correct incorrect DataSet mappings, failed sources, or flawed protection logic.
site.content.05579: The Physical layer carries bits as optical pulses or electrical signals. The complete path from fibre patch cord to SFP transceiver must be healthy.
site.content.05580: Verify optical wavelength, link speed, single-mode/multimode compatibility, Tx/Rx polarity, connector cleanliness, and optical power budget. Copper links also depend on cable quality, termination, and negotiated speed.
site.content.05581: A 132 kV bay IED optical Tx connects through a fibre patch panel to switch optical Rx. Reversed Tx/Rx or incompatible SFPs may prevent link establishment; dirty connectors can cause intermittent errors.
site.content.05582: Fibre/copper, SFP transceivers, patch panels, Ethernet PHY and ports.
site.content.05583: VLANs and priority tags are not Physical-layer functions. Higher-layer configuration may fail even when the optical link is healthy.
site.content.05586: Inspect IED/switch port LEDs, power, and loss-of-signal alarms.
site.content.05587: Compare fibre Tx/Rx, optic type/speed, and receive power; for copper, inspect termination.
site.content.05588: Once the link is stable, establish an approved counter baseline and check whether errors increase.
site.content.05589: Evidence: stable link + acceptable optical levels + no increasing physical errors.
site.content.05592: Inspect the TCP 102 handshake in an approved capture. If there is no SYN/ACK, check listener, ACL, and return path.
site.content.05593: If TCP is healthy, inspect COTP/TPKT, ISO session/presentation, ACSE, and MMS Initiate responses.
site.content.05594: If association is rejected, correlate client limits, selectors/access policy, and vendor diagnostics.

site.content.05641: Does GOOSE require an IP address?
site.content.05642: Conventional GOOSE frame delivery does not require IP. An IED may still have an IP address for MMS or engineering. GOOSE subscription depends on multicast MAC, APPID, control block/DataSet, and configuration.
site.content.05643: What is the main difference between MMS, GOOSE, and SV?
site.content.05644: MMS carries client-server monitoring and control services over TCP/IP. GOOSE distributes events and states through Ethernet publisher-subscriber communication. SV streams sampled current and voltage data through Ethernet publisher-subscriber communication.
site.content.05646: Conventional GOOSE has no TCP acknowledgements. It repeats messages rapidly after a state change and at longer intervals during steady state. stNum identifies state generations, while sqNum identifies retransmissions. Subscribers also supervise message timeouts. Timing is profile/configuration dependent.
site.content.05647: Is MMS breaker position always Boolean?
site.content.05648: No. XCBR.Pos uses double-point status with intermediate and bad-state indications. Interpret the actual data type together with quality and timestamp.
site.content.05649: Does SV always use 4,000 samples per second?
site.content.05650: No. 80 samples/cycle × 50 Hz = 4,000 samples/s is one familiar profile example. Sampling rate, samples per ASDU, and ASDUs per frame depend on the profile. Samples/s and Ethernet frames/s are not necessarily equal.
site.content.05651: Does PTP always run over UDP/IP?
site.content.05652: No. PTP supports Ethernet and UDP/IP transports. Power utility profiles may use Layer 2 Ethernet. Verify the configured profile, domain, and transport; PTP is not interchangeable with SNTP.
site.content.05653: Do PRP, HSR, and VLAN serve the same purpose?
site.content.05654: No. VLANs provide logical segmentation and PCP marks traffic priority. PRP duplicates traffic across independent LANs, while HSR provides duplicate paths around a ring. Fault tolerance depends on the engineered topology and supported endpoints.

site.content.07316: Detailed theory, engineering principles and practical substation examples
site.content.07318: A Substation Automation System (SAS) is an integrated system of intelligent electronic devices (IEDs), communication networks, station controllers, gateways, and SCADA/HMI applications used to monitor, protect, control, and supervise electrical substation equipment. It converts field measurements and equipment states into reliable information, coordinates permitted control actions, and records alarms and events for operators and engineers.
site.content.07319: In a conventional substation, many signals travel through individual copper wires between the switchyard, relay panels and control room. A modern automated substation retains essential hardwired protection and safety circuits while using digital communication for monitoring, reports, interlocking information and selected protection applications. Automation does not eliminate the need for independent protection functions, secure controls, or commissioning tests.
site.content.07321: Read breaker positions, currents, voltages, power, frequency and equipment health.
site.content.07322: Detect faults using protection IEDs and trip affected equipment through approved protection schemes.
site.content.07323: Execute authorized breaker and disconnector operations with local/remote and interlocking checks.
site.content.07324: Exchange standardized data between IEDs, gateways, operator stations and control centers.
site.content.07326: Time-stamp changes, record sequence of events and alert operators to abnormal conditions.

site.content.07378: IEC 61850 is a family of international standards for communication networks and systems used in power utility automation. It defines a common information model, abstract communication services, mappings to communication protocols, and an engineering description language. It is not merely a network protocol or a replacement for every hardwired circuit.
site.content.07379: The main engineering advantage is that different manufacturers can describe substation functions using common names and data structures. Actual interoperability still depends on supported services, compatible data models, configuration and testing.
site.content.07381: • Standardized information models make the meaning of exchanged data clearer.
site.content.07382: • Communication, engineering configuration and conformance are distinct parts of the standard.
site.content.07383: IEC 61850 represents electrical functions through a structured hierarchy. An IED may host one or more logical devices. Each logical device contains logical nodes that represent functions, such as breaker monitoring or overcurrent protection. Logical nodes expose data objects, which in turn contain data attributes.
site.content.07384: For a breaker, the XCBR logical node exposes the Pos data object. Position status, quality and timestamp can be accessed through attributes such as stVal, q and t. The exact reference includes the configured logical-device and logical-node instance names, so it must be checked in the IED model.
site.content.07385: Futuristic IEC 61850 data model hierarchy showing IED, Logical Device, Logical Node, Data Object and Data Attribute, with a circuit breaker position example
site.content.07386: Illustrative IEC 61850 hierarchy. Verify exact data references, values, quality and timestamps against the configured IED; examples in the artwork are illustrative.
site.content.07387: • IED → Logical Device → Logical Node → Data Object → Data Attribute.
site.content.07388: • DataSet membership and reporting are configured separately from the underlying data model.
site.content.07389: IEC 61850 Standard Parts and Their Functions
site.content.07390: IEC 61850-7-2 defines the Abstract Communication Service Interface (ACSI). IEC 61850-7-3 defines common data classes; IEC 61850-7-4 defines compatible logical-node classes and data objects. IEC 61850-8-1 maps services to MMS and Ethernet GOOSE. IEC 61850-9-2 covers sampled-value mappings.
site.content.07391: IEC 61850-6 defines the Substation Configuration Language (SCL) used to exchange engineering information. IEC 61850-10 covers conformance testing. The series also contains other parts, technical reports and extensions relevant to specific applications.
site.content.07392: • Always distinguish a standardized data model from a protocol mapping.
site.content.07393: • Check the applicable edition and the device implementation conformance statement.
site.content.07395: The data model is function-oriented rather than a flat list of vendor-specific register numbers. A logical node groups information for one functional role, and each data object uses an appropriate common data class. This makes status, measurements and controls recognizable across equipment vendors.
site.content.07396: For example, XCBR1.Pos represents a breaker-position function; MMXU1.A can represent measured phase currents. These examples are not a guarantee that every relay exposes the same instance names or optional attributes.
site.content.07397: • Functions are represented by logical nodes.
site.content.07398: • Use the IED SCL file or online model browser to confirm the actual hierarchy.
site.content.07399: IED, Logical Device and Logical Node
site.content.07400: An Intelligent Electronic Device (IED) is a physical or virtual automation device such as a protection relay or bay controller. A logical device groups logical nodes for an application or function, while a logical node is the smallest standardized functional building block.
site.content.07401: A feeder protection relay can contain a logical device with LLN0 for common logical-device information, LPHD for physical-device information, XCBR for breaker status, PTOC for overcurrent protection, and PTRC for trip conditioning. The actual model is vendor- and project-specific.
site.content.07402: • IED is not synonymous with logical device.
site.content.07403: • LLN0 is important for DataSets and report control blocks.
site.content.07404: Data Objects, Data Attributes and Functional Constraints
site.content.07405: A data object represents information such as position (Pos), operation (Op), or measurement. Data attributes hold the values and metadata. Functional constraints classify attributes by use, such as ST for status, MX for measurements, CO for control, CF for configuration and DC for descriptions.
site.content.07406: When browsing an IEC 61850 server, the functional constraint is part of how an attribute is addressed in the service model. Do not confuse a data-object name with the actual value attribute.
site.content.07407: • stVal is a status value; q indicates quality; t provides time information where defined.
site.content.07408: • Use the correct functional constraint when creating or validating signal mappings.
site.content.07409: Common Logical Nodes — XCBR, XSWI, MMXU, PTOC, PTRC
site.content.07410: XCBR models circuit-breaker functions; XSWI models switching devices such as disconnectors; MMXU groups electrical measurements; PTOC models time-overcurrent protection; PTRC represents protection trip conditioning.
site.content.07411: For a 33 kV feeder, an overcurrent element can assert its operation data, the protection logic can initiate a trip, and the XCBR position can change after the physical breaker operates. These are related but separate pieces of information.
site.content.07412: • A protection trip is not the same as breaker position feedback.
site.content.07413: • Select the appropriate logical node and data object for each SCADA point.
site.content.07414: Common Data Classes, Quality and Timestamp
site.content.07415: Common Data Classes (CDCs) specify the attributes and semantics of different data types. Examples include SPS for single-point status, DPS for double-point status, MV for measured values and SPC/DPC for controllable points. The selected CDC determines the structure that a client expects.
site.content.07416: Quality information helps indicate whether a value is valid, questionable or invalid and can carry additional detail. Timestamps help correlate events, but accuracy depends on the source clock and synchronization quality.
site.content.07417: • Never display a value as trustworthy without considering its quality.
site.content.07418: • Time synchronization is essential for meaningful sequence-of-events analysis.
site.content.07420: A DataSet is an engineered collection of data references. It can include status and measurement attributes from different logical nodes. A Report Control Block (RCB) defines how a server reports DataSet changes to an MMS client, including triggers, optional fields and other behavior.
site.content.07421: For a feeder bay, a DataSet might contain XCBR position, protection operation, phase currents and alarm statuses. A configured report can deliver updates to SCADA when the selected trigger conditions occur.
site.content.07422: • A DataSet does not send anything by itself; a service such as reporting uses it.
site.content.07423: • Confirm report enablement, client assignment, DataSet references and trigger options.
site.content.07425: An Unbuffered Report Control Block (URCB) provides event reports while an appropriate client association and reporting configuration are active; it does not provide the same event buffering and recovery behavior as a BRCB.
site.content.07426: A Buffered Report Control Block (BRCB) can retain report entries during communication interruptions within device limits and supports sequence recovery mechanisms. Buffer capacity, entry identifiers, client ownership and configuration must be verified for the actual IED.
site.content.07427: • BRCB is generally preferred where loss of events during temporary disconnections is a concern.
site.content.07428: • Buffered reporting is not a substitute for testing event recovery and overflow behavior.
site.content.07430: MMS client/server communication, as mapped in IEC 61850-8-1, is widely used for monitoring, control and reports between station systems and IEDs. GOOSE provides Ethernet multicast event exchange, commonly for fast inter-IED signaling. Sampled Values carry digitized measurement samples in process-bus applications.
site.content.07431: These services solve different problems. A protection IED may publish GOOSE to peers, send reports to SCADA through MMS and receive sampled measurements from a merging unit when the system design supports it.
site.content.07432: • MMS and GOOSE are not interchangeable.
site.content.07433: • GOOSE and SV require careful VLAN, network and performance engineering.
site.content.07435: IEC 61850 references combine configured names of logical devices, logical nodes, data objects and attributes. A reference such as LD0/XCBR1.Pos.stVal is illustrative; the complete address and separator conventions depend on the service representation and configured IED names.
site.content.07436: Engineers should copy verified references from the actual SCL model or online browser rather than assuming that the logical-device name or logical-node instance is universal.
site.content.07437: • Use the exact configured object reference in mapping and testing.
site.content.07438: • Check naming consistency across SCL, gateway and HMI databases.
site.content.07440: Assume a 33 kV outgoing feeder breaker has 52a and 52b auxiliary contacts. Its digital inputs feed an IED, which evaluates the contact states and updates the breaker position in its IEC 61850 model. The status can be included in a DataSet and reported to the SCADA MMS client.
site.content.07441: During FAT, test breaker OPEN, CLOSED, intermediate and inconsistent-contact states where supported. Verify the SCADA symbol, quality, timestamp, event log and alarm rules rather than relying only on a green network-status indication.
site.content.07442: • 52a/52b interpretation must match the approved wiring and IED logic.
site.content.07443: • SCADA indication and control permission are different engineering checks.
site.content.07445: When current exceeds configured protection criteria, a PTOC function can operate. Protection logic, often represented through PTRC or related nodes, can initiate a breaker trip. The breaker auxiliary contacts then provide independent confirmation of the final position.
site.content.07446: The IED can report protection operation, trip initiation and breaker position as separate signals. This separation helps engineers distinguish an actual fault trip from a control command or a feedback failure.
site.content.07447: • Critical trip paths must follow the approved protection design.
site.content.07448: • Test operation indications, trip circuit and position feedback separately.
site.content.07450: Start by importing the correct ICD/CID/SCD into an IEC 61850 browser or engineering tool. Establish the MMS association, browse the logical-device tree, inspect logical nodes and data attributes, and compare actual values, quality and timestamps with the field condition.
site.content.07451: If SCADA does not update, check the network connection, association, report control block state, DataSet membership, client reservation, trigger options, integrity period, quality and gateway mapping. Capture packets when necessary and compare with the approved signal list.
site.content.07452: • A successful ping does not prove a correct MMS report configuration.
site.content.07453: • Use a structured signal-by-signal FAT/SAT checklist.
site.content.07455: IEC 61850 is a family of international standards for communication networks and systems in power utility automation. It combines standardized information models, abstract services, protocol mappings, engineering configuration and conformance requirements. It is not a single wire protocol or a replacement for every protection circuit.
site.content.07456: A 33 kV feeder IED can expose breaker position through XCBR, report changes to a station HMI, and publish selected protection indications through GOOSE. Different parts of the standard describe these separate capabilities.
site.content.07457: Check the edition, supported services and the actual IED model before assuming interoperability.
site.content.07458: Why IEC 61850 Is Divided into Multiple Parts
site.content.07459: Power utility automation requires consistent terminology, device models, engineering workflows, communication behavior, performance and testing. Dividing the standard into parts allows each discipline to define its requirements while remaining compatible with the overall architecture.
site.content.07460: An IED manufacturer implements data models and communication services; a system integrator builds SCL configurations; a commissioning engineer tests actual signal behavior. Each relies on different IEC 61850 parts.
site.content.07461: Use the applicable part for the task; a protocol connection alone cannot validate data meaning or control safety.
site.content.07463: Part 1 introduces the purpose, scope and fundamental concepts of the IEC 61850 series. It explains the system-oriented approach to communication and interoperability, including the separation of application information from the specific communication technology.
site.content.07464: During project kickoff, use Part 1 to explain why the project specifies standardized logical nodes, engineering files and communication services rather than only vendor-specific register lists.
site.content.07465: Part 1 is orientation material; it is not a detailed IED configuration procedure.
site.content.07467: Part 2 provides terminology used throughout the standard series. Consistent vocabulary matters because words such as logical device, logical node, data object, client, server and data set have defined engineering meanings.
site.content.07468: In a FAT meeting, distinguish an IED (physical or virtual automation device) from a logical device (a grouping within the IEC 61850 information model).
site.content.07470: Part 3 addresses general requirements for communication networks and systems in utility automation environments. Equipment used in substations must be suitable for its intended electrical, environmental and electromagnetic conditions, subject to the relevant requirements and test standards.
site.content.07471: When selecting a station-bus switch or communication device, review the applicable environmental and EMC specifications rather than assuming an ordinary office switch is suitable.
site.content.07472: Do not confuse general equipment requirements with communication-service conformance.
site.content.07474: Part 4 provides guidance concerning system and project management across engineering, integration, testing and maintenance. Coordinated responsibilities and controlled configuration changes are important when several vendors deliver devices for one substation.
site.content.07475: For a 132/33/11 kV project, define who owns the system SCD, who imports IED configuration, who validates GOOSE subscriptions, and who signs FAT/SAT records.
site.content.07476: Keep version-controlled engineering deliverables and change records.
site.content.07478: Part 5 describes communication requirements for functions and device models, including performance considerations for different automation applications. A trip-related message and a slowly changing temperature measurement do not have the same timing requirements.
site.content.07479: A protection engineer identifies time-critical exchanges; a network engineer verifies traffic paths, VLANs, priorities, load and recovery behavior under realistic conditions.
site.content.07480: Performance must be demonstrated for the actual scheme and network, not inferred from protocol labels alone.
site.content.07482: Part 6 defines an XML-based configuration description language for representing substation structures, IED models and communication relationships. Common SCL file categories include ICD, CID, SCD, IID and SSD, with use depending on the engineering workflow.
site.content.07483: A system integrator imports vendor IED descriptions, builds the substation configuration and exports appropriate IED-specific settings. Confirm that imported SCL content matches the deployed IED firmware and project configuration.
site.content.07484: SCL is an engineering description; importing a file does not prove that devices are correctly communicating.
site.content.07486: Part 7-1 explains modeling principles and how abstract information and services relate to practical automation functions. It provides conceptual context for logical nodes, common data classes and the client-server model.
site.content.07487: Model breaker status as an equipment function rather than assigning an arbitrary vendor-only tag without documented meaning.
site.content.07488: The model separates what information means from how a particular protocol transports it.
site.content.07490: Part 7-2 specifies abstract services such as data access, reporting, logging, control and data-set-related operations. ACSI defines the service behavior independently of a particular transport mapping.
site.content.07491: For SCADA breaker status, configure a DataSet and a Report Control Block using supported services; then verify how the actual device maps them to MMS.
site.content.07492: ACSI services are not synonymous with raw Ethernet packets.
site.content.07494: Part 7-3 defines reusable Common Data Classes (CDCs) used to represent types of status, measurement, control and other information. A CDC specifies an organized collection of attributes and their semantics.
site.content.07495: A breaker position commonly uses the DPC common data class, which can expose a double-point status value, quality and timestamp according to the applicable model.
site.content.07496: Validate CDC, functional constraints and mandatory/optional attributes against the actual IED.
site.content.07497: IEC 61850-7-4 — Logical Nodes and Data Objects
site.content.07498: Part 7-4 specifies logical-node classes and their associated data objects. Examples include XCBR for circuit breaker functions, XSWI for switching devices, MMXU for electrical measurements, PTOC for time-overcurrent protection and PTRC for protection trip conditioning.
site.content.07499: For feeder 33-F01, map its breaker position from the appropriate XCBR instance and its measurements from the relevant measurement logical node.
site.content.07500: Do not assume all vendors use identical instance names or implement every optional data object.
site.content.07502: Part 8-1 maps specified abstract communication services to communication technologies, including MMS-based client/server communication and GOOSE messaging over Ethernet. MMS commonly serves station monitoring, reporting and control; GOOSE supports configured event-oriented publisher/subscriber exchanges.
site.content.07503: The HMI receives an MMS report when breaker position changes; a protection IED may publish a GOOSE indication to another IED using a configured multicast address and APPID.
site.content.07504: Check the service mapping and Ethernet settings separately; GOOSE is not carried as an MMS report.
site.content.07506: Part 9-2 defines mapping of sampled-value communication over Ethernet for process-bus applications. Digital samples can represent current and voltage measurements from a merging unit or suitable publishing device.
site.content.07507: In a digital process-bus design, a merging unit publishes sampled measurements and a subscribing protection IED processes them. Verify stream identity, dataset, sampling configuration, time synchronization and network performance.
site.content.07508: Not every substation uses a process bus; conventional CT/VT wiring may remain in service.
site.content.07510: Part 10 defines conformance testing concepts and methods for verifying implementations against relevant IEC 61850 requirements. Conformance testing is different from project-specific interoperability and operational acceptance testing.
site.content.07511: An IED may have a conformance test report but still require integration testing with the chosen HMI, gateway, network switches and other IEDs.
site.content.07512: Perform FAT and SAT against the project signal list, controls, alarms, GOOSE logic and failure scenarios.
site.content.07513: Other Important IEC 61850 Parts and Extensions
site.content.07514: The IEC 61850 series extends beyond the commonly cited substation parts. Other parts and technical reports address application-specific models, engineering guidance, performance and communication technologies. Applicability depends on the project and the editions being specified.
site.content.07515: A utility may use IEC 61850 in applications beyond a conventional transmission substation; project requirements determine which extensions matter.
site.content.07516: Check the current IEC catalogue and procurement specification for applicable editions and amendments.
site.content.07517: How Different IEC 61850 Parts Work Together
site.content.07518: An engineering implementation combines information models, services, mappings and configuration. Part 7-4 defines logical-node classes; 7-3 defines data classes; 7-2 defines services; 8-1 or 9-2 defines mappings; Part 6 describes engineering configuration; Part 10 supports conformance assessment.
site.content.07519: When a feeder breaker opens, the IED updates its XCBR position data, a configured DataSet includes the required attributes, an RCB reports the change over MMS, and SCADA updates the SLD symbol.
site.content.07520: Each stage needs a separate verification point: physical input, model, DataSet, report, client subscription and HMI mapping.
site.content.07521: Consider two 132 kV incomers, two 132/33 kV transformers, 33 kV feeders and 11 kV distribution bays. Protection and control IEDs communicate with station HMI and gateway over an engineered station bus. A digital process bus is optional depending on the design.
site.content.07522: For a 33 kV feeder fault, the protection IED detects the condition, trips the breaker through its approved scheme, updates XCBR position and sends configured events to SCADA. Other IEDs may receive configured GOOSE signals for interlocking or protection coordination.
site.content.07523: Record the actual IEC 61850 object references, report settings, GOOSE subscriptions and timing checks in FAT/SAT documents.
site.content.07525: A reliable integration package typically includes the applicable standards list, IED capability documents, SCL files, network drawings, IP/VLAN tables, DataSet and RCB schedules, GOOSE matrices, SCADA mapping sheets and FAT/SAT test procedures.
site.content.07526: For each breaker indication, document the field contact, IED input, IEC 61850 object reference, quality/timestamp handling, reporting configuration and HMI tag.
site.content.07527: Compliance claims must specify the supported edition, service scope and evidence; interoperability is established through integration testing.
site.content.07529: Interviewers often ask which part defines SCL, logical nodes, common data classes, ACSI, MMS/GOOSE mapping, sampled values and conformance testing. Explain the distinction between data modeling, communication services, protocol mapping and engineering configuration.
site.content.07530: Sample question: “Which IEC 61850 part defines the XCBR logical node?” Answer: IEC 61850-7-4. “Which part defines SCL?” Answer: IEC 61850-6. “Which part maps GOOSE?” Answer: IEC 61850-8-1.
site.content.07531: For commissioning, always verify the real device model and configured behavior rather than memorizing part numbers alone.
site.content.07537: Information models and abstract services are mapped to real communication technologies, while SCL describes the engineered system. Conformance and site testing validate different aspects of the implementation.
site.content.07538: IEC 61850 data hierarchy: the FDR01 IED hosts a server containing logical device FDR01LD0, logical node XCBR1, position object Pos and attributes stVal, q and t. Configured datasets and MMS reports carry selected information to SCADA/HMI.
site.content.07539: IED → Logical Device → Logical Node → Data Object → Data Attribute. Illustrative names; verify the deployed IED model. Selected data reaches SCADA through configured communication services.

site.content.07544: Use the applicable standard edition and your IED’s own model and configuration documentation for project engineering.
site.content.07545: A physical protection IED hosts an IEC 61850 server containing a logical device and XCBR1, MMXU1 and PTOC1 logical nodes. XCBR1 contains Pos with stVal, q and t attributes.
site.content.07546: Logical-node architecture: containment relationships from the physical IED to data attributes. Example names are illustrative.
site.content.07547: 33 kV breaker auxiliary contacts 52a and 52b feed IED digital inputs. XCBR1.Pos exposes stVal, q and t, and an MMS report carries position information to SCADA/HMI.
site.content.07548: Breaker indication path: auxiliary contacts → IED input logic → XCBR.Pos → configured reporting → HMI. Feedback is separate from commands; contact symbols illustrate the open state.
site.content.07549: CT current enters a protection IED. The illustrative application path passes through PTOC, PTRC and a trip output to the circuit breaker.
site.content.07550: Protection path: PTOC operation feeds the configured PTRC/output chain. These internal functional relationships do not imply separate network messages or a mandatory PTRC time delay.
site.content.07551: CT and VT measurements enter the 33-F01 feeder IED. MMXU1 exposes current, voltage, power and frequency information to SCADA through configured MMS reports.
site.content.07552: Measurement path: verify CT/VT scaling, phase identity, units, quality and time. MMXU measurement reporting is distinct from a process-bus sampled-value stream.
site.content.07553: Inside the 33-F01 IED, MMXU supplies measurements, PTOC feeds PTRC and a trip output, CILO supplies a permissive to CSWI and its control output, and XCBR receives breaker feedback. SCADA and the physical breaker are outside the IED.
site.content.07554: Illustrative 33-F01 application: CILO supervises the configured switching-control path; the protection-trip path is separate. XCBR represents returned position feedback. Arrows express functional relationships, not terminal wiring.
site.content.07557: Use the edition and amendments specified by your project, the device MICS/PICS/PIXIT and the deployed SCL to confirm supported behavior. Manufacturer examples are implementation-specific.
site.content.07558: Protection IED server: logical nodes supply data objects and attributes referenced by an ordered DataSet, which a Report Control Block uses to deliver MMS reports to SCADA/HMI.
site.content.07559: DataSet-to-report architecture. The short references are illustrative. Separate scalar stVal, q and t members are not automatically all included in every event report; verify inclusion or use a suitable object-level selection.
site.content.07560: Illustrative interface, not a vendor-tool screenshot. ST is a functional constraint; stVal, q and t are attributes. The shown FCDA elements represent object-level selections.
site.content.07561: BRCB uses a finite buffer and can deliver eligible retained reports after reconnection and resynchronization. URCB has no replay queue for the disconnected period; a read or GI restores current state only.
site.content.07562: Buffered recovery is conditional on retained entries, capacity, configuration and client recovery. Neither a finite BRCB buffer nor a GI snapshot guarantees a complete event history.
site.content.07563: 33-F01 breaker feedback updates the protection IED. The DataSet and BRCB inside the IED produce MMS reports that cross the Ethernet station bus to a SCADA client.
site.content.07564: Reporting indication path: feedback → model/DataSet → configured BRCB → MMS association → SCADA. Packet-shaped arrows show report traffic; the software blocks are not separate network devices.
site.content.07565: Event triggers dchg, qchg and supported dupd produce reports; integrity uses a server timer and GI uses a client request to report the current DataSet.
site.content.07566: Event triggers and current-state snapshots serve different purposes. dupd requires supported data-update notifications; integrity is server-timed and GI is client-requested.
site.content.07567: Isolated FAT/SAT setup: test workstation simulates IED inputs, reports pass through an Ethernet switch to SCADA, and a mirrored port supports MMS capture. Checks cover value, quality, source time, reconnect and overflow.
site.content.07568: Illustrative isolated test arrangement. Use the appropriate simulator or approved input-test interface; a laptop is not wired directly to a live binary input. Capture access and active tests follow the project procedure.

A sender encapsulates information as it moves down the stack; the receiver decodes and decapsulates it on the way up. Real protocol stacks do not necessarily implement each layer as a separate software module.

site.content.08409: Three-Level SAS Architecture: station, bay and process levels with communication buses
site.content.08410: Conceptual illustration. Actual network and field connections depend on the substation design; many sites retain hardwired CT/VT secondary circuits and breaker trips.
site.content.08412: Substation Automation System (SAS) architecture is the engineered arrangement of primary equipment, secondary devices, communication networks, operator workstations and interfaces to the remote control center. It specifies where each function is performed, which devices exchange information, and how the system remains safe and dependable during equipment or communication failures.
site.content.08413: For a 132/33/11 kV substation, the architecture normally separates station-wide supervision from bay-specific protection and control, and from the physical switching and measurement equipment in the yard. The exact division is functional: an IED may combine several roles, and a digital process bus is optional rather than mandatory.

site.content.08425: A feeder breaker changes from Closed to Open. The protection/bay IED updates its status data, and the SCADA client receives an IEC 61850 report or other configured indication. The HMI refreshes the single-line diagram, records the event and raises an alarm if the change meets alarm conditions. The station gateway may forward a mapped point to the RCC using IEC 60870-5-104.

site.content.08428: Bay Level — Protection and Control IEDs
site.content.08429: The bay level contains the intelligence associated with a particular line, transformer, bus coupler or feeder. Protection IEDs detect abnormal electrical conditions, while bay controllers and control IEDs monitor switchgear positions, enforce interlocking conditions and handle authorized local or remote commands.
site.content.08431: A 33 kV feeder relay detects an overcurrent above its configured pickup and, after the applicable time or instantaneous criteria, operates its trip output. The breaker opens through the trip circuit. GOOSE can distribute configured inter-IED signals, but a GOOSE message is not inherently the only trip path.
site.content.08433: An operator requests a breaker Close from SCADA. The bay control function verifies control authority, switching mode, interlocking and any Select-Before-Operate requirements before issuing the configured command. A rejected command must be reported with a useful cause.
site.content.08434: Process Level — Primary Equipment and Field Interfaces
site.content.08435: The process level is where electrical energy is measured, switched and isolated. CTs and VTs provide scaled measurements; circuit breakers interrupt fault current; disconnectors and earthing switches support safe isolation. A merging unit may convert analog inputs into digital sampled values for protection IEDs in a process-bus architecture.
site.content.08437: A conventional installation may connect CT/VT secondaries and breaker contacts directly to IED terminals. In a digital process-bus installation, measurements and selected status/control messages can be exchanged over Ethernet. Both approaches require rigorous protection, safety and timing design.
site.content.08438: Station Bus and Process Bus — Communication
site.content.08440: typically connects bay IEDs, SCADA servers, gateways and engineering workstations. IEC 61850 MMS client/server services support data access, reporting and controls, while GOOSE enables fast event-based multicast exchange between configured devices.
site.content.08447: Example: A bay IED reports a feeder breaker position to SCADA via MMS reporting, publishes a configured GOOSE interlock signal to another IED, and may receive sampled measurements from a merging unit over the process bus. These services have different communication behaviors and must not be treated as interchangeable.
site.content.08449: Substation networks may use a single Ethernet LAN, dual networks, RSTP-based rings, Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP), or High-availability Seamless Redundancy (HSR), depending on equipment capabilities and project requirements. A network drawing should show every switch, IED port, fiber link, VLAN and redundancy domain.

site.content.09390: Step 1: Confirm Bay 52 & Initial CLOSED State
site.content.09391: Verify feeder Bay 52 (CB-33-F03) on the 33 kV Bus is in the initial CLOSED state (XCBR.Pos.stVal = 2, 52a = ON, 52b = OFF).
site.content.09392: SLD, IED LCD, and SCADA/HMI all agree on CB-33-F03 CLOSED.
site.content.09393: Always confirm bay identity and initial apparatus state before any switching test.
site.content.09394: Step 2: Verify Local/Remote Authority & CILO Permissives
site.content.09395: Check 43LR Local/Remote selector status (CSWI.Pos) and verify CILO.EnaOpn / CILO.EnaCls permissives are TRUE.
site.content.09396: Authority and interlock permissives match approved bay logic.
site.content.09397: 43LR prevents simultaneous local panel and remote SCADA control.
site.content.09398: Step 3: Attempt Remote Command in LOCAL Mode (Rejection)
site.content.09399: Switch Authority to LOCAL and issue a remote SBO Select. The IED CSWI must reject the command with AddCause: Blocked-by-mode.
site.content.09400: Red pulse indicates command rejection; breaker remains unchanged.
site.content.09401: In LOCAL mode, remote MMS SBO commands from SCADA are blocked at the IED.
site.content.09402: Step 4: Switch to Approved REMOTE Test Mode
site.content.09403: Return 43LR Authority to REMOTE so the Siemens SIPROTEC 5 IED accepts IEC 61850 MMS SBOw requests from the Station Gateway.
site.content.09404: Authority block turns green (REMOTE ✓) and CSWI.Pos reports remote (2).
site.content.09405: CSWI.Loc = FALSE indicates Remote control authority is active.
site.content.09406: Step 5: Issue SBO Select for Intended OPEN/CLOSE Action
site.content.09407: Send Select-With-Value (SBOw) from Command Control. Yellow/cyan MMS command packets travel SCADA → Gateway → SIPROTEC 5.
site.content.09408: IED reserves control object, sets SBO.StSel = SELECTED, and starts 30 s timer.
site.content.09409: SBO prevents accidental single-action switching by requiring Select then Operate.
site.content.09410: Step 6: Check Select Acknowledgement & Select Timeout (30 s)
site.content.09411: Verify SelectResponse+ acknowledgement and observe the 30-second sboTimeout countdown. If Operate is not sent in time, selection expires.
site.content.09412: Selection automatically cancels upon timeout without operating the breaker.
site.content.09413: sboTimeout ensures a stale selection cannot be operated later unexpectedly.
site.content.09414: Step 7: Issue Operate Within the Select Window
site.content.09415: Click Operate while SBO.StSel = SELECTED. Green command pulses propagate SCADA → Gateway → SIPROTEC 5 → Bay 52 Breaker.
site.content.09416: Breaker transitions cleanly (CLOSED → OPEN or OPEN → CLOSED).
site.content.09417: Operate is accepted only when ctlVal matches the selected action within the timer.
site.content.09418: Step 8: Verify 52a/52b Feedback, Command Termination & SOE
site.content.09419: Trace status feedback Breaker → IED → Gateway → SCADA/HMI. Confirm 52a/52b complement, CommandTermination+, and 1 ms SOE log.
site.content.09420: SOE records Select, Operate, XCBR change, 52a/52b update, and Command Terminated.
site.content.09421: Enhanced security SBO provides CommandTermination+ after physical 52a/52b confirm.
site.content.09422: Step 9: Test Rejected Command with Blocked Permissive
site.content.09423: Block CILO permissive (e.g. Q8 Earth Switch closed) and attempt SBO Select/Operate. Verify IED blocks the unsafe switching request.
site.content.09424: CILO.EnaOpn / EnaCls = FALSE blocks command and logs Interlock Rejection in SOE.
site.content.09425: CILO interlocking is evaluated at the IED before energizing the trip/close coil.
site.content.09426: Step 10: Restore Authority & Original CLOSED Breaker State
site.content.09427: Clear any blocked permissives, restore REMOTE authority, and return CB-33-F03 to its initial CLOSED state (XCBR.Pos.stVal = 2).
site.content.09428: Bay 52 restored to CLOSED (Green) with clean SOE and zero active overrides.
site.content.09429: Always restore normal operating state and remove test blocks before handover.
